7.label: Player moves their queen to an undefended square where it can be captured by a minor piece.
7.description: This feature fires when a player makes a queen move (68% queen moves) that leaves the queen hanging (59% hangs), resulting in a median loss of ~2.0 material (roughly a queen's value minus the piece that captures it). Maia's recommended move is almost always a minor piece (bishop 55%, knight 41%) that captures the queen (100% Maia captures queen), confirming the queen is left en prise. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 386cp lost), with 32% of cases going from winning to drawn and 14% from winning to losing. The tactical analysis confirms hanging_piece as the dominant motif (64%), with common tags including hanging_piece, missed_tactic, and queen_capture. The positions consistently show queens placed on squares attacked by opponent knights or bishops, where the player either overlooked the attack or miscalculated, leaving their most valuable piece undefended. This occurs primarily in the opening and middlegame (100% combined) when piece activity is high and multiple threats coexist.

10.label: Player makes a rook move that neglects an opponent's advanced passed pawn about to promote.
10.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves their rook (52% of activating moves) while failing to address an imminent pawn promotion threat. The material signature shows trades (38%) and hangs (24%), with the median eval loss of 428 centipawns confirming catastrophic blunders. The trajectory (59% losing->losing, 10% winning->losing) shows players already under pressure who then collapse entirely by mishandling the critical promotion race. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags 'promotion_error' (60%) alongside 'passed_pawn' and 'back_rank' motifs, indicating the player redirects their rook to an irrelevant task (capturing material, blocking the wrong threat, or recapturing on an unimportant square) while an enemy pawn on the 2nd/7th rank promotes or forces decisive threats. The top boards consistently show advanced passed pawns (h2, c2, d2, h2) that the opponent ignores in favor of rook exchanges or captures elsewhere. The back_rank motif (20%) appears because promotion often coincides with back-rank mating threats, compounding the error.

13.label: Moving a piece to a square where it (or another piece) becomes undefended, allowing the opponent a tactical shot.
13.description: This feature detects middlegame moves where the player relocates a bishop or rook without capturing, and in doing so leaves material hanging (median net loss of -3.0, i.e., a full piece). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 584 centipawns lost), often converting a defensible or drawn position into a losing one. The Opus analysis reveals the underlying tactical blindness: players miss forks, intermediate moves, or fail to notice that relocating a defender exposes another piece. Common tags include hanging_piece, fork, and missed_tactic. The boards confirm this pattern—pieces are moved to seemingly reasonable squares (Rhf1, Bb7-c6, Rd4-f4) but the player overlooks that the move either walks into a fork, removes a critical guard, or allows an intermediate check that wins material. This is not a trade gone wrong but a pure tactical oversight where a non-capture move drops a piece.

5.label: Moving the queen away from defensive duties, leaving the king fatally exposed in the middlegame.
5.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves their queen (65% of cases) to a square that hangs material (54%) or is merely safe but positionally catastrophic (46%), while the opponent's best response involves capturing with or deploying their queen (85% Maia queen moves, 85% Maia captures a queen). The dominant motifs are king_safety (38%) and hanging_piece (38%), with recurring tags of exposed_king and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 206 centipawns, with positions shifting from drawn-to-losing (27%) or losing-to-even-more-losing (38%), indicating these are defensive positions where the queen was the last line of protection. The concrete examples confirm this: queens abandon critical defensive squares (Qf3 leaving d2/c2 unguarded, Qf8 becoming passive, kings walking into mating nets instead of trading queens). The player fails to recognize that their king's survival depends on the queen's precise placement, and by relocating or misusing it, they allow forced mates or catastrophic material loss.

3.label: Player ignores an undefended bishop capturable by queen in the opening, hanging material instead.
3.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the opponent has an undefended bishop (almost always on g4 or g5) that can be captured for free by the queen (Maia recommends Qxg4/Qxg5 in 100% of cases), but the player instead makes a developing or pawn move (Be2, f3, Ne7, d5, etc.) that ignores the free piece. The material signature shows 62% of moves actually hang material themselves (median net -1.0), and 100% miss winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 75% convert a winning position into a drawn one, 25% into a losing one, with a median cost of 471 centipawns. The boards overwhelmingly show early opening positions (100% opening phase) where a bishop has ventured to g4 or g5 without protection, and the player either chases it inefficiently with f3, blocks their own queen's access with Be2, or simply develops elsewhere. The tactical motif is pure hanging_piece blindness—failing to recognize that an undefended piece in the open can simply be taken.

6.label: Trading queens when the queen was the key attacking piece, squandering a winning or superior position.
6.description: This feature fires on positions where the player captures the opponent's queen (player captured: queen 100%) primarily with a rook (50%) or queen (30%), resulting in a material exchange (trade 80%) with a median net of ~4.0 (reflecting queen-for-queen or equivalent trades). The critical error is revealed by the eval trajectory: 30% go from winning to drawn and 30% remain winning but lose a massive median of 478 centipawns, indicating the queen trade was deeply premature. Maia's recommended moves (queen 80%, giving check 90%) show the engine wanted to keep the queen active and deliver checks rather than simplify. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant tags like 'queen_trade', 'missed_mate_in_one', 'simplification_error', and 'queen_capture_distraction'—players tunnel-visioned on capturing the opponent's queen rather than maintaining their attacking pressure. The example summaries explicitly describe scenarios where trading queens eliminated the piece most responsible for exploiting the opponent's weaknesses, or where the player missed a forced mate by greedily grabbing the queen instead. This is a classic simplification error where material equality is maintained but the position's winning potential is destroyed.

1.label: Trading material for an unimportant pawn instead of supporting or advancing a critical passed pawn in the endgame.
1.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players make exchanges (typically rook captures of pawns) that are materially neutral but positionally catastrophic because they abandon support of a critical passed pawn. The material signature shows 100% trades (net 0.0 material) with rook and pawn moves capturing pawns, while Maia's recommended moves (80% rook, no captures) indicate the correct plan was to keep the rook actively supporting the passed pawn rather than grabbing peripheral material. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (78%), and the tactical summaries repeatedly describe the same pattern: capturing an unimportant kingside pawn while allowing the opponent to eliminate or block a far-advanced passed pawn. The eval trajectory (median 208cp lost, with 40% going from winning to drawn) confirms these trades threw away decisive advantages. All positions are endgames with rook+pawn structures where the passed pawn's advance was the winning plan, but the player prioritized a small material exchange over the strategically decisive pawn promotion race.

11.label: Playing a flashy rook check in an endgame that hangs material or squanders a winning/drawn position by losing critical tempo.
11.description: This feature consistently fires on rook checks (100% rook moves, 100% checks) in endgame positions (88% endgame) that result in material loss (75% hangs, 12% loses, median net -1.0). The eval trajectory shows massive costs (median 329cp lost), with positions shifting from winning to losing/drawn in many cases, and 88% of activations miss winning material. The tactical motifs—rook_endgame, pawn_endgame, passed_pawn, and tempo_loss—reveal the common thread: the player delivers a rook check that looks active but fails to address the critical endgame task (promoting a passed pawn, maintaining piece coordination, or restraining the opponent's pawns). The check either allows the opponent's king to reach a better square, leaves the rook misplaced after the king moves, or abandons defense of a key pawn. Rather than calmly converting technical advantages through proper endgame technique (king activity, pawn advancement), the player opts for a superficially forcing check that disrupts their own coordination and hands the opponent tempo or material.

12.label: Moving a piece that was shielding the queen from a diagonal attack, resulting in queen loss.
12.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves a knight (67%) or other piece that was serving as a critical blocker on a diagonal, exposing their queen to capture by an enemy bishop. The material signature shows the player captures a knight (100%) but loses material (83%, median -3.0 centipawns = net queen-for-knight loss), consistent with winning a knight but immediately losing the queen. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (75%) with discovered_attack (25%), and the tags heavily feature exposed_queen, removed_blocker, diagonal_vulnerability, and queen_loss. The Opus analyses explicitly describe scenarios where a knight on f3 or e4 was blocking a bishop's line to the queen, and moving/exchanging that knight fatally exposes the queen. The eval trajectory (median 519cp lost, with winning->losing 33%) confirms these are catastrophic tactical oversights in the opening (83%). Maia's recommended moves (pawn 50%, queen 33%) suggest the correct play was either to move the queen to safety or advance a pawn to block the diagonal, rather than greedily capturing the enemy knight.

14.label: Player makes a passive or slow move when a decisive tactical capture was immediately available.
14.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position plays a non-capturing move (93% no capture) — typically a pawn, king, or rook move — while a strong tactical capture (Maia captures rook 53%, queen 47%) was available. The material signature shows the moves are technically 'safe' (73%) or hang material (20%), but the critical signal is that 100% of positions had missed winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these are thrown wins: 40% winning->winning (still winning but much less so), 33% winning->drawn, and 13% winning->losing, with a massive median loss of 419 centipawns. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is a hanging piece left uncaptured (50%), combined with tempo loss (25%) — players choose developing, repositioning, or prophylactic moves instead of simply taking free or nearly-free major pieces. Board examples consistently show positions where a knight can capture an undefended rook, a bishop can take a hanging queen, or a pawn can promote/capture decisively, but the player instead makes an aimless move like Rb1, h4, or b4.

4.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that hangs material, missing an available tactical capture (fork, hanging piece) that would have won significant material.
4.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet or non-capturing move (86% no capture) that hangs a piece (47% hangs material, median net loss of -1.0), while a strong tactical capture was available. The Maia-recommended moves overwhelmingly involve captures (37% bishop, 24% rook, 22% knight, 8% queen captures), and 92% of activations show missed winning material. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (60%), with fork (10%) and back_rank (10%) supplementing—indicating the player overlooked an opponent's piece that was en prise or could be won via a simple tactic. The eval trajectory (median 261cp lost) confirms these are consequential mistakes, often in the middlegame (76%), where the player had piece activity or tactical opportunities but chose a passive or misdirected move instead. Tags like 'missed_tactic', 'tempo_loss', and 'calculation_error' reinforce that these are failures of tactical vision rather than positional misjudgments. The top boards consistently show positions with undefended pieces or forks where the player moved a minor piece or pawn aimlessly instead of collecting free material.

2.label: A knight move in the opening that leaves a more valuable piece (typically a queen) undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it.
2.description: This feature identifies a specific recurring blunder pattern where a player makes a knight move during the opening phase that hangs a major piece, typically a queen. The material signature is unambiguous: 100% knight moves, 100% non-captures, 100% hanging material with a median loss of 6.0 pawns (approximately queen value). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: positions shift from drawn to losing with a median cost of ~500 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying cause — players develop or reposition their knight while failing to notice an immediate tactical threat to their queen or other high-value piece. Common motifs include forks (the opponent's piece can capture the hanging piece with additional threats), hanging pieces left undefended, and tempo loss from prioritizing development over addressing urgent threats. The top board examples consistently show positions where a knight move ignores that a queen is en prise (e.g., Nf6 while Qd6 is attacked by Nb5, or Nc3 while Qd3 is attacked by Nb4). This is not a positional misjudgment but a pure tactical oversight — the player focuses on piece development while missing an immediate capture threat against their own material.

15.label: Playing a flashy capture-check with the queen or rook that sacrifices material or squanders a winning advantage.
15.description: This feature detects positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) by capturing a rook with their queen or rook (queen 75%, rook 25% as the moving piece; rook captured 100%), but the move loses material (75% loses, median net -4.0) and costs a median of 204 centipawns. The eval trajectories show positions spanning winning-to-winning, losing-to-losing, and even winning-to-losing — but the common thread is that a seemingly attractive capture-check blinds the player to a stronger continuation. The Opus analysis confirms this: king_safety and exposed_king tags dominate, with recurring themes of missed mates, missed tactics, and deflection motifs. Several examples explicitly describe squandering forced checkmates or dominant advantages by playing crude capture-checks instead of more refined tactical continuations (e.g., choosing a queen trade with check over a mating sequence, or missing a quiet killer move). The lure is the combination of material gain plus check, which feels forcing, but overlooks that the opponent's reply leaves the attacker worse off — either dropping back material, allowing counterplay against an exposed king, or dissolving a winning attack.

0.label: Player makes an irrelevant pawn or piece move while opponent has an unstoppable or near-unstoppable passed pawn promotion threat.
0.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that completely ignores a critical promotion threat on the board. The material signature shows 100% hangs (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -5.0, indicating the player's move allows a devastating consequence rather than addressing the immediate danger. The top boards consistently feature advanced passed pawns on the 7th rank (f7, b7, a7, g7) where one side has a pawn ready to promote. The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of promotion_error (40%) and passed_pawn (40%), with tags like passed_pawn(4) and promotion_threat(2) appearing frequently. Maia's response is uniformly a rook capturing a pawn—consistent with either promoting the pawn or winning the piece that was guarding against promotion. The eval trajectory (losing->losing 60%, losing->winning 40%) suggests these positions are often already difficult, but the player's move—typically an irrelevant pawn push (a4, a3, g5) or misplaced piece move—catastrophically accelerates the loss by abandoning the defense of the promotion square. Example positions show rooks blocking promotion paths being moved away, or tempo being wasted on meaningless pawn advances while the opponent's 7th-rank pawn demands immediate attention.

8.label: King moves that fail to actively participate in endgame play, allowing the opponent to exploit positional advantages or advance passed pawns.
8.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a passive or misguided king move (48% king moves) that costs significant evaluation (median 189cp lost). The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (68%) with the remainder being late middlegame positions. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (77%) — not outright blunders of pieces — yet they lose substantial value positionally, with 67% missing winning material. The dominant motifs (passed_pawn 33%, tempo_loss 22%, positional_mistake 11%) combined with tags like rook_endgame, endgame_technique, and piece_activity reveal that the core error is failing to use the king actively: instead of supporting passed pawns, blockading enemy passers, or creating counterplay, the player makes a passive retreat or sideways shuffle that cedes critical tempi. The trajectory (24% losing->losing, 16% drawn->losing, 7% winning->drawn) shows these moves frequently convert holdable or winning positions into lost ones. The top boards confirm this: Kb7 abandoning counterplay, Ka5 leaving a pawn undefended, Kg2 retreating when active defense was needed. Pawn pushes (21%) and rook moves (20%) in the dataset follow the same pattern — passive choices that lose the thread of endgame technique rather than tactical oversights.

9.label: In the opening, the player makes a quiet pawn or minor piece move that misses a concrete tactical opportunity (usually a free capture or strong developing move), surrendering significant advantage.
9.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake (82% opening) where the player advances a pawn (53%) or retreats/develops a bishop passively (24%) instead of executing the best move—which Maia consistently identifies as a bishop move (100% Maia bishop), often capturing a pawn (35% Maia captures pawn). The material signature shows 'safe' moves 71% of the time (nothing immediately hangs), yet 100% of cases miss winning material, revealing that the error is one of omission rather than commission. The eval trajectory (median 218cp lost, with 35% winning→drawn) confirms these are serious missed opportunities that squander advantages. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' (opponent's pieces left uncaptured), 'positional_mistake', and 'tempo_loss' motifs, plus tags like 'premature_pawn_advance', 'bishop_entombed', and 'development_neglect'. The concrete positions show patterns like retreating Bb3 when Bxb5 wins a pawn, playing b4 when it buries one's own bishop, or making quiet consolidating moves when a sharp tactical blow was available. The unifying thread is choosing a 'safe-looking' but passive continuation in the opening that overlooks a concrete opportunity, typically involving the bishop.

17.label: King moves that lose critical tempo in pawn endgames, allowing the opponent to seize a decisive positional advantage.
17.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player makes a king move (75% king moves) that loses decisive tempo. The material signature shows these are non-capturing moves that are either safe or hang material (50/50), and the best move was typically a pawn capture (Maia recommends pawn takes pawn 100%). The eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 693 centipawns lost—with positions going from drawn to losing (50%) or even winning to losing (25%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (50%), tempo_loss (25%), and passed_pawn (25%), with tempo_loss being the most frequent tag (11 occurrences). Examining the top boards reveals pure or near-pure pawn endgames where the player retreats or sidesteps their king instead of making a critical pawn capture (like gxf5 or fxg5), surrendering the opposition or allowing the opponent's passed pawn to become unstoppable. The consistent pattern is choosing a passive king move when the position demands an immediate pawn exchange to maintain the drawing or winning structure.

19.label: Advancing or promoting a pawn into a square covered by an enemy piece, throwing away a winning endgame.
19.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a player pushes a pawn to promote (100% pawn moves, no captures) but the promotion square or advanced square is directly covered by an opponent's piece—typically a bishop. The material signature shows 80% of these moves 'hang' material (median net loss of -9.0, i.e., a full queen lost immediately after promotion) and the eval trajectory confirms these collapse winning positions into draws or losses (80% winning->drawn, 20% winning->losing, median 379cp lost). The tactical tags strongly reinforce this: 'promotion_error' is the dominant motif (50%), with 'passed_pawn' and 'premature_promotion' recurring throughout. The concrete positions show queens being promoted directly into bishop captures (e.g., a8=Q captured by Bd5, b8=Q captured by Bc7, c8=Q captured by enemy pieces). The player had a strategically won endgame with a passed pawn but failed to first neutralize the defending piece covering the promotion square, converting a powerful pawn into an immediately captured queen.

18.label: King moves that waste critical tempo in pawn endgames, allowing opponent's passed pawns to advance or promote.
18.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player wastes a crucial tempo. The material signature shows 88% king moves with no captures and no checks—these are quiet king retreats or sidesteps rather than active king advances. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (53%), with passed_pawn (20%) and promotion themes appearing frequently. The eval trajectory shows these are all losing->losing positions where the player loses a median of 87 centipawns—making an already lost position significantly worse by misusing the king's limited moves. The board positions consistently show pawn endgames with passed pawns where precise king positioning is critical: instead of blockading or racing toward key squares, the player's king wanders to ineffective squares (e.g., Kc2 instead of Ke4, Kb4 instead of f5/Kd4, Ke3 instead of maintaining central control). The common thread is that in these razor-thin pawn endgames, every single tempo matters for stopping or supporting passed pawns, and the player's king move squanders that tempo.

20.label: Moving a piece that leaves the player's bishop undefended and capturable.
20.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move (typically with a pawn, knight, or queen) that leaves their own bishop hanging or trapped, allowing the opponent to capture it freely. The material signature shows that 54% of activating moves 'hang' a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -2.0 (consistent with losing a minor piece), and Maia's recommended response is always to capture the exposed bishop. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (60%) and trapped_piece (40%), with recurring tags like 'bishop_trapped', 'undefended_piece', and 'move_order' errors. The concrete positions reveal a consistent pattern: bishops on exposed squares (h4, h5, g5) that rely on a specific defender, and the player's move either removes that defender (e.g., Nf3-d2 leaving Bh4 trapped), captures in the wrong order (taking with the knight before exchanging bishops), or simply moves away from the bishop's defense. The eval trajectory is devastating—46% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 19% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 388 centipawns—confirming these are game-deciding oversights rather than minor inaccuracies.

22.label: In a losing endgame, playing a rook check that captures a pawn but loses significant material or allows decisive counterplay.
22.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake pattern where a player in an already losing position plays a rook move that captures a pawn with check (rook 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%), but the move loses material (net median -4.0, meaning typically losing the rook or equivalent). The eval trajectory shows these are losing->losing situations where the move costs a median of 33cp, though several examples show catastrophic drops (484cp, 507cp). The positional analysis reveals these occur in rook endgames and passed pawn scenarios (passed_pawn is the dominant motif at 40%), where the player impulsively checks and captures rather than addressing the critical threats — typically advancing passed pawns or improving king activity. The boards confirm this: positions feature advanced passed pawns (b7, c6, f6, g7 pawns) where the defender plays a desperate rook check/capture instead of the correct defensive technique (king repositioning, blockade). The player sacrifices the rook for a pawn with check, likely hoping for perpetual or stalemate tricks, but instead transitions into a hopeless position.

26.label: Moving a knight to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured for free in the opening.
26.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring opening blunder: a knight is moved (86% of activations) to a square where it hangs with no defenders, costing approximately a full piece (median -3.0 material, 77% classified as 'hangs'). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences—72% of cases shift from a drawn position to a losing one, with a median loss of 444 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (91%) as the dominant motif, with the concrete boards revealing the signature pattern: knights jumping to h4 (or similar rim squares) where they are immediately capturable by an enemy queen on an open diagonal, or knights landing on squares with zero protection. This occurs exclusively in the opening phase (100%), suggesting players are chasing enemy bishops (often a light-squared bishop on f5) with Nh4 without verifying that the landing square is defended—a basic tactical oversight that leaves the piece completely en prise.

16.label: Developing or repositioning a piece while overlooking an opponent's knight fork or tactical leap that wins material or destroys pawn structure.
16.description: This feature fires on opening/early-middlegame positions where the player moves a minor piece or queen (bishop 38%, knight 33%, queen 24%) to a square that appears natural for development or activity, but critically ignores an impending knight tactic. The material signature shows 90% of moves are non-captures and 71% are nominally 'safe' (no piece immediately hangs), yet 100% miss winning material according to Maia comparison, and the median eval loss is a devastating 284 centipawns—with 76% of cases swinging from drawn to losing. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 46%, king_safety 31%, fork 15%) combined with recurring tags like tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and pawn_structure_damage reveal the core pattern: the player's move allows the opponent a tempo-gaining knight jump (Nd4, Nxf6+, etc.) that simultaneously attacks multiple targets, forces retreats, or shatters the pawn shield. The top boards consistently show Italian/Spanish-type openings with knights on d4/f6 exploiting unprotected bishops or queens on vulnerable squares. The player focuses on their own plan (piece placement) while neglecting the opponent's concrete tactical resource, turning an equal or balanced position into a lost one.

21.label: Player makes a quiet or retreating move, missing a forcing continuation (often a check or back-rank tactic) that exploits the opponent's king weakness.
21.description: This feature identifies positions where the player fails to capitalize on king-safety vulnerabilities. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (58%) with no checks played (0%), while Maia's recommended moves deliver check 45% of the time and frequently capture major pieces (queen 32%, rook 21%). The dominant motifs—king_safety (50%), back_rank (25%)—confirm the pattern: the opponent's king is exposed or vulnerable, but the player makes a non-forcing move (often a queen retreat or pawn push) instead of delivering a decisive blow. The eval trajectory (median 312cp lost, with winning→losing/drawn comprising 18%) shows these are game-changing oversights that throw away substantial advantages. The per-position analyses reinforce this: missed mate-in-1, missed Qh4+ as the only good move, failing to exploit back-rank weakness, and self-blocking pieces that could deliver king attacks. The player consistently overlooks forcing sequences involving checks and king-side threats in favor of passive alternatives.

24.label: Player makes a non-queen move that hangs material while their king faces a critical queen attack requiring immediate defensive response.
24.description: This feature captures positions where the player ignores an opponent's dominant queen (Maia recommends queen moves 95% of the time, typically defensive queen repositioning) and instead plays a bishop, king, pawn, or queen move that hangs a piece (55% hangs) or is otherwise unsafe. The king_safety motif (46%) and exposed/uncastled king tags dominate, indicating the opponent's queen is actively threatening the player's king. The median eval loss of 298 centipawns confirms these are severe tactical oversights. The concrete positions show a recurring pattern: the opponent's queen is infiltrating or threatening decisive action (e.g., Qf7, Qg7, Qe2 threats), and the only adequate defense involves the player's own queen (Maia's 95% queen recommendation), but the player instead develops a minor piece, moves the king, or grabs material on the queenside. The trajectory (drawn->losing 15%, winning->losing 6%) shows these mistakes often convert manageable or even favorable positions into lost ones. The common thread is failing to prioritize queen-based defense against an immediate queen infiltration threat, resulting in catastrophic material or positional collapse.

25.label: Failing to resolve critical e4/d5 central tension, allowing a punishing e5 pawn advance that wins tempo or material.
25.description: This feature fires on opening positions (88% opening phase) where the player makes a developing or quiet move (bishop 44%, pawn 31%, king 25% - often castling) instead of addressing the critical central pawn tension (typically d5 vs e4). The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' (94%) - nothing is immediately hung - yet the eval trajectory reveals a devastating positional cost: 88% of cases shift from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 285 centipawns. The Opus analysis consistently identifies the mechanism: by ignoring the central tension, the player allows the opponent to advance e5 with tempo (attacking a knight on f6 or bishop on d6), often creating a pawn fork that wins a piece. Tags like 'tempo_loss' (5), 'pawn_fork' (4), 'center_tension' (3), and 'central_tension_ignored' (2) reinforce this pattern. The top boards uniformly feature classical d5/e4 pawn structures where Maia's recommended move is a central pawn capture (100% pawn moves capturing pawns), while the player instead develops a bishop, castles, or makes a prophylactic move that catastrophically fails to address the tactical time-bomb in the center.

28.label: Moving the queen aggressively without tactical justification, leaving it hanging or losing tempo in the middlegame.
28.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players move their queen (63% of activating moves) to an aggressive-looking square that actually loses material — 68% of moves result in a hanging piece with a median loss of ~1 pawn (net material median -1.0). The eval trajectory shows these mistakes cost a median of 276 centipawns, often converting winning positions to drawn or drawn to losing. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (33%) and king_safety (33%), with tags like 'premature_attack' and 'missed_tactic' appearing frequently. The concrete positions confirm this: players play moves like Qg5, Qd3, Qa5, Qh3 — queen moves that look threatening but lack proper preparation. The Maia alternatives show the engine preferred developing other pieces (rooks 19%, bishops 22%, pawns 19%) or executing concrete tactics (captures 39%, checks 19%) rather than the speculative queen maneuver. In essence, these players launch queen attacks without the necessary supporting moves (sacrifices, deflections, or preparatory threats), allowing opponents to gain tempo against the exposed queen while consolidating their position.

29.label: Playing a quiet or purposeless move that leaves a piece undefended or removes a critical defender, allowing the opponent to win material.
29.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (87% no capture, mostly pawns and rooks moved) that appears safe on the surface but actually hangs a piece (36% hangs) or misses a winning tactic (100% missed winning material). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences—a median loss of 294 centipawns, with positions frequently shifting from drawn to losing (15%) or winning to drawn/losing (12%). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), supported by tags like missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and blocking_own_piece. The per-position analysis reveals the mechanism: players make prophylactic, purposeless, or self-blocking moves (like Kf3 blocking a knight's retreat, or h7h6 while a bishop hangs, or moving a knight that was guarding a critical diagonal) instead of addressing the tactical demands of the position. Maia's recommendations (rooks 47%, queens 23%, knights 18%) suggest that active piece play—often a simple capture or tactical strike—was required. The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (78%) where piece coordination and tactical awareness are paramount, and the quiet moves represent a failure to recognize that the position demanded immediate concrete action.

23.label: Player captures a major piece (trade/safe) but misses a forced checkmate or decisive tactical blow.
23.description: This feature fires when the player makes a rook or queen capture (often taking an opponent's queen or rook) that appears materially reasonable (62% trades, 38% safe moves, median net +5.0) but catastrophically misses a much stronger continuation—typically a forced checkmate or decisive attack. The eval trajectory confirms enormous losses (median 9794 centipawns lost), with positions going from winning to losing/drawn in 24% of cases and remaining 'winning' only nominally in 50%. The Maia reference moves are overwhelmingly checks (100%), revealing that the missed best move involved a checking sequence or mating attack. The tactical motifs (back_rank, king_safety, hanging_piece) and tags (capture_order_error, back_rank) confirm the pattern: the player reflexively recaptures or trades a major piece when a forcing check/mate was available. The concrete positions show scenarios like missing Bf6# to capture on d1, or missing a mate-in-2 by taking a queen instead. The common thread is that a materially 'sensible' capture blinds the player to a lethal tactical shot, usually involving a check or back-rank geometry.

27.label: Player captures material with check instead of delivering a shorter forced mate.
27.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning position (71% winning->winning) executes an aggressive capture—typically with a queen (57%) or rook (43%)—that often delivers check (71%), but misses a faster forced mate. The material signature shows the player capturing rooks (71%), bishops (14%), or knights (14%), yet the move actually loses material net (57%) or results in an unfavorable exchange (43%), with a median cost of -4.0 material. The catastrophic eval loss (median 9254 centipawns) reveals these are positions where forced mates (mate-in-2, mate-in-3, mate-in-4) existed but the player was seduced by a flashy capture or check. The dominant motifs—king_safety (45%), back_rank (18%)—confirm the opponent's king was already fatally exposed. Tags like missed_mate (4), exposed_king (4), and missed_tactic (3) reinforce that the winning combination was available but overlooked in favor of an instinctive 'checks and captures' approach. The Opus examples explicitly describe cases like missing Qd6+ Rd7 Qxd7# by capturing a rook, or exchanging a queen for a bishop when Rf6+ forced mate-in-4. This is the classic 'captures before checkmates' error—grabbing material when a lethal king attack was already decisive.

31.label: Moving the king or major piece to a passive square, losing tempo and allowing the opponent to seize a decisive tactical opportunity.
31.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player makes a non-capturing move (86% hangs material) with a king (29%) or major piece (queen 43%, rook 29%) that retreats to a passive square, losing critical tempo. The median cost is 249 centipawns, and the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), with king_safety and piece_activity as recurring tags. The boards show patterns like Ka1, Kh1, Kh2, Dc1—sideways or backward king/piece shuffles that accomplish nothing while the opponent has a forcing continuation available (typically Maia finds a queen capture 100% of the time). The eval trajectory shows these moves often make already-difficult positions catastrophically worse (43% losing→losing) or throw away advantages (29% losing→winning from opponent's perspective). The tactical summaries confirm 'pointless checks' and king moves that walk into worse squares, classic tempo-wasting retreats that allow the opponent to execute missed tactics like forks or queen invasions.

30.label: Ignoring a knight fork threat in the opening, hanging material to a discovered or direct fork.
30.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player makes a seemingly natural developing or pawn move (pawn 67%, knight 33%) that is not a capture, but hangs material (100% 'hangs' signature, median -1.0 net material). The eval trajectory shows these moves uniformly convert a drawn position into a losing one (drawn->losing 100%, median 423cp lost), indicating catastrophic oversights rather than gradual positional drift. The tactical layer overwhelmingly identifies fork motifs (79%), with dominant tags including 'opening_trap', 'knight_fork', and 'missed_tactic'. Examining the top boards confirms the pattern: nearly all positions feature a knight on b5 or g5 (or similar aggressive outpost) where the opponent's move removes a key defender or opens a fork square, allowing a devastating knight fork winning material. The positions are all in the opening phase (100%), typically involving standard setups (1.d4 Bf4 systems, Fried Liver-adjacent Italian lines, or Sokolsky openings) where one side has aggressively placed a knight and the opponent blunders by ignoring the fork threat—playing moves like ...a6, ...c5, ...c6, or ...Nf6 that either walk into or fail to address the impending knight tactic.

32.label: Active pieces moved to apparently aggressive squares but overlooking critical king safety or tactical vulnerabilities, hanging material.
32.description: This feature captures middlegame blunders (80%) where players move active pieces—primarily bishops (40%) and queens (25%)—to seemingly aggressive squares but catastrophically overlook tactical consequences. The material signature is devastating: 55% hang a piece outright and 25% lose material, with a median loss of 3.0 pawns worth of material. The eval trajectory confirms these are severe mistakes (median 325cp lost), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (25%) or making already losing positions hopeless (25%). The tactical analysis reveals the underlying pattern: players prioritize piece activity (tagged 5 times) while missing tactics (4 times), frequently ignoring king safety threats (33% of motifs), back-rank vulnerabilities (17%), and leaving pieces trapped or hanging. The concrete positions show pieces lunging forward (Qd7, Qxf6, Bh4) while the player's own king or pieces are fatally exposed. Maia's preferred moves are notably more restrained (pawns 30%, defensive rooks 25%), confirming these are overaggressive piece placements that ignore defensive necessities.

33.label: Player sacrifices a piece without adequate compensation, turning a good position into a losing one.
33.description: This feature fires on moves where a player hangs or sacrifices a piece (56% hangs, 11% loses material outright, median net material: -3.0) without sufficient tactical justification. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors: 33% turn winning positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 631 centipawns. The pieces moved are typically rooks (33%), knights (22%), or bishops (22%) — placed on squares where they can be captured for free or where a speculative sacrifice has no real follow-up. The Opus analysis reinforces this with tags like 'failed_sacrifice', 'unnecessary_tactic', 'greek_gift_refuted', and recurring 'hanging_piece' motifs (50%). Concrete examples include a bishop sacrifice for a pawn with no attacking continuation, a rook moved to an undefended square, and capturing the wrong pawn when a more forcing continuation existed. These are not exchanges or trades — the opponent captures nothing in 78% of cases — but rather pieces left en prise or sacrificed into positions where the compensation is illusory. The pattern is overwhelmingly middlegame (89%), where the complexity tempts players into unsound tactical adventures.

36.label: Player makes a passive king or pawn move while their rook hangs to an opponent's doubled rooks on an open file.
36.description: This feature fires when a player makes a non-capture king move (80%) or pawn move (20%) that hangs material worth approximately 5 pawns (median -5.0 centipawns net material, 100% 'hangs' classification). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings—60% winning-to-losing and 40% drawn-to-losing with a median loss of 535 centipawns—indicating the player was throwing away a tenable or winning position. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 50%, overloaded_defender 12%) and tags (rook_endgame, doubled_rooks, c-file_control) reveal a consistent pattern: the opponent has doubled rooks bearing down on an open file targeting an undefended or under-defended rook, and instead of addressing this concrete threat (moving the attacked rook, interposing, or resolving the file tension), the player wastes a tempo on king centralization or an irrelevant pawn push. Maia consistently responds by capturing the hanging rook (100% rook captures). The positions are middlegame rook structures where the player fatally misjudges the urgency of the file pressure.

34.label: Moving a rook to a square where it becomes hanging or trapped, often ignoring critical tactical threats elsewhere.
34.description: This feature fires when a player moves a rook (88% of activations) to a square where it hangs without compensation (62% hang rate, median material loss of -1.0 piece). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 377 centipawns, with many positions converting wins into losses (16% winning->losing) or worsening already difficult positions (20% losing->losing). The dominant motifs—king_safety (33%), hanging_piece (33%), and missed_tactic (11%)—reveal that these rook moves typically ignore urgent threats to the player's own king or leave the rook undefended on vulnerable files/ranks. The concrete positions confirm this: rooks are placed on squares where they become targets for back-rank mates, skewers, or queen attacks (e.g., Rg8 creating back-rank vulnerability, Rh1 walking into a skewer, Re8 landing on an attacked square). Meanwhile, Maia's recommended moves are diverse (knights 24%, bishops 22%, queens 18%) and often involve active tactics like captures (40%) or checks (8%), indicating the player missed a concrete tactical opportunity in favor of a passive or self-destructive rook move.

39.label: Giving a rook check that trades away critical material or activity for insufficient compensation.
39.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a rook check that superficially looks forcing but actually liquidates into a losing position. The material signature shows 100% rook moves delivering check, with outcomes predominantly being trades or outright losses (median net material: -1.0), indicating the check captures a pawn or minor piece but surrenders the rook's superior positional value. The eval trajectory is devastating: 43% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 295 centipawns—these are not speculative sacrifices but misjudged simplifications. The tactical analysis confirms this: tags like 'liquidation_error', 'rook_pair_misuse', and 'dynamic_compensation_squandered' recur, and the per-position summaries consistently describe players trading away a rook (often one of a powerful doubled-rook configuration or a rook dominating the 7th rank) for a mere pawn with check, failing to recognize that the rook's activity was their primary source of counterplay or advantage. The check is visually attractive and feels forcing, but it dissolves the player's dynamic compensation and leaves them in a structurally lost position.

44.label: In drawn endgames, the king moves to a vulnerable square where it can be confined and mated, missing a saving capture.
44.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a king move (100% king moved) that transforms a dead draw into a loss (100% drawn->losing trajectory with catastrophic eval swings, median 10000cp indicating forced mate). The Maia suggestion shows a rook capture was available (100% Maia captures rook), meaning the player missed a crucial material win that would have maintained the draw. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the king walks to an edge or confined square (king_safety, tempo_loss motifs) where it falls into a mating net, rather than taking a hanging rook that would simplify to a drawable position. The boards show classic KBR vs K, KQ vs K+piece, and similar endgame configurations where one critical capture saves the draw but instead the king drifts into a lethal zone.

37.label: King moves away from critical pawns in a losing pawn endgame, accelerating the loss.
37.description: This feature detects a recurring pawn endgame error where a player, already in a losing position, moves their king in the wrong direction—away from critical passed pawns or key squares. All activating positions are pure endgames (100% endgame phase) with king moves that don't capture or give check, and the material situation appears 'safe' (no immediate hanging pieces). However, the eval trajectory shows these moves consistently worsen an already losing position (losing->losing, median 173cp lost), indicating the king is abandoning defensive duties. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (50%), passed_pawn (43%), and tempo_loss (7%)—along with recurring tags like king_activity, tempo_loss, and pawn_race, paint a clear picture: the player's king strays from the 'square' of enemy passed pawns or fails to maintain opposition, allowing the opponent to promote or capture critical pawns. The concrete positions confirm this—kings moving to a5, g6, e6, g5, b5 when they should be staying close to passed pawns or maintaining key defensive posts. This is a fundamental endgame principle violation: the king must remain active relative to passed pawns, and these moves squander tempo in positions where every move counts.

35.label: Leaving a knight en prise to an advancing/attacking pawn in the opening, typically against an e5 pawn.
35.description: This feature captures a specific and recurring opening blunder where a player either moves a knight to a square already attacked by an enemy pawn (especially e5), or pushes a pawn that blocks the knight's escape route, effectively hanging the piece. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' with a median net loss of -2.0 (a minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones with a massive median swing of 435 centipawns. The board positions overwhelmingly feature an advanced e5 pawn that attacks or will capture a knight on f6 (or equivalent), and the tactical motifs are dominated by 'hanging_piece' and 'trapped_piece.' The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the same pattern: the player ignores or fails to recognize that a pawn attacks their knight, either by developing the knight into the attack (e.g., ...Nf6 into e5), playing a move that blocks the knight's retreat (e.g., ...d5 blocking Nd5 escape), or making an unrelated move (e.g., ...e6, ...h6) while leaving the knight hanging. All examples occur in the opening phase, making this a classic opening development oversight against a central pawn advance.

40.label: Player makes a passive or routine move instead of capturing a hanging pawn on e4 with a knight, losing significant advantage.
40.description: This feature fires when a player makes a developing or routine move (bishop 32%, pawn 26%, queen 16%) while ignoring an available knight capture (Maia's recommended move is knight 100% of the time, capturing a pawn 97% of the time). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening phase (74%) where a central pawn—typically on e4—is inadequately defended. The player's move is usually 'safe' (81%) meaning they don't lose material directly, but they miss winning material 90% of the time, resulting in a median eval loss of 230 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows positions going from drawn to losing (26%) or winning to drawn (23%), indicating the missed capture was often the critical moment that squandered an advantage. The Opus analysis confirms this with tags like missed_tactic (7 occurrences), tempo_loss (6), and example summaries explicitly describing failures to capture hanging e4 pawns with Nxe4. The top boards consistently show positions where a knight can profitably capture a central pawn but the player instead castles, develops a piece, or makes a quiet queen move.

38.label: Opening moves that ignore a knight-based discovered attack, hanging material to a tactical shot.
38.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders where the player makes a developing or seemingly natural move (most often a pawn push, sometimes a bishop or king move) that completely overlooks a discovered attack, typically involving a knight on g6 combined with a queen on h5. The material signature is stark: 86% of moves simply hang a piece (median net loss of 5 pawns' worth of material), and in 100% of cases the opponent had a winning tactic available that was missed. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 367cp lost), often converting drawable or slightly worse positions into hopeless ones. The top-activating boards repeatedly show the Nxf7/Ng6 discovered attack pattern where the knight unmasks the queen's attack on a key square, and the player's move fails to address this threat—often continuing routine development or making a pawn move that ignores the tactical emergency. Tags like tempo_loss, development, and missed_tactic confirm the player is prioritizing normal opening principles over concrete calculation of the opponent's forcing sequence.

41.label: King moves instead of recapturing a bishop on f7/h7, losing a piece and tempo in the opening.
41.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: a bishop has been sacrificed (typically on f7 or h7), and the player moves their king (95% king moves) without recapturing the attacking bishop, which Maia consistently identifies as the correct move (Kxf7/Kxh7 in 100% of cases). The material signature shows 'safe' or 'hangs' because the player isn't capturing anything—they're declining a free piece. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 291cp loss), frequently converting drawn or even winning positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 47%). The top boards confirm this: nearly all show a white bishop sitting on f7 or h7 (the classic Fried Liver/Greek Gift squares) with the player choosing Kf8, Kh8, or similar evasions instead of simply taking the bishop. The Opus analysis tags (hanging_piece 40%, tempo_loss 20%, king_safety 27%) reflect that declining the capture leaves a piece hanging, wastes tempo, and often worsens king safety by self-trapping the king. This is an opening-phase error (90% opening) where players instinctively flee rather than accept the sacrifice material.

45.label: Playing a passive pawn or non-forcing move instead of an active rook tactic that wins material or delivers a decisive attack.
45.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (pawn 50%, rook 50%) that loses significant tempo while Maia's recommended move involves an active rook capturing major material (queen 50%, rook 50%). The dominant motifs—tempo_loss, back_rank vulnerability, and hanging pieces—combined with the tags (tempo_loss appearing most frequently, alongside king_safety and missed_tactic) reveal a pattern of choosing passive moves when sharp tactical continuations were available. The eval trajectory shows these moves cost a median of 137 centipawns, sometimes converting winning positions into merely equal ones or turning fightable losses into forced mates. The concrete positions confirm this: h3 instead of a back-rank defense, g3 instead of exploiting tactics, h3 instead of active piece play—all quiet pawn pushes that ignore urgent tactical demands. The phase split (endgame/middlegame) and the 100% missed-winning-material rate confirm these are moments where concrete calculation was needed but the player defaulted to a slow, prophylactic move.

43.label: Ignoring urgent tactical threats in endgames by making passive or tempo-losing moves instead of the critical saving/winning continuation.
43.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (60% endgame, 40% middlegame) where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (95% no capture, pieces moved are king/pawn/knight/rook) that fails to address an immediate tactical obligation. The key signal is that Maia's recommended move delivers check 100% of the time, indicating the correct continuation involved a forcing move (often a knight fork, discovered check, or promotion tactic), yet the player chose a passive alternative. The motifs confirm this: hanging_piece (40%), tempo_loss (20%), passed_pawn (20%), and discovered_attack (20%) all point to situations where a concrete tactical resource was available but ignored. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 287 centipawns, with positions shifting from drawn-to-losing (20%) or winning-to-losing (15%), indicating these tempo wastes are game-decisive. The concrete examples reinforce this pattern: a king move that ignores a hanging knight, a pawn push that misses an immediate promotion tactic, a king retreat to the wrong side allowing a knight to dominate. In each case, the player had a forcing continuation (typically involving check) but instead made an aimless move that squandered the position's critical tempo demands.

42.label: Player makes a move that leaves a piece hanging on a long diagonal controlled by the opponent's bishop, which Maia would exploit by capturing along that diagonal.
42.description: This feature fires when players make moves (predominantly pawn, rook, knight, or queen moves) that ignore a powerful enemy bishop's diagonal pressure, resulting in material being hung (63% of cases). The Maia-recommended response is overwhelmingly a bishop move (90%) that captures along the diagonal (83% bishop captures). The tactical motifs center on hanging pieces (40%), overloaded defenders (40%), and king safety (20%), with recurring tags like 'long_diagonal,' 'bishop_diagonal_exploitation,' and 'removing_the_guard.' The top boards reveal a clear pattern: players attempt to address local threats (e.g., pushing f6 to challenge a knight on e5, or moving a queen to a seemingly active square) while failing to account for the opponent's fianchettoed or centralized bishop slicing through the position on an open diagonal. The median cost is 211 centipawns, with many positions already lost becoming catastrophically worse. The classic example is f7-f6 played to kick a knight while the g2 bishop gains a devastating capture or pin along the a8-h1 or a1-h8 diagonal, or a queen placed on a square doubly attacked including by the long-diagonal bishop.

46.label: Developing a piece in the opening while leaving another piece or tactical opportunity unaddressed, allowing the opponent to win material.
46.description: This feature detects a recurring opening mistake where a player develops a piece (typically a knight or bishop) without first resolving an existing tactical vulnerability—usually a hanging or insufficiently defended piece elsewhere on the board. The material signature shows 100% 'safe' moves (no immediate material loss on the move itself) with no captures, yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: 83% winning->drawn and 17% drawn->losing, with a median loss of 271 centipawns. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (57%), and the tags emphasize tempo_loss, missed_tactic, and development concerns. The concrete positions all arise in the opening (100% opening phase), where the player makes a natural-looking developing move (Nf3, Bg2, Be7, d3) but fails to notice that an existing piece (often a bishop on c4 or knight on e5) is tactically vulnerable. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (67% bishop captures, 33% knight captures), confirming that the opponent could simply take the undefended piece. The pattern is one of prioritizing development routine over concrete calculation—moving forward while a piece is left en prise behind.

47.label: Failing to exploit a weakened diagonal with a devastating queen check in the opening after the opponent's f-pawn advance.
47.description: This feature fires on opening positions where one side has pushed the f-pawn (typically f5 or f4), fatally weakening the e1-h4 or e8-h5 diagonal, and the opponent plays a routine developing move (knight to f6/f3, pawn push, or knight retreat) instead of the crushing Qh4+ or Qh5+ check. The material signature shows the player's move is 'safe' (no material lost immediately) — the mistake is one of omission, not commission. Maia consistently identifies the queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks), confirming the missed tactic is always the same motif. The eval trajectory is devastating: 81% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 316 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the recurring pattern: every position involves king_safety concerns on the weakened diagonal, with 'queen_check' and 'diagonal_weakness' as top tags. The FENs consistently show King's Gambit or similar structures where f2-f4/f5 or f7-f5 has been played, leaving the king exposed along the diagonal, and the opponent ignores the one-move tactical punishment.

51.label: Player ignores a simple pawn capture that wins the opponent's queen, instead making a passive or irrelevant move.
51.description: This feature fires when a player has a pawn that can directly capture the opponent's queen (exf6 capturing the queen on f6 is the recurring motif) but plays an entirely different move—typically a rook relocation or passive piece move. The material signature shows the player's move hangs a piece (62%) or is otherwise costly, while Maia consistently identifies the correct move as a pawn capturing a queen (100% pawn move, 100% queen capture). The eval trajectory is devastating: 88% of cases go from winning to losing with a median loss of 882 centipawns, indicating the player threw away a completely won position. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is a hanging piece (the queen left en prise to a pawn), with tags like 'pawn_takes_queen' and 'missed_capture' recurring. The board positions overwhelmingly feature a pawn on e5 that can capture a queen on f6, but the player overlooks this elementary capture in favor of moves that accomplish nothing strategically.

48.label: Knight or bishop moves that open the center while the player's own king lacks safety, turning drawn positions into losing ones.
48.description: This feature captures a recurring mistake where players make piece moves (predominantly knights at 61%, bishops at 22%) that open or disturb the central pawn structure when their own king is insufficiently sheltered. The king_safety motif appears in 100% of analyzed positions, with tags like 'king_in_center' and 'opening_the_center' confirming the pattern. The material signature shows these moves frequently hang pieces (39%) or end up slightly down (39%), with a median loss of 2.0 material units—suggesting the player misjudges a tactical sequence in the center. The eval trajectory is devastating: 56% of cases convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 344 centipawns. The concrete positions confirm this: players capture pawns or reposition knights into the center (e.g., Nxe4, Ng5, Nxd7, Nxe3) without recognizing that the resulting open lines expose their own king to decisive attacks. The Maia baseline (100% non-captures, mostly pawn moves) suggests the correct approach was typically a quiet consolidating move rather than the aggressive central action chosen.

50.label: Rook moves in the endgame that allow or fall into a skewer or tactical shot, worsening an already difficult position.
50.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a rook move—often a capture of a pawn (83%)—lands the rook on a vulnerable square that permits a tactical refutation, most commonly a skewer (30% dominant motif). The material signature shows the move is nominally 'safe' or even wins a pawn (median net +1.0), but the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 136 centipawns, predominantly making a losing position worse (67% losing→losing) or converting a drawable position into a loss (17% drawn→losing). The recurring pattern across the top boards is a rook actively capturing or relocating to a square that falls on a dangerous diagonal or file, enabling the opponent's bishop or rook to deliver a skewer checking the king while attacking the rook. Tags like tempo_loss, piece_activity, and missed_tactic reinforce that the player prioritizes material grabs or activity without calculating the resulting geometry. Maia's responses (king moves 67%, rook 33%, never capturing) confirm the opponent simply sidesteps and exploits the newly created tactical vulnerability rather than needing to recapture.

54.label: Unsound bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check in the opening, lacking sufficient attacking support.
54.description: This feature detects a highly specific and recurring opening mistake: a bishop captures a pawn on f7 (or f2) with check, sacrificing a full piece for insufficient compensation. The material signature shows bishop moves capturing a pawn with check 100% of the time, with the net outcome being slightly down (median -2.0, i.e., lost a piece for a pawn). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost: 71% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 328 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the core theme—these are premature attacks (tagged 'unsound_sacrifice', 'premature_attack', 'insufficient_compensation') where the player lacks the developed supporting pieces to exploit the exposed king. The top boards confirm this overwhelmingly: nearly all show Bc4xf7+ or Bc5xf2+ in standard opening positions (Italian, Pirc, Sicilian structures) where knights and other pieces remain undeveloped. This is the classic 'coffee-house' Bxf7+ that looks aggressive but simply loses material against accurate defense.

55.label: Player overlooked a knight fork with check that wins the opponent's queen or major material.
55.description: This feature fires when a player misses a devastating knight fork delivered with check. The material/position signature shows Maia recommends a knight move with check in 100% of cases, while the player instead moves various pieces (knights 30%, pawns 19%, bishops 18%) without capturing anything significant (64% no capture). The motif analysis confirms 'fork' in 100% of positions, with dominant tags including knight_fork, missed_tactic, and queen_win. The eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 470 centipawns—consistent with missing a queen-winning tactic—with many positions shifting from winning to losing or drawn. The concrete examples repeatedly show the same pattern: a knight fork with check exploiting the geometric alignment of the opponent's king and queen, where the player instead chose a passive or unrelated move (castling, a pawn push, a premature capture), forfeiting the game-deciding tactical blow.

52.label: Moving the queen away from a winning attacking position, allowing the opponent's king to escape danger.
52.description: This feature fires when a player makes a queen move (67% queen moves) that catastrophically abandons a winning attacking position. The material signature shows these moves lose material (50% loses, 33% hangs) with a median net loss of -6.0, while Maia consistently identifies a queen capture with check as the correct continuation (100% queen, 100% capture, 100% check). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-throwing blunders: 50% go from winning to losing with a massive median eval loss of 1153 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals king_safety as the dominant motif (67%), with tags like mating_attack and queen_infiltration appearing — the player had a winning attack on the enemy king but redirected their queen to an inferior square (often a greedy capture or misguided reposition), missing a forced mating sequence or decisive queen capture with check. The boards show positions where queens are active with exposed enemy kings, but the player's move squanders the attack rather than delivering the killing blow.

49.label: Moving a piece (usually bishop or knight) to a square where it or another piece is left undefended and can be captured for free.
49.description: All three signals converge on a single pattern: the player moves a minor piece (bishop 58%, knight 21%) in a non-capturing move (84% no capture) that simply hangs material (84% 'hangs' outcome, median net material loss of -3.0, i.e., roughly a full piece). The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the motif in 100% of cases, with 'undefended_piece' as the most common tag—the player either places a piece on an unprotected square or moves away from a piece that needed defending, leaving it en prise. The eval trajectory shows these mistakes are catastrophic: 42% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 483 centipawns. The top boards illustrate this clearly—bishops left on open diagonals (a1-h8, a6 squares), knights placed where they can be captured, or moves that abandon defense of another piece. Maia's suggested alternatives often involve the same piece type but in safer configurations (bishop 37%, pawn 32%), frequently including recaptures that would have maintained material balance. This is not an exchange or trade gone wrong—it is a pure oversight where the player fails to notice a piece is undefended after their move.

56.label: Playing routine developing moves while missing a winning queen check that exploits an undefended piece.
56.description: This feature fires on opening positions (93% opening phase) where the player makes a routine, safe move (pawn 55%, bishop 17%, knight 14% — all non-captures 83% of the time) while completely missing a crushing queen check (Maia's move: queen 100%, gives check 100%). The missed tactic almost always involves an undefended piece (hanging_piece motif 77%) that can be won via a queen check, often exploiting a diagonal weakness. The concrete pattern is remarkably consistent across the top boards: a bishop on g4 (or similar piece) is left undefended, and Qa4+ or Qh5+ wins it with check. The eval trajectory is devastating — median 432 centipawns lost, with 62% going from winning to drawn and 10% from winning to losing — confirming these are game-changing missed opportunities. The tags reinforce this: queen_check(6), undefended_piece(9), missed_tactic(10), and deflection(3) all point to the same pattern of overlooking a forcing queen check that exploits a tactical vulnerability in the opening.

53.label: Playing a quiet pawn move instead of capturing a hanging or trapped piece, throwing away a winning position.
53.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, quiet pawn move (100% pawn moves, no captures, material outcome 'safe') while a clearly winning tactical opportunity exists—specifically capturing a hanging or trapped piece with a rook (Maia recommends Rxbishop 100% of the time). The eval trajectory consistently shows winning positions collapsing to drawn (median 370cp lost), indicating the player had a decisive advantage and squandered it. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 40%, trapped_piece 20%, fork 20%) and tags (hanging_piece, missed_tactic, piece_activity) confirm that a concrete capture was available but ignored. The board positions show patterns where bishops or other pieces are en prise or inadequately defended, yet the player pushes a pawn (a5, b5, g6, d3, etc.) instead of taking the free material. This is not a positional subtlety—it's a failure to notice or prioritize an obvious tactical opportunity, choosing a slow move when a decisive capture was on the board.

57.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in the opening, missing that the opponent's knight can fork pieces.
57.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (93% opening) where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (100% no capture) — typically a pawn push (43%), knight development (29%), or bishop move (21%) — that overlooks a knight fork tactic available to the opponent. The dominant motif is 'fork' (75%), and Maia consistently recommends a knight capture (Nxd5-type moves) as the correct alternative. The positions share a recurring structural signature: centralized enemy knights (often on d5) combined with undeveloped or uncoordinated pieces that create fork targets. The eval trajectory is severe (median 346cp loss), frequently converting drawn positions into losing ones (57% drawn->losing). The tactical analysis confirms these are tempo-losing moves that ignore the opponent's knight activity, often leaving pieces hanging on specific squares that the knight can simultaneously attack. The common tags — missed_tactic, tempo_loss, piece_activity, and development — all point to the same underlying error: prioritizing a slow positional plan while a concrete knight fork punishes the lack of coordination.

61.label: Pawn or piece moves that inadvertently leave another piece undefended and capturable.
61.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where a player moves a pawn, rook, or queen and inadvertently leaves another piece unprotected or removes a critical defender. The material signature shows 68% safe moves yet 29% that hang material, with the median eval loss of 319 centipawns confirming these are serious blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The trajectory (36% drawn->losing, 10% winning->drawn) shows these moves frequently turn holdable or winning positions into lost ones. The dominant tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' (43%), supplemented by forks (14%) that exploit the newly undefended pieces. The per-position analyses consistently describe the same pattern: a move that removes a defender (e.g., b7b5 leaving c6 unprotected, Be7-b4 abandoning 7th-rank defense) or creates a tactical vulnerability that allows the opponent to win material with a simple capture or fork. Maia's preferred moves (87% rook moves) suggest the correct continuations involved keeping pieces coordinated and defended, rather than the pawn pushes and piece relocations that created the hanging targets.

60.label: Minor piece moves in the opening that waste tempo or miss tactical threats, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
60.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where players move bishops (67%) or knights (33%) to natural-looking but suboptimal squares, missing stronger tactical continuations. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (67%) rather than outright blunders—the piece isn't immediately lost—but 100% of the time the player misses winning material that was available (e.g., Qxg4 capturing a hanging knight). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%) and tempo_loss (20%), with tags heavily emphasizing development, piece_activity, and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory is severe (median 297cp lost), often converting winning or equal positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 50%, drawn->losing 33%). The concrete positions show classic opening scenarios: developing a bishop to e6/d7/e3 or a knight to a6/h6/a3 when a tactical shot was available. These are 'looks natural but misses the point' developing moves that squander concrete advantages in sharp opening positions.

58.label: Player makes a quiet or slow move, missing a concrete tactical combination that wins material (typically a knight capture available via Maia's suggested bishop/knight moves).
58.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'safe' move (93% safe material outcome) — often a queen move (33%) or other non-forcing continuation — while completely missing a piece-winning tactic. The Maia-recommended move overwhelmingly involves capturing a knight (80%) or other piece via a bishop (87%), indicating a clear tactical shot was available. The 100% 'missed winning material' rate confirms this is not a positional misjudgment but a pure tactical oversight. The eval trajectory (median 319cp lost, with 20% winning->losing and 13% winning->drawn) shows these are game-changing blunders that squander significant advantages. The Opus analysis reinforces this with motifs of hanging pieces, trapped pieces, forks, and explicitly tagged 'missed_tactic' and 'piece_winning_missed' patterns. Concrete examples include missing Bxc6/Qxc6 combinations, failing to play Nxg4, and making slow developing moves while a forcing capture sequence was available. The positions are in opening/middlegame phases where sharp tactical awareness is critical, and the player instead chose a passive or tempo-losing alternative.

59.label: In endgame positions, player makes a move that leaves a piece or pawn undefended and immediately capturable, throwing away a winning or drawn position.
59.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame blunder pattern where players hang material through careless piece placement. The material signature shows 75% of moves are non-captures that hang a piece (with median -5.0 material loss), and the phase is 100% endgame. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% go from winning to losing and 25% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 1290 centipawns—indicating these are game-deciding errors. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (60%), with promotion_error (20%) as a secondary theme. The concrete positions reveal the pattern clearly: rooks placed on squares where pawns can capture them (Rd5 into e6xd5), pawns advanced to block their own rook's defense (a7 allowing Kxa7 capturing the rook), queens traded for single pawns in won positions, and pieces moved into the capture path of enemy units. The rook_endgame tag (7 occurrences) and passed_pawn tag (5) confirm these are simplified positions where one inattentive move immediately drops decisive material. Players appear to lose focus or miscalculate simple tactics in technically won endgames.

62.label: Wasting a critical tempo in a winning position, allowing the opponent to escape a decisive attack or mate.
62.description: This feature detects positions where a player holds a winning advantage but plays an irrelevant or passive move that squanders a decisive tempo. The material signature shows pieces being moved (queens 28%, rooks 26%) without capturing (72% no capture), and 63% of moves are 'safe' yet 68% miss winning material—indicating the move itself doesn't hang anything but fails to execute an available tactic. The eval trajectory confirms these are overwhelmingly 'throwing a win': the median cost is 579cp, with winning->winning (28%) masking that the advantage shrinks drastically, plus winning->drawn (7%) and losing->winning (9%) showing massive swings. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (43%), combined with back_rank threats (29%) and missed mates (3 tags), revealing that the player had a forcing continuation (often a back-rank mate or queen invasion) but instead played a slow developing move, king walk, or flank pawn push that gave the opponent a crucial defensive tempo. The example positions consistently show forced mates or crushing tactics available (f6, Qf6, Rh3) that were missed in favor of aimless moves like h4, Kh2, or Rc3.

63.label: In the opening, player makes a routine move instead of exploiting a Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice fork/discovered attack that would win material and disrupt the opponent's king.
63.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where the player has a bishop on c4 aimed at f7, often with a knight on f3 ready to follow up, and the opponent's king remains in the center (frequently with a bishop on g4 pinning). The player makes a quiet developing move (castling, h2h3, Be3, Bg5, Bb3) instead of the crushing Bxf7+! sacrifice, which Maia consistently identifies as the correct move (100% bishop moves capturing a pawn with check). The material signature shows 'safe' moves (96%) meaning the player didn't lose material directly—they simply missed the tactic. The eval trajectory is devastating: 67% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 246 centipawns, meaning roughly 2.5 pawns of advantage evaporates. The dominant motifs are fork (60%) and discovered attack (20%), reflecting that Bxf7+ typically sets up a knight fork (Ng5+) or discovered attack winning the pinning bishop on g4.
