The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 46%, king_safety 23%) and tags (missed_tactic, hanging_piece, tempo_loss) confirm that these are middlegame positions (86%) where the player overlooks a one- or two-move combination and instead plays a slow, purposeless move (like a quiet king move, a pawn push, or an aimless rook shuffle), immediately dropping from a won position to a lost one. The examples consistently show players ignoring available checks, captures, or threats that would win decisive material, choosing instead moves that leave their own pieces en prise or allow the opponent to seize the initiative.

130.label: Knight on f3 moves despite being pinned by a bishop to the queen, allowing queen capture.
130.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: a knight (100% of moves are knight moves) on f3 is pinned by an opponent's bishop (typically on g4) to the queen on d1, and the player moves that pinned knight anyway (most commonly Ne5). The material signature confirms catastrophic loss (median -5.0 material, corresponding to queen loss), with 55% losing material outright and 46% hanging material. The eval trajectory shows massive swings (median 550cp lost), turning drawn or winning positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis tags are overwhelmingly consistent: pin (50%), hanging_piece (50%), with recurring tags of queen_hanging, queen_loss, moving_pinned_piece, and pin_exploitation. The phase is 100% opening, and the OPUS summaries explicitly describe the same scenario repeatedly—White plays Ne5 while the Nf3 is the only piece blocking the Bg4-Qd1 diagonal, allowing the bishop to simply capture the queen. This is a classic beginner-level tactical oversight in the opening.

131.label: Player hangs major material by failing to address an unstoppable passed pawn threat.
131.description: This feature fires on middlegame/endgame positions where the player makes a move that hangs a piece (92% hangs, median -5.0 material) while completely ignoring a critical passed pawn threat. The Opus analysis confirms that passed pawns are the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with tags like 'unstoppable_promotion' and 'piece_priority_error' indicating the player moves a rook, queen, or knight to an irrelevant square instead of addressing an advanced passed pawn. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median 9375 centipawns lost, 33% winning->losing), consistent with allowing a promotion or losing material to a promotion threat. Maia's recommended moves often involve captures (rook 33%, knight 17%, queen 17%) that would either eliminate the passed pawn's support or win decisive material from the promotion threat. The concrete positions confirm this: e7 promotion threats left unaddressed, advanced h/f-pawns ignored, and pieces moved to squares that don't interact with the critical pawn at all.

128.label: Moving a rook to a natural-looking square (often d1 or d8) that surrenders a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative and equalize or take over.
128.description: This feature fires on positions where a player, typically holding a winning or near-winning advantage (median eval lost: 274cp, with 67% going from winning to drawn), plays a seemingly logical rook move (83% rook moves) that fails to maintain pressure. The boards overwhelmingly show rook lifts to open files (Rad1, Rad8, Rac1) that look natural but squander tempo at a critical moment. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (38%), with the common tags emphasizing missed_tactic and piece_activity—the player had a forcing continuation available (often a check, capture, or central pawn push like e5 or Qc3+) but instead chose a quiet developing move. The material signature confirms these aren't blunders in the traditional sense (83% 'safe', no captures), yet the eval trajectory shows catastrophic positional collapse. Maia's responses frequently involve checks (50%) or active queen/pawn moves that exploit the gifted tempo. The pattern is a player who has built a winning position but, at the critical moment requiring concrete action, defaults to a 'routine' rook centralization that lets the opponent consolidate or counterattack.

134.label: Unsound knight sacrifice on f7 in the opening that lacks sufficient compensation.
134.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: a knight capture on f7 (or f2 from Black's perspective) that constitutes an unsound sacrifice. The material signature shows knight moves capturing pawns (87%) with a slightly_down outcome and median net material of -2.0, indicating the player gives up a knight for only a pawn — a full piece sacrifice. The eval trajectory is devastating: 79% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 281 centipawns, showing these sacrifices fundamentally misjudge the position. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant tags of 'unsound_sacrifice', 'insufficient_compensation', and 'king_safety' — the player hopes for a kingside attack or fork after Nxf7, but the king simply captures and the attack fizzles due to insufficient development. The top boards overwhelmingly show the classic Ng5-Nxf7 pattern in the opening where White prematurely lunges at f7 before having the piece coordination to sustain the initiative.

129.label: Player makes a developing or quiet move while overlooking an opponent's knight delivering a devastating fork or tactical blow.
129.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable but passive move (pawn, queen, knight, or king move—rarely capturing anything) while completely ignoring a powerful knight-based tactical threat from the opponent. The material signature shows 42% of moves hang material and 50% are 'safe' only superficially—meaning the player didn't lose material on the move itself but left a critical tactical vulnerability unaddressed. Maia consistently recommends capturing the threatening knight with a bishop (Bxf6, Bxf4, etc.), indicating the correct response was to neutralize the knight. The eval trajectory is severe: 67% of cases go from drawn to losing with a median loss of 411 centipawns, showing these are game-deciding oversights. The tactical motifs confirm this: fork (38%), hanging_piece (38%), and tags like 'knight_fork', 'hanging_queen', 'ignored_threat', and even 'checkmate_in_one' all point to players failing to recognize an active enemy knight as an immediate tactical danger—whether it threatens a fork on e2+, a discovered attack, or even mate on h6. The boards consistently show a white or black knight on an aggressive square (g4, f4, f6, d5, N5-squares) that the player neglects to address.

132.label: Ignoring or worsening a pin/tactical threat in the opening, allowing the opponent to win material.
132.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (97% opening) where the player makes a seemingly quiet developing move (pawn 26%, bishop 24%, knight 19%) that ignores a critical tactical threat—most commonly a pin (33%), hanging piece (25%), or tempo loss (17%). The moves are overwhelmingly non-captures (89% capture nothing) and appear 'safe' on the surface (73% safe material outcome), yet Maia consistently recommends a pawn move (100% pawn), suggesting the correct response was a simple, concrete prophylactic pawn push to address the threat. The eval trajectory is devastating: 37% of cases transition from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 265 centipawns—typically a full piece. The top boards make the pattern vivid: players castle into a pin, develop a piece that worsens a pin on another piece, or make natural-looking moves (g6, Qd7, Bd7, O-O) that catastrophically overlook an existing pin or tactical motif. These are classic opening traps where the player's move is positionally reasonable in isolation but tactically blind to the opponent's concrete threat exploiting a pin or alignment.

138.label: Player moves queen aimlessly instead of capturing opponent's hanging queen in a won endgame.
138.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in an endgame (80%) with a winning position, moves their queen (80% of moves) without capturing anything, while the opponent's queen is hanging and could be taken for free. The Maia best-move analysis confirms that in 100% of cases, the correct move was a queen capture (Qxq). The eval trajectory shows these are devastating mistakes—60% convert winning positions to drawn ones, with a median loss of 497 centipawns. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 67%, missed_capture tags appearing 4 times, queen_hanging appearing twice) all converge on the same pattern: the player overlooks a trivially available queen capture. The concrete positions show queens that could be taken (Qxf2, Qxc5, Qxe2) but instead the player makes an irrelevant queen move—sometimes a purposeless check, sometimes stepping into a square where their own queen hangs. This represents a fundamental oversight of free material rather than a complex tactical error.

137.label: Developing a bishop to a square where it is immediately vulnerable to a pawn fork or capture in the opening.
137.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake where a player develops their bishop (94% bishop moves) to a square that is tactically vulnerable, most commonly to a central pawn advance that creates a fork. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase (100%), and the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (38%) and fork (31%), with recurring tags like pawn_fork, central_pawn_advance, and opening_trap. The classic pattern is ...Be6 walking into d5 forking the bishop and a knight, or Be3 placing the bishop where it can be captured by an opponent's piece. The eval trajectory shows these are consequential mistakes—56% turn drawn positions into losing ones and 28% throw away winning positions, with a median loss of 331 centipawns. The material signature shows 33% of these moves directly hang the piece while 67% appear superficially safe but create devastating tactical vulnerabilities one move later. This represents a failure to account for the opponent's most natural central pawn thrust when choosing a development square for the bishop.

133.label: Player makes a quiet king or rook move while an opponent's rook hangs en prise to a minor piece or other attacker.
133.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a simple one-move capture of an undefended enemy rook. The material signature shows the player almost never captures anything (97% no capture) and instead moves their king (52%) or rook (23%) passively, while Maia's recommended move captures a rook 100% of the time—typically with a bishop or knight. The hanging_piece motif appears in every single position (100%), and the tactical summaries consistently describe scenarios where an opponent's rook sits completely undefended on a square attacked by the player's piece, yet the player makes an irrelevant move instead. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 39% convert a winning position into a losing one and 36% turn a win into a draw, with a median cost of 671 centipawns—roughly the value of the missed rook. The positions split evenly between middlegame and endgame, often featuring rook endgames or simplified positions where the hanging rook should be visually obvious. The 23% 'hangs' material outcome reflects cases where the quiet move itself drops material in return, compounding the error.

135.label: Player makes a slow or irrelevant move in the endgame while opponent's passed pawn advances to promotion.
135.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (78%) where the player makes a materially 'safe' move (91%) that nonetheless loses a median of 250 centipawns. The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (44%), tempo_loss (22%), and promotion_error (22%), indicating the player squanders critical tempi needed to stop or blockade an enemy passed pawn. The top boards consistently show advanced passed pawns (often on the 7th rank) where the player's piece abandons its restraining duty or the king wanders to an irrelevant square. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve rooks and bishops giving check (35%) to gain tempo against the promotion threat, confirming the player missed the urgency. The eval trajectory shows positions already deteriorating (39% losing→losing) but also 17% drawn→losing and 13% winning→losing, meaning the player often throws away a holdable or even winning position by ignoring the promotion race. The concrete examples—rook leaving blockade duty, king stepping onto a check diagonal enabling promotion with check, capturing a trivial pawn while the opponent queens—all reflect the same pattern: failing to prioritize the opponent's passed pawn in a critical endgame moment.

139.label: Moving the king in the opening instead of capturing/developing, permanently forfeiting castling rights and exposing the king.
139.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake where the player moves their king (100% king moves, 100% opening phase) instead of making the superior developing/capturing move identified by Maia (100% bishop captures knight). The material outcome is 'safe'—nothing is immediately hung—but the eval trajectory shows a median loss of ~198 centipawns, typically pushing drawn positions into losing ones or making already-losing positions significantly worse. The dominant motifs (king_safety 30%, tempo_loss 20%) and tags (king_trapped, development) confirm the positional nature: the king move forfeits castling rights, blocks piece development (especially bishops), and wastes critical tempo in the opening. The top activating boards vividly illustrate this with Ke7 moves that leave the king exposed on e7 while a strong knight sits on d6, when Bxd6 (or similar captures) would have addressed the threat while maintaining king safety. This is not a tactical blunder or material loss per se, but a positional catastrophe rooted in choosing a passive king retreat over an active piece interaction.

141.label: Player makes a natural-looking move while missing a forced checkmate (typically mate in 2) involving a queen delivery with check.
141.description: This feature fires when players overlook a forced checkmate, almost always mate in 2 or fewer moves. The three signals converge clearly: (1) The material/position signature shows Maia's best move is always a queen capture with check (queen 100%, captures pawn 100%, gives check 100%), while the player instead makes quiet or positionally-motivated moves (bishops, pawns, knights) that are often safe or involve exchanges — they're doing something 'reasonable' rather than delivering the killing blow. (2) The eval trajectory shows a catastrophic median loss of 9772 centipawns — consistent with missing a forced mate while remaining in a merely winning or even drawn position. The winning->winning 58% cases represent going from 'mate in N' to just 'large advantage.' (3) The Opus tactical analysis confirms this overwhelmingly: dominant motifs are king_safety (75%) and back_rank (25%), with tags including missed_mate(5), mate_in_2(3), queen_bishop_battery(4), and kingside_attack(3). The example summaries explicitly describe missed mate-in-2 sequences (Qxb6+ Ka8 Qb7#, Qxg6+ Qg7#) where batteries and back-rank weaknesses were already in place. Players consistently chose superficially active or defensive moves while the decisive queen check was available.

136.label: Misjudging passed pawn dynamics in simplified positions, either allowing blockade or trading into lost pawn endings.
136.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where players fatally misjudge positions involving passed pawns. The material signature shows checks (57%) and piece moves (rooks/knights) that often hang material or lose significantly (median net material -1.0), with a devastating eval cost (median 385cp lost) frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (29% winning->losing, 29% winning->drawn). The tactical analysis reveals the unifying thread: passed_pawn appears in 40% of motifs and 4/7 tagged positions, with errors including premature pawn advances that allow blockade (e7+ creating a permanent Ke8 blockade), catastrophic exchanges that create unstoppable enemy passers (Rxf7 enabling gxf7 passed pawn), and misjudged king activity in resulting pawn endgames. The concrete positions confirm late middlegame/endgame scenarios (71% middlegame, 29% endgame) where players make seemingly active moves—checks, exchanges, pawn pushes—that fundamentally misread how passed pawn dynamics will resolve, often because the 'threat is stronger than the execution' principle is violated or the opponent's king activity in simplified positions is underestimated.

142.label: Critical tempo errors in king-and-pawn endgames where the player wastes a move instead of capturing or advancing decisively.
142.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame mistakes where the player loses a critical tempo, typically costing 500+ centipawns. All positions are endgames (100%) with kings and pawns, and the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (27%), pawn_endgame (33%), and passed_pawn (27%). The player frequently moves a king or pawn passively—retreating, advancing the wrong pawn, or failing to capture an available pawn (Maia's recommended move captures a pawn 100% of the time)—when the position demands an immediate capture or the most direct path in a king race. The eval trajectory shows these errors convert drawn positions to lost ones or make losing positions hopeless (median 530cp lost), reflecting how in pure pawn endgames a single wasted tempo can decide whether a passed pawn promotes or a king arrives in time. The board positions consistently show razor-sharp king races with passed pawns on both sides where precise move order is everything.

140.label: Passive or misdirected moves that ignore critical king safety threats, allowing tactical exploitation via back-rank or kingside attacks.
140.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a seemingly safe or neutral move (49% safe, 73% no capture) — often with a rook, bishop, or king — while neglecting urgent king safety concerns. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), supplemented by fork threats (33%), and the tags highlight missed tactics, back-rank vulnerabilities, weakened kingside, and queen invasions. The eval trajectory shows a massive median cost of 283 centipawns, with many positions going from drawn to losing (14%) or from losing to deeply lost (19%). Maia's recommended moves are predominantly rook moves (65%) that address active defense or counterplay, often involving captures (33%). The top boards show exposed kings (e.g., kings on g7, h6, g6, open files) where the player's move fails to address the opponent's attacking resources — moving a piece passively or to the wrong square while the opponent has concrete threats against the king. The pattern is not a material blunder per se but a positional failure to prioritize king safety, allowing the opponent's initiative to become decisive.

145.label: Player makes a non-checking move that misses a powerful bishop check or discovered attack, losing significant material or positional advantage.
145.description: This feature fires when players miss a strong checking move involving a bishop (Maia's move is 100% bishop, giving check 100% of the time) and instead play passive or tempo-losing moves (pawns 26%, queens 26%, bishops 17%, knights 15%) that are overwhelmingly non-captures (91%). The missed winning material rate is 100%, confirming these are all cases where a forcing tactical blow was available but ignored. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: median loss of 356 centipawns, with 24% converting winning positions to drawn and 13% going from drawn to losing. The dominant motifs (king_safety 60%, tempo_loss 20%) and tags (missed_tactic, uncastled_king, open_lines_against_king) reveal the pattern: the opponent's king is vulnerable, a bishop check (often Bxf7+ or similar discovered/direct check) would exploit this decisively, but the player instead makes a routine developing or positional move (b3, Be3, O-O-O, Qf3) that squanders the tactical moment. The boards consistently show positions with exposed kings where a forcing bishop check would win material or deliver a mating attack.

146.label: Bishop captures or moves that release positional tension, allowing the opponent to win material or seize initiative.
146.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a bishop (56% of cases) in a way that releases critical positional tension, often capturing a pawn (48%) or making a non-capture that hangs material (30%). The median net material outcome is -2.0 with 70% of cases missing winning material, indicating these moves consistently overlook stronger tactical alternatives. The eval trajectory shows these are game-changing errors (median 313cp lost), frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (winning->drawn 26%, drawn->losing 22%, winning->losing 13%). The Opus analysis reveals the core pattern: positional_mistake (38%) and hanging_piece (38%) dominate, with tempo_loss and missed tactics as recurring tags. The concrete positions confirm this—multiple instances show bishops capturing on d4 in Italian Game structures where maintaining tension was critical, bishops exchanging themselves for lesser pieces or pawns while abandoning attacking prospects, and bishop moves that release pawn tension (like d5-d6 releasing a strategic outpost). The player trades positional pressure for immediate but insufficient material, failing to recognize that the tension itself was the source of their advantage.

144.label: Player makes a safe-looking developing or retreating move, wasting a critical tempo and missing a forcing tactical shot that would have maintained or extended a winning advantage.
144.description: This feature captures positions where the player holds a winning advantage but squanders it by playing a move that appears safe or natural (often a king move, queen recapture, or knight development) while missing a forcing tactic—typically involving a check, discovered attack, or piece activity surge. The material signature shows the played moves are mostly 'safe' (no immediate material loss) yet Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve pawn advances or queen moves that deliver check (100% check rate). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions that remain technically winning but hemorrhage enormous centipawn value (median ~9487cp loss, indicating missed mates or decisive combinations). The recurring tags—tempo_loss (appearing in all examples), missed_tactic, king_safety, and piece_activity—reveal the common thread: the player had a narrow critical moment requiring the one forcing continuation but instead made a passive or misdirected move, losing the initiative and allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape. Examples include walking the king into a pawn storm (Kh7), recapturing a piece instead of delivering a winning check (Qg7+), and developing a knight instead of exploiting a tactical shot (Nxb5+).

143.label: Trading knights on a central square that exposes the player to a devastating fork or tactical blow.
143.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player recaptures (or initiates a trade of) a knight on a central square (e5 or d5), achieving material equality in the immediate exchange but catastrophically overlooking a resulting fork or tactical shot. The material signature shows 100% knight captures resulting in trades (net 0 material), yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 343 centipawns with 88% of cases going from drawn to losing — indicating the trade itself is not the blunder but rather what it permits. The top boards almost exclusively show ...Nxe5 or ...Nxd5 recaptures in standard opening structures (Philidor, French, Slav setups) where a white knight has planted on e5/d5. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'fork' (54%), meaning the recapture allows a devastating fork (often a pawn fork on d4/c4/f4 winning a piece back with interest, or a discovered attack). The phase is overwhelmingly opening (82%), consistent with premature simplification on outpost squares before the position is ready. Players are lured by the natural-looking recapture but miss that the resulting structure or piece placement permits a tactical blow that wins material.

147.label: Premature Bxf7+ sacrifice in the opening that lacks sufficient tactical follow-up, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
147.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening mistake: the player sacrifices a bishop on f7 (or f2 from Black's side) with check, capturing a pawn but losing a full piece without adequate compensation. All 12 top-activating positions show a bishop moving to f7/f2 with check (bishop moved 100%, pawn captured 100%, check given 100%), resulting in a net material loss of approximately 2 pawns (piece for pawn). The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 373cp lost), confirming these are not sound sacrifices. The tactical analysis tags (unsound_sacrifice, insufficient_compensation, premature_attack) and king_safety motif (100%) reveal the positional error: players attempt a pseudo-Fried Liver or Greek Gift style attack in the opening, but the position lacks the necessary piece coordination (undeveloped pieces, closed center, no follow-up threats) to justify the material investment. The opponent simply captures and consolidates, leaving the sacrificing side down a full minor piece with no attack.

152.label: Player makes a safe-looking move while ignoring an opponent's undefended piece that could be captured for free.
152.description: This feature fires when a player makes a materially 'safe' move (no material is lost immediately—net material median 0.0) but misses a clear tactical opportunity to win hanging material. The dominant motif is overwhelmingly hanging_piece (85%), and the tags consistently reference missed_tactic, hanging_piece, and missed_queen_capture. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve capturing major pieces (queen 67%, rook 33%), confirming that the opponent had undefended or inadequately defended high-value pieces available for capture. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 385 centipawns—often converting a winning position into something drawn or even losing (winning->losing 33%, winning->drawn 33%)—consistent with squandering a full rook or more of advantage. The board positions confirm the pattern: players develop pieces, reposition knights, or make reflexive recaptures while a free queen or rook sits undefended elsewhere on the board. The common thread is 'tunnel vision'—the player focuses on their own plan (development, tempo, recapture reflex) and completely overlooks that the opponent has left a piece en prise.

151.label: Queen moves that fail to give a critical check, allowing the opponent to deliver checkmate or seize a decisive advantage.
151.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their queen (76% of activations) but crucially fails to deliver check, while Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100% Maia check rate vs 0% player check rate). The positions are predominantly middlegame/endgame scenarios involving exposed kings (king_safety 45%, exposed_king tags) where perpetual check or forcing sequences were available as defensive resources. The median eval loss of 420 centipawns confirms these are catastrophic oversights—often turning drawable positions into losses (drawn->losing 17%) or allowing immediate checkmate (forced_mate tag appears 3 times). The material signature shows 79% non-captures with 31% hanging the queen outright, consistent with quiet queen moves that ignore the urgency of the position. The tactical summaries repeatedly describe scenarios where the player's queen retreats passively or makes a non-checking move, forfeiting perpetual check opportunities or walking into mating nets. The core error is choosing a queen move that neglects a critical checking resource that was the only way to maintain the balance or survive.

148.label: Retreating or misplacing a knight in the opening, abandoning a strong central post and hanging material.
148.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake where a player moves their knight away from a powerful central square (e4 is the most common), either retreating it or redirecting it to an inferior square. The material signature shows knight moves that result in hanging a piece or losing material (median -1.0 pawns), with 100% of cases missing winning material that was available. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—positions swing from winning or drawn into losing, with a median loss of 349 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying pattern: the knight abandonment leaves pieces undefended (hanging_piece 44%), compromises king safety (33%), and loses tempo (11%). Tags like 'king_in_center', 'undefended_knight', and 'opening_blunder' confirm these are early-game decisions where the player either retreats a well-placed knight (e4→f6, e4→d6) or makes a speculative knight move (e4→f2, e4→g5) that loses the initiative and exposes tactical vulnerabilities. The positions consistently show Italian Game or similar e4-e5 structures where Black's knight on e4 was a dominant piece, and moving it away concedes the center and allows White's pieces (especially Bc4, Re1, Nf3) to exploit the resulting weaknesses.

149.label: Rook moves to a passive square, abandoning active defense or attack and allowing back-rank or tactical exploitation.
149.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a rook (64% of cases) to a passive or aimless square, typically in endgames or simplified middlegames. The material signature shows these are safe moves (86% nothing hangs immediately), yet the median eval cost is 257 centipawns—indicating a severe positional or tactical concession despite no immediate material loss. The trajectory confirms these are often game-turning errors: winning→drawn (21%) or winning→winning but with massive advantage squandered (29%), consistent with throwing away a won position through passivity. The Opus analysis reveals the underlying motifs: back-rank vulnerabilities exposed by moving the rook away from defensive duties (Re3 leaving e1 unguarded), tempo loss (rook retreats that cede initiative), missed tactics (failing to play the one active rook move like Rxb2), and skewer/pin vulnerabilities created by rook repositioning (Nc7 allowing Rb8+ skewer). The boards consistently show rook endgames or simplified positions where one precise rook move was required, but instead the player chose a quiet, passive rook move that either abandoned a critical file/rank or allowed a devastating tactical reply.

150.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move that neglects urgent king safety issues, missing a tactical resource involving checks or attacks on the exposed king.
150.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions (88%) where the player makes a move that is materially 'safe' in isolation (72% safe moves, no captures 73%) but catastrophically misses a tactical opportunity or defensive necessity related to king safety and hanging pieces. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (50%), with tags highlighting exposed kings, missed intermezzos, and missed tactics. The median eval loss of 297 centipawns confirms these are severe mistakes. Critically, Maia's suggested moves frequently involve checks (20%) and captures (67% capture something), meaning the correct move exploited forcing sequences—especially checks against exposed kings—to win material or save the game. The player instead plays a non-forcing, non-capturing move (often a bishop, rook, or pawn repositioning) that ignores the tactical urgency of the position, failing to exploit or defend against king vulnerability. The trajectory shows roughly even distribution across all eval categories, indicating these aren't positional subtleties but missed concrete tactics that punish across all game states.

153.label: Developing a minor piece to a passive or purposeless square in the opening, ignoring concrete tactical threats and losing critical tempi.
153.description: This feature identifies opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where a player develops a bishop (45%), pawn (30%), or knight (25%) to a square that ignores an existing tactical threat, resulting in a position swing from drawn to losing (90% of cases) with a median loss of 322 centipawns. The material signature shows that 50% of these moves hang a piece while 95% are non-captures, meaning the player makes a quiet developing move while missing that an opponent's tactical shot (usually a pawn capture worth material, as Maia's response captures a pawn 95% of the time) is available. The Opus analysis confirms motifs of hanging_piece (33%), tempo_loss (22%), and positional_mistake (22%), with recurring tags of development, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic. The concrete positions show patterns like Bb2 ignoring dxc3 winning a piece, Bb5+ wasting two tempi, and Nf3 walking into a discovered attack on the f-pawn—all cases where a natural-looking developing move overlooks that the opponent has a concrete tactical resource exploiting the player's previous commitments.

155.label: Player ignores an available queen capture while already losing, allowing the position to deteriorate further.
155.description: This feature fires when a player who is already in a losing position fails to capture an opponent's queen that is available for taking. The material/position signature shows that Maia's recommended move captures a queen in 100% of cases, confirming the queen is consistently available for capture. The player instead makes a 'safe' or 'hanging' move with a knight, rook, pawn, or king—never capturing anything. The eval trajectory shows all cases go from losing to more losing (median 185cp lost), indicating this isn't about throwing a winning position but rather failing to find the one defensive resource that limits damage. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'queen_capture_missed' and 'hanging_piece' as dominant motifs, and multiple example summaries explicitly describe failing to take an undefended or capturable queen. The positions are concentrated in the opening and middlegame phases where the opponent's queen is aggressively placed (often on unusual squares like g6, d7, g3, d1) and the player overlooks the capture in favor of a routine or panicked move.

154.label: Advancing a passed pawn one square too early, allowing the opponent to win the pawn or neutralize the promotion with tempo-gaining tactics.
154.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake: pushing a passed pawn toward promotion prematurely, when the opponent has a tactical resource (typically a check, rook interposition, or king maneuver) that gains the tempo needed to stop or capture the pawn. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures, occurring 78% in endgames, where 40% of moves hang the pawn outright. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (46%) and passed_pawn (31%), and Maia's recommended responses frequently involve the king (52%) or rook (30%) — consistent with the opponent exploiting tempo to catch the pawn. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 171 centipawns, with many cases converting wins to draws or drawn positions to losses (winning->drawn 18%, drawn->losing 12%). The top boards consistently show pawns on the 2nd/7th rank being pushed to the promotion square one move too soon, where an intermezzo check or rook swing neutralizes the threat. Tags like tempo_loss (9 occurrences) and missed_tactic (7) confirm the player misjudges the race and fails to recognize the opponent's intermediate resource.

158.label: Player moves a piece passively when the opponent's best reply was to trade queens, squandering a significant positional or material advantage.
158.description: This feature detects middlegame positions where the player makes a 'safe' (non-capturing, non-hanging) move—most often retreating or repositioning a queen, king, or major piece—while missing that the opponent's strongest continuation (Maia's move is queen-takes-queen in 100% of cases) would have involved a queen trade that the player should have either forced on favorable terms or avoided by maintaining tension. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 273 centipawns, with 50% of cases going from winning to still-winning but with a dramatically reduced advantage, consistent with squandering a dominant position. The tactical motifs are uniformly 'positional_mistake' with tags like simplification_error, queen_trade_misjudgment, and open_file_dominance_squandered—indicating the player either allowed or invited a queen exchange under unfavorable structural conditions, or retreated when maintaining the queen's active placement was critical. The boards confirm complex middlegame positions where the queen was the linchpin of the attack, and the player's passive move enabled a simplifying trade that collapsed their advantage.

156.label: King moves to wrong square in lost endgame, allowing forced mate or decisive promotion.
156.description: This feature detects king moves in endgame positions that catastrophically worsen an already losing situation. The material signature shows the player always moves their king (100%), makes no capture, and the move appears 'safe' in immediate material terms—yet misses a knight capture that Maia identifies (100% missed winning material). The eval trajectory confirms these are losing positions that become catastrophically worse (median 9251cp loss), typically converting a slow loss into forced mate. The positional analysis reveals the dominant context: passed pawn endgames (45%) where precise king placement is critical, with fork motifs (18%) indicating the king often steps into tactical patterns. The boards confirm king-and-pawn endgames with advanced passed pawns where the king retreats or sidesteps to the wrong square, missing the only defensive resource (often capturing a knight or blocking a promotion path). The common tags—tempo_loss, piece_activity, passed_pawn—reinforce that these are king moves that lose a critical tempo in races to promote or stop enemy pawns.

157.label: Queen captures a defended pawn in the opening, leaving the queen hanging or trapped.
157.description: This feature fires on early-game queen sorties that greedily capture a pawn only to lose the queen. The material signature shows queen moves capturing pawns with a catastrophic net loss (median -8.0, i.e., losing the queen), confirming these are not equal trades but outright blunders. The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (median 618cp lost), indicating a position that was otherwise balanced is destroyed by one impulsive capture. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' — the queen lands on a square where it is captured by a defender the player overlooked. Tags like 'early_queen_development', 'pawn_grab_punished', and 'tempo_loss' reinforce the classic pattern: bringing the queen out early to snatch a pawn, failing to verify whether the target is defended (e.g., by a rook on an open file or a bishop along a diagonal), and immediately losing the queen. The concrete board examples show exactly this — Qh5 walking into an h-file rook, Ba6 captured by a defending piece — all in the first few moves of the game.

160.label: Player makes a passive move instead of playing a pawn fork that wins material by simultaneously attacking two pieces.
160.description: This feature fires when players miss a winning pawn fork, overwhelmingly in middlegame and endgame positions. The material/position signature shows that the player's actual moves are mostly safe but passive (pawn 40%, knight 30%, rook 20%), while Maia's recommended moves consistently involve checks (100% check rate) with pawns or knights. The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the median eval loss of 221 centipawns confirms these are costly oversights. The tactical analysis is dominated by fork motifs (75%), with 'pawn_fork' and 'missed_tactic' as the most common tags. The top activating positions are strikingly similar—many share the exact same tactical theme of ...f5+ forking a king and rook on adjacent diagonals. The trajectory (winning->winning 50%, losing->winning 30%) shows these opportunities arise across various evaluation states, but the player consistently fails to execute the decisive blow, instead making quiet developing or prophylactic moves that squander a significant tactical opportunity.

163.label: Trading queens in a pawn endgame that allows an unstoppable passed pawn promotion.
163.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame error: the player voluntarily trades queens (75% queen moves, 75% capturing a queen, 100% with check) in positions where the queen was the only piece preventing a passed pawn from promoting. The boards are universally late endgames with advanced passed pawns (tags: passed_pawn 12x, pawn_promotion 3x, queen_trade_error 3x). The material signature shows 'trade' (75%) because the queen exchange is roughly equal in piece value, but the positional consequence is catastrophic—median eval loss of 529cp, with trajectories going from drawn->losing (50%) or making a losing position decisively worse (50%). The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the same pattern: the queen provided perpetual check threats or blockade capabilities that were the sole drawing resource, and once queens leave the board, the opponent's king activates to escort a passed pawn to promotion. The concrete positions confirm this—nearly all feature a far-advanced pawn (7th rank) with the queen trade immediately enabling its unstoppable advance.

162.label: Player captures material instead of delivering a forced checkmate sequence.
162.description: This feature fires when a player has a forced checkmate available but instead plays a materially 'safe' capture—typically taking a rook or trading pieces—driven by material greed rather than calculating the mating attack. The SEE signature shows the player capturing a rook (100%) with the move assessed as 'safe' materially, yet missing winning material (100%), indicating they chose a materially sound but tactically inferior move over a decisive mating continuation. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic missed wins (median 9530 centipawns lost), consistent with converting a checkmate-in-N into merely a winning or unclear position. The tactical analysis tags overwhelmingly point to material_greed, back_rank_mate, missed_checkmate, and one_move_mate—the player sees a hanging piece or available capture and reflexively takes it, ignoring that the opponent's king is trapped (often on the back rank by its own pawns) and a forced mate existed. Maia's recommended moves (giving check 100%) confirm that the correct continuation involved checking sequences leading to mate rather than the greedy capture chosen.

159.label: Moving a rook to a square where it becomes trapped, forked, or fatally exposed on the back rank.
159.description: This feature fires on moves—predominantly rook moves (42%) and queen moves (26%)—that appear safe on the surface (68% 'safe' material outcome) but walk into devastating tactical refutations. The median eval loss of 454 centipawns confirms these are game-changing blunders, not minor inaccuracies. The dominant motifs (back_rank 30%, fork 20%, trapped_piece 10%) reveal the recurring pattern: the player repositions a major piece (usually a rook) to a square that looks active or purposeful, but overlooks that the destination square is tactically poisoned—either allowing a back-rank mate, a knight/bishop fork picking up the piece, or leaving the rook with no escape squares. The concrete positions confirm this: Ra1 walks into a trapping pattern, Rc1 allows a knight fork on e2, Rxd2 removes a back-rank guard. Maia's preferred moves (king 37%, rook 21%) suggest the engine often wants to address king safety or keep the rook on its current strong square rather than rerouting it. The 47% missed-winning-material rate and the spread of trajectory outcomes (winning->losing 16%, drawn->losing 16%) show these are moments where the player had reasonable or even winning positions but self-destructed by placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square without calculating the opponent's forcing replies.

165.label: Moving a piece or pawn to a square where it (or another piece) is left undefended and immediately capturable.
165.description: This feature fires on moves that leave a piece hanging, costing substantial material (median -6.0 pawns, with 89% of moves classified as 'hangs'). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (93%), and the tactical analysis consistently shows pieces moved to squares attacked by opponent pieces, resulting in immediate capture. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic blunders—33% turn winning positions into losing ones, 22% turn wins into draws—with a median loss of 456 centipawns. The pattern spans opening (56%) and middlegame (44%) phases, where the player makes a developing or repositioning move without noticing the opponent's tactical threat. The top boards illustrate this clearly: queens moved to knight-attacked squares, bishops developed to undefended diagonals, and pawns pushed while leaving major pieces en prise. Maia's suggested moves (capturing bishop 44%, knight 22%, rook 11%, queen 11%) confirm the opponent had an immediate winning capture available in nearly every case.

161.label: Playing a knight check in a won endgame instead of capturing a critical pawn, squandering a decisive advantage.
161.description: This feature captures a specific endgame mistake where a player delivers a knight check (knight moved 100%, check given 100%) that is materially 'safe' (nothing is immediately lost) but catastrophically wastes tempo in a position that required precise pawn-related play. The eval trajectory shows these checks convert winning positions into draws or losses (median 1049cp lost), indicating the player had a decisive advantage that evaporated. Maia consistently recommends capturing a pawn with the knight instead (Maia captures pawn 100%, no check), revealing that the correct move was a simple material/structural gain rather than a flashy check. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: dominant motifs include passed pawns (31%), hanging pieces (31%), and tempo loss (8%), with 'tempo_loss' being the most frequent tag (9 occurrences). The board positions are all deep endgames with sparse material where one tempo or one pawn decides the game. The player repeatedly chooses an attention-grabbing knight check over the prosaic but winning pawn capture, fatally disrupting their own pawn promotion plans or allowing the opponent to activate/escape.

166.label: In endgames with passed pawns, player fails to give a critical rook check that would gain tempo or stop promotion.
166.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (95% endgame phase) where the player moves a rook (52%), king (28%), or pawn (16%) but critically fails to deliver a check—Maia's recommended move is always a rook move (100%) that gives check (100%). The missed check costs a median of 228 centipawns, often converting drawn positions to losing ones (15%) or accelerating losses (30%). The dominant motifs are passed pawns (38%) and promotion errors (25%), indicating the check was needed to gain tempo against an advancing passer or to prevent/force promotion. The boards confirm rook endgames with advanced pawns where a well-timed rook check would either blockade a pawn, gain a crucial tempo, or activate the king. Instead, players make 'safe' moves (74%) that appear reasonable but surrender the initiative at the decisive moment, allowing the opponent's passed pawn to advance unimpeded or the opponent's king to reach a winning square.

168.label: Knight moved to an undefended square in the opening, immediately dropping material.
168.description: This feature captures a specific recurring opening blunder where a player moves their knight (100% knight moves) to an undefended or tactically vulnerable square, resulting in the piece being hung (60% hangs, median -3.0 material loss, consistent with losing a full minor piece). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions to losing (60%) or winning positions to drawn (40%), with a median cost of 286 centipawns—indicating a serious tactical oversight rather than a subtle positional error. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (62%), with tempo_loss (25%) reflecting that these knight moves often appear aggressive or 'tricky' but ignore immediate threats or leave the knight en prise. All positions occur in the opening phase (100%), and the concrete examples show knights lunging to squares like f4, e5, g5, d5, h5, or b4 where they can be immediately captured by pawns or minor pieces. The player misjudges the forcing nature of their knight move, overlooking that the destination square is undefended and accessible to the opponent's pieces.

169.label: Moving a bishop to a long diagonal square where it is immediately capturable for free in the opening.
169.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder where a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) to an aggressive-looking but completely undefended square—typically along a long diagonal to h3, h6, or a6/a3—where it is immediately captured by an opposing bishop that already controls that diagonal. The material signature confirms these are non-captures that hang a piece (100% hangs, median -3.0 pawns = a full minor piece). The eval trajectory shows these uniformly turn drawn positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 544cp loss). The top boards reveal the concrete pattern: Bc8-h3 walking into Bf1xh3, Bc1-h6 into Bg7xh6, or Bf1-a6 into Bb7xa6—all in the opening phase (100% opening). The bishops are placed on squares that look active but are tactically refuted by an opposing bishop already aimed at that exact square, resulting in an immediate free piece capture with no compensation.

164.label: Player makes a developing or repositioning move that ignores critical central tension, allowing the opponent to seize material or positional advantage.
164.description: This feature fires on moves where a player develops or repositions a piece (bishops 33%, knights 17%, rooks 17%) while neglecting urgent central or tactical demands. The material signature shows that 50% of these moves hang a piece and the median net material is -1.0, indicating the player loses material not through a direct tactical oversight like a one-move blunder, but by playing a move that looks reasonable developmentally while ignoring the concrete tension on the board. The dominant tags — tempo_loss (appearing twice), central_tension_ignored, and premature_development — confirm that the core error is prioritizing piece placement over resolving immediate pawn or piece conflicts in the center. The eval trajectory (winning→drawn at 230cp median loss) shows these are positions where the player had an advantage but squandered it by failing to address the critical moment. Maia's suggested moves (100% pawn moves, often captures) reveal that the correct response was typically a concrete pawn action resolving central tension, not further development. The board positions consistently show rich central pawn structures (e4/d4/e5/d5 complexes) where the player chose a quiet piece move instead of the forcing pawn break or capture that was required.

170.label: Playing a showy check with a minor piece that abandons a winning attack or hangs material.
170.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers check (100% of activations) with a knight or bishop (94% combined), but the move is tactically disastrous—hanging the piece 47% of the time with a median material loss of 2.0 and a median eval cost of 269 centipawns. The dominant motifs (king_safety, back_rank, tempo_loss, trapped_piece) and tags (missed_tactic, missed_mate) reveal that the player had a much stronger continuation available—often a forced mate or decisive attack—but was seduced by the superficially forcing nature of a check. The Opus analyses confirm the pattern: checks that 'look forcing but achieve nothing constructive,' abandoning beautifully placed pieces or back-rank combinations for an aimless check that loses tempo and material. The eval trajectory shows 63% missed winning material, with many positions going from winning to drawn or drawn to losing, indicating these aren't desperate last-resort checks but rather impulsive moves that squander real advantages. This is the classic amateur trap of 'always check, it might be mate'—prioritizing the forcing appearance of a check over calculating whether it actually accomplishes anything.

167.label: Player makes a quiet or greedy move while missing that the opponent's queen delivers a critical check or perpetual, often costing the game.
167.description: This feature identifies positions where the player (across middlegame and endgame) makes a move—often a pawn push, king move, or greedy queen capture—while completely ignoring a queen check that was available or needed to be addressed. The material signature shows Maia recommending a queen move with check 100% of the time, yet the player never plays a check themselves. The 'missed winning material' rate is 100%, and the median centipawn loss is enormous (410cp), with trajectories showing drawn positions collapsing to losses or wins evaporating to draws. The dominant motifs are king_safety (71%) and tempo_loss (29%), with recurring tags like exposed_king, missed_perpetual, and checkmate_in_one. The concrete positions confirm this: players push pawns or capture material greedily (e.g., Qxg7 grabbing a pawn instead of maintaining perpetual check, or making quiet king/pawn moves while a forced checking sequence wins or draws). The core error is a failure to recognize the urgency of queen checks—either delivering them for perpetual/checkmate or defending against the opponent's checking motifs—resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings.

174.label: Player moves queen (or blocks a diagonal) to a square where it hangs to an enemy bishop along an unobstructed diagonal.
174.description: This feature fires on positions where the player places their queen on a square that is undefended along an open diagonal, allowing the opponent's bishop to simply capture it. The material signature is stark: 94% of moves are non-captures that hang a piece, with a median material loss of -6.0 (approximately queen value), and queens are the most commonly moved piece (47%). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings—32% go from drawn to losing and the median centipawn loss is 495, consistent with losing a queen for nothing or near-nothing. The Opus tactical analysis confirms this with 100% 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, supplemented by 'diagonal_oversight' and 'undefended_queen' tags. The top activating boards repeatedly show queens landing on squares (especially h3) that sit on open diagonals leading directly to enemy bishops (e.g., Qh3 hanging to a bishop on e6 via the d7-h3 diagonal). This is a pure one-move tactical oversight in the opening or early middlegame where the player fails to notice a bishop's line of attack on the queen's destination square.

173.label: Player makes a routine developing or repositioning move instead of executing a winning tactical strike.
173.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing piece move (92% safe, 100% no capture) — typically with a knight, rook, or queen — while a decisive tactical opportunity goes unexploited. The Maia reference consistently recommends a knight capture (100% knight, 97% capturing a pawn), revealing that the engine saw a concrete knight tactic (fork, exploitation of geometry) that the player overlooked. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly missed wins: 47% go from winning to drawn and 13% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 300 centipawns. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant motifs of tempo_loss (43%) and missed_tactic (29%), plus recurring tags like missed_tactic, knight_fork, and concrete_over_general. The boards consistently show middlegame positions (79%) where the player chose a natural-looking developing or consolidating move (Bg5, Rc1, Na4, Rf1) instead of a crushing tactical blow — often Nxd5 or Nxb5 — that would have won material through forks or geometric exploits. This is not a positional misjudgment but a failure to calculate a concrete tactical shot, defaulting to routine play at a critical moment.

172.label: Giving a futile queen check in the endgame that allows the opponent to improve their position or force a winning simplification.
172.description: This feature fires on queen checks in endgame positions (90% endgame) that serve no constructive purpose. The player always moves their queen (100%) and always delivers check (100%), yet the best move according to Maia was typically a quiet pawn advance or king move (pawn 70%, king 10%) rather than a check. The tactical analysis repeatedly identifies 'pointless_check' and 'tempo_loss' as dominant tags, with the checks either improving the opponent's king placement, allowing a lethal interposition that forces a queen trade into a lost pawn endgame, or creating tactical vulnerabilities like forks. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 353 centipawns, with positions going from winning-to-losing (20%), winning-to-drawn (20%), or drawn-to-losing (30%). The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (60%) — nothing is immediately captured or lost — but the positional damage is severe. The pattern is a player reflexively giving check without calculating the consequences, particularly failing to recognize that keeping queens on the board or making a quiet improving move was essential to maintaining their position in the endgame.

171.label: In endgame positions, the player makes a move that ignores an immediate tactical threat (hanging piece or missed capture with check), losing decisive material through a fatal move-order or tempo error.
171.description: This feature captures a specific endgame mistake pattern where the player, in a winning or drawn position, makes a move that completely ignores the most urgent tactical demand of the position. All positions are endgames (100%), and the median eval loss is a catastrophic 1375 centipawns, often converting wins into losses (40% winning->losing, 20% drawn->losing). The material signature shows 60% of moves simply hang material—these aren't trades or complex sacrifices but rather moves that leave pieces undefended (hanging_piece appears in 67% of motifs). The dominant tags (tempo_loss at 9 occurrences, hanging_piece at 4, move_order at 2) reveal the core pattern: the player makes a move that is plausible in isolation (developing a knight, pushing a pawn, capturing a low-value target) but catastrophically ignores either an attacked piece, a capture-with-check opportunity, or a forced sequence the opponent has. The Maia analysis confirms this—the correct move was almost always a queen move (80%) capturing high-value material (queen 60%, rook 40%) with check (100%), meaning the player missed a forcing tactical shot that was both urgent and winning. Examples like playing Qxg2 instead of Qxd7+ or moving a knight while leaving the queen en prise perfectly illustrate this tempo-blindness in simplified positions.

175.label: Player makes a non-critical move while missing a strong rook maneuver that exploits king safety or hangs material.
175.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a knight, pawn, or minor piece (often hanging it—43% hangs) while the engine strongly recommends a rook move (Maia plays rook 82% of the time). The missed winning material rate is 100%, with a median cost of 251 centipawns, indicating these are serious tactical oversights. The dominant motifs are king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (50%), suggesting the correct rook move typically either defends the king, activates along a rank/file to exploit the opponent's king weakness, or picks up a hanging piece. The eval trajectory shows positions transitioning from drawn to losing (18%) or remaining losing (18%), meaning these errors either throw away a holdable position or accelerate collapse. The player appears distracted by local piece maneuvers (knight repositioning, pawn pushes) while missing the critical rook lift, rook swing, or rook activation that addresses the most urgent feature of the position—often a vulnerable king or an undefended piece that a rook can target along an open line.

176.label: Squandering a winning position by making a non-urgent rook or pawn move instead of the decisive active continuation.
176.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a winning advantage (median eval lost: 255 centipawns, with 67% winning->drawn trajectory) but throws it away by playing a passive, non-urgent move—typically a rook retreat/sidestep (67%) or a slow pawn push (33%)—rather than executing the critical tactical or active continuation. The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' (nothing is immediately hung or traded), which is precisely the problem: the player avoids risk but squanders a decisive advantage. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss and passed_pawn issues, with positions frequently involving rook endgames or advanced passed pawns where one precise move would convert. The Opus analyses consistently describe scenarios where the winning move required immediate decisive action (exploiting a pin, activating the queen, pushing a passed pawn) but the player instead made a quiet, aimless move that allowed the opponent to reorganize or find perpetual check resources. The positions are predominantly middlegame-to-endgame transitions where concrete calculation was needed rather than general moves.

179.label: Capturing a piece while fatally ignoring an unstoppable passed pawn in the endgame.
179.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a materially 'safe' capture (most often a knight taking a bishop) but catastrophically misallocates tempo away from the critical task of stopping or racing a passed pawn. The material signature shows 100% bishop captures that are objectively safe (median net +3.0 material), yet the eval trajectory reveals these moves swing the position by a median of 505 centipawns—typically from drawn to losing (67%) or even winning to losing (33%). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is passed pawns (88%), with tempo_loss and promotion_error as recurring tags. The concrete pattern across boards is consistent: the player grabs material (a bishop on a2, a bishop on d2, a piece off the board) while an enemy passed pawn on the 6th or 7th rank advances to promotion unimpeded. The correct moves universally involve king activity toward the pawn or direct blockade rather than the tempting capture. This is a classic endgame pattern-recognition failure where short-term material gain is irrelevant compared to pawn promotion tempo.

177.label: Premature piece exchange in the opening that concedes positional compensation (central pawns, tempo, or exposes hanging pieces).
177.description: This feature fires on opening-phase trades (92% opening) where a bishop or knight captures an enemy piece (77% capturing knights) in what appears materially equal (92% trade, median net 0.0), but the exchange is strategically catastrophic—costing a median of 300 centipawns in evaluation. The dominant pattern is a player initiating a piece exchange without accounting for the positional consequences: after the recapture, the opponent gains a powerful central pawn (e.g., exd5 cramping the position), wins tempo against an exposed piece, or reveals an undefended piece left behind (38% hanging_piece motif). Maia's preferred moves (77% non-captures) confirm the engine wanted to delay or avoid the exchange entirely. The eval trajectory shows these trades frequently turn drawn or winning positions into losing ones (winning->losing 23%, drawn->losing 31%), indicating the player threw away their position by exchanging at the wrong moment. Tags like king_safety, center_control, and ignored_threat reinforce that these trades overlook broader positional factors in favor of a superficially 'equal' swap.

181.label: Queen captures a promoting pawn with check but loses the queen or allows a draw in a won endgame.
181.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player uses their queen to capture a pawn (often a passed pawn near promotion) with check, but this move actually loses massive material (median -8.0, consistent with losing the queen). The boards consistently show positions with advanced passed pawns on the 7th rank (a7, b7, h7, g7) where the opponent has a promotion threat. The player's queen captures the pawn with check, but this either allows the opponent to promote anyway, results in a stalemate/draw, or the queen is lost to a discovered attack or skewer after the king moves. The eval trajectory confirms this costs ~534 centipawns on average, often converting a winning position into a draw. The tactical motifs (promotion_error, passed_pawn, tempo_loss) and the Opus analysis confirm that these are cases where the queen—the strongest piece—is sacrificed or trapped by capturing a promotion-square pawn, when better moves (typically quiet king moves or rook maneuvers) would maintain the win. The pattern is a reflexive 'stop the pawn' capture that backfires catastrophically in the endgame.

178.label: In rook endgames, playing purposeless rook moves (often pointless checks) that waste critical tempo needed to address passed pawns.
178.description: This feature captures a highly specific rook endgame mistake pattern. The material/position signature shows the player almost exclusively moves a rook (89%) without capturing anything, and the move is technically 'safe' (89% don't immediately hang material), yet 78% of the time a winning tactic was missed. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 366 centipawns, with positions shifting from winning to drawn/losing or from losing to completely lost. The tactical analysis reveals the core mechanism: tempo_loss (42%) and passed_pawn (42%) are co-dominant motifs, with tags like 'pointless_check' and 'piece_activity' reinforcing the picture. The player moves their rook to an irrelevant square—often giving a meaningless check that improves the opponent's king—when the critical task was to blockade, attack, or race against passed pawns. The Opus summaries explicitly describe 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' errors and rooks drifting away from the key defensive or offensive axis. All 12 positions are pure rook endgames (100% endgame phase), confirming this is a specialized pattern of wasting tempo with aimless rook activity when passed pawn dynamics demand precise timing.

182.label: In the opening, a minor piece is left hanging due to overlooking a simple tactical threat.
182.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening-phase blunder (91% opening) where the player moves a minor piece (bishop 39%, knight 27%) or pawn (20%) without noticing that it leaves material hanging (36% hangs outcome). The eval trajectory is devastating: 68% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 371 centipawns—consistent with dropping a full piece. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 50%, king_safety 38%, fork 12%) and tags (missed_tactic, hanging_piece, ignored_threat) confirm that the player simply overlooks an existing or newly-created threat to their own piece. Maia's recommended moves (77% bishop captures, 23% bishop moves, often with check) reveal that the correct response was almost always to capture an opponent's piece or address the threat directly. The example summaries reinforce this: a bishop left en prise to a pawn, a pawn push leaving pieces tactically vulnerable, or an aggressive-looking knight move that actually drops material. These are not complex sacrifices or positional errors—they are straightforward cases of failing to notice a hanging piece in a developing position.

185.label: Developing the bishop to a square that leaves a pawn undefended, allowing immediate capture.
185.description: This feature fires on a specific recurring opening mistake where a player develops their bishop (100% bishop moves) to a square that inadvertently leaves a pawn hanging (material outcome: hangs 100%, median net material -1.0). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 285cp lost), indicating a significant blunder rather than a minor inaccuracy. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (46%) and tempo_loss (15%), with common tags including undefended_pawn and missed_tactic. The top activating positions overwhelmingly show French Defense structures where Be3 (or Bd2) leaves the b2 pawn undefended while a black queen on b6 is perfectly positioned to capture it. Maia's recommended response is consistently a pawn capture (pawn 100%, captures pawn 100%), confirming the opponent immediately wins the hanging pawn. This is a pattern of premature bishop development in the opening that neglects concrete pawn defense duties.

180.label: Giving a check with the queen that hangs it immediately, squandering material or a winning position.
180.description: All three signals converge on a single recurring blunder: the player delivers a queen check (queen moved 92%, check given 100%) that hangs the queen outright (hangs 100%, median net material lost -5.0, i.e., roughly a queen's value). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors—median 677 centipawns lost—often converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones. The Opus tactical summaries reinforce this: players place the queen on an aggressive-looking checking square without noticing the queen can simply be captured (e.g., 'Qh1+ simply loses the queen for nothing,' 'on f3, the queen can be captured by Black's queen'). Maia's recommended alternatives are typically quiet moves (rook moves, non-captures) that maintain material and positional advantage, showing the check was unnecessary. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece, king_safety, tempo_loss—describe a player seduced by the forcing nature of a check who overlooks that the queen lands on an undefended square visible to an opposing piece. This is not a trade or exchange; no opposing piece is captured. It is a pure tactical oversight where the allure of giving check blinds the player to an elementary hanging-queen refutation.

184.label: Passive or premature pawn moves in simplified positions that squander a winning or drawn advantage.
184.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame mistakes where the player pushes or moves a pawn (75% pawn moves) in a simplified position, throwing away a winning or drawn game. The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% go from winning to drawn, 25% from drawn to losing, and 25% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 392 centipawns. The positions are overwhelmingly pawn endgames (64% motif) with kings and pawns, where the player misses the single correct continuation (often a king move or a specific pawn timing). Maia's recommendations frequently involve checks (38%) or captures, suggesting the player overlooked active king play or tactical pawn breakthroughs. The common tags (tempo_loss, pawn_structure, passed_pawn) reveal that these errors typically involve wasting a critical tempo, mishandling pawn structure, or failing to create/stop a passed pawn. The boards confirm king-and-pawn endings where one mistimed pawn advance (like f3-f4, h7-h5, g5-g4, b4-b5) ruins a carefully calculated position.

188.label: Player makes a slow or irrelevant move while leaving a major piece completely undefended and capturable.
188.description: This feature fires when a player ignores a critical hanging piece (usually their own queen or rook) and instead plays a slow, non-urgent move—often a pawn push or minor piece maneuver—that allows the opponent to simply capture the undefended piece for free. The material signature shows 75% of moves 'hang' material with a median loss of ~8 pawns worth (consistent with losing a queen), and 67% of cases swing from winning to losing. The Opus analysis confirms 100% hanging_piece motifs with tags like 'hanging_queen', 'undefended_piece', and 'one_move_tactic'. Maia's response is overwhelmingly queen captures (75%) or rook captures (25%), frequently with check (83%), indicating the opponent's refutation is trivial and immediate. The boards show middlegame positions where the player had a perfectly playable or even winning position but played a move completely ignoring that a major piece sits en prise on an open line, resulting in catastrophic material loss.

183.label: Giving a check that hangs a major piece (queen or rook) to a simple recapture or interposition.
183.description: This feature identifies positions where the player delivers a check with a queen or rook (100% checks, queen 50%, rook 50%) that catastrophically loses material (median net material: -5.0, with 50% hangs and 30% loses). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (50%) and king_safety (50%), with tags like 'checks_not_always_best', 'queen_blunder', and 'pawn_captures_queen' reinforcing that the player impulsively chose a flashy check without calculating that the checking piece lands on a square where it can be trivially captured. The eval trajectory shows these occur overwhelmingly in already-losing positions (losing->losing 30% with median 227cp further lost), suggesting a desperate or panicked attempt to harass the opponent's king that only accelerates defeat. Maia's recommended moves (queen 60%, rook 30%, mostly non-captures and non-checks) indicate that quiet defensive or regrouping moves were far superior. The concrete examples—such as Qe4+ where a pawn captures the queen, or Rf8+ walking into a back-rank trap—illustrate the recurring pattern: the allure of check blinds the player to the hanging piece left behind.

186.label: Abandoning an active rook position or wasting a critical tempo in a winning endgame, converting a win into a draw or loss.
186.description: This feature captures a specific endgame mistake pattern where players squander winning positions by misplacing rooks or losing tempo. The material signature shows the best move was always a rook move (Maia's move: rook 100%), but players instead moved pawns (28%), rooks to wrong squares (28%), or kings (26%), with 89% being non-captures—these are positional misjudgments rather than tactical oversights. The eval trajectory confirms these are 'throwing away wins': 41% go from winning to drawn and 4% from winning to losing, with a massive median loss of 269 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying mechanism through dominant tags: rook_endgame (6), tempo_loss (5), piece_activity (4), and rook_activity (3). The concrete examples consistently show players abandoning dominant rook positions (leaving the h-file, failing to play Rd4 or Re2), making premature pawn advances that create structural weaknesses, or allowing counterplay through tempo-losing king moves. The endgame (52%) and middlegame (48%) phase split with rook_endgame as a top motif confirms these are late-game positions where precise rook placement is paramount and one inaccurate move dissipates the advantage.

189.label: King or pawn moves that squander critical tempo in pawn endgames, allowing the opponent to consolidate or promote.
189.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a king move (67%) or pawn push (33%) that loses critical tempo. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (appearing in 8 of 9 positions), combined with passed_pawn and pawn_endgame themes. The eval trajectory shows these moves are costly (median 249cp lost), typically turning drawn positions into losses (22%) or worsening already-losing positions (67%). The material signature shows these are 'safe' moves (89%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet 67% miss winning material, indicating the player chose a passive or misguided king walk/pawn push instead of the one critical action needed (capturing a pawn, blockading, or racing). The board positions confirm classic pawn endgame scenarios where precise calculation of tempi determines whether a passed pawn promotes or a king reaches a critical square in time, and the player consistently chooses the wrong moment to advance or retreat.

187.label: Knight recapture or trade in the opening that misses a winning Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice with check.
187.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a knight capture (often recapturing or trading knights) that appears materially safe but misses a critical Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice giving check. The material signature shows knight moves capturing knights with a 'safe' outcome, yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic swing from winning to drawn (median ~296cp lost). Maia consistently recommends bishop captures on pawns (Bxf7+) delivering check, and the missed tactic tags dominate (7 occurrences). The boards are overwhelmingly Italian Game / Two Knights Defense positions where the Bc4 eyes f7 and a forcing Bxf7+ (or Nf6# discovered attack) exists. The motifs—king safety, tempo loss, forks, and discovered attacks—all point to the same pattern: the player chooses a routine-looking knight trade instead of exploiting the vulnerable f7 square with a check-based combination that would maintain or increase the advantage. The 100% opening phase confirms these are well-known tactical patterns in open games that club players routinely miss in favor of 'safe' piece exchanges.

190.label: Player misses a winning knight fork with check in the endgame, turning a winning or drawn position into a lost one.
190.description: This feature identifies endgame positions where the player had a decisive knight fork available (typically with check, winning the opponent's queen or major piece) but instead played a passive or irrelevant move. The material signature shows the player's actual moves are a mix of king and knight moves that don't capture anything, with 50% hanging material—indicating the move itself wasn't a capture but left the position collapsing. Meanwhile, Maia consistently recommends knight moves (often with check and capturing a pawn or initiating the fork sequence). The eval trajectory is catastrophic: a median loss of 966 centipawns, swinging from winning or drawn positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies fork motifs (67%), with tags emphasizing missed_tactic, knight_fork, and queen_win—confirming the player repeatedly fails to execute a knight fork that would win the opponent's queen. The board positions consistently show endgame scenarios with knights positioned one move away from a devastating fork on the enemy king and queen, but the player moves the knight elsewhere or makes an unrelated king move, squandering the tactical opportunity.
