191.label: Pushing a pawn on the flank or in a non-critical area while missing a tactical opportunity involving a fork or hanging piece.
191.description: This feature captures a highly specific mistake pattern: the player pushes a pawn (95% of activations) in the opening or middlegame (100% combined), typically a quiet, non-capturing move (99% no capture) that ignores a concrete tactical opportunity. The dominant motifs are forks (42%) and hanging pieces (33%), meaning the opponent has a vulnerable piece or the player's own move creates a tactical vulnerability. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly piece moves—knights (31%), bishops (19%), queens (12%)—often capturing material (22% captures), indicating the correct move was an active piece deployment exploiting the tactic. The eval trajectory is severe: median 275cp lost, with 18% going from drawn to losing and 12% from winning to drawn, confirming these pawn moves throw away significant advantages. The board examples reinforce this: b4 ignoring central tension, a3 walking into a fork, b3 losing tempo while a piece hangs, f3 allowing a fork, f4/g4 weakening the king while tactics exist. The common thread is a slow, often flank pawn push that neglects the immediate tactical demands of the position.

194.label: Premature pawn advance in a losing endgame that drops material or wastes a critical tempo.
194.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves in king-and-pawn endgames (67% endgame phase) where the player, already in a losing position, pushes a pawn that hangs material (100% hangs, median -1.0 net material). The eval trajectory shows these are losing->losing positions where the pawn advance costs a median of 111 centipawns, making an already dire situation significantly worse. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (54%), passed_pawn (38%), and tempo_loss (8%)—along with recurring tags like king_activity and pawn_structure, reveal that these are positions demanding precise calculation of pawn races and opposition. Instead of maintaining defensive structure or optimizing king placement, the player prematurely advances a pawn (often creating or responding to passed pawns) that either gets captured, creates a losing tempo in a pawn race, or abandons a critical defensive square. The top boards confirm this: positions like pure K+P endings where moves like ...c4, ...f5, ...h4, or ...b3 push pawns forward impulsively rather than attending to the delicate tempo and king-position requirements of the endgame.

195.label: Player gives a purposeless queen check instead of capturing the opponent's queen, throwing away a winning position.
195.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a queen check (player moved: queen 100%, played a check: 100%) instead of taking the opponent's available queen (Maia's recommended move captures a queen 100% of the time). The move itself doesn't lose material immediately (safe 100%), but the eval trajectory shows a catastrophic collapse from winning to drawn (100%, median loss of 10000 centipawns — i.e., a forced mate or trivially won endgame is squandered). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant pattern: the player passes up a decisive queen trade (tags: queen_trade, missed_capture, pointless_check, unnecessary_check) that would yield a won pawn endgame (pawn_endgame motif 45%) or simply win the opponent's hanging queen outright (hanging_piece 18%). The summaries explicitly describe 'patzer sees a check' syndrome — choosing a flashy but purposeless check over the simple, game-ending capture. This is not a material blunder in the traditional sense; the queen is not lost. Rather, it is a failure to simplify into a trivially won position, driven by the psychological compulsion to give check.

196.label: Player overlooks a forced checkmate in one move, typically a queen delivery with check, playing an inferior move instead.
196.description: All three signals converge on the same pattern: players missing an immediate checkmate in one. The material/position signature shows Maia unanimously recommending a queen move that captures a pawn and gives check (100% across all three), while the player instead makes quiet moves with pawns, kings, or knights that don't give check (0% check rate). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders with a median loss of 9475 centipawns—consistent with converting a forced mate into a lost or drawn position (winning->drawn 12%, winning->winning 12% where they were already mating but stayed winning). The Opus analysis explicitly identifies 'checkmate_in_one' and 'missed_mate_in_one' as tags, with example summaries describing missed Qxf7# and Qxf2# mates. The positions (88% opening phase) are overwhelmingly from Italian Game / Fried Liver style openings where tactical queen sacrifices or queen deliveries on f7/f2 are available. The king_safety motif (67%) and back_rank_diagonal tags confirm the queen's mating access along diagonals to the king. Players instead make developing moves, castle, or capture unrelated pieces, completely overlooking the one-move kill.

192.label: Knight delivers a check that abandons its strong post, losing tempo and often the piece itself.
192.description: This feature fires on knight moves that give check (100% knight moved, 100% check) but sacrifice positional value for a meaningless tempo gain. The material signature shows 40% of these moves hang the knight outright and only 44% are safe, with a median material loss of -1.0 (a full piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly blunders: median 305 centipawns lost, with many converting winning positions to drawn or drawn to losing. The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern — 'pointless check' and 'tempo loss' dominate the motifs (33% tempo_loss, tags include pointless_check as the most frequent). The per-position summaries repeatedly describe knights leaving powerful centralized squares (e4, e3) to deliver checks that accomplish nothing, as the opponent simply sidesteps and the knight ends up trapped, misplaced, or captured. This is overwhelmingly a middlegame phenomenon (80%) where the knight's positional value on a strong outpost far exceeds the fleeting disruption of a check. Players are seduced by the forcing nature of check without evaluating whether the knight's relocation improves their position.

199.label: Retreating or misplacing the queen in the opening instead of capturing a free/winning pawn, losing tempo and turning a drawn position into a losing one.
199.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes (100% opening) where the player moves their queen (75%) or bishop (25%) to a passive or retreating square instead of capturing available material. Maia consistently recommends capturing a pawn with the queen (100% Maia queen moves capturing a pawn), indicating the missed opportunity is concrete and tactical. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (64%) and hanging_piece (29%), with common tags emphasizing development, piece_activity, and missed_tactic. The material outcome of the played move is mostly 'safe' (75%), meaning the player doesn't immediately lose a piece—they simply waste time repositioning (e.g., Qd5-d8, Qd5-a5, Qd4-c3) rather than grabbing a free pawn or maintaining central pressure. The eval trajectory is uniformly drawn->losing (100%), with a median loss of 276 centipawns, showing that these tempo-wasting queen moves in the opening convert a balanced position into a clearly losing one. The concrete pattern across the top boards is Scandinavian/center-pawn structures where the queen is already developed early but retreats to a passive square instead of taking the hanging d4/d5 pawn or maintaining active centralization.

198.label: In the opening, player makes a non-capture move that leaves a minor piece (usually knight) undefended and en prise.
198.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a player moves a pawn, knight, or bishop (89% of cases) without capturing anything, yet leaves a piece hanging (99% 'hangs' outcome) for a median loss of ~335 centipawns (approximately one minor piece). The phase is almost exclusively the opening (99%), and the tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'hanging_piece' (92%). The eval trajectory shows these moves typically transform drawn positions into losing ones (68% drawn->losing), indicating the player had a viable position before the blunder. The top boards reveal the concrete pattern: in French/Caro-Kann/Scandinavian-type structures with a pawn on e5, players develop or move their knight to f6 where it is immediately captured by the e5 pawn, or they play irrelevant moves (like h3, d3, c4) while a piece is under direct attack. Maia's recommended moves (54% knight, 25% bishop) suggest the correct response was typically developing or repositioning the threatened piece to safety. This is a one-move tactical oversight in familiar opening positions where the player ignores an immediate threat to their own piece.

193.label: In already-losing positions, player makes a move that ignores immediate king safety threats, allowing forced checkmate or catastrophic material loss.
193.description: This feature fires on moves where a player in an already-losing position (44% losing->losing, 32% losing->winning for opponent) makes a critical defensive error that accelerates their demise. The material signature shows 64% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material), with rooks (36%) and kings (28%) being the most commonly moved pieces—suggesting desperate but inadequate defensive attempts. The dominant motif is king_safety (58%), supported by tags like tempo_loss, missed_tactic, exposed_king, and mating_attack. The Opus analysis reveals a recurring pattern: positions where the player is already worse but still has defensive resources, yet plays a move that allows forced checkmate (often in 1-7 moves) or catastrophic material loss. The boards confirm this—many feature exposed kings with attacking pieces nearby (e.g., FEN with Nf8+Qh5 attacking, or Rg6+Bf6 threats), where the player's move fails to address the primary king safety concern. Maia's suggested moves (which miss winning material 80% of the time) often involve pawn pushes or king moves that better address the defensive requirements. The median 34cp loss understates the damage because many positions go from 'lost but playable' to 'immediate checkmate,' averaged with smaller inaccuracies.

201.label: Player makes a routine developing move instead of executing a winning Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7/h2.
201.description: This feature fires on positions where a player has a classic Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+ or Bxh2+) available but fails to execute it, instead making a safe, non-capturing move with a minor piece or queen. The material signature shows the player's move is overwhelmingly 'safe' (85%) with no captures (96%), while Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a pawn with check—the hallmark Bxh7+/Bxh2+ sacrifice. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly missed opportunities: 46% of cases transition from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 216 centipawns. The tactical analysis is definitive: 100% king_safety motif, with 'greek_gift' and 'Bxh7_sacrifice' as dominant tags. The top boards all show French Defense or similar pawn structures where a bishop on d3 or c2 has a clear sacrificial path to h7 against a castled king, and the player instead retreats or develops passively (Be2, Be3, Nf1, O-O, etc.), squandering a textbook attacking opportunity in the opening phase (85% opening).

197.label: Moving an actively placed piece away from a critical square, leaving another piece or tactical resource undefended.
197.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a well-placed piece (often a rook, queen, or bishop) away from a key square, inadvertently leaving another piece hanging or abandoning a crucial tactical threat. The material signature shows 63% of moves are 'safe' in the sense that no immediate capture occurs, yet 23% result in a hung piece — the player doesn't lose material on the move itself but exposes something else. The eval trajectory is devastating: 29% go from winning to drawn and 11% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 329cp, indicating these are game-changing errors that squander significant advantages. Maia strongly preferred rook moves (66%), suggesting the correct continuation usually involved maintaining rook activity on key files or ranks. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: dominant motifs include hanging_piece (30%) and discovered_attack (10%), while tags like tempo_loss, piece_activity, undefended_rook, and open_file_control recur. The concrete positions show pieces being moved off active squares (Nf4 abandoning Nf6+ threats, Bd3 retreating instead of Rd1, Kg2 wasting tempo while a bishop hangs). The core mistake is repositioning an active piece without recognizing it was the linchpin holding a tactical or defensive resource together.

203.label: Moving a bishop away from a critical task in the endgame, hanging material or missing a decisive capture.
203.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their bishop to an inferior square, hanging it or leaving material undefended, while a superior bishop capture (typically taking an unprotected knight or key piece) was available. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves that are non-captures resulting in a hang (median -1.0 material), while Maia consistently identifies a bishop capturing a knight as the correct move. The eval trajectory is devastating—100% of cases go from winning to losing with a median loss of 793 centipawns, indicating these are thrown wins. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: the dominant motifs include hanging_piece and pawn_endgame contexts, with tags like passed_pawn, piece_activity, and tempo_loss recurring. The positions are almost exclusively simplified endgames where the bishop had one critical job (defending a promotion path, capturing an undefended piece, or maintaining an active post), and the player carelessly relocated it, forfeiting a decisive advantage.

200.label: Pawn captures (especially recaptures or central exchanges) that open lines or diagonals enabling opponent's tactical shots like forks, skewers, or attacks on hanging pieces.
200.description: This feature identifies pawn moves—particularly pawn captures (88% pawn moves, 39% capturing pawns, 50% hanging material)—that open critical lines for the opponent's pieces, enabling devastating tactical consequences. The material signature shows these moves overwhelmingly hang material (50%) or result in unfavorable trades (42%), with a median loss of 1.0 material unit. The eval trajectory confirms these are serious errors costing a median of 286 centipawns, frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (28%) or throwing away wins (15% combined winning->drawn/losing). The tactical analysis reveals the recurring mechanism: pawn captures that open diagonals or files (e.g., cxd5 opening the a2-g8 diagonal, dxe5 allowing a skewer, exd5 enabling forks), where Maia's recommended moves were typically piece moves (knight 34%, king 17%, bishop 12%) rather than the tempting pawn exchange. The positions cluster in opening/middlegame (100%) where central pawn exchanges feel natural but inadvertently expose the player to latent tactical motifs—forks (20%), hanging pieces (40%), and skewers (10%)—that the opponent's already-developed pieces can immediately exploit.

204.label: In winning endgames, player overlooks a simple hanging piece capture (usually a rook), converting a won position into a lost one.
204.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player has a winning advantage but makes a 'safe' move (no material lost directly, median net 0.0) while completely missing a free capture of a major piece. The material signature shows the player moved their king or pawn instead of capturing, while Maia's recommendation captures a rook 100% of the time. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 100% winning-to-losing with a median loss of 1016 centipawns. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (80%), with tags like missed_capture and missed_tactic reinforcing that the opponent left a piece en prise. The concrete positions confirm this: a knight that could take an undefended rook on c1, a king move instead of capturing a hanging rook on e6, pawns advanced while rooks sit undefended. The player appears to be on autopilot in the endgame—making natural-looking king centralizations or pawn pushes—while being blind to a trivially available capture that would clinch the game.

202.label: Developing or moving pieces while ignoring an immediate mating or king-safety threat on a vulnerable diagonal or square.
202.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes a structurally reasonable or developing move (often a knight or pawn, sometimes a queen or bishop) but catastrophically ignores an existing king-safety threat. The material signature shows 71% of these moves simply hang material (non-captures that drop a piece or allow mate), with a median net loss of -1.0 pieces, and the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of ~95 pawns (effectively mate), confirming these are game-ending oversights rather than gradual positional errors. The Opus tactical analysis tags king_safety at 100% across all positions, with recurring sub-motifs of f7/f2 weakness, queen-bishop batteries aimed at the king, and scholar's-mate-type patterns. The top boards consistently show positions where a diagonal or f-file weakness is already targeted by opponent pieces (e.g., Qf3+Bc4 on f7, or queen+bishop trained on f2 with check), and the player plays a developing move (Nc3, Be2, d6) that neither blocks the threat nor moves the king, resulting in immediate checkmate or decisive material loss. Maia's recommendations (mostly pawn moves or queen moves) suggest the correct response was typically a defensive pawn block or king move, reinforcing that the blunder is a failure to recognize urgent king danger.

205.label: A pawn move in the opening that leaves a piece undefended and immediately capturable, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
205.description: This feature detects a specific and recurring opening blunder pattern: the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) that inadvertently hangs a piece (100% 'hangs' material outcome, median net material -1.0 indicating a full piece lost). The eval trajectory confirms these are consistently drawn positions turning losing (100% drawn->losing, median 231cp lost), meaning the player had equality and threw it away with a single careless pawn push. The tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (83%), supported by tags like 'opening_blunder', 'development', and 'tempo_loss'. The concrete positions show classic scenarios: pushing d5 when it can be captured without adequate recapture, playing e4 when it drops a pawn to an already-placed knight, or advancing a pawn that exposes a piece (like Ba6 being left en prise after a pawn push). These are not positional subtleties—they are straightforward one-move oversights where the pawn advance either directly hangs itself or uncovers an attack on another piece, all occurring in the opening phase (100%) before the player has fully developed.

206.label: Playing a check that gains no tempo and leaves the checking piece or another piece hanging.
206.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player delivers a check (100% of activations) most often with a queen (53%) that results in hanging a piece (62%) with a median material loss of 3.0 points and ~325 centipawns of evaluation damage. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (45%), hanging_piece (27%), and back_rank (18%)—combined with tags like 'pointless_check' and 'perpetual_check_missed' reveal the underlying error: players see a check and reflexively play it without verifying whether the checking piece survives or whether the check accomplishes anything strategically. Maia's recommended moves (0% checks, spread across queens, rooks, pawns, knights) confirm that the engine sees quiet developing or consolidating moves as superior. The eval trajectory shows this mistake is devastating across all game states—turning wins into losses (7%), draws into losses (9%), and deepening existing losing positions (18%). The example positions consistently show checks that drive the opponent's king to a better square, lose a tempo, or simply leave material en prise, often missing perpetual check sequences or concrete winning continuations that required calculation rather than the superficially forcing check.

207.label: A queen check that loses tempo or hangs the queen by moving it to an inferior square without constructive purpose.
207.description: This feature fires on queen moves that deliver check (100% of activations) but serve no constructive purpose and frequently result in hanging material (76% hangs, median net material -9.0, i.e., losing the queen). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses (median 158 centipawns lost), often converting drawable or even defensible positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 24%, losing->losing 35%). The tactical analysis repeatedly identifies the 'pointless check' motif—the queen checks on a square where it can be captured, blocked with a counter-threat, or forced into an unfavorable exchange. Tags like 'queen_misplacement', 'tempo_loss', and 'king_safety_neglect' confirm that these checks relocate the queen from an active post to a vulnerable one, often allowing the opponent to interpose with tempo or force simplification. The Maia responses (71% non-captures, often king moves or queen interposes) show that the opponent calmly sidesteps the check while the checking side's position collapses. This is the classic amateur mistake of giving check 'because it's check' without verifying that it improves the position.

208.label: Player makes a non-checking move while a winning queen check (often with decisive threats) was available, leaving pieces hanging.
208.description: This feature fires when players miss a critical queen check that would have won material or delivered a decisive blow. The material/position signature shows that Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100% check rate), while the player's actual move never gives check (0%). The player typically moves a queen (55%) or other piece to a square that is safe (73%) or even hangs material (18%), but critically misses the forcing queen check. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: the median eval loss is 867 centipawns, with positions frequently transitioning from winning to losing (18%) or winning to drawn (9%). The tactical analysis shows 100% hanging_piece motifs—by failing to deliver the queen check, the player often leaves their own piece (frequently the queen itself) on an undefended or tactically vulnerable square. The board positions consistently show middlegame scenarios where a powerful queen check along a diagonal or file would have been decisive, but the player instead makes a quiet or misdirected move, overlooking the forcing nature of the check.

215.label: Moving the queen (or other major piece) to a square where it can be immediately captured, throwing away a winning or equal position.
215.description: This feature captures moves where the player actively hangs a major piece—most often the queen (71% queen moves)—resulting in catastrophic material loss (median net material: -4.0, with 43% hangs and 43% loses). The eval trajectory confirms these are game-destroying mistakes: 29% swing from winning to losing and 29% from winning to drawn, with a median eval drop of 547 centipawns. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (60%) and tags like 'queen_blunder', 'piece_safety', and 'material_loss'. The positions show players relocating their queen or major piece without noticing that the destination square (or the square vacated) leaves a piece en prise to an opponent's tactic—such as an undefended rook captured by a knight fork, or a queen placed where it can be taken with tempo. Maia's recommended moves (57% queen, 29% rook) typically keep the piece safe or find a constructive alternative, confirming the blunder is an oversight rather than a forced concession.

210.label: Trading or exchanging rooks in a winning position, allowing the opponent to equalize or seize the advantage.
210.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players initiate or allow rook exchanges (rook moved 56%, rook captured 56%) that squander a winning advantage. The material outcome is predominantly 'trade' (50%), confirming these are exchange decisions rather than outright blunders. The eval trajectory shows winning->drawn (31%) and winning->losing (12%) as dominant patterns, with a median loss of 273 centipawns — indicating players are throwing away substantial advantages through premature simplification. The tactical analysis reinforces this with tags like 'simplification_error', 'rook_endgame', and 'piece_activity', suggesting players trade rooks when their rook activity or coordination was a key component of their winning advantage. The concrete positions show rook-heavy middlegames and endgames where the player exchanges into an equal or lost position (e.g., exchanging rooks on d1, trading on c7) instead of maintaining piece pressure. Maia's recommended moves frequently avoid these trades (Maia captures 'none' 81% of the time), preferring to maintain tension with active piece play or deliver checks (38% check rate), confirming the human error is choosing liquidation over sustained pressure.

209.label: Player makes a passive or developing move instead of a forcing Bxc3+ (or similar bishop check) that wins decisive material through a tactical sequence.
209.description: This feature fires on opening positions (96% opening phase) where the player has a bishop that can deliver a forcing check—typically Bxc3+—initiating a tactical sequence that wins significant material (median 355 centipawns lost). Instead of playing the critical bishop move (Maia recommends bishop 100% of the time, capturing a knight 96% with check 100%), the player makes a passive or non-forcing move: developing a knight to a rim square (25%), retreating a bishop (33%), pushing a pawn (29%), or castling. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (43%) and fork (43%), reflecting that the missed Bxc3+ check often sets up a queen fork winning material. The material signature shows 83% no capture and 33% hangs—the player's move doesn't take anything and frequently leaves material vulnerable. The eval trajectory (29% drawn->losing, 25% winning->drawn) confirms these are game-changing missed opportunities in the opening where the king remains in the center (king_in_center tag), making the check particularly devastating.

214.label: In drawn endgames, the king moves passively instead of capturing a critical pawn, allowing the opponent to win.
214.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern. The material/position signature shows the player always moves their king (100%) without capturing anything, while the best move (Maia's suggestion) consistently involves capturing a pawn (100%). The positions are exclusively endgames (100%) where the game is objectively drawn, but the passive king move transforms it into a losing position (drawn->losing 100%, median loss of 589 centipawns). The tactical analysis reveals hanging pieces (56%) and promotion errors (22%) as dominant motifs, with 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss' as the most frequent tags. Examining the top boards confirms this: simplified endgame positions (kings + few pieces/pawns) where the player's king retreats or sidesteps instead of actively capturing a critical pawn or piece that would maintain the draw. The player loses a crucial tempo, allowing the opponent to promote a pawn or achieve a decisive material advantage. This is fundamentally a failure to recognize that in these simplified positions, the king must actively engage with enemy material rather than drift passively.

213.label: Premature rook exchange or capture that converts a defensible endgame into a lost pawn endgame by surrendering piece activity.
213.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes (100% endgame phase) where a rook (75% of moves) captures a pawn (67%) or makes a rook move that simplifies the position into a pure pawn endgame, forfeiting critical piece activity. The dominant motif is 'pawn_endgame' (47%), indicating that the key error is transitioning into a worse pawn ending. The trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly losing->losing (83%) positions where the player makes a bad position significantly worse (median 133cp lost), rather than throwing a winning position. The tactical summaries consistently describe moves like Rxa7, Rxb2, Rf2 that trade off the rook or reduce its activity, converting difficult-but-defensible rook endgames into trivially lost pawn endgames. Maia's suggested alternatives (king moves 67%, maintaining the rook 17%) emphasize keeping piece activity alive rather than simplifying. The boards confirm this: rook-vs-rook endings with passed pawns where one side prematurely exchanges or repositions the rook passively, losing the dynamic counterplay that kept the position defensible.

212.label: Player ignores a free rook capture available to their bishop along an open long diagonal.
212.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, materially safe move (pawn 33%, knight 27%, etc. with no captures) while completely overlooking that their bishop can capture an undefended rook along the long diagonal (Maia's move is always bishop capturing rook). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening or early middlegame (67% opening, 33% middlegame), where one side has fianchettoed or developed a bishop onto the long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1) while the opponent's rook remains undefended — typically because a pawn moved (like ...g6 or ...b6) without the rook having escaped or been shielded. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 80% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 381 centipawns, consistent with missing a free exchange. The tactical tags (long_diagonal 8/15, hanging_rook 4/15, missed_capture, hanging_piece 100%) and the per-position analyses all converge on the same pattern: a bishop has a clean capture of an unprotected rook along an open long diagonal, but the player makes an irrelevant developing or prophylactic move instead, squandering a decisive material advantage.

216.label: Advancing or capturing with a pawn that fatally ignores tactical threats, losing tempo and allowing opponent counterplay.
216.description: This feature fires on pawn moves (100% pawn played) that overwhelmingly result in material loss (62% hangs, 31% trades, median -1.0 material) with a severe eval drop (median 343 centipawns). The positions are predominantly middlegame (69%) where the player pushes or captures with a pawn—most frequently advancing to b2 or pushing a passed pawn—while missing that the opponent has strong tactical resources (92% missed winning material). The Opus analysis reveals the recurring pattern: players push pawns prematurely (often passed pawns or captures on b2) without first addressing critical threats like back-rank attacks, piece coordination, or king safety. The dominant motifs (king_safety 44%, passed_pawn 22%, tempo_loss tags) show these pawn moves ignore immediate tactical dangers—mating patterns, blockade opportunities, or developing threats—giving the opponent free tempo to consolidate or attack. The eval trajectory (31% drawn->losing, 23% winning->drawn) confirms these moves frequently throw away favorable or balanced positions by prioritizing a slow pawn advance over addressing urgent tactical needs.

217.label: Losing a drawn endgame by allowing opponent's passed pawn promotion or hanging a piece in a simplified position.
217.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a drawn position collapses into a lost one (drawn->losing 100%, median 530cp lost). The material signature shows king moves (50%), knight (25%), and bishop (25%) — typical endgame piece maneuvering — with no captures, yet 50% of moves hang material. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%), promotion_error (20%), and passed_pawn (20%), all united by the common endgame theme of failing to address critical pawn promotion threats or dropping pieces in simplified positions. The top boards confirm this: minimal-material endgames (often K+piece vs K+piece/pawn) where the player makes a single catastrophic error — either failing to capture a dangerous piece (e.g., missing Nxb6 capturing a queen), mishandling a promotion race, or losing a piece to a simple tactic in a position that was objectively holdable. The tempo_loss tag (13 occurrences) suggests these mistakes often involve wasting a critical tempo when every move counts in the race to promote or blockade.

211.label: Moving a knight to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured, or moving a knight while ignoring a hanging piece elsewhere.
211.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player moves a knight (50% of moves) to a square where it is left undefended and immediately capturable, or moves a knight while ignoring a critical hanging piece elsewhere on the board. The material signature shows 50% of moves result in a 'hang' (a non-capture that drops a piece) with a median material loss of -2.0 (roughly a full piece), and the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (67%) with 'undefended_piece' appearing in 4 of the tagged positions. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors—median 409 centipawns lost, with 33% converting drawn positions to losing ones. The concrete positions reinforce this: Nd3 leaving itself capturable (boards 1, 3, 10), knights moving while queens or other pieces hang (board 1's Nd3 ignoring the attacked queen on e3), and knights relocating to squares with no support. The Opus analysis explicitly identifies 'move-order errors' where the knight move neglects a more urgent defensive need, and pieces left en prise after the knight relocates. This is fundamentally a tactical oversight—the player focuses on developing or repositioning the knight while failing to notice it (or another piece) is left hanging.

219.label: Moving the queen away from essential defensive duties, fatally exposing the king to mating attacks.
219.description: This feature identifies positions where a player moves their queen (74% of activations) away from a critical defensive role, typically capturing a pawn (65%) that appears tempting but is strategically irrelevant. The dominant motif is king_safety (71%) with recurring tags of exposed_king, mating_attack, and forced_mate. The Opus analyses consistently describe the same pattern: the queen leaves its defensive post—where it was the sole guardian against back-rank or mating threats—to grab material or reposition offensively, allowing the opponent's pieces to deliver devastating attacks against the now-undefended king. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 412 centipawns, with positions shifting from winning to losing or drawn to losing. The material signature shows 'loses' and 'hangs' categories (52% combined), reflecting that while the queen captures a pawn, the resulting position collapses due to the tactical consequences of the exposed king rather than a simple piece-for-piece exchange. The concrete board positions repeatedly show queens moving to aggressive-looking squares (Qxh6, Qxc3, Qxe3, Qxe4) while the player's own king sits dangerously exposed on an open file or rank.

218.label: Advancing a pawn with check in the endgame that concedes critical squares or tempo, often converting a winning/drawn position into a worse one.
218.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake: pushing a pawn to deliver check (100% checks, 82% pawn moves, no captures in 98% of cases) that proves positionally counterproductive. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (72%) — the pawn isn't immediately lost — yet the median eval cost is 228 centipawns, indicating severe positional damage. The trajectory (22% winning->drawn, 18% drawn->losing) confirms these are game-altering errors that squander advantages. The tactical analysis reveals why: the dominant motifs are positional_mistake (33%) and tempo_loss (33%), with tags emphasizing pawn_structure, king_activity, and passed_pawns. The concrete examples are illuminating — c5+ fixes pawn structure and gifts blockading squares, e4+ releases control of key squares and frees the opponent's king, g4+ collapses a winning position to equality. In each case the player is seduced by the forcing nature of a check but the pawn advance permanently weakens their position, cedes key squares, or disrupts their own pawn structure in a phase (76% endgame) where such concessions are decisive.

220.label: Moving a piece (often the queen) to a square where it becomes vulnerable to a knight fork, losing significant material.
220.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves a high-value piece—most frequently the queen (34%)—to a square that is tactically vulnerable to a knight fork or discovered attack. The OPUS analysis overwhelmingly identifies fork motifs (90%) with dominant tags including knight_fork, queen_loss, and geometric_vulnerability. The material signature shows 66% 'safe' moves (non-captures that appear harmless) and 26% 'hangs' (the piece becomes exposed), indicating the player doesn't realize the destination square is tactically poisoned. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 497 centipawns, with 13% of cases turning drawn positions into losing ones and 9% throwing outright wins. The concrete board examples consistently show queens or kings landing on squares where an enemy knight can execute a devastating fork (e.g., Ne2+, Nd3+, Nf6+). Maia's recommendations frequently involve king moves (26%) or repositioning the queen safely (36%), suggesting the correct response was to address the knight's tactical access rather than ignoring it. This is a pattern of tactical blindness to knight geometry—players place valuable pieces on vulnerable squares without computing the opponent's forking possibilities.

222.label: Playing a passive or slow move that leaves a piece undefended, allowing the opponent a free capture or winning tactic.
222.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, non-urgent move (typically a pawn push or minor piece recapture) that completely overlooks a hanging or undefended piece on the board. The material signature shows the player's move hangs material 67% of the time with a median net loss of -5.0 (roughly a full piece), while Maia consistently finds a rook capture with check as the punishment. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 67% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 783 centipawns. The tactical analysis emphasizes hanging_piece and tempo_loss motifs—the player wastes a tempo on a slow move (like g2-g3, c3-c4, or a prophylactic rook lift) while a concrete tactical shot exists, either capturing their undefended piece or winning a decisive exchange. All positions occur in the middlegame where tactical alertness is critical, and the common thread is 'material blindness'—failing to notice that a piece lacks adequate defense before playing a move that doesn't address the threat.

221.label: Hanging a rook (often by capturing a passed pawn) that converts a winning endgame into a lost pawn ending.
221.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves a rook to a square where it can be immediately captured (100% hangs, median -5.0 material = a full rook), converting a winning position into a losing one (100% winning->losing, median 1157cp lost). The boards show king+rook+pawns vs pawns endgames where the rook impetuously captures or blocks a passed pawn on a square defended by the opponent's king, gifting the rook and leaving a hopelessly lost pawn ending. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs: pawn_endgame (29%), hanging_piece (21%), and passed_pawn (14%), with tags reinforcing that these are rook endgames transitioning into lost pawn races. The check signal (100% played a check) combined with the concrete FENs shows these are often rook captures on the promotion square that deliver check but allow the king to simply take the rook. Maia's recommended move is consistently a quiet pawn push (100% pawn, no capture, no check), indicating the correct plan was advancing a passed pawn rather than the flashy but fatal rook lunge.

224.label: Moving a minor piece while leaving the queen undefended on an exposed square.
224.description: This feature captures a specific tactical blunder pattern where the player moves a knight or bishop (63% combined) while their queen is left hanging or inadequately defended. The material signature shows 54% hangs and 42% loses with a devastating median net loss of -6.0 (approximately a queen's value), and Maia's recommended move is the queen 90% of the time—indicating the queen urgently needed to move or be defended. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (75%), with common tags including queen_hanging, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders (median 394cp lost), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (35% drawn->losing, 10% winning->losing). The per-position analyses consistently show the player making a minor piece move (developing, capturing, or repositioning) while overlooking that their queen sits on an undefended square vulnerable to attack—a classic case of move-order error where the queen's safety should have been addressed first.

225.label: Player makes a passive rook move instead of finding a saving or winning check that exploits the opponent's exposed king.
225.description: This feature fires when players (predominantly moving rooks, 48%) make passive or aimless moves in positions where Maia identifies a critical check (Maia gives check 100% of the time). The material signature shows these moves are often 'safe' (58%) or 'hangs' material (30%), meaning the player doesn't immediately lose a piece but catastrophically misses the tactical resource. The eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences: median 308cp lost, with many positions flipping from drawn-to-losing (21%) or winning-to-losing (12%). The tactical analysis reveals the missed checks often involve back-rank threats, perpetual check resources, or enabling passed pawn promotion sequences. Concrete examples show players moving rooks to passive squares (Rab7, Rd7) when Re3+ perpetual check draws, or Re2+ wins material, or when a check enables a forcing promotion sequence. The positions cluster in middlegame (67%) and endgame (33%) scenarios where king exposure creates tactical opportunities that require precise calculation of checking sequences rather than routine piece placement.

228.label: Player makes a slow move in a won endgame instead of delivering the available checking sequence that forces faster mate.
228.description: This feature fires when a player in a won endgame (75% endgame phase) plays a non-capturing pawn or piece move that is technically safe (75% safe, no material lost) but misses a much more forcing continuation. The key signal is that Maia's recommended move delivers check 100% of the time, typically with a rook (58%) or knight (25%), while the player's move gives check only 8% of the time. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), meaning the player wastes time with passive moves when aggressive checking sequences are available. The eval trajectory shows most positions remain winning->winning (33%) with a median of 0 centipawns lost, which aligns with the example summaries showing moves that extend mating distance rather than lose material outright—the player is already winning but plays inefficiently by not utilizing checks to accelerate the mate. The boards confirm endgame positions with exposed kings where rook or knight checks would tighten the net immediately.

230.label: Player makes a routine move instead of a winning bishop tactical shot (Bg5, Bg4, Bc6, etc.) that would have won material.
230.description: This feature fires when a player misses a concrete winning bishop move. The Maia signal is striking: in 100% of cases, the engine recommends a bishop move, and in 100% of cases the player missed winning material. The player instead plays a variety of piece moves (pawns 27%, bishops 24%, knights 22%, queens 19%) that are mostly safe (54%) or involve equal trades (30%), but which squander a significant advantage (median 261cp lost, with 30% going from winning to drawn and 8% from winning to losing). The tactical motifs involve tempo loss (50%), hanging pieces (25%), and forks (25%), with tags like 'missed_tactic', 'deflection', and 'exchange_winning_opportunity' recurring. The concrete examples consistently show the same pattern: a bishop move (Bg5, Bg4, Bc6) exploiting geometric alignments—pins along diagonals, forks of queen and rook, or attacks on undefended pieces—is available but the player opts for a natural developing or routine move instead. This occurs predominantly in the middlegame (78%) and opening (22%), where tactical alertness to bishop geometry is most critical.

226.label: Moving a major piece (queen/knight) to an unsafe square, ignoring king safety and losing significant material.
226.description: This feature fires when players move their queen or knight to a square where it hangs (62% of moves result in a hung piece, median material loss of -5.0), typically in the middlegame (75%). The tactical analysis reveals that king_safety (50%) and tempo_loss (50%) are the dominant motifs — players are making moves that ignore urgent threats to their own king or waste critical tempo, allowing the opponent to exploit tactical vulnerabilities. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 417 centipawns), with positions sometimes collapsing from survivable to forced mate. Examining the boards confirms: players move pieces to exposed squares (e.g., Ng4 walking into tactics, Qd4 ignoring back-rank/king issues, Bd4 dropping material) while their king is under pressure or the opponent has active pieces aimed at the king. The Maia responses frequently involve capturing with rooks/queens (63% captures), confirming the opponent is winning the hung piece. This is not a trade or exchange — it's a one-sided material loss caused by prioritizing an irrelevant plan while king safety demands immediate attention.

234.label: King or piece moves onto a line where a discovered attack wins material.
234.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves their king (56% of cases) or another piece onto a square that enables a devastating discovered attack. The material signature shows 56% of moves hang a piece (median net material loss of -1.0, i.e., a full piece), and the eval trajectory is catastrophic—median 421 centipawns lost, with 56% of cases converting drawn positions into losing ones. The dominant tactical motif is discovered_attack (55%), supported by tags like discovered_check and geometric_motif. The concrete positions reveal a recurring pattern: a king steps onto a diagonal or file where an enemy piece can unmask an attack (e.g., Kh8 walking onto the a1-h8 diagonal allowing a bishop discovery, or Kb8 breaking a perpetual by stepping into a discovered geometry). Maia's preferred moves (89% king moves) suggest the correct defense usually involved the same piece but to a safe square. The player fails to recognize the geometric relationship between the attacker, the screening piece, and the square they're moving to.

232.label: A knight moves to a central square (typically e4 or e5) where it is inadequately defended and immediately lost.
232.description: This feature captures a highly specific and recurring blunder pattern: a knight is moved (88% of activating moves are knight moves) to a central square—overwhelmingly e4 or e5 based on the top boards—where it hangs with no compensation (100% 'hangs' with no capture made). The eval trajectory shows these moves predominantly turn drawn positions into losing ones (70% drawn->losing), with a median cost of 237 centipawns, indicating a full piece or near-piece loss. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (45%), with positional_mistake (27%) reflecting cases where the knight move looked natural or thematic (e.g., occupying a central outpost) but the piece was tactically unprotected or subject to discovered attacks. The positions cluster in the opening-to-middlegame transition (46% opening, 55% middlegame) in closed/semi-closed structures where central knight maneuvers are common but the player misjudges the tactical safety of the target square. Maia's recommended moves diverge significantly (only 36% knight), confirming these knight centralizations are objectively unsound despite appearing strategically motivated.

227.label: Knight captures a pawn but loses the knight to a minor piece recapture, surrendering central dominance and development advantage.
227.description: This feature detects a recurring pattern where a knight (86% of moves) captures a pawn (100% capture target) in the opening or early middlegame (69% opening, 31% middlegame), resulting in a net material loss of approximately 2 pawns (median -2.0, classified as 'slightly_down'). The boards reveal a strikingly consistent motif: knights jumping to central squares (d4, d5, e4, e6) to grab a pawn, only to be recaptured by a piece that then occupies a superior post. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic positional consequences—38% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 321 centipawns far exceeding the material deficit, indicating the damage is primarily positional. The Opus analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are hanging_piece (44%), positional_mistake (33%), and tempo_loss (22%), with recurring tags of piece_activity, development_advantage, and king_in_center. The canonical example is 5...Nxd4 'trading an actively-placed knight merely for a pawn while gifting White a dominant centralized knight.' Maia's responses (bishop 45%, queen 14%) confirm the recapture restores material while seizing initiative. This is fundamentally a bad exchange decision—capturing a pawn with a knight that was performing valuable positional duties, resulting in the opponent gaining a dominant piece placement, superior development, or dangerous initiative.

231.label: Player makes a non-checking move while missing a forced checkmate exploiting back-rank or king-safety weakness.
231.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a forcing checkmate sequence (typically involving a queen check exploiting back-rank vulnerability or an exposed king) and instead plays a quiet or irrelevant move. The material signature shows the player's move is spread across pieces (rook 25%, queen 23%, pawn 18%, knight 15%) with no check delivered (0%), while Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a queen move (58%) that delivers check (100%). The 96% missed-winning-material rate and median eval loss of 376 centipawns confirm these are catastrophic oversights. The Opus analysis identifies back_rank (50%) and king_safety (40%) as dominant motifs, with tags like back_rank_mate, missed_mate_in_one, and exposed_king recurring throughout. The concrete positions consistently show situations where a queen check would have delivered immediate or short-sequence checkmate via the back rank or against an exposed king, but the player instead made a materialistic capture, a positional move, or retreated a piece—completely missing the tactical shot. The eval trajectory (winning->losing 8%, drawn->losing 5%) confirms many of these represent thrown wins where the mating opportunity was the decisive moment.

233.label: Player makes a developing or positional move while overlooking that their opponent's queen can capture a hanging or inadequately defended piece.
233.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a piece (most often queen, bishop, or pawn) without capturing anything (61% non-captures), and the resulting position allows the opponent's queen to win material—Maia's recommended response is overwhelmingly a queen capture (94% queen moves, 100% captures). The material signature shows the player's move frequently loses or hangs material (27% loses, 24% hangs), with a devastating median eval loss of 421 centipawns. The eval trajectory shows these errors are game-changing: 36% turn drawn positions into losing ones, and 12% throw away winning positions. The tactical motifs reveal the underlying causes: players overlook king safety issues (uncastled or centralized kings), miss knight forks that win material after the queen recaptures, lose tempo allowing devastating queen interventions, or fail to recognize hanging pieces that the opponent's queen can scoop up. The positions are predominantly middlegame (73%) with active piece play where the queen's long-range attacking power is maximized. The common thread is that players focus on their own plans while failing to account for the opponent's queen having a powerful tactical capture available.

236.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move when a forcing check (often a queen check) wins material or delivers a decisive attack.
236.description: This feature fires when a player makes a non-capturing, non-checking move (100% no capture, 0% checks played) while Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100% queen, 100% check) that wins significant material (100% missed winning material). The positions are overwhelmingly middlegame (95%) and the cost is severe (median 410cp lost), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losses (drawn->losing 33%, winning->drawn 14%, winning->losing 10%). The tactical motifs—tempo_loss (50%), back_rank (25%), hanging_piece (25%)—reveal that the missed checks exploit concrete vulnerabilities: back-rank mates, loose pieces, or forcing sequences that gain decisive tempo. The per-position analyses confirm players retreat passively or play aimless moves when a queen check (sometimes a sacrifice initiating a forcing sequence) would have been decisive. The player's actual moves (rooks 29%, queens 24%, knights 24%, pawns 14%) are quiet repositioning moves that squander the initiative entirely.

229.label: Retreating the queen passively in the opening instead of executing a tactical capture, losing critical development tempo.
229.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern where Black has an early queen on d5 (typically from a Scandinavian-type structure) alongside a bishop on g4, and instead of playing the tactically correct Bxf3 capture (winning a knight or disrupting White's structure), the player retreats the queen to a passive square (Qd8, Qd7, Qe6, or Qa5). The material signature shows 100% queen moves with no captures, all rated 'safe' in isolation—nothing is immediately hung—yet the eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn->losing with a median loss of 311 centipawns. The boards are almost entirely identical positions (Nc6/Bg4/Qd5 vs Nc3/Nf3/d4), confirming this is one recurring opening scenario. The Opus analysis and tags (tempo_loss 83%, missed_tactic, development, piece_activity) reveal that the queen retreat wastes a critical tempo in the opening, allowing White to seize a commanding development advantage, while the missed Bxf3 tactic would have maintained equality by exploiting the pin or winning material. The mistake is tactical in nature: a concrete tactic exists but is missed in favor of a passive retreat.

237.label: King moves that leave the player's queen hanging or ignore capturing the opponent's undefended queen in endgame positions.
237.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (88% king moves) in a way that catastrophically overlooks queen-level tactics. The material signature shows 62% of moves hang a piece and the median eval loss is 10000 centipawns (full point swing or mate), with 62% of cases converting a winning position into a losing one. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motif is hanging_piece (91%) with recurring tags of missed_capture, hanging_queen, and queen_blunder. The concrete pattern across the top boards is strikingly consistent: in won endgame positions, the player makes a passive or aimless king move while either (a) their own queen is left undefended and capturable, or (b) the opponent's queen is en prise and could be taken freely—often by a simple pawn capture. Maia's suggested moves confirm this, showing queen moves (50%) and captures of the opponent's queen (100%) as the correct continuations. This represents a fundamental attention failure in endgames where the player, perhaps focused on king activity or pawn promotion, completely overlooks immediate queen-level tactical obligations.

235.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move that neglects king safety or tactical threats, allowing the opponent to exploit exposed pieces or attack the king.
235.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make quiet, non-capturing moves (100% no captures, 0% checks) — typically pawn pushes (43%) or queen moves (29%) — that fail to address critical tactical demands in the position. The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (71%) in the immediate sense (nothing is directly hung), yet they miss winning tactics 43% of the time, indicating the player chose a passive continuation over an active one. The dominant motifs of king_safety (50%) and hanging_piece (33%), combined with tags like missed_tactic, tempo_loss, and exposed_king, reveal that these are positions where the player needed to act decisively — either exploiting the opponent's weak king or defending their own — but instead played a slow, positional-looking move. The eval trajectory (median 124cp lost, with positions going from drawn to losing or getting worse) confirms these aren't catastrophic one-move blunders but significant positional/tactical oversights where tempo and initiative are squandered. The boards show middlegame positions with open lines, exposed kings, and tactical tension where a concrete forcing move was required but the player defaulted to a quiet developing or prophylactic move instead.

238.label: Player makes a non-forcing move instead of delivering a winning queen check that Maia consistently identifies.
238.description: Across all top-activating positions, Maia's recommended move is always a queen check (100% queen, 100% check), while the player instead plays passive pawn moves (42%), queen moves to suboptimal squares (33%), or rook moves (25%) that fail to exploit the position's tactical potential. The material signature shows 42% of these moves hang material and 100% miss winning material, indicating the player squanders a decisive attacking opportunity. The eval trajectory confirms severe consequences: a median loss of 250 centipawns, with positions going from winning to drawn (25%) or winning to losing (17%). The positional tags—exposed_king_not_exploited, attacking_potential_squandered, queen_misplacement—all converge on the same theme: the player had a powerful queen check available that would have won material or delivered a decisive attack against an exposed king, but instead played a quiet or repositioning move that allowed the opponent to consolidate. The board positions consistently show queens already on strong diagonals or files near the enemy king, with the missed check being the critical blow.

239.label: Losing critical tempo in won or drawn endgames by making aimless king or piece moves instead of executing the winning technique.
239.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material lost immediately, no captures) but catastrophically loses winning chances through tempo loss. The material signature shows king moves (50%), rook moves (25%), and queen moves (25%) with no captures—these are quiet repositioning moves, not tactical blunders. The eval trajectory is devastating: median 9443 centipawns lost, with positions going from winning to losing or drawn to losing. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (46%), appearing in nearly every example. The concrete positions reveal the pattern clearly: simplified endgames (KR vs K, KQ vs K+pieces, rook endgames) where the player had a forced mate or decisive advantage but played an aimless move that either let the opponent escape (mate-in-14 becoming mate-in-25, or forced mate collapsing to +557). The tactical analyses confirm this—moves like Rh3 instead of a constructive approach, or king retreats that allow defensive resources. These are players who reached winning endgames but lacked the technique to convert, wasting moves while the opponent's defensive chances improve or drawing mechanisms activate.

240.label: Player makes a passive or structural move instead of executing a forcing sequence that exploits advanced passed pawns.
240.description: This feature fires in middlegame positions where the player has an advanced passed pawn (often on the 6th or 7th rank) and a concrete forcing sequence available—typically involving a rook exchange or simplification that leads to promotion—but instead plays a passive or structurally weakening move (rook retreats, pawn pushes that weaken squares, quiet queen moves). The material signature shows mostly safe moves (67%) that don't immediately hang anything, yet the median eval loss of 205 centipawns indicates a substantial missed opportunity. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%) that capture rooks, suggesting the correct plan involves exchanging rooks to clear the path for the passed pawn. The dominant motifs (passed_pawn 50%, pawn_endgame 50%) and tags (advanced_passed_pawns, forcing_sequence_missed, exchange_then_promote, simplification) all converge on the same theme: the player fails to calculate the concrete tactical sequence that converts the passed pawn advantage, opting instead for slow moves that allow the opponent to reorganize. The trajectory (winning->winning 67%, winning->drawn 11%) shows these are positions where the win is slipping rather than immediately thrown away, consistent with a failure to execute rather than a gross blunder.

242.label: Bishop or queen moves that fatally expose the player's own king to tactical threats.
242.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a bishop (67%) or queen (33%) to capture material (pawn 67%, rook 33%), but in doing so fatally compromises their own king's safety. The material signature shows the move is slightly losing (median net -2.0), and the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences (median ~100 pawns lost in eval), with games swinging from winning to drawn or drawn to losing. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are king_safety and hanging_piece, with tags including exposed_king, queen_penetration, and subtle_king_move. The concrete positions show patterns where a piece capture or aggressive piece move neglects the king's vulnerability—for instance, moving a king to f8 exposes it to a lethal knight+queen attack, or capturing a knight on g3 leaves a critical piece undefended. The opponent's best response typically involves a king move (67%) that escapes or a pawn advance, while recapturing the now-undefended bishop (67%) or knight (33%). The core mistake is prioritizing material gain or piece activity while overlooking that the resulting position leaves the player's king dangerously exposed to immediate tactical exploitation.

243.label: Player makes a passive queen move instead of delivering or pursuing checkmate, throwing away a decisive attack.
243.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing queen move that catastrophically misses a forced checkmate or winning tactical sequence. The material signature shows 100% queen moves with no captures and no checks—these are passive queen repositionings rather than active attacking moves. The eval trajectory reveals a median loss of ~9361 centipawns, indicating missed mates or near-mate conversions (winning->winning with massive eval drop, or losing->drawn where the opponent similarly squandered a mate). The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) and fork (33%), with tags including missed_mate_in_one, exposed_king, and back_rank_pattern. Maia's recommended moves consistently deliver check (100%) using queens or rooks, often involving rook-to-seventh, queen-rook coordination, or knight forks—all aggressive continuations the player failed to find. The boards show positions ripe with mating nets (Re7#, Ndb5+, back-rank threats) where the player instead played an aimless queen shuffle, allowing the opponent to escape or equalize.

241.label: Ignoring central captures or developing moves in the opening, wasting tempo on passive or irrelevant moves that allow the opponent to seize the initiative.
241.description: This feature detects a specific opening-phase blunder pattern where a player, facing a position with available central pawn captures or natural developing moves, instead plays a passive or tempo-losing move (often a pawn push or quiet minor piece move) that hangs material or cedes a decisive positional advantage. The material signature shows 67% of moves hang something (non-captures that leave pieces or pawns en prise), with a median net loss of -1.0, and critically 100% of positions are in the opening phase. The trajectory is stark: every instance converts a drawn position into a losing one, with a median eval loss of 288 centipawns—indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding mistakes. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is tempo_loss (43%), with recurring tags of development, pawn_structure, and center_control. The concrete examples consistently show players ignoring strong central captures (dxe5, exd5, cxd5) in favor of quiet moves like Nf3, Be2, b3, or f4 that fail to address the tactical demands of the position. Maia's recommended moves (83% pawn captures) confirm that the correct play was almost always to take in the center, maintaining equality, while the played moves squander the position by losing critical tempo.

246.label: Trading rooks when an intermediate tactic (check, fork, or zwischenzug) should have been inserted first.
246.description: This feature fires on positions where a player voluntarily trades rooks (100% rook moves capturing rooks, net material median 0.0 confirming an exchange rather than a blunder) but misses a much stronger intermediate tactic. The Maia-recommended moves are knight moves (100%), often delivering check (100%), indicating that a knight fork or zwischenzug check was available before committing to the rook trade. The dominant motifs — fork (40%), king_safety (40%), and move-order tags (zwischenzug, intermediate_check, knight_fork) — all point to the same pattern: the player executed a reasonable-looking rook exchange but in the wrong move order, forfeiting a winning tactic (100% missed winning material). The eval trajectory (median 189cp lost, with positions going from winning to still winning but much less so, or even losing to winning for the opponent) confirms these are costly move-order errors in the middlegame where inserting a forcing intermediate move first would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate.

245.label: Playing a slow move (often f3) instead of capturing a pinned piece, throwing away a winning advantage.
245.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing move—most often a pawn push like f3—while missing a decisive tactical capture of a pinned knight (Maia's move is 100% bishop capturing knight). The positions overwhelmingly arise in the opening (76%) with a bishop pinning a knight (pin motif 23%, hanging_piece 31%), and the player chooses a tempo-losing prophylactic move instead of exploiting the pin immediately. The eval trajectory confirms this is a devastating missed tactic: 81% of cases go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 366 centipawns. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies move-order errors where playing f3 before the critical Bxf6 capture allows the opponent to escape the pin, permanently squandering a piece-winning opportunity. The boards consistently show a Bg5/Bb5 pinning a knight with ...Bg4 also present, and the player wastes time with f3 rather than executing the capture.

248.label: King moves that waste tempo in won pawn endgames near promotion, slightly delaying a forced win.
248.description: This feature identifies king moves in clearly won pawn endgames (100% endgame phase, 100% winning->winning trajectory) where the player plays a king move instead of the optimal pawn advance (Maia consistently recommends pawn moves). The material outcome is 'safe' with negligible centipawn loss (median 3cp), meaning the position remains completely won but the path to victory is marginally suboptimal. The top boards reveal a highly specific pattern: positions with advanced passed pawns on the 6th/7th rank where the player moves their king instead of pushing the pawn toward promotion. The motifs—passed_pawn (33%), tempo_loss (27%), promotion_error (13%), pawn_endgame (13%)—collectively paint a picture of unnecessary king shuffling when the critical decision is pawn promotion timing. The positions (e.g., Kf6f7 instead of g7, Kh6h7 instead of g7, Ke7e8 instead of f8=Q) show players instinctively centralizing or advancing their king when the pawn push is more precise, costing tempi in the mating sequence without jeopardizing the result.

244.label: Failing to address a dominant enemy knight, losing tempo and allowing tactical exploitation in the opening/middlegame.
244.description: This feature fires when players make slow, non-confrontational moves that ignore a powerfully-placed enemy knight, resulting in severe evaluation drops (median 279cp lost). The material signature shows the player's move is often 'safe' (67%) or 'hangs' a piece (30%) — meaning they aren't trading or capturing but instead playing passive moves while a dominant knight sits unchallenged. The Maia best-move signal is emphatic: 80% of the time the correct response was a knight move, and 93% of suggested captures target an enemy knight — indicating the critical missed action was capturing or challenging that knight. The tactical analysis confirms this with tempo_loss (50%) as the dominant motif, along with tags like missed_tactic, piece_activity, and knight_outpost. The top boards repeatedly show positions with strong centralized knights (Nd5, Ne4, Nd4, Ne5) where the player ignores the knight to castle, develop passively, or make a slow rook move. The eval trajectory (28% winning→drawn, 17% drawn→losing, 8% winning→losing) shows this is predominantly a 'throwing the advantage' pattern occurring in openings (63%) and middlegames (37%), where one tempo of inaction against a dominant knight allows the opponent to consolidate or launch a decisive attack.

247.label: Opening moves that leave the queen en prise on a diagonal, typically to an active bishop.
247.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where a player makes a routine developing or pawn move while completely overlooking that their queen is hanging — almost always along a diagonal attacked by an enemy bishop. The material signature shows the move itself is primarily a non-capture pawn or knight move that 'hangs' a piece (75% hangs), and the missed winning material is 100%, meaning the opponent always had a strong capture available. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (91%) with the most common tag being 'queen_hanging' (5 occurrences). Concrete examples show patterns like Bg4 attacking Qd1 along the diagonal while White plays an oblivious pawn push, or Nf6 moving away and leaving Qd8 exposed to Bg5. The eval trajectory is catastrophic — median loss of 859 centipawns — flipping positions from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-losing. This is a pure one-move tactical oversight in the opening where the player fails to notice their queen is directly attacked.

251.label: Pawn moves in the opening that fatally weaken king safety, ignoring hanging pieces or tactical threats.
251.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (72% opening) where the player pushes a pawn (38%) or makes a minor piece move that catastrophically weakens their king's position while ignoring a superior knight retreat or capture recommended by Maia (98% knight). The material signature shows 57% 'safe' and 28% 'hangs'—meaning the move itself doesn't always lose material immediately, but it creates devastating tactical vulnerabilities. The dominant motifs are king_safety (42%) and hanging_piece (33%), with the concrete positions showing classic patterns: f6/f3 weakening diagonals near the king, ignoring undefended knights, or making pawn moves that open lines toward their own king. The eval trajectory is severe—55% of cases swing from drawn to losing with a median loss of 322 centipawns—indicating these are not positional inaccuracies but game-deciding tactical oversights. The missed winning material rate of 77% confirms that a strong tactical resource (usually a knight maneuver) existed but was overlooked in favor of a structurally or defensively catastrophic pawn push.

252.label: Passive or aimless moves that ignore mounting king safety threats, often in already difficult positions.
252.description: This feature identifies moves where the player neglects critical king safety concerns. The material signature shows mostly non-capturing moves (89% no capture) with rooks, pawns, and kings that are frequently unsafe (43% hang material), yet the dominant motif is overwhelmingly king_safety (73%). The eval trajectory reveals these occur predominantly in already-losing positions (39% losing->losing), suggesting players who are under pressure make passive or misdirected moves rather than addressing the tactical threats against their king. Maia's recommended moves are often active rook moves (64%) that frequently deliver check (32%) or capture pawns (43%), indicating the opponent had concrete attacking resources that the player failed to counter. The example positions consistently show exposed kings with active enemy pieces nearby, and the player's chosen moves (like Kg1, Kh3, Kg3) are often king retreats or quiet piece shuffles that fail to address the incoming attack, sometimes accelerating checkmate. The positions are almost entirely middlegame (96%), where king safety is most critical.

249.label: Player overlooks a simple back-rank checkmate in one move, making an irrelevant move instead.
249.description: All three signals converge on a single, clear pattern: players missing an immediately available back-rank checkmate. The Opus analysis identifies back_rank as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with tags like 'missed_mate_in_one', 'one_move_mate', and 'back_rank_mate' appearing repeatedly. The material/position signature shows Maia (the engine) always recommends a check (100%) using the queen or rook to capture on the back rank, while the player instead makes a 'safe' but purposeless move (75% safe, no capture 50%) — often a queen or pawn move that ignores the winning tactic entirely. The eval trajectory is devastating: the median eval lost is over 100 pawns (mate missed), with 50% of cases flipping from losing to winning for the opponent, confirming these are positions where an immediate mate was available but the player's random move hands the advantage (or the game) back. The boards confirm kings trapped on the back rank (h1, k1, k8) with queens and rooks perfectly positioned to deliver mate, yet players move elsewhere out of pattern blindness.

250.label: Unsound early bishop/knight captures on f7/f2 with check that lose material after the king recaptures.
250.description: This feature identifies a very specific opening mistake pattern: playing a bishop or knight to capture the f7 (or f2) pawn, usually with check, in the early opening. The material signature shows the player always captures a pawn (100%) with a bishop (62%) or knight (38%), delivers check (69%), but ends up slightly down (net -2.0, meaning they lose roughly a minor piece for a pawn). The eval trajectory confirms this is catastrophic: 100% of cases go from drawn to losing, with a median loss of ~300 centipawns. The boards make the pattern crystal clear—nearly every position shows Bxf7+ or Nxf7 (or the mirror ...Bxf2+/Nxf2) on move 3-6, the classic 'cheapo' attempt that looks aggressive but is tactically unsound because the attacking piece has no support and the king recapture leaves the attacker down material with no compensation. The Opus analysis tags (unsound_sacrifice, premature_attack, tempo_loss) confirm these are speculative sacrifices without adequate follow-up, not legitimate gambits.

254.label: Moving a major piece (rook or queen) to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured.
254.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a major piece—most often a rook (50%) or queen (25%)—to a square where it hangs undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it outright. The material signature is stark: 75% of moves result in a 'hangs' classification (a non-capture that drops a piece), with a median net material loss of -5.0 points, and Maia's recommended move captures a rook 100% of the time, confirming the piece was left en prise. The Opus tactical analysis reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (71%), supported by tags like queen_blunder, hung_piece, en_prise, and undefended_piece. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings (median -9743 centipawns lost), indicating these aren't subtle positional errors but game-ending blunders. Concrete examples include a rook moved to e2 where it's captured by Re1, a queen placed on a square attacked by a rook, and failing to notice a piece is unguarded on its destination square. The pattern is consistent: the player overlooks that the square they're moving their major piece to is directly attacked, resulting in immediate material loss.

253.label: Playing a routine developing or pawn move in the opening while missing a free capture of an undefended enemy piece.
253.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening-phase blunder (91% opening) where the player pushes a pawn (82%) or makes a developing move that is itself safe (96% safe material outcome), but completely overlooks that an opponent's piece is hanging and can be captured for free. The eval trajectory confirms these are serious mistakes—median 366cp lost, with 55% converting a winning position into a drawn one and 18% going from drawn to losing. The Opus analysis is decisive: 67% hanging_piece motif, with recurring tags like missed_capture, free_material, and opening_blunder. The concrete positions show a striking pattern: bishops on g4 or b4 left en prise while the player plays f3, d3, or Nd4 instead of simply taking the piece (e.g., Qxg4 or cxb4).
