Maia's recommended moves confirm this—64% of best moves are bishop captures. The player gets absorbed in their own development plan and fails to notice the opponent left a piece undefended.

255.label: Player moves their queen to an undefended square where it can be captured for free, squandering a winning or significant advantage.
255.description: All three signals converge on a consistent pattern: the player moves their queen (57% of moves played) to a square where it hangs with no compensation, resulting in catastrophic material loss (median -9.0 material, 82% 'hangs' classification). The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with the Opus summaries explicitly describing queens placed on undefended squares. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 9225 centipawns—essentially converting wins or near-mates into drastically worse positions (46% winning->winning suggests they still had enough advantage to survive, 18% losing->winning reflects the opponent's perspective improving). The top boards corroborate this: queens on d3, f4, e3, g5, e6, c5 are placed where they can be immediately captured. Maia's suggested moves frequently involve captures (rook 21%, bishop 14%, pawn 25%), indicating the engine saw the tactic to win the hanging queen. This is a pure tactical oversight—not an exchange or positional error—where the player simply fails to notice their queen is unprotected on its destination square.

258.label: Trading a piece into a losing pawn endgame where the removed piece was essential for defense.
258.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player initiates a trade (bishop captures knight/bishop, or rook captures rook) that transitions into a lost pawn endgame. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves making trades (net material median 0.0), confirming these are exchanges rather than blunders. The eval trajectory shows all cases go from losing to deeper losing (median 123cp lost), indicating the player made an already difficult position decisively worse. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags these as pawn_endgame (92%) with recurring themes of simplification_error, passed_pawn exploitation, and king_activity — the player fatally misjudges the resulting pawn structure after removing their last defensive piece. The traded piece (bishop, knight, or rook) was providing critical long-range defense, blockading capabilities, or compensating for a passive king, and without it the opponent's pawn majority or passed pawn becomes unstoppable. The FENs confirm sparse endgame positions where one side voluntarily exchanges into a technically lost pawn ending.

256.label: Playing a slow or misdirected piece move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate a previously lost position.
256.description: This feature fires on moves where a player holds a winning or advantageous position but squanders it through a tempo-losing move instead of executing the decisive continuation. The material signature shows diverse piece types being moved (pawns, knights, bishops, rooks roughly equally) with 83% being non-captures—these are quiet, repositioning moves rather than active strikes. Critically, 44% of these moves hang material, yet the median net material is 0.0, suggesting the immediate loss isn't always captured material but rather positional collapse. The eval trajectory confirms this is primarily a 'throwing away a win' pattern: winning->drawn (19%) and drawn->losing (19%) with a massive median loss of 305 centipawns. The Opus analysis is dominated by tempo_loss (50% of motifs, plus king_safety and missed_tactic tags), showing players making slow moves—retreats, prophylactic shuffles, or move-order errors—at moments demanding immediate tactical execution. The Maia baseline (97% pawn moves) suggests the correct continuation was typically a straightforward pawn advance or breakthrough, but the player instead chose a piece move that lost the initiative. The concrete examples reinforce this: Ng5 before Bxf7+ (move-order error), Qa6 losing tempo against an uncastled king, Bf4 developing passively when only one move works. The unifying thread is a failure to strike at the critical moment, choosing a 'natural' but slow move that lets the opponent escape.

259.chip: Losing Rook Trade Into Pawn Endgame
259.label: Trading rooks into a lost king-and-pawn ending by misjudging the resulting pawn structure or king activity.
259.description: This feature fires when a player initiates or accepts a rook exchange (100% rook captures rook, net material median 0.0 — a clean trade) that transitions into a losing pawn endgame. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 311 centipawns, with 50% of cases going from drawn to losing and 43% making an already difficult position decisively worse. The Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags these as pawn_endgame transitions (86%) where the player misjudged critical factors like king proximity to passed pawns, pawn structure weaknesses, or tempo. Maia's recommended alternatives are non-capturing rook moves (100% no capture), indicating the correct plan was to maintain the rook on the board and preserve defensive resources. The top boards confirm the pattern: simplified rook endgames where one side trades into a technically lost K+P ending, failing to recognize that the opponent's king activity, passed pawn potential, or pawn structure advantages become decisive once rooks leave the board.

261.label: Knight moves to vulnerable squares in the opening, getting trapped or creating hanging pieces.
261.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening-phase mistake where players move knights (59% of moves) to squares that appear active but are tactically vulnerable. The positions are 100% opening phase, and the dominant motifs are trapped_piece (40%) and hanging_piece (30%), with common tags emphasizing tempo_loss and development issues. The eval trajectory shows these moves typically convert drawn positions into losing ones (76% drawn->losing), with a median cost of 285 centipawns—approximately a full minor piece. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern: knights jump to central squares like d4 or e5 where they look aggressive but can be attacked with tempo (e.g., ...c6 hitting both a knight and bishop, or pawns trapping the knight). Maia's preferred moves (88% knight moves) suggest the correct idea often still involves the knight but to a safer square. The 35% 'hangs' rate confirms these knights are being placed where they can be won outright, while the 47% 'missed winning material' rate shows players are choosing flashy knight hops over concrete tactical opportunities already available in the position.

264.label: Advancing a passed pawn without adequate king support in the endgame, allowing it to be captured or neutralized.
264.description: This feature detects a highly specific endgame error where a player pushes a passed pawn prematurely (pawn moves account for 100% of activating moves) without first establishing the necessary king support or coordination. The material signature shows these moves overwhelmingly hang material (75%), with a median cost of -1.0 (the pawn itself), because the advanced pawn is simply captured. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: a median of 507 centipawns lost, often converting wins into draws or drawn positions into losses. The positional analysis reinforces this with dominant motifs of pawn_endgame (36%), passed_pawn (27%), and promotion_error (9%), along with recurring tags for king_activity and tempo_loss. The concrete positions all show pure pawn endgames or bishop+pawn endgames where the correct plan involved king centralization or maneuvering before advancing the pawn. Instead, the premature push allows the opponent's king or piece to capture the pawn or reach a critical square, squandering the advantage the passed pawn provided.

260.label: Moving the king into an exposed position where the opponent has a forced checkmate or devastating check sequence.
260.description: This feature detects positions where a player moves their king (57% of moves are king moves) into a square that allows the opponent to deliver check (Maia gives check 100% of the time in response) with a mating net or forced mate sequence. The dominant tags—exposed_king(7), mating_net(3), forced_mate(3), king_walk(2), tempo_loss(5)—all point to the king voluntarily walking into danger. The position summaries explicitly describe kings walking into mating nets, onto open files, or into squares vulnerable to back-rank checks. The eval trajectory shows 50% losing->losing (accelerating an existing loss by allowing immediate mate instead of prolonged resistance) and 43% losing->winning (likely mislabeled or reflecting positions where the opponent gains a forced mate). The material signature shows 'safe' 64% because the move itself doesn't hang a piece—it hangs the king by walking into a tactical mating pattern. The missed winning material at 100% confirms these players consistently overlook the opponent's knight or rook delivering check with mate to follow. This is fundamentally a king safety tactical error in middle-to-endgame positions.

257.label: In simplified endgame positions, the player makes a move that leaves a piece or major unit completely undefended and capturable.
257.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions (75% endgame phase) where the player makes a move that hangs a piece outright (75% 'hangs' outcome, meaning a non-capture that drops material). The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 90%, and the tag 'rook_endgame' appears in half the examples, indicating these are typically simplified positions with rooks and pawns. The median material cost is -4.0 (roughly a whole rook), and the median eval lost is 697 centipawns — catastrophic blunders. The tactical analysis reveals a consistent pattern: players make slow moves (pawn advances, king walks, or repositioning moves) while ignoring that their own piece is en prise or will become en prise. Maia's recommended moves give check 100% of the time and frequently capture hanging material, confirming that the opponent's piece was simply left undefended. The trajectory (50% losing->losing, 25% winning->drawn) shows these often occur when players are already under pressure and lose focus on piece safety in the simplified position, or when they had a won endgame and threw it away with a careless move that drops a piece.

263.label: Ignoring concrete tactical threats in the opening, leaving pieces hanging or allowing forks.
263.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players in the opening phase (100% opening) make developing or natural-looking moves (pawns, bishops, knights) that ignore concrete tactical threats already present on the board. The material signature shows 75% of moves simply hang a piece (non-captures that leave material en prise), with a median cost of ~262 centipawns—typically converting a drawn position into a losing one (62% drawn->losing). The Opus analysis reveals the common thread: players prioritize development or routine moves while overlooking opponent batteries, forks, and tactical pressure (dominant motifs: hanging_piece 50%, fork 25%). Tags like 'missed_tactic', 'piece_activity', 'development', and 'tempo_loss' confirm these are moves that look reasonable from a strategic standpoint but fatally ignore immediate tactical obligations. Examples include ignoring Bc4+Ne5 pressure on f7, overlooking discovered attacks after Nxc6, and making illusory 'active' knight sacrifices with no compensation. The pattern is specifically an opening-phase failure to prioritize tactics over development.

265.label: Moving a key attacking piece away from its optimal diagonal or square, squandering a winning initiative.
265.description: This feature fires when a player moves a bishop or queen away from a critical attacking position, abandoning a winning tactical opportunity. The material signature shows bishops (26%) and queens (23%) are the most commonly moved pieces, with 72% involving no capture—these are repositioning moves rather than exchanges. The devastating median eval loss of 380 centipawns with 98% missed winning material confirms these moves squander concrete tactical wins. The trajectory (winning->drawn 26%, drawn->losing 15%) shows players throwing away favorable positions. The motif layer reveals why: pins (33%), trapped pieces (11%), and king safety themes (11%) were available but ignored. The tactical analyses consistently describe players moving an attacking piece away from its optimal square—abandoning a pin, releasing pressure on a critical diagonal, or missing a geometric exploitation—when the position demanded maintaining or intensifying the attack. Maia overwhelmingly preferred bishop moves (92%), suggesting the correct continuation typically involved keeping the bishop on its attacking diagonal rather than rerouting it.

262.label: Player makes a minor move while leaving a piece undefended or ignoring an opponent's tactical threat, resulting in significant material loss.
262.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a seemingly routine move (often a pawn or knight move, 50% combined) that hangs material (53% of outcomes) rather than addressing a critical tactical threat on the board. The median material loss of -2.0 confirms pieces are being dropped, not traded. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (90%), suggesting the correct response typically involved activating or repositioning a rook to defend a threatened piece or exploit an existing tactical opportunity. The Opus analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (50%), with 'tempo_loss' (25%) indicating these moves waste time on non-urgent tasks while a concrete threat demands attention. The eval trajectory shows massive damage (median 341cp lost), often converting drawn positions to lost ones (33%) or deepening existing disadvantages. The concrete examples reinforce this: Qd2 ignoring Bxh1, capturing on a6 before saving an undefended bishop on g4, taking a pawn instead of trapping a piece. In each case, the player pursues a secondary goal while a primary tactical obligation—defending or exploiting a hanging piece—goes unaddressed.

267.label: Pieces abandon active posts in endgames, hanging material or squandering winning advantages.
267.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player moves a piece (most often a king or rook) away from an active or critical post, leaving material undefended or surrendering a decisive positional advantage. The material signature shows 61% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material) with a median cost of -1.0 material, predominantly in endgame positions (68%). The eval trajectory confirms these are primarily advantage-squandering errors: 39% convert winning positions into drawn ones, with a median loss of 244 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (44%), passed_pawn (22%), and tempo_loss (22%), with common tags including rook_endgame, piece_activity, and missed_tactic. The concrete examples consistently show rooks leaving dominant files (e.g., Rxh7 abandoning the c-file), kings stepping into vulnerable squares (e.g., Ke5 leaving pawns undefended), or passive moves that surrender tempo and allow the opponent to activate. The pattern is distinctly about misplacing pieces in simplified positions where activity and piece coordination are paramount.

266.label: King moves in endgames that miss available captures of hanging or undefended pieces, worsening an already difficult position.
266.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern in endgame positions where the player moves their king (75% of moves are king moves) instead of capturing available material. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (75%) with the dominant motif being hanging_piece (43%) and the most common tags including missed_capture (6 instances). The Maia engine consistently recommends capturing pieces (queen 50%, knight 25%, rook 25%), indicating that significant material was freely available but overlooked. The material outcome is mostly 'safe' (75%) meaning the king move itself doesn't immediately lose material, but the missed captures represent substantial missed opportunities — 100% of positions show missed winning material. The eval trajectory shows these occur in already-losing positions (50% losing->losing, 50% losing->winning), with a median cost of 81 centipawns, though several examples show catastrophic collapses. The concrete examples confirm this: retreating a king instead of capturing an undefended queen (Kb6 instead of cxd5), moving a king instead of capturing a knight (Kc3 instead of taking on d4), and passive king moves that ignore hanging pieces throughout the endgame phase.

268.label: Premature pawn advance in a won pawn endgame that throws away the win by destroying critical pawn structure or losing tempo/opposition.
268.description: This feature fires on a highly specific and recurring endgame mistake: in a pure pawn endgame (100% endgame phase, 83% pawn_endgame motif), the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) that appears safe (no material is immediately lost) but catastrophically squanders a winning or drawn position (88% winning->drawn, 12% drawn->losing, median 538cp lost). The tactical analyses reveal the mechanism: these pawn advances prematurely break pawn structure, surrender opposition or tempo, or dissolve connected pawn advantages that were the foundation of the win. Tags like tempo_loss, opposition, theoretical_draw, and connected_pawns confirm the positional nature of the error—the player pushes a pawn when patient king maneuvering (king_activity) was required. The boards consistently show positions where alternatives like king penetration or maintaining pawn tension would have preserved the advantage, but the instinct to advance pawns converts technically won positions into theoretical draws.

270.label: Moving a piece that was guarding a long diagonal, leaving material hanging to an opponent's fianchettoed bishop.
270.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves a piece (most often a bishop or pawn, sometimes a knight) that was serving as the sole defender of a square on a long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1), leaving a pawn or piece hanging to the opponent's fianchettoed bishop. The material signature shows 96% of moves are non-captures that hang material (median loss of ~1 piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings—39% go from drawn to losing with a median cost of 367 centipawns. The tactical analysis unanimously tags 'hanging_piece' as the motif, with recurring themes of fianchetto_exploitation, long_diagonal pressure, and king_safety concerns. The top boards consistently show an opponent's bishop on b2 or b7 in a fianchetto structure, and the blundering move removes the only piece blocking or defending along that diagonal (e.g., Bf1-d3 leaving g2 unguarded, or Bf8-c5 abandoning defense of g7). This occurs overwhelmingly in the opening (64%) or early middlegame (36%), when players develop pieces without recognizing their defensive role on the long diagonal.

269.label: Player executes a check or capture with a bishop that trades material but loses critical tempo or misorders the tactical sequence.
269.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers check (83% of cases) with a bishop (67%) that captures a rook (67%), resulting in a material trade (58%) rather than a clean win. The median eval loss of 244 centipawns reveals these aren't neutral exchanges—they're costly tactical errors. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss, promotion_error, premature_combination) combined with tags like move_order_error and premature_combination paint a clear picture: the player rushes to execute a forcing sequence (check + capture) before completing the necessary preparatory moves. Maia's preferred moves (pawns, knights, queens with no checks) suggest the engine sees quieter, more patient continuations. The boards confirm this—positions like Bxf7+ before Nc4 activation, or premature queen promotions, or bishop captures that simplify when the position demanded maintaining tension. The trajectory shows these often throw away winning or drawn positions (winning->drawn 8%, drawn->losing 8%), with 67% missing winning material entirely. The pattern is a player who sees a flashy forcing line and pulls the trigger one move too early, settling for an exchange when precise move ordering would have won decisively.

271.label: In a losing endgame, the player makes a king move that fatally neglects an opponent's advanced passed pawn, allowing immediate promotion or forced mate.
271.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a way that is materially 'safe' in the immediate sense (no hanging pieces), but catastrophically misses the critical need to address the opponent's passed pawn. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (100%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss and deflection—the king move either loses a crucial tempo or allows the opponent to advance/promote a passer with tempo. The eval trajectory shows these are already losing positions that become utterly hopeless (median 9452 centipawns lost), converting slow technical losses into forced mates or immediate promotions. Maia consistently finds king captures of pawns or pawn-stopping moves that the player overlooked. The concrete board positions confirm the pattern: advanced passed pawns on the 6th/7th rank where the player's king wanders away from the promotion square, allowing unstoppable queening. This is not a material blunder in the traditional sense but a fundamental endgame error of prioritization—failing to respect the most dangerous passed pawn.

272.label: Queen recaptures a bishop on e2/e7 without noticing a hanging piece or missed intermediate move, turning a viable position into a serious deficit.
272.description: Across all top activations, the player uses their queen to recapture a bishop (usually on e2 or e7), completing what appears to be a simple exchange. The material signature confirms a trade (net 0.0), yet the eval trajectory shows catastrophic positional loss (median 369cp), shifting from drawn to losing or winning to drawn. The tactical layer reveals why: in 67% of cases a piece is left hanging after the queen recapture, and in most positions there was a critical intermediate move (zwischenzug) or better move order that should have been played first. By reflexively recapturing with the queen, the player misses tactics like capturing with tempo, exploiting pins, or maintaining piece coordination. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening/early middlegame phase where development and piece activity matter most, and the premature recapture forfeits these advantages. This is not a material blunder in the traditional sense but a trade-execution error: the exchange itself is reasonable, but the timing and move order make it a serious positional mistake.

278.label: Moving a piece (typically knight or bishop) to a square where it can be captured for free, dropping approximately a minor piece.
278.description: All three signals converge on a clear pattern: the player moves a minor piece (knight 29%, bishop 23%) or occasionally a queen (15%) to a square where it is simply left undefended and captured. The material signature shows 76% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -1.0 (consistent with losing a minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly blunders—median 267 centipawns lost—with 16% swinging from drawn to losing positions. The Opus tactical analysis tags 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif at 75%, and the example summaries explicitly describe pieces placed on squares where they are trivially captured (e.g., queen placed where a bishop simply takes it, knight moved to an undefended square). The player typically isn't capturing anything (89% no capture), just relocating a piece to a tactically vulnerable square without noticing the opponent's attacking resources. This is a pure oversight blunder rather than a positional misjudgment or unfavorable trade—the piece is simply left en prise.

274.label: Hanging a minor piece in the opening by making a premature or misguided knight/bishop move that leaves it undefended.
274.description: This feature detects opening-phase blunders where a player moves a knight (67%) or bishop (33%) to a square where it is left hanging or inadequately defended, costing approximately a full minor piece (median -3.0 material, median 396 centipawns lost). The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing to losing (100%), indicating these are not speculative sacrifices but genuine oversights. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (64%), with supporting tags of opening_mistake, premature_attack, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show recurring patterns: bishops capturing defended pawns (e.g., Bxe7 capturing a pawn defended by multiple pieces, or Bxf2+ winning a pawn but losing the bishop), or knights/bishops moving to squares where they can be captured for free. Maia consistently recommends simple bishop-takes-pawn recaptures (100% bishop moves capturing pawns), confirming that straightforward developing captures were available. These are not positional misjudgments or exchange decisions—they are pure tactical oversights in the opening where a piece is left en prise or sacrificed for grossly insufficient material.

279.label: Playing a bishop check or move that leaves the piece hanging with no compensation in the opening.
279.description: This feature detects a recurring opening mistake where a player moves a bishop (often delivering check or entering an apparently active square) but leaves it en prise with no adequate recapture or compensation. The material signature shows 100% bishop moves that hang material (median -2.0, consistent with losing a minor piece), while Maia preferred a quiet pawn move instead. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic: positions go from drawn to losing with a median loss of 427 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this with dominant 'hanging_piece' motifs (89%) and tags like 'opening_trap' and 'piece_left_en_prise.' The concrete examples repeatedly show bishops being placed on squares where they can simply be captured—Bb5+ into ...a6, Bg5 where it cannot be adequately defended, Bxb5 where a knight recaptures with tempo. The common thread is an impulsive, aggressive-looking bishop move (frequently a check) that overlooks a simple refutation, typically a pawn or piece capture that wins the bishop outright.

277.label: Player makes a non-forcing move while an enemy bishop on g4 pins or pressures pieces, missing the tactical need to address it immediately.
277.description: Across the top activating positions, a striking visual pattern emerges: in nearly every board, Black has a bishop actively placed on g4, pinning or pressuring White's knight on f3 against the queen on d1. The player (usually White) makes a quiet, non-urgent move (pawn pushes like a4/a5, rook moves like Rc1/Rb1, or piece shuffles like Bf4/Bd2/Kf2) that fails to address the tactical tension created by this bishop. The material signature shows safe moves (78%) that aren't outright hanging pieces, but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic cost: 67% go from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 258 centipawns. The motifs confirm tempo_loss (36%) and hanging_piece (21%) — the player wastes a critical tempo while Maia consistently identifies capturing the g4 bishop (via hxg4 pawn capture, as noted in the example summaries) as the only good continuation. The player ignores the tactical urgency of the Bg4 pressure, allowing the opponent to maintain or escalate the pin/attack, squandering a winning advantage into equality or worse.

276.label: In winning endgames, advancing or capturing with a pawn instead of using a rook to deliver check or support promotion, squandering a decisive tempo advantage.
276.description: This feature captures a highly specific endgame mistake pattern. The material/position signature shows the player almost always moves a pawn (86%), rarely captures anything (71% no capture), and frequently gives check (57%) — yet Maia's recommended move is overwhelmingly a rook move (86%) that always gives check (100%). The eval trajectory is devastating: 50% of cases convert winning positions to draws, with a median loss of 431 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern through dominant motifs of passed_pawn (44%) and tempo_loss (33%), with rook_endgame and missed_tactic as universal tags. The concrete positions reveal the story: players have winning rook+pawn endgames with passed pawns but push the pawn prematurely (or make a pawn capture) instead of using their rook actively — typically to give a critical check that deflects the opponent's king, cuts off a rank/file, or supports promotion. The pawn advance feels natural but surrenders the critical tempo needed to convert, allowing the opponent's king to blockade or the opponent's rook to activate. This is a 'push before you deflect' error where impatient pawn advancement replaces the necessary preparatory rook check.

281.label: Player makes a non-capturing move that leaves a piece (typically a rook) hanging on an open diagonal to an enemy bishop.
281.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (most often a pawn push, sometimes a rook or queen move) that either opens a critical diagonal or ignores an existing diagonal threat, leaving a piece undefended and en prise. The material signature shows 100% hangs with a median loss of ~2.0 (consistent with losing the exchange, i.e., a rook for a bishop). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights: 52% of cases swing from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 298 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags 'hanging_piece' (90%), with recurring themes of 'exchange_loss', 'undefended_rook', 'diagonal_attack', and 'ignored_threat'. The concrete positions repeatedly show the same pattern: a pawn move (like b3, d4, or d5) either removes a diagonal blocker or wastes a tempo while an enemy bishop on a long diagonal (often a6-f1) attacks an undefended rook. The phase is predominantly middlegame/opening where these long diagonals are most active but easily overlooked amid development.

282.label: Knight captures a pawn on d4/e4/e5 but leaves itself hanging on the captured square.
282.description: This feature detects a highly specific recurring blunder pattern: a knight (84%) captures a pawn (96%) on a central square — overwhelmingly d4 or e5 based on the board positions — in the opening or early middlegame (100% opening/middlegame), where the capture appears materially safe (84% 'safe' outcome by simple material count) but actually leaves the knight hanging or tactically vulnerable. The hanging_piece motif dominates at 80%, and the eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 343cp), often swinging from equal/slight advantage to losing. The top boards reveal a strikingly consistent pattern: knights jumping to d4 or e5 to capture a pawn, where the square appears inviting but the knight is insufficiently supported and can be captured or trapped. Maia's recommended moves (bishop 40%, knight 24%) suggest quiet developing moves were far superior. The 88% 'missed winning material' rate confirms these positions often had strong tactical alternatives the player overlooked in favor of the tempting but poisoned pawn capture.

275.label: Moving a bishop (or queen) aggressively to an undefended square where it is immediately lost, typically collapsing a playable position.
275.description: This feature consistently fires on middlegame positions where the player lunges a bishop (70%) or queen (30%) to an attacking square—most often h3, h6, or h4—without adequate support, leaving the piece hanging (90% of moves result in a hung piece). The material signature shows a median loss of 3.0 (i.e., a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (median 358cp lost), frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (30% drawn→losing, 30% winning→losing, 20% winning→drawn). The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (58%), with secondary themes of tempo_loss (25%) and king_safety (17%): the piece moves to an aggressive-looking square that appears to threaten something (often the opponent's king) but is tactically refuted because the piece lacks protection or the attack is premature. The top boards overwhelmingly show bishops going to h3 or h6 (e.g., Bh3, Bh6, Bh3, Bh6) or queens relocating aggressively (Qh5, Qh4) without sufficient compensation, creating the illusion of an attack while simply dropping material.

280.label: Player makes a quiet developing move in the opening, missing a devastating queen check that exploits the opponent's exposed king.
280.description: This feature fires when a player makes a seemingly reasonable developing move (typically a knight or pawn move, 47% and 22% respectively) during the opening (92%) while completely missing a crushing queen check. The material signature shows the move itself is usually 'safe' (81%) — nothing is immediately hung — but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic cost: a median of 322 centipawns lost, with 40% of positions going from winning to drawn and 8% from winning to losing. The key diagnostic is that Maia's recommended move is a queen move 100% of the time, delivers check 100% of the time, and 100% of positions involve missed winning material. The tactical motifs overwhelmingly involve king_safety (89%), with tags like exposed_king, open_diagonal, and missed_mate. The concrete pattern from the top boards shows positions in the opening where the opponent's king is vulnerable on a diagonal (typically e1-h4 or e8-h5), and moves like Qh4+ or Qg3+ would win material or force devastating follow-ups, but the player instead makes a slow development move like Nf6, Ne7, d6, or Nc6 that completely ignores the tactical opportunity.

273.label: Moving a rook (or queen) to a passive square that loses tempo and allows the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit a tactic.
273.description: This feature identifies a recurring pattern where players move major pieces—predominantly rooks (56%) and queens (22%)—to squares that fail to address the critical demands of the position, resulting in severe tempo loss. The material signature shows 98% non-captures with 44% of moves hanging material, yet the pieces aren't literally dropped in simple blunders; rather, the passive placement allows the opponent to exploit tactics (missed_tactic 12%), attack the king (king_safety 25%), or win material through initiative. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (38%), visible across the top boards where rooks shuffle to squares like b1, e1, or d1 without purpose while the opponent has concrete threats. The eval trajectory (median 273cp lost, with 16% drawn->losing and 8% winning->drawn) confirms these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-changing errors where a slow move squanders a significant advantage or tips the balance. Maia's recommendations frequently involve active moves—captures (23%), checks (14%), and piece development—highlighting that the position demanded forcing play, not the passive regrouping the player chose. The middlegame phase dominance (83%) fits the pattern of positions where piece activity and initiative are paramount, and a wasted tempo proves catastrophic.

283.label: Opening moves that miss a winning queen check-fork capturing an undefended piece.
283.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening blunder pattern where the player makes a quiet developing move (pawn, bishop, or knight — 81% of activations) while missing a devastating queen check (Maia recommends a queen move with check 100% of the time) that simultaneously attacks an undefended piece, typically a bishop pinned or exposed on b4/b5. The material signature shows the played move is usually 'safe' (82%) — meaning nothing immediately hangs — but the missed tactic costs a median of 366 centipawns, with 50% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one and 16% into a losing one. The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (97%), featuring Indian/Nimzo-type structures where a bishop has sortied to b4 or b5 without adequate protection. The dominant motifs — fork (33%), hanging_piece (33%), and tempo_loss (25%) — all point to the same underlying pattern: a queen check forks the king and an undefended minor piece. Tags like queen_fork(5), queen_check(4), undefended_piece(3), and opening_blunder(4) further confirm this is a missed elementary tactical shot in well-known opening positions where the opponent's piece placement creates a dual-target vulnerability exploitable only by a forcing check.

286.label: Playing a slow pawn move that ignores an opponent's devastating passed pawn or promotion threat.
286.description: This feature fires when a player makes a passive or slow pawn move (67% pawn moves, no captures in 83% of cases) in the middlegame while an opponent's passed pawn—typically on the 6th rank—poses an immediate and decisive threat. The eval trajectory shows massive drops (median 347cp lost), often converting drawn or already difficult positions into clearly lost ones. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (71%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss, promotion_threat, and back_rank tactics. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%), often involving rook captures or active rook play to contest files or eliminate the passed pawn. The concrete positions repeatedly show a passed pawn on c6 or d5 that the player ignores in favor of irrelevant flank pawn pushes (a6, a5, c5, f6), allowing the opponent's rooks to dominate open files and either promote the pawn or execute crushing tactical combinations. The mistake is fundamentally positional—failing to prioritize the most urgent threat on the board—rather than a miscalculation or material blunder.

285.label: Pushing a pawn forward in the endgame that permanently fixes the structure, eliminates dynamic tension, or loses tempo.
285.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player advances a pawn (always a non-capturing pawn push, often giving check) that irreversibly damages their position. The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' in the immediate sense—nothing is hung—yet they cost a median of 109 centipawns in already-losing positions. The tactical analysis reveals the consistent theme: passed pawn mismanagement, tempo loss, and structural fixing. Across the top boards we see moves like g6+ (blocking the pawn against g7 forever), a5 (locking the queenside and eliminating counterplay), h4 (wasting a critical tempo), a4 (creating a target while freeing the opponent's passed pawn), and f5 (closing the position prematurely). In every case, the player had a pawn advance available that felt natural or aggressive but actually eliminated future flexibility, froze the pawn structure in the opponent's favor, or squandered a tempo that was needed for king activity. Maia consistently preferred capturing a pawn instead, suggesting these advances miss concrete pawn exchanges that maintain dynamic possibilities. The 100% endgame phase confirms this is specifically about late-game pawn handling where such structural commitments are most consequential.

284.label: Moving the king to an unsafe square that allows tactical exploitation or accelerates the opponent's attack.
284.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their king (45% of moves are king moves) into a vulnerable square, ignoring critical king safety concerns. The dominant motif is king_safety (60%), with tags like exposed_king and back_rank reinforcing that the core error is voluntary king exposure. The material signature shows 44% of moves 'hang' something—not necessarily the king itself, but the king's misplacement leaves other pieces or mating nets exploitable. Maia strongly prefers king moves (99%) but to safer squares, confirming the player chose the wrong king destination. The eval trajectory (median 214cp lost) shows these are severe mistakes, often in already-losing positions (32% losing->losing) or converting draws to losses (11% drawn->losing). The concrete examples show kings walking into tactical forks (Ke5 in a K+R endgame), castling into pressure (O-O-O with imprisoned bishop and Nd6+ ideas), and kings stepping onto exposed diagonals/files. The phase split (65% middlegame, 35% endgame) shows this happens both when the king should stay sheltered and when active king play goes wrong in the endgame.

287.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while their own queen hangs undefended, allowing opponent to capture it for free.
287.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a non-capture move (89% no capture) that hangs a major piece (67% 'hangs' outcome), with a catastrophic median material loss of -9.0. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-deciding blunders: 67% convert winning positions into losing ones, with a median eval swing of 1375 centipawns. The tactical analysis strongly reinforces this: 82% of positions are tagged with 'hanging_piece', and the per-position summaries repeatedly describe scenarios where the player's own queen is undefended and the opponent can simply capture it. The common tags 'queen_hanging', 'hanging_queen', and 'missed_capture' all point to the same pattern — the player plays a purposeless or passive move (king retreats, knight maneuvers, pawn pushes) while completely overlooking that their queen is en prise. Maia's recommended moves confirm this: 67% involve queen moves (presumably saving or using the queen) and 56% involve capturing the opponent's queen, indicating the correct response was either to defend or to capture first in mutual-hanging situations. The boards show endgame and middlegame positions where both sides have exposed queens, and the player fatally loses tempo by ignoring the tactical emergency.

289.label: Recapturing bxc6 in the opening allows a devastating Bxc6+ bishop fork winning material.
289.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening mistake where a player captures a knight on c6 with the b-pawn (bxc6), failing to recognize that the bishop on b5 can then recapture on c6 with check, forking the king and rook. All top activating positions occur in the opening phase with 100% pawn captures of a knight, and 100% of cases miss a winning queen move (Maia's recommendation). The material signature shows a 'trade' (pawn takes knight), but the eval trajectory reveals a median 236 centipawn loss, typically converting a drawn position into a losing one (86% drawn->losing). The dominant motifs are fork (46%) and king_safety (31%), with recurring tags like bishop_fork, exposed_king, and opening_trap. The pattern is almost exclusively from Ruy Lopez or Italian-style positions where White has placed a bishop on b5 and knight on c6, and Black reflexively recaptures bxc6 without first interposing or preparing with moves like Qd7, falling into a well-known tactical pattern.

288.label: In a winning endgame, plays an inaccurate move that hangs material or misses the critical continuation, squandering a decisive advantage.
288.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of endgame conversion failures. The material signature shows that 86% of moves result in hanging a piece (non-capture that drops material), with a median net material loss of -1.0, and 86% of positions are in the endgame phase. The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions being squandered: 71% remain winning but lose a median of 602 centipawns, while 14% collapse from winning to drawn. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying causes: players miss captures of undefended pieces (hanging_piece), fail to properly handle passed pawns (passed_pawn), make promotion errors (promoting without first eliminating blockaders), and lose critical tempi (tempo_loss). The concrete positions show king-and-pawn endgames, rook endgames, and minor piece endgames where the player had a decisive advantage but chose a move that either allowed counterplay, failed to execute the winning technique (e.g., not removing a defender before promoting), or simply hung material by overlooking the opponent's tactical resources. The common thread is that 86% of positions had a winning capture or tactic available (missed_winning_material) that would have maintained the full advantage.

291.label: Promoting a passed pawn with check instead of maintaining its positional power, allowing the opponent to capture the new queen.
291.description: This feature detects a specific endgame blunder where a player promotes a pawn (often with check) but the resulting queen is immediately capturable or tactically lost, converting a drawn or winning position into a losing one. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves that deliver check yet hang material (median -9.0, i.e., losing a queen's worth). The eval trajectory confirms these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones (median 302cp lost). The tactical analysis strongly corroborates this: 'promotion_error' is the dominant motif (38%), with tags like 'premature_promotion', 'passed_pawn', and 'pawn_endgame' recurring throughout. The board positions consistently show endgames where a player promotes to a queen with check rather than making a patient king move or keeping the pawn as a positional asset. The promoted queen lands on a square where it can be captured (often by the opponent's king), squandering the pawn's restraining power and the game's outcome.

292.label: Player makes a quiet or repositioning move, missing a strong queen check or capture that wins significant material.
292.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a seemingly safe, non-capturing move (84% safe, 77% no capture) — typically with a knight (32%) or queen (26%) — while completely missing a powerful tactical opportunity. The Maia best-move signal is overwhelmingly a queen move (81%) that delivers check (97%) and captures material (pawn 42%, knight 36%, bishop 10%, rook 6%). The missed winning material rate is 97%, confirming that nearly every activation involves overlooking a concrete tactic. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 289 centipawns, with many cases going from winning to drawn (19%) or involving missed forced mates. The Opus analysis confirms dominant motifs of missed_tactic and king_safety, with tags including back_rank and forced_mate. The positions cluster in the opening (58%) and middlegame (42%), where the opponent's king is vulnerable to a queen check that simultaneously wins material or delivers mate, but the player instead develops a piece or makes a structural move, completely overlooking the forcing continuation.

290.label: King or piece moves that squander tempo in won or winning endgame positions, allowing the opponent to draw or complicate.
290.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player, typically with a winning or near-winning advantage, makes a king move (57%) or knight move (29%) that loses critical tempo. The material signature shows these are not capture-related errors (no captures in 100% of cases) and the pieces are mostly 'safe' (86%), meaning nothing is immediately hung—yet the median eval loss is a massive 553 centipawns, with 57% going winning->winning (but much less winning) and 29% going winning->drawn. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (50%), passed_pawn (21%), and tempo_loss (21%)—confirm these are positional tempo errors in simplified positions where precise king activity and pawn timing are paramount. The concrete examples show kings stepping to inferior squares (Kf6 abandoning a mating net, Kh5 losing coordination), knights decentralizing (Ne7 losing control), and impulsive checks (Nf4 ruining a mating geometry). The common thread is a player who has a technically won endgame but wastes a crucial tempo on a purposeless or counterproductive move, allowing the opponent to activate their king, block a passed pawn, or reach a theoretical draw.

293.label: Moving the king to an exposed square that allows tactical punishment via checks, forks, or perpetuals.
293.description: This feature identifies positions where the player voluntarily moves their king (50% of moves are king moves) to an unsafe square, squandering a winning or drawn position. The eval trajectory is devastating (median 542cp lost), with 31% converting winning positions to drawn and 12% drawn to losing — consistent with throwing away wins via king misplacement. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs are king_safety (43%) and fork (29%), with tags like king_exposure, perpetual_check, and tempo_loss recurring. The concrete positions show kings retreating or advancing to squares where they become vulnerable to perpetual checks (Kb3 walking into a perpetual check net), tempo-gaining rook checks (Ke4 allowing Rd4+), or tactical forks. Maia's preferred moves (81% king moves) suggest the king needed to move, but the player chose the wrong square — one that exposes it rather than shelters it. This is not a material blunder in the traditional sense (75% 'safe' material outcome) but a positional catastrophe where the king's placement enables the opponent's tactical resources.

297.label: Player makes a quiet move while an opponent's major piece hangs undefended, turning a winning position into a losing one.
297.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a free capture of a major piece (usually a queen). The material signature shows 82% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave pieces en prise) while Maia's recommended response captures a queen 91% of the time — meaning the opponent's queen was already hanging and the player simply didn't take it. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 82% swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 955 centipawns (~a queen's worth). The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (85%) with tags like 'missed_capture' and 'hanging_queen' dominating. The board positions repeatedly show scenarios where a queen sits undefended on an open diagonal or file, yet the player makes a passive or irrelevant move (a king retreat, a rook shuffle, a pawn push) instead of simply capturing it. Several OPUS summaries explicitly note 'pawn takes queen' or 'Qxc7' being missed — psychologically easy to overlook captures that were the only move to maintain the advantage.

298.label: Moving the queen to a passive square instead of capturing material or delivering a forcing check.
298.description: This feature fires when players move their queen (75% of cases) to a non-forcing, passive square—missing a strong tactical opportunity that Maia identifies as a queen move with check (100%) that also captures material (pawn 75%, bishop 25%). The material signature shows the played move hangs a piece 50% of the time while the rest are merely safe but purposeless, and 100% of cases miss winning material. The eval trajectory confirms significant losses (median 562 centipawns), indicating these are costly missed tactics rather than subtle positional errors. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (50%) and hanging_piece (50%)—along with tags like 'aimless_check' and 'missed_tactic' paint a picture of players either retreating their queen without purpose or making superficially active moves (like the example of a pointless check that Black easily blocks) when a forcing queen capture with check was available. The positions are predominantly middlegame (75%) with active piece play on both sides, where the correct move involved the queen aggressively entering with check to win material, but the player instead chose a quiet or retreating queen move that surrendered the initiative entirely.

299.label: Ignoring an undefended queen on an open diagonal during the opening, allowing its immediate capture.
299.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a player's queen (almost always on g4) is left hanging on an open diagonal while the player makes an irrelevant developing move or pawn capture (knight 50%, pawn 50%). The material signature shows catastrophic losses (median -8.0, consistent with losing a queen) with 67% outright losing and 33% hanging material. The eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences: 83% winning->losing and 17% drawn->losing with a median loss of 711 centipawns—essentially throwing away a winning or equal position in one move. The Opus analysis unanimously tags hanging_piece (100%) with dominant labels of hanging_queen, ignored_threat, and open_diagonal. The concrete positions repeatedly show White's queen on g4 being capturable by Black's c8-bishop along an unobstructed diagonal (after ...d5 clears the path), while White plays moves like Nf3, exd5, or Nxd5 completely ignoring the threat. Maia consistently recommends queen moves (100%), confirming the correct response was simply to move the queen to safety.

294.label: Trading a strong bishop for a rook when superior tactical continuations existed, collapsing a winning or equal position.
294.description: This feature detects positions where a player trades their bishop (91% of moves) for a rook (82% of captures) in what is technically an exchange (material outcome: trade 100%, median net +2.0 suggesting the rook-for-bishop exchange), but catastrophically misjudges the position. The eval trajectory shows massive losses (median 440cp), with 36% going drawn->losing and 23% winning->losing, indicating the player threw away a favorable position. The tactical motifs (fork 33%, hanging_piece 33%, discovered_attack 11%) reveal that the traded bishop was either defending against an imminent fork, maintaining control of a critical diagonal, or the position contained a superior tactical continuation (missed_tactic appears in 6/22 cases). The boards confirm this: players capture rooks on f8, a8, or e8 with their bishops, failing to see that the bishop was a cornerstone piece whose removal enables devastating knight forks, discovered attacks, or even checkmate sequences. Maia's recommended moves (knight 27%, pawn 23%, queen 23%) suggest quiet developing or defensive moves were far superior to the greedy exchange capture. The tags 'piece_activity' (7) and 'tempo_loss' (5) confirm the bishop was an active, well-placed piece whose removal cost critical tempi and positional compensation far exceeding the nominal exchange gain.

296.label: Player gives a pointless check that sacrifices their best-placed knight or bishop, losing material for no compensation.
296.description: This feature captures a highly specific mistake pattern: the player delivers a check (100% of activations) with a knight (70%) or bishop (30%) that results in hanging the piece (50%) or losing significant material (40%), with a median loss of 3.0 pawns worth of material. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors (median 414cp lost), often turning drawn or losing-but-defensible positions into hopeless ones. The Opus tactical analysis reveals the unifying theme: these are 'useless checks' or 'desperate checks' where the player trades away their most active, best-placed piece for a check that accomplishes nothing strategically—the opponent simply captures or sidesteps, and the checking piece is gone. The tags 'pointless_check', 'desperate_check', and 'tempo_loss' appear repeatedly. In multiple examples, the knight being sacrificed was the player's strongest piece (e.g., an intruder on a2 tying down the opponent's king, or a centralized knight on e5 defending critical squares). The Maia recommendations (60% queen moves, 0% checks) confirm that the engine sees no reason to deliver check—better moves exist that maintain piece activity. This occurs primarily in openings and middlegames where piece activity matters most, and the player succumbs to the temptation of 'check is always good' rather than preserving their best-placed piece.

301.label: Capturing or advancing a pawn/bishop before executing a forcing intermediate move, leaving a piece undefended.
301.description: This feature identifies a recurring opening/early middlegame mistake where the player makes a pawn or bishop move (often a capture that appears to be a fair trade) but uses the wrong move order, leaving a piece hanging. The material signature shows 57% trades and 29% hangs—seemingly reasonable exchanges that go wrong because a critical intermediate move (often a check, as Maia's response involves check 86% of the time) was missed. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors (median 364cp lost), typically turning drawn or slightly losing positions into hopeless ones. The Opus analysis repeatedly flags 'move_order' (6 occurrences) and 'hanging_piece' (7 occurrences) as the core issue: the player recaptures or exchanges in the wrong sequence, failing to notice that their opponent can interpose a forcing move (usually a discovered or direct check) that wins the now-undefended piece. The positions cluster in the opening phase (71%) where development and piece coordination make move order critical—exemplified by the case where capturing on c3 before first playing Bxd7+ left the a4 bishop completely unprotected.

295.label: Ignoring a central pawn threat in the opening by making a developing or non-urgent move that hangs material.
295.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player makes a seemingly natural developing move (bishop deployment, pawn advance, or quiet preparation) while ignoring a concrete tactical threat to a central pawn—most often e5 or d5. The material signature shows 100% 'hangs' with no captures, meaning the player's move is a non-capture that leaves material en prise (median -1.0, typically a pawn). The eval trajectory is severe: 75% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 25% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 328 centipawns—far more than just a pawn, because the positional damage compounds the material loss. The tactical analysis confirms this through recurring tags of 'hanging_piece,' 'tempo_loss,' 'central_tension_ignored,' and 'missed_tactic.' The concrete positions all arise around moves 3-6 in standard openings (Scotch, Italian, Catalan, Advance French structures) where the opponent has created tension on a central pawn, and the player responds with a move-order error—developing a piece, fianchettoing, or making a flank move—before addressing the critical central threat. Maia consistently punishes by capturing the hanging pawn. The pattern is not a complex tactical oversight but rather a prioritization error: choosing development or structure over an immediate concrete obligation in the center.

302.label: Player trades or captures a piece, abandoning a promising kingside attack in favor of material considerations.
302.description: This feature fires when players in the middlegame (92%) abandon active attacking positions—particularly against the opponent's king—in favor of material-oriented moves. The king_safety motif (60%) and attack_abandonment/tempo_loss tags reveal the core pattern: the player had a dangerous initiative or mating attack but chose a move that relieved pressure. The material signature shows 36% hangs and 14% trades with median net material of 0.0, meaning these aren't simple blunders but rather moves where the player either exchanged an attacking piece for a passive one, captured material that wasn't the priority, or made a quiet move when a forcing continuation existed. Maia overwhelmingly preferred queen moves (66%) suggesting the engine wanted to maintain queen-led attacks. The trajectory (median 356cp loss, with winning->drawn 14%, winning->losing 10%) confirms these players were throwing away won or promising positions. The example summaries crystallize this: capturing a knight instead of continuing a mating attack, exchanging a dominating piece for a passive one, choosing material gain over a devastating king attack. The player prioritizes tangible material over intangible but decisive attacking momentum.

300.label: Aimless king moves in completely won positions that miss faster wins or allow counterplay.
300.description: This feature fires on positions where a player has a massive winning advantage (evaluations consistently +700 or higher) and plays a safe but aimless king move instead of converting decisively. The material signature shows 75% king moves that are 'safe' or 'hang' material—not blunders in the traditional sense since the position remains winning (winning->winning with 0cp median loss), but the missed opportunities are significant: 100% of the time Maia identifies a capture (usually taking a rook) or forcing move that would end the game faster. The dominant motifs—king_safety, hanging_piece, back_rank—reflect that these players are passively shuffling their king when crushing tactical finishes exist (checkmates, decisive captures). The boards confirm this: multiple positions with dual queens, massive material advantages, where the player walks the king (Kf2, Ka3, Kc3, Kh3, Kg3) instead of delivering checkmate or capturing remaining material. One example explicitly shows missing a one-move checkmate (Qxh8#) in favor of Kg3. These are endgame conversion failures—technically not losing moves, but wasteful king shuffles that reflect a lack of calculation when the game is already won.

303.label: Moving the king into a forced mating net when already in a losing or critical position.
303.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their king (62% of activating moves are king moves) directly into a mating net or fatally weakens their king's shelter (e.g., pushing a shielding pawn). The material signature shows 77% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop everything, i.e., the game), and in 100% of cases the player missed winning material—specifically Maia consistently identifies a queen capture as the correct move. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders (median 9177cp lost), mostly in already-losing positions (62% losing->losing), meaning players in desperate situations make their position immediately terminal rather than finding the one defensive resource. The tactical analysis is unanimous: king_safety is the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with tags like 'mating_net', 'king_walk_blunder', 'exposed_king', and 'forced_mate' recurring throughout. The concrete positions show kings stepping onto open files/diagonals controlled by enemy queen-rook batteries (e.g., Kg7 into Q+R control, Ka3 into Q+R mating corridors), or pawn moves that fatally open the king's shield. All positions are middlegame, where heavy pieces are still active and mating attacks are decisive.

306.label: Developing a bishop to a square where an opponent's pawn fork wins material in the opening.
306.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening mistake pattern where a player develops a bishop (54% of moves are bishop moves) to a square that walks directly into a pawn fork, typically in the opening phase (94% opening). The dominant tactical motif is overwhelmingly 'fork' (73%), with 'pawn_fork' being the most common tag. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into losing ones (71% drawn->losing) with a massive median cost of 327 centipawns—roughly a full minor piece. The concrete examples confirm this: bishops are placed on d6 where e4-e5 forks bishop and knight, or pieces are developed to squares vulnerable to natural pawn advances. The moves themselves are 'safe' in the sense that nothing is immediately hanging (94% safe), but they create a one-move tactical vulnerability to a pawn advance that wins material. Maia's preferred moves (51% pawn moves) confirm the refutation is typically the pawn thrust that executes the fork. This is not a positional subtlety—it's a concrete tactical oversight where piece development ignores the opponent's most natural pawn break.

304.label: Developing a bishop or pawn in the opening that leaves an unprotected knight hanging to a simple capture.
304.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a bishop (64%) or occasionally a knight/pawn in well-known open game positions (100% opening phase), neglecting that their centralized knight (often on d4 or e5) is left undefended. The material signature shows 73% of moves 'hang' a piece with a median loss of 3.0 pawns (roughly a full minor piece), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings—82% going from drawn to losing. The Maia analysis corroborates this, as the engine's recommended move is always a knight capture (Nxd4, Nxc6, etc.), exploiting the newly unprotected piece. Opus analysis highlights recurring tags: hanging_piece, missed_tactic, development errors, and tempo loss, with specific examples showing bishops blocking defensive lines (Bd3 blocking the queen's protection of Nd4) or development moves (Bd2, Bg5) that ignore tactical obligations to the centralized knight. The positions are overwhelmingly from Sicilian and Italian/Scotch structures where White places a knight aggressively on d4/e5 early, then 'develops' another piece without noticing the knight has lost its support.

312.label: Avoiding a decisive queen exchange that would convert to a trivially won pawn endgame.
312.description: This feature fires when a player in a winning endgame position fails to execute a queen trade that would lead to a trivially won pawn endgame. The material signature shows the player moved their king (75%) or pawn (25%) instead of trading queens — Maia consistently recommends queen captures (100% queen moves capturing queens). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 511 centipawns, with 25% of cases flipping from winning to losing. The Opus analysis is definitive: dominant tags include 'queen_trade_missed', 'missed_simplification', and 'pawn_endgame_conversion', with example summaries explicitly describing players who 'avoided the decisive queen trade' leading to 'a trivially won pawn endgame.' The positions are overwhelmingly endgames with passed pawns where the simplification was the only winning path, and the player's alternative move (typically a king move) exposed them to perpetual check or counterplay.

305.label: Pawn captures in the opening that open lines or release tension, exposing tactical vulnerabilities like discovered attacks or hanging pieces.
305.description: This feature fires on opening pawn exchanges (100% pawn moves, 94% pawn captures, 94% opening phase) where the player prematurely releases central tension through a trade (72% trade outcome, median net material 0.0). The eval trajectory shows these trades are devastating positionally: 56% transition from drawn to losing with a median loss of 236 centipawns—far exceeding the material exchanged. The tactical analysis reveals why: these pawn captures leave pieces hanging (50% hanging_piece motif), create discovered attack vulnerabilities (20%), or concede forks (10%). The common tags (missed_tactic, development, piece_activity, king_in_center) confirm these are premature central captures that open lines before the player's position can handle them—exposing underdeveloped pieces, uncastled kings, or creating outposts for the opponent. The concrete positions (dxe5, exd4, dxc5, d5xc6) all show players grabbing or exchanging central pawns that inadvertently open the position to the opponent's better-developed forces.

309.label: Moving a rook to a passive or purposeless square instead of exploiting a back-rank or tactical threat with tempo.
309.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a rook (50% of cases) to a square that is objectively safe (80% nothing hangs) but catastrophically wastes tempo, forfeiting a winning or near-winning advantage. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (56%) and back_rank (33%), indicating that the correct move typically involved a rook check or back-rank threat that would have gained a crucial tempo. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly rook moves (90%) with 40% delivering check, confirming the missed tempo-gaining continuation. The eval trajectory shows 50% of cases go from winning to drawn with a median loss of 230 centipawns—these are thrown wins, not positional subtleties. The concrete positions repeatedly show rooks being placed on quiet squares (Rf4, Re1, Rh6, Re8) when a forcing check or back-rank invasion was available, squandering the initiative and allowing the opponent to equalize or consolidate.

308.label: King moves that surrender tempo or activity in lost pawn endgames.
308.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames (100% endgame phase) where the player is already losing (losing->losing 100%). The material outcome is 'safe' (no pieces hang or are exchanged), yet the dominant motifs—passed_pawn (38%), pawn_endgame (23%), and tempo_loss (15%)—reveal that the king retreats or sidesteps in a way that concedes critical tempo against advancing passed pawns or allows the opponent's king to gain activity. The boards consistently show bare pawn endgames with passed pawns where the losing side's king drifts to a passive square (e.g., retreating to the back rank, stepping away from the promotion path, or moving laterally without purpose). While the eval trajectory shows minimal median centipawn loss (the position is already lost), the practical effect—as noted in the Opus analyses—often shortens the mating distance or transforms a stubborn defense into a trivially won position for the opponent. The mistake is not a material blunder but a positional/tempo failure: the king fails to contest the critical squares around passed pawns or actively resist.

310.label: In already lost positions, playing moves that hang pieces or walk the king into mate instead of finding the best defensive resource.
310.description: This feature captures moves made in already-losing positions (100% losing->losing trajectory) that massively accelerate the loss. The material signature shows 100% hangs—non-captures that drop material (median -3.0 net)—while Maia's recommended moves consistently deliver check (100%), indicating the player missed critical tactical threats. The eval trajectory shows a staggering median loss of 8727 centipawns, meaning these moves turn a difficult but potentially prolonged defense into immediate catastrophe. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: kings walking into mating nets (Kg5 into forced mate), bishops placed on undefended squares for free capture (Bd1 allowing Qxd1), and passive moves that ignore the opponent's crushing initiative. The common tags—king_safety, missed_tactic, hanging_piece, passive_retreat, king_walk_into_mate—all point to players who, already in desperate positions, fail to find the one remaining defensive resource and instead collapse instantly through either resignation-mode carelessness or active blunders that accelerate their demise.

307.label: In a king-and-pawn endgame, the player moves their king away from the critical squares needed to escort or stop a passed pawn, throwing away a won or drawn position.
307.description: All three signals converge on a highly specific endgame blunder. The material/position signature shows 100% king moves with no captures in pure endgame positions, where Maia's recommended move was always a pawn push—indicating the pawn (promotion) was the critical resource. The eval trajectory reveals catastrophic swings (median 542cp lost, with many positions going from forced mate to dead draw), consistent with the binary nature of pawn promotion races. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'promotion_error' as the dominant motif (60%) and 'pawn_endgame' (27%), along with recurring tags like passed_pawn, tempo_loss, and king_activity. Examining the top boards reveals minimal-material KP vs K or KPP vs KPP positions where the winning side needs precise king placement to shepherd a passed pawn to promotion (or the defending side needs to maintain opposition). Instead, the player moves their king to a square that loses the opposition or abandons the key promotion-support squares, converting a theoretical win into a draw. Classic examples include positions like Kd6+Pc6 vs Kc8 where Kd6-c5 fatally loses control of the promotion square.

311.label: In already-lost endgame positions, passive king or rook moves that allow the opponent to exploit piece coordination failures, often trapping a piece or accelerating a forced loss.
311.description: This feature fires on moves in lost endgame positions (losing->losing 100%, endgame 100%) where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material immediately hangs, no captures involved) with the king (50%) or rook (50%) that catastrophically worsens their position by a median of 410 centipawns. The boards show simplified endgames with queens, rooks, or minor pieces where the dominant motifs are trapped_piece (23%), passed_pawn (23%), and king_safety (23%). The recurring pattern is a king or rook repositioning that fails to address the critical threat—often allowing the opponent's queen or rook to trap a piece, exploit a passed pawn, or deliver a mating net. Tags emphasize tempo_loss (9 occurrences) and piece_activity (10), indicating these moves squander defensive coordination rather than blundering material directly. The player drifts their king or passively retreats a rook when precise defensive placement was required, turning a difficult but sometimes defensible position into an immediate forced loss.

314.label: Player makes a developing or quiet move while an opponent's knight on h4 (or similar outpost) creates a tactical threat that goes unaddressed.
314.description: Across the top activating positions, a striking pattern emerges: the opponent frequently has a knight on h4 (visible in many of the FENs) that creates tactical threats—often a capture opportunity like Nxh4 or exploitation of the knight's position. The player instead makes a quiet developing move (bishop deployment 36%, knight move 23%, pawn push 23%) that is nominally safe (68% safe material outcome) but misses a concrete tactical opportunity flagged by Maia's overwhelming preference for knight captures (97% Nxsomething). The eval trajectory shows these are costly mistakes (median 290cp lost), frequently converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones (32% drawn->losing, 23% winning->drawn, 10% winning->losing). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs: hanging pieces left unaddressed (50%), tempo loss from ignoring the threat (25%), and missed tactics (tagged 3 times). The player prioritizes generic development or prophylaxis over the urgent concrete need to address or exploit an exposed enemy knight, losing significant material or positional advantage as a result.

313.label: Moving the rook (or king) passively instead of exploiting an active tactical opportunity, hanging material or squandering a winning position.
313.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a passive rook or king move that hangs material (58% hangs) rather than finding the critical forcing continuation. The material signature shows rook moves (58%) and king moves (25%) that are non-captures (96%) with a median cost of ~295 centipawns. Maia's recommended moves frequently give check (42%) and capture winning material (88% missed winning material), indicating the player overlooked forcing sequences. The motifs (king_safety 36%, back_rank 18%, hanging_piece 18%, tempo_loss 9%) reveal that these passive moves fail to exploit the opponent's vulnerable king or back-rank weaknesses, often doubling rooks on irrelevant files or retreating the king when an attacking blow was available. The eval trajectory shows positions transitioning from drawn/winning to losing (drawn->losing 25%, winning->drawn 12%), confirming these are moments where tactical opportunities were squandered in favor of aimless piece shuffling. The concrete examples reinforce this: Kf1 instead of Qc8+ exploiting an exposed king, Re7 in an equal position instead of maintaining tension, Rah8 missing checkmate in one, and Kf4 abandoning pawn defense.

315.label: Trading into a losing pawn endgame by capturing a piece that simplifies away the player's winning advantage.
315.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player uses a rook to capture a bishop with check, resulting in a slight material loss (median -2.0, consistent with exchanging a rook for a bishop in a simplifying trade). The critical pattern is that the player was winning but threw away the win catastrophically (median 9358 centipawns lost, remaining winning only by the narrowest technical definitions or transitioning to vastly worse positions). The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (46%) and passed_pawn (15%), with tempo_loss also prominent. The Opus analysis confirms the recurring theme: players trade their rook for a bishop (or simplify analogously), converting into a pawn endgame where the opponent has superior pawn structure, passed pawns, or king activity. Maia's recommended moves are quiet rook moves (no capture, no check), indicating the correct plan was to maintain the rook's activity rather than cash in the material. The boards show rook-vs-bishop endgames where the rook side had a decisive advantage but threw it away by capturing the bishop and entering a drawn or lost pawn ending.

318.label: Moving the queen away from critical defensive duties, allowing devastating king attacks.
318.description: This feature captures queen moves that neglect king safety obligations. The material signature shows the player always moves their queen (100%) without capturing anything (75%), while Maia's recommended moves consistently deliver check (100%), often capturing material in the process. The dominant motifs are king_safety (44%), back_rank (22%), and exposed_king tags, indicating the queen is being displaced from defensive squares. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 222 centipawns, with positions spanning losing-to-losing (50%) and losing-to-winning (25%), suggesting these are often desperate positions where the queen's defensive role is paramount. The concrete examples reinforce this: a queen capturing on h6 removes it from covering f7, allowing a mating attack; a queen going to c4 leaves the king vulnerable to a knight fork; queen moves to passive squares while the opponent has forced mates available. The pattern is consistently one of the queen being moved to tactically irrelevant squares while the king faces immediate threats.

317.label: Leaves a piece or pawn undefended in the opening by ignoring basic threats or violating development principles.
317.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where a player makes a non-capture move (100% no capture) that hangs material (88% hangs, median -1.0 material). The moved pieces are predominantly pawns (62%) or bishops (25%), and the motifs are dominated by hanging_piece (60%) and tempo_loss (20%). The eval trajectory shows severe consequences—median 287 centipawns lost, with half the cases flipping from drawn to losing.
