The material signature shows the move itself doesn't capture anything (85% no capture) but hangs material 35% of the time, with the median eval loss of 301 centipawns confirming a severe tactical oversight. The dominant motif is 'fork' (46%), with knight_fork appearing as the most common tag (6 occurrences). The eval trajectory shows these mistakes often convert drawn positions to losing ones (35%) or deepen an already losing position (30%), indicating players fail to notice knight geometry when repositioning their rook. The concrete positions repeatedly show rooks moving along files or ranks into squares where an enemy knight has a forking check or dual-attack resource—often Nf4+, Nxe3+, or similar patterns that simultaneously attack the king and the newly-placed rook.

572.label: Placing a piece on an undefended square attacked by an opponent's piece or pawn in the opening, immediately losing material.
572.description: This feature detects a very specific type of opening blunder where a player moves a piece (most often a bishop or knight) to a square that is immediately capturable for free. The material signature shows 100% hangs with a median net loss of -3.0 (a full piece), confirming these are not trades but outright gifts. The eval trajectory is catastrophic, with a median loss of 575 centipawns—converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones. All positions occur in the opening phase, and the dominant tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' (50%), supported by tags like development, tempo_loss, and piece_blunder. The concrete examples reinforce this: Bg4 placed on a queen-attacked diagonal, Ng5 left undefended for a queen capture, Bf4 placed on a pawn-attacked square. These are elementary one-move oversights where a developing piece lands on an immediately attacked square, representing a fundamental failure to check whether the destination square is safe.

571.label: Player makes a quiet developing or positional move while a strong tactical capture (usually queen taking a piece) was available, squandering a winning advantage.
571.description: This feature fires when a player makes a safe, non-capturing minor piece or pawn move (bishop 26%, pawn 24%, knight 21% — with 99% no capture) while the engine's best move was overwhelmingly a queen capture (Maia's move: queen 63%, capturing a bishop 46% or knight 33%). The positions are in the opening or middlegame (100% combined), and 100% of activations involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic missed opportunities: 36% go from winning to drawn, 7% from winning to losing, with a median loss of 418 centipawns — nearly a full piece advantage evaporated. The tactical analysis shows 75% involve a hanging piece the player simply failed to take, and common tags include tempo_loss and missed_tactic. The concrete examples consistently show the player ignoring an undefended or inadequately defended enemy piece (often on an open file or central square) that the queen could capture immediately, instead playing a slow preparatory move that allows the opponent to consolidate. This is not a case of hanging material or making a bad trade — it is the failure to recognize and execute an available winning capture.

573.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move, missing a winning queen capture or combination that exploits hanging pieces, forks, or back-rank threats.
573.description: This feature fires when the player makes a seemingly safe, non-capturing move (90% no capture, 80% 'safe' material outcome) — typically a pawn push or minor piece move — while the best move involved a queen action (Maia's recommended move is a queen 93% of the time, usually capturing a piece: knight 60%, rook 13%, bishop 7%). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic cost: median 392 centipawns lost, with 53% of cases converting a winning position into drawn or losing. The dominant tactical motifs (hanging pieces 40%, forks 20%, back-rank 20%, pins 20%) and repeated 'missed_tactic' tags confirm the player overlooked a forcing queen combination — a capture, fork, or back-rank exploitation — and instead played a passive developing or consolidating move. The positions are predominantly middlegame (73%) where the queen's tactical power is at its peak, and the examples consistently show a single critical queen move (Qxd5, Qxd4, Qxd2) that was the only way to maintain the advantage.

575.label: Moving the knight in the Petrov Defense and falling into a discovered attack by the queen on e2/e4 that wins material.
575.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern in the Petrov Defense (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nxe4) where one side has placed their queen on e2 (or e4) creating a battery along the e-file against the opponent's king. The player moves their knight away from e4 (or e5), failing to recognize that this exposes them to a discovered attack along the e-file by the queen, which typically wins a full queen's worth of material (~458 centipawns median). All positions are in the opening phase, the player always moves a knight (without capturing anything meaningful), and the correct move was invariably a queen move (100% Maia queen moves). The discovered_attack motif dominates at 77%, and the positions universally transition from drawn to losing. The boards confirm the recurring structure: knights on e4/e5 with a queen lurking on e2/e4, and the player blindly relocates the knight, walking into a devastating discovered attack.

574.label: Moving the king in a won endgame that allows the opponent to escape via stalemate or perpetual, throwing away a forced win.
574.description: This feature captures a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player with a completely winning position (often mate-in-N) makes a king move that catastrophically hangs the game's outcome. The material signature shows 100% king moves that are non-captures and non-checks, yet result in 'hanging' material (median -9.0, indicating a queen-equivalent loss). The eval trajectory confirms these are winning positions collapsing to drawn (100% winning->drawn, median 9945 centipawns lost — i.e., forced mates being thrown away into draws). The board positions reveal queen+king vs king endgames or similar technically won positions where the player moves their king into a fork, stalemate setup, or position allowing perpetual check, when the correct move was a queen maneuver to deliver or approach checkmate. The Opus analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (78%), with the hung piece being the queen exposed to a fork or the win itself dissolving into stalemate. The top boards (e.g., Kc4-d4 walking into a knight fork, Ke6-d6 in a K+R endgame creating stalemate) show kings wandering into tactically vulnerable squares in positions that required precise technique rather than casual king centralization.

576.label: A bishop delivers a premature, easily-blocked check in the opening that wastes tempo and often leaves the bishop stranded or hanging.
576.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions (100%) where the player moves a bishop to deliver check (bishop 100%, check 100%), but the check is purposeless—easily blocked or parried—costing critical development tempo. The material signature shows the bishop frequently hangs (67%) with a median net loss of -2.0 (roughly the bishop itself), and the eval trajectory confirms catastrophic consequences: 78% of cases transition from drawn to losing with a median loss of 315 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly tags 'tempo_loss' (73% dominant motif, 9/12 positions), with supporting tags like development and piece_activity reflecting the wasted moves. The top boards reveal a concrete recurring pattern: Bb5+ or Bb4+ in the opening where the check accomplishes nothing strategically—the opponent blocks with a developing move or pawn that simultaneously creates a threat, and the bishop must retreat or is trapped, having squandered two or more tempi in a phase where development is paramount. Maia's preferred alternatives (knight 56%, pawn 33%) suggest natural developing moves that maintain coordination rather than chasing a frivolous check.

577.label: Player makes an active move (capture or repositioning) that leaves a major piece undefended and immediately capturable.
577.description: This feature detects moves where a player repositions or captures with one piece while leaving another major piece (queen or rook) completely unprotected and hanging. The material signature shows 38% hangs and 31% loses with a median net loss of -4.0 (consistent with losing a full piece or more), and the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 100%. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic oversights—median 553 centipawns lost, with many positions swinging from drawn or winning to losing. The Opus analysis reveals a consistent pattern: players make seemingly purposeful moves (captures, repositioning) without noticing that their action either removes a defender, opens a line to an unprotected piece, or relocates a piece that was performing a critical defensive function. Tags like 'unprotected_piece', 'rook_hanging', 'queen_hanging', and 'opened_diagonal' confirm that the core error is tunnel-vision on one part of the board while a major piece elsewhere becomes a free target. Maia's recommended moves (90% non-captures, 44% rook moves) suggest the correct play was typically a quiet defensive or consolidating move rather than the aggressive/greedy action chosen.

578.label: Trading pieces when holding a dynamic advantage, surrendering attacking potential and tempo for an equal material exchange.
578.description: This feature fires on positions where a player initiates a trade (57% material outcome is 'trade', median net material 0.0) — typically with a bishop (50%) or pawn (36%) — that squanders a significant dynamic advantage. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 235 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or losing (21% winning->drawn, 7% winning->losing), indicating the player was throwing away a won position. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (50%), and the tactical analysis reveals tags like 'premature_simplification', 'queen_trade_error', and 'dynamic_advantage_squandered'. Maia's recommended moves (64% queen moves, 93% non-captures) suggest maintaining piece activity and pressure rather than exchanging. The concrete positions confirm this: trading queens when ahead in development (d1d4 vs the centralized black queen), exchanging bishops that were key attacking pieces (f5d3 surrendering a strong bishop), or simplifying pawn structures that were cramping the opponent (e4f3). In each case, the player chose material equivalence over maintaining dynamic tension, relieving their opponent's defensive burden during the opening/middlegame phase.

579.label: Player makes a quiet or inferior move, missing a forcing check or fork that would have won significant material.
579.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a powerful forcing move—typically a check or fork—that the engine (and Maia's predicted best move, which gives check 76% of the time) would have found. The material signature shows the player's move is often 'safe' (52%) or 'hangs' a piece (29%), meaning they played something passive or outright losing instead of the available tactic. The player frequently moves a knight (33%) or queen (29%) but fails to capture anything (67% no capture), while the best move almost always involved winning material (86% missed winning material). The eval trajectory confirms these are costly mistakes (median 369cp lost), with many positions going from winning to drawn or drawn to losing. The tactical motifs—forks, trapped pieces, king safety, exposed kings—combined with Maia overwhelmingly recommending checks (76%), paint a clear picture: the player had a forcing continuation available (a check, fork, or attack on an exposed king) but instead played a retreat, a quiet move, or an inferior capture, squandering a decisive tactical opportunity in the middlegame.

581.label: A rook delivers a showy check that hangs the rook or loses major material by overlooking a simple recapture or defensive resource.
581.description: This feature consistently fires on middlegame positions where a player delivers a rook check (100% rook moves, 100% checks) that catastrophically loses material (76% hangs, median net material -4.0, median eval loss 680 centipawns). The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly positions where wins are thrown away (35% winning->losing). The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: players are seduced by a 'flashy check' that blinds them to simple defensive resources like recaptures by knights or bishops sitting on the landing square's vicinity. The better moves identified by Maia are quiet piece moves (bishops 29%, pawns 24%, knights 18%) — none of which give check — suggesting the player fixated on forcing moves rather than consolidating their advantage. Tags like 'premature_attack', 'unnecessary_forcing_move', and 'exchanging_active_for_passive' reinforce that these checks are impulsive rather than calculated, often allowing the opponent to trade off a passive piece for the intruding rook or simply capture it outright.

583.label: Throwing away a winning endgame by giving a meaningless check that hangs the queen.
583.description: This feature detects a specific and devastating endgame mistake pattern: the player moves their queen to deliver a check (100% checks), but the check is tactically meaningless because the opponent's king simply captures the queen (Maia's king captures on 100% of responses). The material signature shows the queen is hung outright (non-capture that drops a piece, net material median -9.0), and the eval trajectory confirms these were all winning positions converted to draws (100% winning->drawn, median 10000cp lost — i.e., stalemate or complete collapse). The board positions reveal simplified endgames where the player had an overwhelming advantage but threw it away with a flashy but hollow check. The tactical analysis tags (queen_blunder, missed_tactic, endgame_technique) and example summaries confirm the pattern: queens placed on squares where they are simply captured for free, eliminating the very piece needed to convert the win. Several positions also involve promotion errors (underpromotion or failure to promote) that compound the endgame collapse.

585.label: Player makes a quiet move while an opponent's piece hangs undefended, missing a simple free capture.
585.description: This feature fires when a player overlooks a completely undefended enemy piece that could be captured for free. The material/position signature shows that the player's move is a non-capture (captured: none 100%) that is often safe but sometimes hangs material itself, while Maia consistently recommends capturing an enemy bishop (Maia captures: bishop 100%). The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the eval trajectory shows a median loss of 337 centipawns—typically squandering a winning position while remaining ahead (winning->winning 75%, winning->drawn 25%). The Opus tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (82% of motifs) with tags like 'missed_capture' and 'undefended_piece' appearing repeatedly. The concrete positions confirm the pattern: in each case, an opponent's piece (usually a bishop) sits completely undefended on the board, capturable by a rook or pawn, but the player instead makes a slow positional or aimless move (a king retreat, a pawn push, a rook shuffle), gifting the opponent a tempo to rescue the hanging piece. This is not a complex tactical oversight but rather a simple failure to notice a free capture sitting on the board.

582.label: King or piece moves in drawn endgames that lose a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to create a decisive passed pawn with check.
582.description: This feature identifies a specific endgame mistake pattern where the player makes a 'safe' move (no material is immediately lost) with a king, bishop, or knight, but fatally misplaces the piece or wastes a tempo. The eval trajectory is remarkably consistent: every activation transitions from a drawn position to a losing one, with a median cost of ~315 centipawns. The positions are predominantly pawn endgames or simplified piece endgames where precise timing is everything. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (appearing in 5/6 annotations), pawn_endgame, and passed_pawn—reveal that the mistake enables the opponent to achieve a pawn break or advance with tempo (often a check, as Maia's response is 100% pawn captures giving check). The boards confirm this: kings walking into squares where pawn forks hit with tempo (Kg7 allowing f6+), or passive moves that let the opponent execute a critical pawn exchange creating an unstoppable passed pawn. The player's move looks natural but ignores the razor-thin timing demands of the endgame.

580.label: Player withdraws a critically active rook (or queen) to a passive square, abandoning attacking pressure and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit back-rank/tactical vulnerabilities.
580.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a rook (77%) or queen (15%) to a passive square without capturing anything (100% non-capture, 100% materially 'safe' in the immediate sense). The massive median eval loss of 459 centipawns and the trajectory (winning->drawn 31%, winning->losing 23%, drawn->losing 23%) confirm these are game-ruining mistakes that throw away advantageous or tenable positions. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying pattern: the moved piece was the player's most active attacker, and its retreat abandons critical pressure—often along a rank or file that was creating threats. The dominant motifs (back_rank 33%, positional_mistake 22%) and tags (missed_tactic, tempo_loss, piece_activity) show that by pulling back the active piece, the player both loses tempo and exposes their own back rank or allows the opponent's pieces to activate. The concrete positions confirm this: rooks retreating from aggressive second-rank posts (b2->b8), rooks leaving open files where they pressured the opponent, queens moving away from coordinated mating patterns. Maia's recommended moves (69% give check, 38% capture pawns) show that the correct continuation was to maintain or increase aggression, not retreat. The feature captures the archetypal positional blunder of voluntarily deactivating one's best-placed piece.

584.label: Throws away a winning position by missing critical tempo or technique in simplified positions.
584.description: This feature captures positions where a player holds a winning advantage—often in middlegame-to-endgame transitions or pure endgames—and makes a move that converts the win into a draw (60% winning->drawn trajectory, median 200cp lost). The material signature shows diverse piece moves (rooks, bishops, pawns, kings) that are often objectively 'safe' (60%) yet catastrophically inaccurate in context. The dominant motifs (passed_pawn 22%, pawn_endgame 22%, back_rank 22%, tempo_loss 11%) combined with tags like tempo_loss(4), endgame_technique(2), and missed_tactic(3) reveal that these errors stem from failing to execute precise technique: advancing the wrong pawn, capturing in the wrong move order, or allowing counterplay that neutralizes a decisive advantage. The boards confirm this—positions with passed pawns on the 7th rank, king-and-pawn endgames, and simplified positions where only one move maintains the win. The 80% missed-winning-material rate shows Maia consistently found superior continuations, indicating these are narrow decision points where the player relaxes or miscalculates at the moment of conversion.

586.label: In won endgame positions, plays a safe but non-optimal move that fails to convert the advantage efficiently.
586.description: Across all top activating positions, the phase is exclusively endgame (100%), and the material outcome of the move is always 'safe' (no material is lost or traded). The player typically moves a pawn or king—slow, consolidating moves—while Maia's suggested alternatives often involve more active king moves or checks (29% check rate). The positions are overwhelmingly won (advanced passed pawns, extra material, dominant king placement) yet the eval trajectory shows 0 centipawns lost at median, suggesting these are technically non-losing but suboptimal moves that delay or complicate conversion. Examples include pushing a pawn to b6 instead of using the knight or king more aggressively, promoting to a queen when a different approach forces faster mate, or making a passive king move when a check or more active continuation was available. The pattern is one of playing 'safe but slow' in positions where precise technique would win faster or more cleanly.

589.label: Player moves queen passively instead of capturing a hanging piece with it, squandering a winning position.
589.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player has a winning advantage but fails to use their queen to capture a hanging or tactically vulnerable piece. The material signature shows the player moves their queen 56% of the time without capturing anything (89% no capture), while Maia's recommended move is always a queen capture (100% queen, capturing knights 44%, pawns 22%, rooks 22%, bishops 11%). The 'missed winning material' flag is 100%, confirming every activation involves overlooking a concrete capture. The eval trajectory is devastating—median 637 centipawns lost, with 33% going from winning to drawn and 22% from winning to losing. The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (80%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, missed_capture, and tempo_loss. The player retreats or repositions their queen (often to passive squares) when a forcing capture was available, effectively throwing away a won game by overlooking simple material gains.

587.label: Player makes a move that completely overlooks an existing tactical threat, hanging material worth roughly a minor piece or more.
587.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move (most often a pawn or rook move) that ignores an immediate tactical threat on the board, resulting in material being hung (92% hangs, median net material loss of -3.0, i.e., roughly a minor piece). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 184 centipawns, consistent with dropping a piece rather than a catastrophic blunder. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%) and king_safety (40%), with common tags like 'missed_tactic', 'ignored_threat', and 'tempo_loss'. The concrete positions show patterns like ignoring a bishop attacking a queen (FEN with Bf3 hitting Qd1), making a passive rook move while a passed pawn advances, or pushing a pawn while a piece is en prise. Maia's recommended moves frequently involve captures (33% pawn, 25% bishop, 8% knight), suggesting the correct response was to address the threat by trading or capturing the attacking piece. The phase is predominantly middlegame (75%), where tactical threats are most dense and overlooking them is most costly. This is not a positional misjudgment or a bad trade—it's a failure to recognize or prioritize an existing concrete threat on the board.

588.label: Playing a slow or passive move that allows the opponent to exploit tactical themes like forks or trapped pieces.
588.description: This feature captures moves where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing piece relocation (93% no capture) that appears safe on the surface (50% 'safe' material outcome) but critically misses a strong tactical opportunity or walks into a tactical vulnerability. The 43% 'hangs' rate indicates that many of these passive moves leave pieces en prise or vulnerable to subsequent tactics. The dominant motifs—trapped_piece (50%) and fork (50%)—combined with tags like deflection, missed_tactic, and knight_on_rim reveal a pattern where the player places a piece on a passive or rim square instead of executing or preventing a tactic. The eval trajectory (median 356cp lost, with 21% winning→losing and 21% winning→drawn) confirms these are game-changing errors that throw away advantages. Maia's recommended moves heavily involve captures (36% pawn, 36% bishop, 14% queen) and checks (21%), underscoring that the player chose a slow repositioning move when a sharp tactical blow was available. The example summaries explicitly describe placing knights on passive rim squares (Na5) instead of exploiting forks/exposed kings, and making slow approach moves that give opponents time to activate trapped pieces.

590.label: Moving the king in a way that leaves pieces or back-rank squares undefended, allowing the opponent to win significant material or deliver checkmate.
590.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) without capturing anything, and the move directly hangs material (100% 'hangs' outcome with a median net loss of -5.0 material points). The tactical motifs are dominated by king_safety (38%), hanging_piece (38%), and back_rank threats (12%), indicating that these king moves expose the player to immediate tactical exploitation—either leaving pieces unprotected, walking into back-rank mates, or abandoning defensive duties. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 283 centipawns, with positions spanning from already-losing situations made worse to outright game-losing blunders (including forced mates). The top boards confirm the pattern: kings stepping to squares like g2, e2, f1, f8, h7, g5 where they either walk into mating nets or abandon protection of key pieces (especially rooks). Maia's responses overwhelmingly involve rook captures (75%) or queen strikes (25%), confirming that the opponent immediately exploits the newly-hanging material or delivers decisive checks. This is fundamentally a king-safety tactical oversight occurring primarily in endgame positions where the king is active but overstepping its safe zone.

593.label: Player makes a passive or irrelevant move while a free capture (their own or opponent's hanging piece) demands immediate attention.
593.description: This feature fires when a player, typically in a winning or advantageous position, plays a quiet or passive move (rook repositioning, king move, pawn push) while a critical hanging piece — either their own undefended piece or an opponent's freely capturable piece — goes unaddressed. The material signature shows the played move frequently hangs material (33%) or loses material (33%), with a median net loss of -2.0, while Maia's recommended move is almost always a knight or rook capture (100% captures). The eval trajectory is devastating: 67% of cases swing from winning to losing, with a median eval loss of 901 centipawns — indicating these are not marginal oversights but game-losing blunders. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' in 100% of cases, with common tags including tempo_loss, mutual_attack, and capture_first errors. The concrete pattern across boards shows positions with mutual piece tension or undefended pieces where the player ignores the tactically forcing capture in favor of an irrelevant move, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or simply collect free material.

595.label: Moving a piece (often knight or queen) directly into an opponent's capture range, hanging it for no compensation.
595.description: This feature fires on moves where a player places a piece en prise with no adequate compensation. The material signature shows 46% losses and 33% hangs with a median net material cost of -5.0 (roughly a full piece), dominated by knight (42%) and queen (25%) moves. The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 86%, with example summaries describing pieces moved directly into capture range or undefended squares. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 262 centipawns, often converting already-losing positions into completely lost ones (46% losing->losing) or throwing away drawn/winning positions (25% combined). The concrete board examples reinforce this: Ne5+ walking into fxe5, Qxh7 overlooking Rxh7, Bb5 hanging to an undefended bishop, and Qf5 dropping a queen to a knight fork. These are simple one-move oversights where the player fails to check whether the destination square is defended.

594.label: Trading or exchanging a key tactical piece (often a bishop) before exploiting a concrete advantage it supported.
594.description: This feature fires on positions where the player initiates a piece exchange—most commonly trading a bishop for a knight (bishop moved 50%, knight captured 50%)—that appears materially neutral (62% trades, median net material 0.0) but is strategically catastrophic (median eval lost: 354 centipawns). The eval trajectory shows these trades throw away winning or drawn positions (25% winning->drawn, 19% drawn->losing, 12% winning->losing). The tactical analysis reveals the core pattern: the exchanged piece was a linchpin maintaining tactical tension (e.g., a Bg5 pinning or pressuring that justified a follow-up Nxe4), and removing it prematurely eliminates a concrete tactical opportunity. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (33%), tempo_loss (17%), and move-order errors—confirm that the player chose a routine exchange when the piece's presence on the board was essential for a stronger continuation. Multiple examples show Bg5xf6 exchanges that relieve tension instead of exploiting it, or developing moves played instead of capturing hanging pawns (Nxg5, Nxe4). The mistake is not the trade itself being materially unsound, but rather that it dissolves the position's tactical energy at exactly the wrong moment.

592.label: Sacrificing major pieces (rooks/queens) without adequate compensation, often via pointless checks or misguided captures that lose significant material.
592.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players sacrifice major pieces—primarily rooks (54%) and queens (38%)—in positions that are already difficult or roughly equal, causing catastrophic material losses (median net material: -4.0, median eval lost: 316 centipawns). The trajectory shows 54% of these occur in already-losing positions (making them worse), while 30% swing from winning or drawn to losing, indicating desperation-driven or hallucinated tactics. The OPUS analysis reveals the common thread: players execute captures or checks that appear active but have no follow-up—pointless checks (like Qb8+ where Kxb8 leaves no continuation), premature captures of passed pawns that walk into traps (Rxe7 allowing Re1 recapture), or grabbing material while ignoring promotion threats. The motifs of tempo_loss (22%), hanging_piece (22%), and the prevalence of passed_pawn tags (6 occurrences) confirm these are cases where players prioritize an immediate but illusory tactical idea over the critical positional demands (stopping promotion, maintaining piece coordination), resulting in catastrophic material hemorrhage with no compensation.

591.label: In the opening, capturing a piece with a pawn on the h-file (hxg) that destroys the king's pawn shield, turning a balanced or favorable position into a losing one.
591.description: This feature identifies a highly specific opening mistake where a player uses their h-pawn to capture a piece (usually a bishop or knight on g5/g4), resulting in a material trade that appears reasonable but catastrophically compromises king safety. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves that are technically trades (median net +2.0 suggests capturing a minor piece), yet 100% of the time the player misses winning material — indicating they chose a superficially attractive capture over a much better alternative. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median 368cp loss, with 64% of cases going from drawn to losing and 18% from winning to losing. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is king_safety (92%), with recurring tags of pawn_shield_destruction and open_file. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show ...hxg5 or hxg4 moves in the opening, where recapturing on g5/g4 with the h-pawn opens the h-file against the player's own castled king or removes a critical pawn shield, allowing the opponent's rook or queen to exploit the newly opened lines. Players are lured by winning material in a trade but fail to recognize the positional catastrophe of exposing their king.

596.label: Player greedily captures material or repositions a piece while fatally ignoring back-rank mate vulnerability.
596.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a knight or rook move—often capturing a bishop or queen (material outcome appears 'safe' at surface level)—while catastrophically overlooking back-rank threats against their own king. The eval trajectory is devastating: 60% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 669 centipawns, indicating these are game-deciding blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is back_rank (60%), with recurring tags of king_safety, back_rank_mate, and material_greed. The pattern is consistent: the player's greed for material (capturing a piece or making an aggressive move) blinds them to the fact that their back rank is fatally weak—often with only one defender preventing immediate checkmate. Maia consistently recommends quiet knight moves (100% knight, no captures), suggesting the correct play was a defensive consolidation or prophylactic piece placement rather than the aggressive capture chosen. The phase is primarily opening/early middlegame (60%/40%), when players are still developing but back-rank issues can already be lethal due to uncastled or poorly sheltered kings.

599.label: Giving a check that loses significant material with no follow-up attack or compensation.
599.description: This feature identifies checks (100% of activating positions involve giving check) delivered primarily by rooks (70%) and queens (26%) that result in catastrophic material loss (39% hang a piece, 35% lose material, median net material of -4.0). The eval trajectory confirms these are devastating mistakes (median 289 centipawns lost), often worsening already-losing positions (37% losing->losing) or throwing away winning ones (11% winning->losing). The Opus tactical analysis repeatedly identifies 'pointless check' and 'piece sacrifice without compensation' — moves where the player delivers a check with no constructive follow-up, often trading away their most active piece for nothing or hanging it outright. The example summaries explicitly describe giving away a rook for a 'meaningless check with no follow-up' and eliminating one's own counterplay through a check that simplifies into a hopeless position. Maia's preferred moves (72% non-captures, only 17% checks) confirm the engine sees quiet developing moves as superior, highlighting that the check was an impulsive tactical choice rather than a sound one.

600.label: In winning endgames, trading or moving active pieces that were critical for converting the advantage, often surrendering key defenders of passed pawns or allowing tempo loss.
600.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes where a player with a winning position makes a king move (100% king moves) or piece exchange that is nominally 'safe' in material terms but strategically undermines their winning plan. The eval trajectory shows these are almost always winning->winning with small centipawn losses (median 9cp), but the example summaries reveal catastrophic cases too—trading away key defensive/offensive pieces for pawns, or losing tempo in critical pawn races. The dominant motifs (passed_pawn 40%, tempo_loss 20%, pawn_endgame 20%) combined with the boards showing pawn endgames and piece-vs-pawn scenarios indicate the recurring mistake is mishandling the conversion phase: the player makes a 'safe' king move instead of advancing or supporting a passed pawn (as Maia suggests with 100% pawn moves), losing critical tempo or allowing the opponent counterplay. The positions are all endgames with passed pawns where precise technique—particularly king activity and tempo—determines the outcome.

597.label: Player makes a quiet pawn move while ignoring an immediate checkmate or decisive tactical threat from the opponent's queen.
597.description: This feature consistently fires when a player makes a slow, non-capturing pawn move (71% pawn moves, 86% no capture) while completely missing a critical tactical opportunity or ignoring a lethal threat. The Maia best move is overwhelmingly a queen move (71%) that delivers check (100% of Maia moves give check), indicating the player missed a forcing queen continuation or failed to address an incoming mating attack. The dominant motifs—king_safety (25%), back_rank (17%), and hanging_piece (33%)—combined with tags like missed_tactic (9/12) and king_safety (8/12) confirm the player is oblivious to immediate threats against their own king or missed a decisive tactical blow. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 253cp), with positions shifting from winning to losing/drawn (58% combined). The concrete positions reinforce this: in multiple cases the player pushes g3, f5, or c5 while a queen checkmate or devastating check sits on the board. The move is 'safe' in that the pawn itself isn't immediately captured (57%), but the position collapses because the real danger—a mating attack or winning tactic—was completely overlooked.

598.label: Player makes a non-capturing move in the opening that leaves a knight undefended, allowing the opponent to win it cleanly.
598.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (queen moves 38%, king moves/castling 25%, bishop moves 25%) that fatally neglects the safety of a knight. The material signature is stark: 88% of moves 'hang' material with a median loss of -3.0 (a full piece), and Maia's recommended response is always capturing a bishop or exploiting the hanging knight. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders—88% shift from drawn to losing, with a median cost of 473 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern: players either misplace their queen away from defending a critical knight (Qf3 leaving Ne5 undefended, Qa5 ignoring Ne4's vulnerability), castle prematurely while a knight is tactically exposed, or develop a piece that ignores existing tension around a knight. The positions all occur in the opening (100%), typically in Sicilian or French-type structures where knights on e4/e5 are centralized but require tactical support. The common thread is a 'tactical oversight' where the player makes a reasonable-looking developing move but fails to notice their knight is en prise or forkable.

601.label: In endgames, moving a piece (often king or pawn) that leaves another piece undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it for free.
601.description: This feature identifies a specific endgame blunder pattern where the player makes a non-capturing move (100% no captures) that hangs material (62% hangs) in pure endgame positions (100% endgame). The moves are predominantly king or pawn moves (38% each) that inadvertently abandon defense of another piece. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (90%), with missed_capture (6/8) indicating the player overlooked they could have simply taken an opponent's piece instead. The eval trajectory shows these are catastrophic errors—median 883 centipawns lost—typically converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (63% winning->drawn/losing). The concrete positions reveal the pattern clearly: kings move away from pieces they were defending (e.g., Ke6-f5 abandoning a knight on d5), pawns advance when a capture was available (g3-g2 instead of Kxg5), or pieces relocate leaving material en prise. The opponent's best response (Maia) is overwhelmingly a capture (100% captures: 62% rook, 25% bishop, 12% knight), confirming these are straightforward hanging-piece blunders in simplified positions where the player lost track of defensive obligations.

603.label: Player makes a quiet or passive move while a free capture of an opponent's hanging piece is available.
603.description: This feature consistently fires when players overlook simple captures of undefended enemy pieces. The material signature shows the player's actual moves are predominantly quiet king moves (32%), rook moves (28%), and pawn moves (17%) with 87% making no capture at all, while Maia's recommended moves heavily involve capturing major pieces (70% rook captures, 21% queen captures). The 100% 'missed winning material' rate confirms every activation involves failing to take free material. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%), tempo_loss (38%), and missed_tactic (12%)—reinforce that the opponent had undefended pieces available. The eval trajectory (40% winning->winning, 38% losing->winning) with median 0.0 centipawn loss suggests these positions are often already decided, so the miss doesn't always flip the game result, but the concrete examples confirm the pattern: overlooking Bxd6 capturing a free rook, missing Nxd2 winning an undefended rook, and prioritizing slow pawn moves over immediate piece captures. The 'hangs' outcome at 23% shows that sometimes the passive move itself leaves the player's own pieces vulnerable, compounding the error.

604.label: Playing a quiet developing or retreating move while leaving a piece undefended and capturable by the opponent.
604.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'safe' move (no material exchanged, nothing immediately lost on the move itself) that is passive or routine—typically a knight retreat, a rook move, or a quiet pawn push—while overlooking that one of their pieces is hanging and can be freely captured. The material signature shows 100% safe moves (no capture, no immediate loss), yet Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly captures (rook, bishop, knight, queen in 80%+ of cases), confirming that the opponent had a free piece to take. The hanging_piece motif appears in 100% of Opus analyses, and common tags like 'missed_capture', 'tempo_loss', and 'development_over_tactics' reinforce that the player prioritized routine development or repositioning over concrete tactical awareness. The eval trajectory (median 360cp lost, with 40% of positions going from winning to drawn) shows these oversights are severely punishing—often converting a won game into one where the advantage has evaporated. The boards confirm the pattern: knights left en prise on g5, h4, or e5 while the player develops or retreats, queens that could capture freely ignored in favor of positional shuffling.

605.label: Player delivers a check (often with a rook) that wastes tempo or abandons a stronger continuation, missing winning material.
605.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a check (90% of activating positions involve check) predominantly with a rook (60%), but the check is suboptimal compared to a much stronger alternative. The missed winning material rate is 100%, meaning every activation involves passing up a superior move—typically a Maia-recommended rook or queen capture that wins significant material without giving check. The eval trajectory shows that in most cases the position remains winning (50% winning->winning), so the check isn't catastrophic, but it squanders a decisive advantage or delays conversion. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 50%, king_safety 25%, tempo_loss 25%) and tags like 'check_first', 'zwischenzug', and 'tempo_loss' confirm the pattern: players are seduced by the forcing nature of a check rather than calmly collecting material or maintaining an attack. The Opus analyses reinforce this—several examples note that checking first costs only a few centipawns (extending mate or slightly worsening eval) while others show the check actively throws away a winning position by moving an attacking piece away from where it's needed. The core cognitive error is prioritizing the 'forcing' feel of a check over calculating the objectively strongest continuation.

608.label: Moving a piece to an active square while leaving it or another piece undefended and capturable.
608.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where a player actively moves a piece (queen or bishop, typically) to an aggressive or seemingly purposeful square, but in doing so leaves material hanging—either the moved piece itself lands on an unprotected square, or the move abandons defense of another piece. The material signature shows 50% hangs (non-captures that drop a piece) and 50% trades, indicating the player either places a piece where it's freely captured or initiates an exchange that loses material due to the hanging piece. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (40%), overloaded_defender, and tempo_loss—confirm this is about undefended pieces rather than deep tactical oversights. The eval trajectory (losing->losing, median 188cp lost) shows these occur in already-difficult positions where the player, under pressure, prioritizes activity or counterplay over piece safety. Concrete examples include Nd4+ landing on a square captured by the queen, Bc4 ignoring an undefended bishop on a5, and Ne4 where recaptures open fatal lines. The common thread is wrong prioritization: choosing an active-looking move while overlooking that a piece is left en prise.

607.label: Playing a knight check that abandons a critical defensive or active piece in the endgame, losing material for no compensation.
607.description: This feature consistently fires on endgame positions where the player delivers a knight check (100% knight moves, 100% checks) that is objectively terrible—hanging the knight or losing material (50% hangs, 50% slightly down, median net -2.0). The positions are universally endgames with simplified material, where the knight was serving a vital defensive or restraining role. The Opus analysis repeatedly identifies the pattern: the knight was the key piece holding the position together (guarding pawns, restricting the opponent's king, or maintaining a blockade), and the player sacrifices it for a meaningless check or an insignificant pawn capture. The tactical tags (hanging_piece, tempo_loss, calculation_error) confirm the player is seduced by the check's forcing nature without calculating that the knight will be lost or that the resulting position is hopeless. The eval trajectory shows varied starting positions (winning, losing, equal) but the common thread is that the check accomplishes nothing strategically—it's a reflexive 'check is always good' impulse rather than sound endgame technique.

606.chip: King Tempo Loss in Pawn Endgame
606.label: King moves to a suboptimal square in a won pawn endgame, losing critical tempo in the race to promote or blockade passed pawns.
606.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure pawn endgames (100% endgame phase, 100% king moves, no captures) where the player retains a winning position but squanders tempo. The material signature shows these moves are overwhelmingly 'safe' (80%) — nothing is immediately hanging — yet the median eval loss of 81 centipawns indicates a significant strategic cost. The dominant motifs are pawn_endgame (53%), passed_pawn (27%), and tempo_loss (13%), with tags confirming king_activity and tempo_loss as central themes. Examining the boards reveals pure king-and-pawn positions where the winning technique requires precise king maneuvering — opposition, outflanking, or supporting a passed pawn — and the player instead drifts the king to a square that loses a critical tempo, allowing the opponent's king to reach a key defensive post or enabling counterplay. The trajectory (winning->winning, ~81cp lost) shows these aren't game-losing blunders but meaningful inaccuracies where the player had one clearly superior path (often a single best move) and chose a plausible but inferior king step that slows the winning process.

609.label: Player overlooks a forced back-rank checkmate (or mating sequence) and plays an aimless or materialistic move instead.
609.description: This feature fires when a player has a winning back-rank mating combination available but fails to execute it. The material signature shows that 53% of moves hang material and the net median is -1.0, indicating the player's move is not only non-productive but often leaves pieces undefended. Crucially, Maia's recommended moves deliver check 100% of the time (predominantly with queen at 60% or rook at 33%), confirming that the missed opportunity involves a checking/mating sequence. The Opus tactical analysis identifies back_rank as the dominant motif in 71% of cases, with tags like back_rank_mate, missed_mate, and catastrophic_blunder recurring. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 420 centipawns, with positions shifting from winning to losing (20%) or drawn to losing (7%), indicating these are game-deciding oversights. The concrete examples consistently show players choosing quiet or materialistic moves (Kxe2, Nf3, h4, pawn pushes) when forced checkmates in 1-3 moves existed via back-rank exploitation. The pattern is a player who either doesn't see the back-rank vulnerability or gets distracted by other considerations, squandering a decisive tactical opportunity.

610.label: Ignoring an undefended or freely capturable piece during the opening to make a passive developing move instead.
610.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player makes a developing or quiet move (typically a bishop or knight move, 56% and 22% respectively) while completely overlooking a hanging or undefended enemy piece that could be captured immediately. The material signature shows 67% of moves result in hanging a piece with a median loss of -2.0 material units, and 78% of positions occur in the opening phase. The eval trajectory is devastating: 67% go from winning to losing and 22% from drawn to losing, with a massive median eval drop of 933 centipawns. The OPUS analysis confirms the dominant motif is hanging_piece (88%), with recurring tags of opening_blunder, missed_capture, and ignored_threat. The concrete examples show a strikingly consistent pattern: players develop a piece to a passive square (Bb7, Be6, Nh6, Bf6) while an enemy queen or bishop sits completely undefended and capturable. The mistake is not about making a bad trade or positional concession—it is pure tactical blindness in the opening, where the player follows general development principles instead of addressing an immediate tactical reality.

602.label: In a won endgame, player makes a safe queen move instead of a queen check that wins material or accelerates the win.
602.description: Across all activating positions, the player has a dominant queen in an endgame and plays a safe move (often capturing a pawn) rather than Maia's recommended queen check. The material signature shows 100% queen moves that are objectively safe but miss winning material (100% missed winning material). Maia always recommends a queen check instead. The 0 centipawn eval loss suggests these positions are already winning, so the mistake doesn't throw the game — it just delays victory by choosing materialistic or quiet moves over forcing checks that would have won faster or captured more. This is a technique/efficiency error in converting endgames, where the player defaults to 'safe' grabs rather than calculating the most forcing continuation.

611.label: Automatically promoting to a queen in the endgame when underpromotion or a different move was required to avoid tactical refutation.
611.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (91%) where a player advances a pawn to the promotion square and reflexively chooses a queen, ignoring critical tactical consequences. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures, and the Opus analysis overwhelmingly tags 'promotion_error' (69%) as the dominant motif. The eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of 551 centipawns, with 55% of cases going from winning to still winning but with drastically reduced advantage, and 27% converting wins into draws or losses. The concrete boards confirm the pattern: players promote to queens when underpromotion (to rook or bishop to avoid stalemate), or an entirely different non-promotion move (like a king move or check) was necessary. Maia's suggested alternatives frequently involve rook moves (36%) or giving check (55%), indicating the engine sees immediate tactical threats—back-rank mates, skewers, or stalemate traps—that the reflexive queen promotion either enables or ignores. The 'back_rank' (15%) and 'skewer' (8%) motifs confirm that the new queen often becomes immediately vulnerable or the promotion overlooks a mating net against the player's own king.

616.label: Player ignores an invading bishop attacking their queen, making a routine move instead of addressing the immediate threat.
616.description: This feature fires when a player in the opening phase makes a routine developing or pawn move (bishop 50%, pawn 50%) while completely ignoring a critical tactical threat—specifically, an enemy bishop that has invaded a key square and is directly attacking their queen. The boards consistently show White's bishop on c7/e7/B7 squares attacking Black's queen (or analogous setups), and the player responds with casual development (Bg7, Nf6, d6, etc.) rather than capturing the invading bishop or moving the queen. The material signature confirms catastrophic loss (median -5.0 material, net eval swing of ~1031 centipawns), and Maia consistently identifies Qxbishop as the correct recapture. The dominant tag cluster—hanging_piece (80%), ignored_threat, queen_loss, missed_tactic, opening_trap—all converge on the same pattern: the player simply fails to register that their queen is under direct attack from an invading bishop, resulting in a swing from winning to losing in a single move.

612.label: Player makes a developing or routine move while overlooking an opponent's bishop bearing down on an unprotected piece along an open diagonal.
612.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly natural move (pawn 28%, knight 24%, queen 22%, bishop 18%) that hangs material (46% of moves result in a hang) by failing to notice an enemy bishop's unobstructed diagonal attack. The Maia best move is overwhelmingly a bishop move (96%), indicating the correct response involved either deploying or repositioning a bishop to exploit or defend against diagonal threats. The tactical analysis confirms this: 43% hanging_piece motif combined with recurring tags like 'unblocked_diagonal', 'bishop_captures_queen', and 'opening_oversight'. Multiple example summaries describe players making developing moves without recognizing that an opponent's bishop has a clear path to a high-value target (often the queen on d8 via g5-d8 diagonal). The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly drawn positions turning losing (54%), with a median loss of 253 centipawns — consistent with hanging a minor piece or allowing a devastating bishop tactic. The phase split (46% opening, 54% middlegame) confirms these occur during development when diagonals first open up and players focus on their own plans rather than scanning the opponent's piece activity along long diagonals.

614.label: Player makes a slow developing move in the opening, missing a forcing tactical shot (often a capture or fork) that wins material.
614.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (97% opening) where the player moves a minor piece or pawn quietly (knight 31%, bishop 28%, pawn 28%) without capturing anything (100% non-capture), while the engine's preferred move was almost always a bishop or knight capture (Maia captures: bishop 72%, knight 24%). The eval trajectory shows a severe cost (median 320cp lost), frequently converting drawn positions to losing (28%) or winning positions to drawn/losing (42% combined). The tactical motifs—fork (29%), tempo_loss (29%), hanging_piece (29%)—and the per-position analyses consistently describe the same pattern: the player chose a slow, developmental, or prophylactic move when a concrete tactical sequence (a capture, fork, or forcing sacrifice) was available that would have won material or delivered a decisive attack. The positions show typical opening structures where tactical tension exists (pieces on active squares, open diagonals, unresolved central contact) but the player defaults to a routine developing move instead of calculating the critical forcing line.

615.label: Playing a safe but passive move instead of executing a winning knight fork or tactic in the middlegame.
615.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player had a winning knight tactic available (almost always a fork) but instead played a 'safe' move—typically a knight or pawn move that doesn't capture anything and doesn't lose material directly, yet squanders a decisive advantage. The material signature shows 75% safe moves with no capture (69%), confirming the player isn't blundering a piece but is simply missing the winning shot. Maia consistently recommends knight moves (100%), and the missed winning material rate is 100%, indicating a clear tactic was available every time. The dominant motifs are fork (55%) and missed_tactic (36%), with tags like 'missed_fork' and 'exchange_win_missed' reinforcing that a concrete knight fork or combination was on the board. The eval trajectory (winning→drawn 69%, median loss 271cp) shows these are cases of throwing away a winning position by failing to find the critical knight maneuver—often the only move that maintains the advantage. The example summaries repeatedly reference missed Nc6, Nd3, or Nxc6 as the single winning move, confirming the pattern of overlooking a decisive knight fork.

613.label: Player castles or makes a developing move that walks into an existing tactical threat, leaving pieces hanging or the king exposed.
613.description: This feature captures positions where the player makes a seemingly natural developing or safety move—most prominently castling (4 of the top 12 positions show castling as the played move)—that walks directly into an existing tactical threat. The material signature shows 33% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that drop a piece) with no checks played, and 72% involve no capture, indicating these are quiet moves that overlook danger. The eval trajectory is severe (median 344cp lost), with transitions like drawn->losing and winning->drawn, showing these moves throw away the position. The tactical analysis confirms the pattern: hanging_piece (40%), fork (20%), and king_safety (20%) are the dominant motifs, with recurring tags of missed_tactic, undefended_piece, and king_safety. The example summaries explicitly describe castling into positions where pieces are left undefended or attacked. Maia's recommended moves (44% queen moves, 22% captures of knights) suggest the correct response was to address the tactical threat rather than complete development. This is not a trade gone wrong but rather a failure to recognize that a quiet, 'natural' move ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability.

618.label: Developing or repositioning a bishop (or other piece) to a square where it can be captured for free, squandering a significant advantage.
618.description: This feature identifies moves—predominantly bishop moves (57%)—that leave the moved piece undefended ('hangs' in 71% of cases), resulting in a median loss of ~3 pawns worth of material and a catastrophic eval swing (median 513 centipawns lost). The trajectory shows these errors frequently convert winning or drawn positions into drawn or lost ones (winning->drawn 29%, drawn->losing 14%), indicating advantages being thrown away rather than positions already being bad. The Opus tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs are hanging_piece (50%) and tempo_loss (50%), with tags like 'material_advantage_squandered' and 'missed_tactic' reinforcing that the player had a good position but made a careless developing or repositioning move that overlooked a tactical vulnerability. The top boards show middlegame positions (71%) where pieces are actively being developed or rerouted, but the destination square is tactically compromised—often the opponent can simply capture the piece or exploit the tempo lost. Maia's suggested alternatives (pawn 57%, bishop 43%) indicate that quieter, more consolidating moves were available.

617.label: Playing a passive or cosmetic move instead of an available tactical piece activation that wins material or tempo.
617.description: This feature fires when players make a passive or aesthetically-motivated move (often with a pawn, bishop, rook, or knight) while missing a concrete tactical opportunity involving a bishop or knight activation (Maia recommends bishop 56%, knight 38%). The material signature shows 84% non-captures with 32% hanging pieces afterward, confirming the player chose a quiet move that leaves material vulnerable rather than seizing the available tactic. The eval trajectory (median 259cp lost, with 11% drawn->losing and 7% winning->drawn) shows these are significant missed opportunities that often throw away a game's result. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (33%), fork (22%), positional_mistake (22%), hanging_piece (11%)—along with tags like missed_tactic, overloaded_defender, and wrong_piece all point to the same pattern: the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (retreating a knight from an outpost, pushing a quiet pawn, making a cosmetic rook move) when a forcing piece activation would have exploited a concrete tactical vulnerability. The top boards consistently show positions where active piece placement (Ng4 attacking f2, Bg4 winning the exchange, moving a bishop to safety) was available but the player chose a passive alternative.

622.label: Developing or pushing a piece in the opening that ignores an immediate tactical threat, hanging material.
622.description: This feature fires on opening-phase moves (100% opening) where the player develops a piece or pushes a pawn while ignoring a concrete tactical threat on the board. The dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (50%), supported by tags like 'ignoring_threats', 'opening_blunder', and 'development_before_tactics'. The moves themselves are non-captures (100% no capture) that frequently result in hanging material (50% hangs). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences—a median loss of 445 centipawns, often transitioning from drawn to losing positions. The concrete examples consistently show the same pattern: a natural-looking developing move (Be2, Nf3, c4, Be7) that overlooks an opponent's pawn or piece ready to capture an undefended piece. The player prioritizes routine development over addressing the immediate tactical reality, losing roughly a minor piece worth of material in the process.

619.label: Releasing central tension or making premature exchanges that squander a winning advantage.
619.description: This feature fires on moves where a player prematurely resolves tension—typically with pawn captures/exchanges or minor piece moves in the center—collapsing a winning position into a drawn or losing one. The material signature shows mostly safe or trade outcomes (62% safe, 19% trade) with pawns and knights as the most common pieces moved, indicating these aren't tactical blunders but strategic misjudgments. The eval trajectory is devastating: 36% winning->drawn and 9% drawn->losing, with a median loss of 300 centipawns, confirming these moves throw away substantial advantages. The Opus analysis reveals dominant motifs of positional_mistake (38%) and tempo_loss (25%), with tags emphasizing piece_activity and missed_tactic. The top boards consistently show moves like exd5, cxb3, axb6, and fxe5—premature captures that release pawn tension, open lines for the opponent, or trade off attacking potential. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly quiet pawn advances (93%), suggesting the correct approach was to maintain tension and improve piece placement rather than clarify the position. The opening/middlegame phase split (48%/52%) confirms these occur when strategic tension is at its peak and should be preserved.

620.label: Failing to recapture or address a bishop on an attacked square in the opening, leaving a piece hanging.
620.description: This feature detects a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a player moves a bishop (67%) or pawn (25%) to a square where it is immediately hanging, typically failing to recapture an opponent's piece that has just captured on a key square. The material signature shows 92% of moves hang a piece (non-capture that drops material), with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full minor piece). The eval trajectory is devastating: 83% of cases swing from drawn to losing and 17% from winning to losing, with a median cost of 514 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (83%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, development, and tempo_loss. Examining the concrete positions reveals the signature scenario: after a bishop exchange (often Bxf6 or Bxf3), the player develops a piece to the now-attacked square (e.g., ...Be7 into Bxe7, or Be2 into Bxe2) instead of recapturing, or ignores the hanging piece entirely to make a developing/castling move. Maia consistently identifies the recapture (capturing bishop 100% of the time), confirming these are straightforward recapture oversights in the opening phase.

621.label: King moves in won pawn endgames that squander promotion tempo, hanging material or converting forced wins into merely technical advantages.
621.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame mistake: the player makes a king move (100% king moved) in a pawn endgame (endgame 100%) that hangs material (net -1.0, typically a critical pawn) while already in a winning position (winning->winning trajectory, but losing a median of 472 centipawns). The dominant motifs—passed_pawn (44%), pawn_endgame (22%), and promotion_error (11%)—combined with tempo_loss as the most frequent tag, reveal the core pattern: instead of pushing a passed pawn to promote (or taking the immediately winning continuation), the player makes a king move that loses a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to address the promotion threat. The top boards consistently show positions with advanced passed pawns (g6, a7, d6, f5) where promotion is imminent, but the king wanders to capture a less important pawn or reposition unnecessarily. The Maia baseline (100% pawn moves) confirms that the natural/intuitive move was a pawn push. Though still winning, these moves convert forced mates or immediate promotions into drawn-out technical endgames, representing a failure to execute the final blow in king-and-pawn endings.

626.label: Pushing a pawn forward that loses tempo, weakens king safety, or hangs material in the middlegame.
626.description: This feature fires on pawn moves (100% pawn played) that are predominantly non-captures (68% no capture) resulting in hanging material (47%) or trades (24%), with a median material loss of -1.0. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences: median 319 centipawns lost, with 18% converting winning positions to drawn and 9% winning to losing. The tactical analysis reveals the core motifs are king_safety (30%), tempo_loss (30%), and positional_mistake (20%), with tags like premature_pawn_advance, missed_tactic, and piece_activity. The top activating boards confirm the pattern: pawns pushed to g6, b6, h3, g3, and e6 that either weaken the king's shelter, waste tempo in critical positions, or miss stronger piece-based continuations. These are not aggressive pawn breaks but ill-timed advances that squander positional advantages or create fatal weaknesses, often when the player should have been pursuing a tactical opportunity with a piece instead.

625.label: Pieces move into losing positions against advanced passed pawns, often capturing or blocking them but falling into tactical refutations.
625.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where a player moves a piece (typically a rook or knight) into contact with an advanced passed pawn, only to lose significant material through a tactical refutation. The material signature shows 42% loses and 33% hangs with a median net loss of -4.0 (roughly a full piece), indicating these aren't trades but genuine material losses. The dominant motif is passed_pawn (43%), and the board positions consistently feature advanced passed pawns (e7, c7, g2) where the player's piece engages with the pawn but gets trapped or allows a recapture sequence that wins material. The eval trajectory shows 46% losing->losing and 25% drawn->losing, with a massive median eval drop of 429cp — these moves often turn holdable positions into lost ones. The tactical analysis confirms players are walking into forced sequences: capturing passed pawns that are actually protected by lurking pieces, or abandoning blockade duties. Maia's preferred moves (rook 46%, king 29%) suggest the engine wanted defensive/consolidating moves rather than the greedy or panicked piece contact with the passed pawn.

623.label: Rook moves that ignore or create back-rank mating threats, allowing decisive tactical punishment.
623.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a rook (62% of cases) in a way that either exposes their own back rank or fails to address an existing back-rank weakness. The material signature shows a mix of trades and hangs (38% each), indicating these moves aren't pure blunders but rather moves that overlook a critical tactical vulnerability. The dominant motifs—king_safety (50%), back_rank (33%), and hanging_piece (17%)—confirm the pattern: the player makes a move that looks reasonable but neglects the paramount concern of king safety along the back rank. The tags reinforce this with king_safety (5), missed_tactic (4), back_rank (3), and forced_mate (2) appearing frequently. The eval trajectory is varied (winning->winning 25%, losing->losing 25%), suggesting these mistakes occur across different evaluation contexts but often transform survivable positions into immediate losses, as seen in multiple examples where the eval swings by thousands of centipawns due to sudden mate threats. The concrete positions show kings on the back rank with insufficient protection, rooks being moved away from defensive duties, and opponents having pieces aligned for back-rank exploitation.

628.label: Giving unnecessary checks or intermediate moves instead of immediately promoting a passed pawn in a won endgame.
628.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame mistake pattern. The material/position signature shows rook moves delivering check (100%) in endgame positions that are already winning, where the engine preferred a pawn move (Maia's move: pawn 100%) — strongly indicating a missed promotion opportunity. The eval trajectory confirms these are trivial inaccuracies (median 5cp lost, winning→winning), not game-losing blunders. The Opus tactical analysis clinches it: the dominant motif is promotion_error (54%) combined with tempo_loss (15%) and passed_pawn (23%), with example summaries explicitly describing 'unnecessary intermediate checks that slightly delay the cleanest conversion' and 'promoting immediately' being the better option. The top boards corroborate this perfectly — positions with pawns on the 7th rank (a7, b7, c7, h7) where the player plays a rook check instead of pushing or promoting the pawn. This is the classic endgame principle violation of giving pointless checks rather than executing the immediate promotion, costing small amounts of precision but not the result.

627.label: Player hangs a piece by playing an aggressive-looking move (often with check) that leaves material undefended.
627.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make aggressive moves—frequently checks (44%) or attacks with minor pieces and pawns—that appear threatening but actually hang material (74% of moves result in hanging a piece, median net material loss of -2.0, median eval loss of 234 centipawns). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (50%) and king_safety (50%), with tags indicating undefended pieces and tempo loss. The positions are primarily in the opening/middlegame (97%), where the player launches a premature attack or plays a move that looks forceful (check, tempo-gaining pawn push, piece lunge) but overlooks that a piece is left en prise. The eval trajectory shows these often convert drawn positions to losing ones (26% drawn->losing), indicating the player had a reasonable position before the blunder. The top boards confirm this: moves like Nxe5, Qh5+, Nc7+, and Bf6+ all look aggressive but leave pieces hanging or fail to account for the opponent's tactical response. The Opus analysis highlights 'tempo illusions'—moves that appear to gain time but actually lose material.

631.label: In queen-vs-pawns endgames, the player wastes a critical tempo with a king move instead of using checks or captures to address advancing passed pawns.
631.description: This feature fires on a specific recurring endgame mistake pattern. The material/position signature shows the player almost always moves their king (75%) without capturing anything, while the engine recommends a queen move (100%) that captures a pawn with check. The positions are uniformly endgame queen-vs-pawns scenarios where passed pawns and promotion threats are the central tension. The eval trajectory shows these are mostly minor inaccuracies (median 11cp lost) that don't change the game outcome (winning stays winning 75%), but in 25% of cases the tempo loss costs enough to shift from losing to drawn. The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (21%), passed_pawn (29%), and promotion_error (21%)—along with tags like queen_vs_pawns, king_activity, and missed_mate, reveal a consistent pattern: the player moves their king passively when the position demands immediate tactical action with the queen (checks, pawn captures, or mate threats) to neutralize advancing passed pawns before they promote. The boards confirm this—nearly all are sparse endgames with dangerous passed pawns where precise timing is everything.

630.label: King moves that waste tempo and miss winning queen promotions in pawn endgames.
630.description: This feature captures a specific endgame blunder pattern where a player makes a safe king move (100% king moves, no captures, no checks) in positions with advanced passed pawns nearing promotion. The eval trajectory shows these moves convert losing positions into winning ones for the opponent (losing->winning 100%, median eval lost: -10550 centipawns), indicating the player threw away a completely won game. Maia consistently identifies queen moves capturing pawns with check as the correct continuation, confirming that the missed resource involves promotion or queen activity exploiting the advanced pawn. The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are tempo_loss (43%), hanging_piece (29%), and king_safety (29%), with recurring tags of passed_pawn, promotion_threat, and missed_tactic. The concrete positions all feature advanced pawns on the 7th rank (a7, c7, g7, f7, etc.) where the player needed to execute a tactical sequence involving promotion but instead played a passive or misdirected king/piece move that squandered the critical tempo needed to promote or defend against the opponent's counter-promotion. The player consistently fails to recognize that in these razor-sharp pawn race endgames, a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to promote first or generate decisive counterplay.

629.label: Player makes a passive or retreating move that misses a critical knight maneuver, often leaving pieces poorly coordinated or trapped.
629.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-capturing move (90% no capture) with a pawn, bishop, or knight that is objectively safe (73% safe material outcome) but catastrophically misses a strong knight move (Maia suggests knight 100% of the time). The median eval loss of 234 centipawns with 98% missed winning material confirms these are serious oversights. The dominant motifs—trapped_piece (38%), overloaded_defender (25%), and king_safety (25%)—combined with tempo_loss as the most common tag (6 occurrences) reveal the pattern: players make passive, tempo-wasting moves (retreating knights to b1, playing Be7 when a rook is exposed, shuffling kings) instead of active knight moves that would exploit tactical vulnerabilities. The trajectory (23% drawn->losing, 8% winning->drawn, 4% winning->losing) shows these mistakes frequently convert holdable or winning positions into lost ones. The positions are complex middlegames (65%) and openings (35%) where piece activity is paramount, and the player's instinct toward safety or consolidation causes them to miss the dynamic knight resource that maintains pressure on trapped pieces or overloaded defenders.

632.label: King moves that allow drawing resources or lose critical tempo in won endgame positions.
632.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions where the player is already winning but makes a suboptimal king move that either costs tempo or risks stalemate/drawing chances. The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures in endgame positions that are nominally 'safe' (nothing hangs immediately). The eval trajectory is predominantly winning->winning with small centipawn losses, but the Opus analysis reveals several catastrophic cases where king moves turn forced mates into merely winning positions or even drawn/lost ones (e.g., Kf6 losing 536cp in a drawn position, or missing promotion with b8=Q). The top boards show a clear pattern: simplified endgames (often K+Q vs K, K+R vs K, or pawn endgames) where the winning side plays a king move instead of the optimal technique—often approaching in a way that gives stalemate, loses opposition, or wastes a critical tempo when a pawn promotion or mating net was available. The dominant motifs of promotion_error, tempo_loss, and pawn_endgame confirm these are technique failures in won endings rather than tactical oversights in complex positions.

633.label: Player makes a quiet or repositioning move, missing a forcing continuation (often involving check) that would have delivered a decisive attack.
633.description: This feature fires when a player, usually in the middlegame, plays a move that looks safe or even aggressive (often moving a queen or rook) but catastrophically misses a winning tactical continuation that Maia identifies—most frequently a checking move (Maia gives check 49% of the time). The material signature shows the played move is overwhelmingly non-capturing (63% no capture) and superficially safe (63% 'safe' outcome), yet the eval trajectory reveals a median loss of 469 centipawns, with many positions flipping from winning to losing or drawn (18% combined). The Opus analysis highlights king_safety and back-rank vulnerability as dominant motifs alongside mating attacks and missed tactics: the player's piece repositioning or pawn push ignores a forcing sequence (often a check, skewer, or mating net) that would have decided the game. The top boards confirm this—positions are rich with tactical potential (batteries, exposed kings, back-rank themes) where the player chose a passive continuation instead of the one decisive blow.
