824.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern: the player delivers a check (100% of activating positions) — most often with a knight (40%) but also with bishop, rook, or pawn — that hangs material (80%) or loses material (20%), with a median cost of -3.0 material (roughly a minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms these are devastating mistakes: 60% convert a winning position into a drawn one, with a median loss of 574 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals that the checks are impulsive tempo moves that overlook hanging pieces (40%), lose tempo (40%), or ignore back-rank vulnerabilities (20%). Maia's recommended responses involve capturing significant material (rook 60%, bishop 20%, knight 20%) — the very pieces that were left hanging by the ill-considered check. The common tags (missed_tactic, king_safety, material_sacrifice_unsound) confirm these are not sacrificial brilliances but unsound checks where the player prioritized delivering check over board safety, missing that the opponent simply captures the checking piece or a now-undefended piece elsewhere.

819.label: Moving a piece to a square where it (or another piece) is left undefended and can be captured for free.
819.description: The three signals converge on a clear pattern of leaving pieces en prise. The material signature shows 69% of moves result in a 'hang' (non-capture moves that drop a piece), with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full piece), and the pieces moved are predominantly knights (31%) and queens (23%)—pieces that are frequently misplaced on aggressive-looking but undefended squares. The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors: 23% flip from winning to losing, with a median cost of 260 centipawns, indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders. The Opus tactical analysis seals it: the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' at 55%, with tempo_loss (27%) as a secondary theme—players move a piece aggressively (often with a check or attack) but overlook that it leaves material undefended elsewhere. The top boards illustrate this repeatedly: a bishop moves to f4 leaving a queen on g7 hanging, a knight jumps to g5 overlooking defensive needs, pieces are developed to squares where they or the pieces they were protecting become free captures. The tempo_loss tags reflect that many of these hanging moves are pseudo-active (threats or checks that accomplish nothing) while the real cost is the undefended material left behind.

825.label: Player makes a natural developing move in the opening but misses a powerful knight fork or knight tactic that wins material.
825.description: This feature fires on opening-phase positions (96% opening) where the player makes a safe, natural-looking move (pawn 30%, bishop 17%, king 17% - often castling or quiet development) but misses a knight tactic that Maia consistently identifies (Maia's move is knight 100%). The missed winning material rate is 100%, and the dominant motifs are fork (42%) and tempo_loss (50%), with knight_fork appearing as the most common specific tag. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show Italian Game and similar open-game structures where a knight jump (typically ...Nd4 or Nd5) simultaneously attacks an exposed queen and another piece, winning material cleanly. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly oversights: 56% go from winning to drawn and 17% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 235 centipawns. Players instead castle, develop a bishop to a natural square, or push a pawn - all reasonable-looking moves that fatally ignore the tactical opportunity sitting on the board.

817.label: Trading or capturing pieces in rook endgames that eliminates drawing resources or winning chances by simplifying into a lost position.
817.description: This feature fires on endgame mistakes (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a capture or exchange involving rooks (rook moved 60%, captured pawns/rooks 80%) that results in material loss (net median -4.0) or a strategically inferior simplification. The dominant motif is rook_endgame (43%), with tags like simplification_error, passed_pawn, and rook_activity reinforcing that these are technique failures rather than tactical oversights. The eval trajectory shows significant damage (median 154cp lost) spanning various scenarios—throwing wins into draws, turning drawn positions into losses, or worsening already bad positions. The tactical analyses reveal a consistent pattern: players make intuitive-looking captures (taking passed pawns, trading rooks, exchanging queens) without calculating intermediate moves (checks, forcing sequences) that would have maintained superior endgame positions. The checks played (80%) suggest aggressive-looking moves that actually backfire by enabling unfavorable exchanges or exposing the player's own weaknesses. The Maia alternatives (100% non-captures, 60% giving check) confirm that quieter, more patient moves—often intermediate checks or prophylactic plays—were correct.

827.label: Failing to address critical passed pawn promotion threats in king-and-pawn endgames, losing decisive tempo.
827.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a move that ignores or mishandles a critical passed pawn promotion threat. The material signature shows mostly safe moves (67%) that aren't outright blunders of pieces, yet the eval drops a median of 226 centipawns—indicating positional/tempo catastrophes rather than hanging material. The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (36%) and promotion_error (36%), with tempo_loss as a recurring tag (7 appearances). The boards uniformly feature advanced passed pawns (often on the 7th rank) where precise king positioning or piece activity is essential. Instead, the player moves the king in the wrong direction, wastes a tempo with an irrelevant pawn push, or repositions a piece away from the critical promotion square. The trajectory (67% losing→losing, 33% drawn→losing) shows these mistakes typically convert holdable or marginally lost positions into completely lost ones, often allowing immediate queening or forced checkmate sequences.

823.label: Castling (or tempo-wasting) into a position where opponent's pieces already target the kingside, allowing devastating tactical combinations.
823.description: This feature captures a highly specific pattern where the player—most often by castling kingside (or making a tempo-losing move like a4 or a pawn grab)—walks their king directly into a prepared attack. The material signature shows 82% 'safe' moves (no immediate material exchange), yet the eval trajectory is catastrophic: median 393cp lost, with 35% drawn->losing and 24% winning->losing, indicating the player threw away a tenable or winning position. The OPUS analysis reveals the dominant motifs are king_safety (38%) and pin (46%), with recurring tags like 'castling_into_attack', 'deflection', and 'missed_tactic'. The concrete positions overwhelmingly show a setup where the opponent has a bishop aimed at h2 (often Bd6), a piece on g4 pinning or pressuring f3, and tactical shots like Bxh2+ followed by capturing an undefended queen on d1 via the open d-file. The player fails to recognize that the standard 'safe' developing move of castling actually triggers a forced tactical sequence exploiting pre-existing piece coordination against the kingside.

822.label: Failing to find a desperate but necessary tactical resource (check, sacrifice, or intermediate move) that was the only way to maintain the position.
822.description: This feature captures positions where a player makes a passive or natural-looking move while missing a critical tactical resource—often a desperado sacrifice, intermediate check, or forcing sequence—that was the sole path to survival or maintaining an advantage. The material signature shows pieces being hung (60%) or lost (20%) with a median cost of -3.0 material and 502 centipawns of evaluation, indicating severe blunders. The eval trajectory spans winning->losing, winning->drawn, and drawn->losing, confirming these are positions where the player threw away a good or holdable position. Maia's suggested moves frequently involve checks (60%) and captures (queen, knight, rook), contrasting with the player's passive moves. The tactical analysis reveals the dominant pattern: positions with a single critical saving move (Bxc2+ desperado, Qxc3+ capture, Rb1+ sacrifice) that the player failed to find. Tags like missed_tactic (6), intermediate_check (2), deflection (2), and desperado (1) reinforce that the common thread is overlooking a forcing tactical resource. The board positions show complex middlegame and endgame situations where quiet moves allow the opponent to consolidate, while the missed moves exploit geometric tactics (checks along diagonals/files, promotion threats, piece sacrifices).

826.label: Moving the queen to a passive or vulnerable square where it becomes tactically exposed or loses coordination.
826.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where the player moves their queen (92% of cases) to a square that hangs material (67% of moves result in hanging a piece, with a median net material loss of -1.0). The key distinction is that these are non-capture queen moves—the player isn't trading poorly but rather repositioning the queen to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable. The OPUS analysis reveals the underlying themes: the queen moves often resolve tension poorly (queen_tension_resolved_poorly), lose tempo, or miss concrete tactics (missed_tactic appears in 3/4 of analyzed positions). Looking at the boards, we see positions with active queen confrontations (e.g., queen vs queen tension on open files/diagonals) where the player retreats or sidesteps to an inferior square instead of the correct tactical continuation (often capturing something). The eval trajectory shows a median cost of 257 centipawns, with positions spanning winning->drawn and drawn->losing, indicating these queen repositions squander significant advantages or turn equal positions into lost ones. The common thread is a queen that had an active role but was moved to a passive, hanging, or tactically exploitable square.

828.label: A quiet pawn move in the opening that leaves a piece undefended on a long diagonal, typically hanging a rook to a fianchettoed bishop or centralized queen.
828.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn moves (100% pawn played, 100% opening phase) that are non-captures yet catastrophically hang material (100% 'hangs' outcome, median -5.0 material). The eval trajectory uniformly shows drawn positions collapsing into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 384cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' with recurring tags of 'long_diagonal', 'hanging_rook', and 'undefended_piece'. Examining the concrete positions reveals a clear pattern: players make routine-looking fianchetto or development pawn moves (g7-g6, b7-b6, e7-e6) without recognizing that a fianchettoed bishop on b2 or a centralized queen on d4 already x-rays through to an undefended rook on a8 or h8. The move itself appears natural—a standard hypermodern setup—but in this specific position the long diagonal is already weaponized, and the pawn advance either opens the diagonal further or fails to address the existing threat. The result is an immediate loss of roughly a rook's worth of material from an otherwise equal position.

831.label: Player initiates a pawn trade that releases central tension, costing significant positional value.
831.description: This feature detects pawn exchanges (97% pawn moves, 93% capturing pawns, 80% resulting in trades) that release pawn tension prematurely, particularly in the opening and middlegame (37% opening, 63% middlegame). The eval trajectory shows these trades are costly—median 248 centipawns lost—with many positions going from drawn to losing (13%) or remaining losing (18%). Examining the top boards reveals a consistent pattern: players capture on squares where pawn chains interlock (e4xf5, f3xe4, c6xd5, e5xf4, f5xg4), resolving central or structural tension that was better maintained. Maia's preferred alternatives are diverse piece moves (knight 24%, bishop 16%, queen 13%) rather than the pawn recapture, suggesting the engine sees developing or repositioning as superior to the simplifying exchange. The mistake is strategic—releasing tension hands the opponent open lines, outpost squares, or initiative that the closed structure was denying them.

829.label: Knight moves to an aggressive-looking square but is left hanging or tactically refuted, costing significant material.
829.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where a knight (96% of moves) is played to an apparently active or threatening square—often a deep infiltration (f7, b6, c2, e3, f2)—but the move actually hangs the piece (46% hang outright) or loses material (median net -1.0, median eval lost 362cp). The tactical motifs include forks (33%) and tempo loss (33%), suggesting the knight jumps look aggressive but either miss that the knight itself is undefended, or allow the opponent a tactical refutation. The eval trajectory shows these are game-changing errors: 23% turn draws into losses and 19% turn wins into losses. Maia's recommended moves are diverse (rook 23%, knight 31%, pawn 19%), indicating the correct play was often a quiet or consolidating move rather than the speculative knight lunge. The board positions confirm knights landing on squares like f7, c2, f2, b6, e3—squares that appear to create threats but where the knight lacks support and is immediately captured or the resulting complications favor the opponent.

830.label: Moves that ignore the player's own uncastled or exposed king, allowing the opponent's pieces to exploit open lines and create decisive threats.
830.description: This feature identifies moves where a player, often in a middlegame position with an uncastled or exposed king (KQ castling rights still available in many top boards), makes a developing, pawn-pushing, or queen-moving decision that fatally neglects king safety. The material signature shows these are predominantly 'safe' moves (78%) — not blunders of hanging pieces — yet they cost a median of 327 centipawns, frequently turning drawn or winning positions into losing ones (33% drawn->losing, 22% winning->drawn, 6% winning->losing). The dominant tactical motif is king_safety (60%), with recurring tags of uncastled_king, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic. Maia's recommended responses are universally king moves (100%), suggesting the opponent's punishment directly targets the exposed king. The concrete positions confirm this: players push pawns (a3-a4, d3-d4, b7-b5, f2-f4), grab material greedily (Qxf2), or retreat bishops when they should be castling. The single correct move is often simply O-O. These are positional oversights where the player underestimates the urgency of king safety, not material miscalculations.

832.label: Moving the queen to a passive or irrelevant square instead of trading or delivering a decisive blow, squandering a winning or balanced position.
832.description: This feature captures a specific pattern where the player moves their queen (100% queen moves, 0% captures) to a square that either hangs material (50%) or is merely safe but pointless (50%), while the engine's recommended response involves a queen capture (Maia captures queen 100%). The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic — converting winning positions to drawn (50%), winning to losing (25%), or drawn to losing (25%), with a median loss of 406 centipawns. The dominant motifs are king_safety (60%) and tempo_loss (20%), with recurring tags of exposed_king, queen_misplacement, and critically missed_simplification/queen_exchange_declined. The concrete pattern across the boards is clear: the player declines a queen trade or fails to deliver a decisive queen blow, instead retreating or repositioning the queen passively. This leaves the opponent's king threats unanswered or allows the opponent to force a winning queen exchange. The 75% check rate suggests these queen moves often look aggressive (giving check) but are actually hollow — the check gains nothing while missing the decisive continuation. The core error is choosing an aesthetically active but strategically vacuous queen move over the objectively winning simplification or forced sequence.

833.label: Bishop ventures unprotected into enemy territory in the opening and is immediately captured for free.
833.description: This feature fires when a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves) aggressively into enemy territory during the opening phase (100% opening) where it has no support, leaving it en prise to an enemy queen or other piece. The material signature shows the move either hangs the piece outright (33%) or results in a severe material loss like trading a bishop for a mere pawn (67% slightly_down, with piece_for_pawn appearing in 6/12 tags). The eval trajectory confirms the catastrophic nature: every instance converts a drawn position into a losing one, with a median loss of 510 centipawns—consistent with losing a full minor piece. The tactical analysis unanimously identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif, and the concrete positions show a recurring pattern: Bf4-c7 being captured by the queen, Bb2xg7 being recaptured by Bf8, or similar premature bishop raids deep into the opponent's camp where the piece is completely undefended. The Maia recommendation (100% pawn moves, no captures) suggests the engine preferred quiet developing moves rather than these speculative bishop lunges.

835.label: Trading a knight for a pawn when a stronger knight capture (typically winning the exchange by taking a rook) was available.
835.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a knight capture of a pawn that results in an even trade, but Maia's analysis shows the knight could have captured a rook instead — meaning the player missed winning the exchange (knight for rook). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic errors, with 100% going from winning to losing positions (median loss of 452 centipawns). The tactical analysis highlights hanging pieces (80%) and missed tactics as the dominant motifs: in each case, a piece was available for capture that the player overlooked while settling for an inferior knight trade. The boards confirm this pattern — positions where a knight has access to multiple captures, and the player chose the wrong target (a pawn trade instead of the rook), throwing away a winning position. This is fundamentally a target-selection error on a knight fork or knight attack where the player grabs the less valuable piece.

834.label: Playing a showy check that squanders a winning deflection or intermediate move, converting a winning position into a draw.
834.description: This feature fires when a player delivers a check (44% of moves are checks) with a queen or rook that appears safe or even trades material evenly (median net material 0.0), but catastrophically misses a stronger tactical continuation—typically a deflection sacrifice or critical intermediate move. The eval trajectory (median 441cp lost, 56% winning→drawn) shows these are thrown wins, not incremental errors. The missed Maia moves (100% give check themselves, often with rook or bishop) confirm that the correct line also involved a forcing move, but with superior move order. The dominant motifs—king_safety (44%), tempo_loss (22%), and the recurring tags 'missed_tactic', 'deflection', 'premature_check', and 'move_order'—all point to the same pattern: the player sees a flashy check and plays it impulsively, but this drives the opponent's king to safety or disrupts a precise tactical sequence (e.g., a deflection sacrifice or intermezzo) that would have won decisive material. The per-position analyses repeatedly describe checks that improve the opponent's king position or skip a necessary intermediate move, destroying the winning combination.

839.label: Player gives a check instead of capturing an undefended or available enemy piece, throwing away a winning position.
839.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player delivers a check (100% check rate) but misses a critical capture opportunity (Maia recommends capturing the queen 100% of the time, missed winning material 100%). The positions are exclusively endgames where the player is already winning, yet the unnecessary check costs a massive median of ~97 pawns worth of evaluation—typically converting a forced mate or decisive material advantage into merely a winning position, or allowing the opponent's queen to survive. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (62%) and tempo_loss (38%), with tags like 'unnecessary_check', 'premature_check', and 'forced_mate_missed' appearing repeatedly. The concrete pattern from the boards and summaries is clear: in positions with an undefended enemy queen or a forced mate sequence available, the player reflexively delivers a flashy but purposeless check rather than simply collecting the hanging material. The check gives the opponent's king an escape route and preserves their counterplay resources, squandering a trivially won position through tactical impulsiveness.

837.label: Player makes a non-queen move that ignores a critical queen maneuver, allowing a devastating positional or tactical collapse.
837.description: This feature fires when players make moves (predominantly pawns at 31% and non-queen pieces) while the best move was almost always a queen move (Maia recommends queen 90% of the time). The material signature shows 54% safe and 36% hangs—meaning the moves themselves often leave pieces en prise or create tactical vulnerabilities, not through direct exchanges but through neglect. The median eval loss of 316 centipawns is severe, with 98% missing winning material. The dominant motifs—fork (40%), positional_mistake (20%), tempo_loss (20%), king_safety (20%)—reveal that by failing to deploy or reposition the queen (the one correct move), players leave tactical vulnerabilities unaddressed: knights on rim squares, undefended pieces susceptible to forks, or king safety issues that a queen move would have resolved. The board examples confirm this: positions where the queen needed to centralize, defend, or create threats (Qe2, queen repositioning) but instead the player pushed a pawn, moved a knight to the rim, or made a tempo-losing move, collapsing the position from equal/winning to losing.

838.label: Player makes a quiet pawn or queen move while missing a strong knight maneuver that exploits king safety or tactical opportunities.
838.description: This feature fires when players make seemingly safe moves (pawns 42%, queens 25%) that are materially innocuous (75% safe, median net 0.0) but miss a critical knight resource. In all 12 positions, Maia's recommended move is a knight move (100%), often capturing a pawn (75%) or initiating a tactical sequence. The eval trajectory shows severe consequences—median 219cp lost—with positions swinging from winning to losing/drawn (17%+17%+17%). The tactical analysis reveals king_safety (67%) and missed_tactic (33%) as dominant motifs, with tempo_loss and piece_activity as recurring tags. The boards consistently show positions where knights have powerful outpost squares or tactical jumps (Nxe5, Nd4, Nf-type moves) that exploit loose king positions or win material, but the player instead makes a passive pawn advance or repositioning move that ignores the concrete tactical opportunity. The pattern is one of positional timidity—playing 'normal' moves while a sharp knight blow was required.

841.label: Player makes a move that overlooks a devastating discovered attack, typically involving a knight on g6 with queen on h5.
841.description: This feature fires on positions where players fail to address a critical discovered attack threat, most commonly in opening positions (90%) featuring the classic Ng6+Qh5 battery pattern. The material signature shows 60% of moves 'hang' material (non-captures that leave pieces en prise) with a median loss of 2.0 material units, while Maia's recommended move captures a piece 80% of the time (usually a knight), indicating the correct response was to eliminate the attacking piece. The dominant motif is discovered_attack (75%), and the eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 409 centipawns), often converting drawn positions to losing ones (30%) or making already-losing positions completely hopeless (50%). The concrete board positions repeatedly show the Ng6/Qh5 setup where the knight's movement will uncover the queen's attack (or vice versa), and players respond with irrelevant pawn moves or king walks instead of the only saving move—typically capturing or blocking the discovered attack source.

840.label: Player makes a quiet move that overlooks the opponent's forcing sequence (often a capture with check) that wins material or converts to a winning endgame.
840.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-capturing move (91% no capture) that hangs material (55% hangs, median -1.0 net material), typically in the middlegame (91%). The opponent's best response frequently involves a knight, rook, or bishop capture (Maia captures: knight 55%, rook 36%, bishop 9%), often with a forcing transition such as a recapture with check or a simplification into a won endgame. The eval trajectory shows these are overwhelmingly thrown wins (36% winning->drawn, 9% winning->losing), with a steep median loss of 315 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: the blunder is a quiet king move, pawn push, or rook move that ignores a tactical shot — usually a capture with check (rook_exchange_with_check tag) or a forcing simplification that the opponent exploits to enter a winning pawn endgame or grab hanging material. Tags like passed_pawn, forced_transition, and pawn_endgame_conversion indicate the missed tactic often involves a transition to a technically won simplified position. The player's move looks natural but overlooks that the opponent has a concrete forcing sequence (check, exchange, or fork) that fundamentally changes the position's evaluation.

836.label: Ignoring threats to one's own king while making an otherwise plausible but irrelevant move.
836.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move (most often a pawn push, queen move, or piece relocation) that completely ignores a critical king safety threat. The material signature shows 46% of moves hang material and 88% involve no capture—these are non-forcing moves played while the opponent has a dangerous attacking setup. The eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences: a median loss of 254 centipawns, with many positions swinging from drawn to losing or from salvageable to hopeless. The Opus tactical analysis reveals the dominant motif is king_safety (60%), with supporting tags like checkmate_threat_ignored, queen_on_h_file, and missed_tactic. The concrete examples show players capturing pieces on irrelevant squares while mate threats loom (e.g., ignoring Qxh7#), pushing pawns that weaken their own king shelter (f4, g6, h4), or relocating pieces away from defensive duties. Maia's recommended moves (91% pawn moves, likely defensive pawn blocks like ...g6 or ...f5) confirm that the engine sees simple prophylactic king-safety moves as correct. The pattern is a player who fails to recognize the urgency of their king's vulnerability and plays a 'normal' move instead of addressing the immediate tactical danger to their monarch.

843.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing queen or piece move when the position demands immediate tactical action, squandering a winning or tenable position.
843.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player makes a passive, non-capturing move (73% no capture) — most often with the queen (56%) — that fails to exploit a concrete tactical opportunity. The material signature shows 39% of moves 'hang' something (leaving pieces undefended or allowing the opponent to seize the initiative) and 42% appear superficially 'safe' but miss winning tactics (68% missed winning material). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and king_safety (33%), indicating the player chose a quiet repositioning or prophylactic move when the position demanded forceful play. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 324 centipawns, with 24% of cases converting drawn positions to losing and 17% converting winning to drawn. The per-position analyses consistently describe 'slow, improving' moves that ignore immediate tactical shots, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counter-attack. This is not a material blunder or bad trade — it is a failure to recognize that the position's tension required concrete action rather than passive maneuvering.

842.label: Moving the queen to a passive square when active play (checks, threats, or perpetual) was required to maintain or salvage the position.
842.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves their queen (48% queen moves) to a passive or retreating square, hanging material or squandering a winning/drawing resource. The material signature shows 48% of moves hang a piece and the median net material loss is -1.0, indicating the queen itself isn't immediately captured but the resulting passivity allows the opponent to execute decisive tactics. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic swings (median 548cp lost), with many positions going from winning to losing or losing to hopelessly lost. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring tactical thread: king_safety (33%), back_rank (33%), and tempo_loss (17%) dominate — the retreating queen abandons critical attacking lines, checking diagonals, or perpetual check resources. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (87%) that stay active with checks (30% give check), confirming that the correct approach was to maintain pressure rather than retreat. The concrete examples reinforce this: Qd6-h2 abandoning a dominant centralized queen, Qh8-h2 retreating when king pressure was needed, Qa5-d8 walking into a back-rank pattern, and Qc8-d8 allowing a forced mating sequence. The common thread is a queen retreat that surrenders the initiative at the critical moment when only active play could hold or win.

846.label: Playing a quiet or retreating minor piece move that leaves material hanging, missing a critical tactical opportunity.
846.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a bishop or knight (79% combined) without capturing anything (100% non-captures), and the move hangs material 64% of the time (median net material: -1.0). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 369 centipawns), with positions shifting from drawn-to-losing or winning-to-drawn. The dominant motif is hanging_piece (50%), combined with tags like missed_tactic, missed_mate, and undefended_piece. The Opus analysis reveals that in these positions, strong tactical shots existed (forced mates, winning captures like Bxf5 winning a queen) but instead the player made a passive, non-forcing minor piece move—often a retreat or repositioning (Bc8, Bd6, Ne4)—that ignores the tactical demands of the position and leaves their own material undefended. The opponent's best response (Maia line) frequently involves captures (64% capture rate) or checks (21%), exploiting the newly hanging pieces. This is fundamentally a tactical blindness pattern: choosing quiet development or defense when the position demanded concrete action.

847.label: Moving a minor piece or ignoring queen safety while leaving one's own queen undefended and capturable.
847.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a developing or secondary move (bishop, knight, or queen relocation) while leaving their own queen en prise—typically hanging on an open file or central square where the opponent's queen can simply capture it. The material signature shows 56% hangs with a median loss of 3.0 (a queen's relative value in many contexts) and Maia's recommended response is always a queen capture (100%), often with check (83%). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 61% convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 541 centipawns. The tactical analysis reinforces this: 'hanging_piece' dominates at 60%, with recurring tags like 'hanging_queen' and 'undefended_piece.' The top boards show a recurring pattern in the opening/early middlegame where players develop pieces (Bg4, Nc6) or reposition their queen without noticing that their queen on e5 or similar central squares is completely undefended and immediately capturable by the opponent's queen. Players attend to secondary threats while missing the most basic tactical reality on the board.

844.label: In a winning position with an active attack (often involving a knight on g5), the player retreats their king instead of capturing/recapturing, hanging a piece to the opponent's queen.
844.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening/early middlegame pattern where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a non-capture that hangs material (100% hangs, median -3.0 material loss). The opponent's best response is always a queen capturing a knight (Maia: queen 100%, captures knight 100%). The positions almost exclusively arise in the opening (86%) and share a common tactical signature: the player's king is already exposed (often on f7/f1 after earlier play), typically facing a knight on g5 in a Fried Liver or similar Italian Game attacking structure. Instead of playing the one correct defensive or counter-attacking move (frequently recapturing a piece with the queen), the player retreats their king to a passive square (e8, g6, g8, g1, f8, e7), which drops a knight that was previously defended or leaves a piece en prise to the opponent's queen. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—71% swing from winning to losing, 29% from winning to drawn, with a median loss of 626 centipawns. The dominant motifs (hanging_piece 58%, king_safety 33%) confirm the player prioritizes perceived king safety over material, failing to recognize the concrete tactical requirement to maintain their extra piece. This is a panic retreat that squanders a winning position.

845.label: Player makes a pawn or knight move that fatally ignores deadly diagonal attacks (batteries, mate threats) against their king.
845.description: This feature captures positions where the player moves a pawn (38%) or knight (28%) while completely overlooking critical diagonal threats to their king. The material signature shows 55% of moves hang a piece and the median cost is -1.0 (a full piece), with 76% missing winning material. The dominant motif is king_safety (57%), supported by tags like queen_bishop_battery, diagonal_mate, and light_square_weakness. The concrete examples are striking: g7-g6 moves that open the king to Qxg6+ mate sequences, c4 pushes that ignore lethal diagonal batteries aimed at g2/h1, and piece moves that neglect forced checkmate threats along diagonals. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic consequences (median 284cp lost), with 28% going from drawn to losing and 28% making losing positions even worse. Maia consistently recommends knight (55%) or bishop (17%) moves that address the diagonal threats—either blocking, retreating, or developing defensively. The pattern is a player who becomes tactically blind to diagonal geometry, often making seemingly reasonable developing or space-gaining moves while a queen-bishop battery or diagonal mate threat demands immediate attention.

851.label: King moves to an unsafe square, exposing it to tactical threats and causing a significant evaluation drop.
851.description: This feature identifies middlegame positions where the player moves their king (75% of activating moves are king moves) to a square that critically worsens king safety. The dominant motif is king_safety (64%), supported by tags like exposed_king, tempo_loss, and missed_tactic. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic: median 276 centipawns lost, with 50% turning drawn positions into losing ones. The concrete examples reinforce this — Kf3 stepping onto a dangerous diagonal, Kc1 abandoning the only safe square, Kg6 walking into an attack. These are not material blunders in the traditional sense (50% are materially 'safe' immediately) but positional catastrophes where the king voluntarily moves to a vulnerable square, enabling opponent tactics (skewers, checks, attacks) that were previously impossible. The player fails to recognize that their king's current square was safe and that moving it opens lines or creates tactical vulnerabilities.

848.label: King moves that waste critical tempo in queen-vs-pawn or pawn-promotion endgames, allowing the opponent to consolidate or convert.
848.description: This feature fires on king moves in deep endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player loses tempo at a critical moment involving passed pawns and promotion threats. The material signature shows all king moves with no captures and no checks, meaning these are quiet repositioning moves rather than tactical blunders—yet they cost a median of 93 centipawns. The eval trajectory (80% losing→losing, 20% drawn→losing) indicates these moves typically make already-difficult positions worse or convert holdable draws into losses. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (43%), supported by passed_pawn (21%) and promotion_error (14%), painting a clear picture: in positions where pawn promotion races or queen-vs-pawn tablebase knowledge is critical, the player's king steps to the wrong square, losing a crucial tempo. The top boards confirm this—nearly all feature advanced passed pawns, promotion squares, and queen-vs-pawn scenarios where one tempo determines whether a position is drawn or lost. The king retreats or sidesteps when a specific square was required to maintain drawing chances or coordinate with a promoting pawn.

850.label: In rook endgames with passed pawns, the player makes a tempo-losing or misdirected move that ignores the critical promotion threat.
850.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (82%) involving rook moves (55%) and pawn moves (27%) where the player neglects or mishandles a passed pawn promotion race. The material signature shows moves are mostly 'safe' (82%) — nothing is immediately hung — yet the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic positional collapse (median 463cp lost), often converting drawn positions into losses (27%) or even wins into losses (9%). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motifs: passed_pawn (45%), tempo_loss (27%), and promotion_error (27%). The concrete positions all feature advanced passed pawns (often on the 7th rank) in rook endgames where the player either gives a purposeless check that improves the opponent's king position, captures the wrong pawn, or otherwise wastes a critical tempo in a promotion race. Maia consistently recommends rook moves (100%) that address the promotion threat directly, while the player's actual moves squander the position by failing to prioritize the queening race. The common thread is losing a tempo or misidentifying the critical passed pawn in time-sensitive endgame positions.

849.label: Rook or king moves that allow immediate back-rank checkmate by neglecting the vulnerable back rank.
849.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves their rook (71%) or king (29%) in a way that fatally exposes their back rank to checkmate. The dominant motif is overwhelmingly back_rank (75%), with tags confirming back_rank(8), back_rank_mate(2), and missed_tactic(10). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic swings — positions that were losing but playable suddenly become immediate checkmate (losing->losing 57% reflects already-difficult positions made terminal, while losing->winning 29% and drawn->winning 14% show cases where the opponent was actually worse but the blunder gifts them an instant win). The Opus analysis consistently describes 'catastrophic evaluation shifts' to #+1 or #-1, with rooks being moved away from critical defensive files or kings stepping onto vulnerable squares. The material signature shows 'safe' 71% because these aren't capture blunders — the moved piece itself isn't hanging — but the positional consequence is lethal. The phase split (endgame 57%, middlegame 43%) reflects that back-rank vulnerabilities peak in simplified positions where pawns haven't advanced to create luft and fewer pieces remain to defend.

853.label: Advancing a pawn or minor piece that removes a critical defender, leaving material hanging in the opening.
853.description: This feature detects opening-phase moves (71% opening) where players advance pawns (42%) or develop minor pieces (25% knight, 21% bishop) without capturing anything (100% non-captures), yet hang material 62% of the time with a median cost of ~242 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the mechanism: tempo_loss and hanging_piece motifs dominate, with recurring themes of queenside overextension and center weakness. The concrete positions show pawn advances (c3-c4, f2-f4, a4-a5, d4-d5) or piece moves that remove key defenders or create tactical vulnerabilities. Maia's recommended alternatives are typically quiet developing moves (42% bishop, 42% knight), suggesting the player rushed a pawn advance or repositioning that ignored defensive obligations. The eval trajectory (25% drawn->losing, median 242cp loss) confirms these are consequential positional errors where structural/tempo considerations were overlooked, not simple tactical oversights.

855.label: In won endgames, plays a passive king or pawn move instead of capturing/activating the rook against an enemy knight.
855.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern in technically won endgames (100% endgame phase, 100% winning->winning) where the player makes a 'safe' king move (80%) or pawn push (20%) that wastes tempo, costing a median of 120 centipawns. The boards consistently show rook-vs-knight endgames where Maia recommends Rxknight (100% rook capturing knight), often with check (60%). The dominant motifs—tempo_loss (25%), passed_pawn (33%), and hanging_piece (17%)—along with tags like piece_activity and missed_tactic confirm that the player squanders a decisive advantage by making an aimless move rather than cleanly winning material with the rook. The positions all feature sparse endgame material where the opponent's knight is tactically vulnerable, but the player opts for a slow consolidating move instead of the concrete Rx capture that simplifies to an easily won position.

856.label: Player ignores an available queen capture, making a passive or irrelevant move that squanders a decisive advantage.
856.description: This feature fires on positions where the player had a straightforward queen capture available (Maia's move is overwhelmingly queen capturing queen, 100% capture rate) but instead played a different piece (rook 40%, queen 20%, pawn 20%, king 20%) with no capture 80% of the time. The result is catastrophic: 100% of these positions involve missed winning material, with a median eval loss of 9350 centipawns—indicating transitions from winning/drawn positions into losses or draws. The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (58%) and missed_capture/missed_tactic tags, confirming the player overlooked an undefended or takeable queen sitting on the board. The per-position analyses reinforce this: one player took a pawn instead of capturing the opponent's queen, another made a passive king move while a bishop could capture the queen, and others played aimless moves while a winning queen capture was available. The phase spans middlegame and endgame, and the trajectory shows these are game-deciding oversights—winning positions converted to draws or losses due to failing to notice the simplest tactical opportunity on the board.

858.label: In the opening, player makes a routine developing move instead of deploying a bishop to pin or trap the opponent's exposed queen.
858.description: This feature fires on opening positions where the player has a strong bishop move available (Maia consistently recommends a bishop move in 100% of cases) that would exploit an exposed queen via a pin or diagonal attack, but the player instead makes a safe, routine developing move (knight 36%, bishop 27%, king/castling 18%). The material signature shows these moves are 'safe' (82%) - nothing is immediately lost - yet the eval trajectory reveals a massive median cost of 361 centipawns, with 55% of cases converting a winning position into a drawn one. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant pattern: the missed move is almost always a bishop deployment that pins the queen to the king along a diagonal (pin 29%, pin_to_king tag) or traps an exposed queen (trapped_piece 14%, exposed_queen tag appears 4 times). The boards consistently show early middlegame positions where an opponent's queen sits vulnerably on c3 or similar squares, and a bishop check/pin from b4 or b5 would win decisive material. Instead, players opt for natural but passive development, squandering their tactical opportunity.

854.label: Player makes an irrelevant move while opponent's advanced passed pawn or promotion threat demands immediate attention.
854.description: This feature fires when players ignore critical promotion threats in the middlegame. The material signature shows that 67% of moves hang material (non-captures that drop pieces) while Maia's recommended moves overwhelmingly involve capturing a queen (83%) or rook (17%) — indicating the player missed winning major material tied to the promotion theme. The dominant motifs are promotion_error (50%) and passed_pawn (25%), with promotion_threat appearing in half the positions and forced_mate in a third. The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 9181 centipawns lost), consistent with missing a promotion-based tactic that either wins the game outright or loses it immediately. Examining the boards confirms this: positions feature pawns on the 7th rank (e7, P on h7, b6, c6) where the opponent's advanced pawn creates mating threats or forces major material gain, yet the player makes diversionary moves — capturing irrelevant pawns, delivering pointless checks, or developing pieces — instead of addressing the existential promotion threat. The combination of 'hangs' material outcome with Maia suggesting queen captures indicates these positions had winning captures available that would neutralize the promotion, but the player's attention was elsewhere.

852.label: Misplaying rook endgames by allowing unfavorable exchanges or leaving rooks en prise, typically losing the rook for nothing or a pawn.
852.description: This feature detects a specific pattern of rook mishandling in endgame positions. The material signature shows 96% rook moves with a median net loss of -5.0 (consistent with hanging or losing a rook worth 5 pawns), where 58% are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop the piece) and 34% are 'loses' (capturing a pawn but losing the rook). The tactical analysis confirms 56% of positions are tagged as rook_endgame motifs, with common themes of passed pawns, king activity, and pawn endgame transitions. The eval trajectory shows most errors occur in already-losing positions (40% losing->losing) with a massive median eval loss of 259 centipawns, suggesting players in difficult rook endgames make desperate or careless rook moves—either grabbing a pawn while allowing a rook trade into a lost king-and-pawn ending, or placing the rook where it hangs. The Opus summaries consistently describe trading the active rook for a pawn and entering a hopeless pawn endgame, or allowing rook exchanges that create unstoppable passed pawns. Maia's preferred moves (46% rook, 34% pawn, 18% king) suggest the correct approach was often a quieter rook reposition, pawn push, or king maneuver rather than the aggressive/greedy rook action that was played.

859.label: Retreating or misplacing a piece to a passive square, abandoning coordination and leaving pieces or key squares undefended.
859.description: This feature captures middlegame mistakes where the player moves a piece (most often a rook, queen, or knight) to a passive or inferior square, resulting in a large evaluation drop (median 341 centipawns) that frequently shifts the position from drawn to losing (53%). The material signature shows these are overwhelmingly non-captures (88%) that are nominally 'safe' (59%) or hang material (41%)—meaning the piece itself isn't immediately lost but the repositioning catastrophically weakens the position. The tactical motifs (hanging_piece 40%, king_safety 20%, overloaded_defender 20%) combined with tags like tempo_loss, centralization_loss, and piece_activity reveal the recurring pattern: the player retreats or sidelines an active piece (e.g., Ng3 retreating a centralized knight, Kh1/Kf1 misplacing the king, Re1 pulling a rook off an active file, Nd3 retreating an attacking knight), which immediately creates tactical vulnerabilities—hanging pieces, overloaded defenders, or king exposure. Maia consistently recommends active rook moves (often rook captures), confirming that the correct plan involved maintaining piece activity rather than retreating. The positions are complex middlegames where the player chose passivity over engagement, surrendering the initiative decisively.

860.label: King moves in pawn endgames that lose tempo or cede critical squares without immediate material loss.
860.description: This feature fires on king moves in pawn endgames (100% king moves, 100% endgame phase, no captures, material outcome 'safe') where the player makes a suboptimal but often low-cost king retreat or sidestep that loses a tempo or abandons an active position. The eval trajectory shows these are mostly occurring in already-losing positions (60% losing->losing) with a median cost of only 3 centipawns, indicating minor inaccuracies rather than catastrophic blunders—though occasional severe cases exist (e.g., the 9488cp loss converting a defensible position into forced mate). The dominant motifs (pawn_endgame 47%, tempo_loss 20%, passed_pawn 13%) and tags (tempo_loss, piece_activity, king_activity) confirm the recurring pattern: the king steps to a less active square, losing a critical tempo in positions where opposition, outflanking, or proximity to passed pawns is paramount. The top boards uniformly show minimal-piece pawn endgames where the king moves away from optimal squares (Kd5 instead of maintaining opposition, Kc1 retreating passively, Ke7 losing contact with key pawns).

861.label: Player captures a pawn or makes a safe rook move in the endgame, missing an immediate checkmate or mating sequence.
861.description: This feature identifies a highly specific and painful type of chess mistake: in rook endgames (or near-endgames), the player makes a 'safe' rook move—often capturing a pawn—while completely overlooking a forced checkmate, typically in one or very few moves. The material signature shows rook moves (86%) that are materially safe (100%), yet Maia's recommended move is always a rook delivering check (100%), and winning material is missed 100% of the time. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 355 centipawns despite most positions remaining winning, indicating the player threw away a decisive tactical finish. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant tags of missed_mate_in_one (5/7), king_safety (62%), and back_rank (23%). The concrete examples repeatedly show players grabbing pawns (Rxh5, Rxa5, Rxa8) or making routine rook maneuvers while a back-rank mate or mating net was available. This is the classic 'tunnel vision on material' error where the player focuses on pawn-grabbing rather than examining the opponent's king vulnerability.

862.label: Launching an unsound early queen sortie (often a Scholar's Mate attempt) that hangs the queen or loses massive material after the opponent's simple refutation.
862.description: All three signals converge on the same pattern: aggressive but premature queen moves in the opening that backfire catastrophically. The material signature shows 80% queen moves delivering check, yet 80% result in a hung piece with a median net loss of -8.0 (roughly a queen). The eval trajectory confirms these aren't minor inaccuracies—they swing drawn or winning positions into losing ones by a median of 455 centipawns. The tactical tags are remarkably consistent: scholars_mate_attempt, premature_attack, unsound_sacrifice, insufficient_compensation, and tempo_loss all appear repeatedly. The top boards make the concrete pattern unmistakable: Qh5 and Qh4 lunges (and one Bxf7+ sacrifice) in the first 4-12 moves, classic Scholar's Mate or pseudo-Scholar's Mate ideas that are easily refuted because the attacking side lacks supporting pieces. Maia's recommended alternatives (pawn moves, knight development) confirm that quiet developing moves were far superior. The phase is 100% opening, cementing this as an early-game aggression blunder where the queen becomes trapped or is won outright after the opponent calmly defends.

863.label: Player makes a quiet or non-forcing move, missing a forcing queen check that wins significant material.
863.description: This feature identifies positions where the player makes a non-capturing, non-checking move (70% no capture, only 3% checks played) while Maia's best move is invariably a queen check (100% queen, 100% check). The material signature shows 29% of moves hang a piece and 98% miss winning material, with a massive median eval loss of 353 centipawns—consistent with overlooking a decisive tactical blow. The eval trajectory confirms these are game-changing errors: winning positions become losing (12%), drawn positions become losing (12%), and even winning positions lose significant advantage. The tactical motifs (tempo_loss 33%, back_rank 17%, overloaded_defender 17%, hanging_piece 17%) and tags (missed_tactic, king_safety, exposed_king_ignored) all point to the same pattern: the player fails to recognize that their queen can deliver a check that exploits king vulnerability—often involving back-rank themes or discovered attacks—and instead plays a passive or aimless move that surrenders the initiative and often material. The concrete positions confirm this: many feature exposed kings where a queen check would win material or force decisive gains, but the player moves a rook, knight, or pawn instead.

867.label: Developing a knight to a square attacked by an enemy pawn in the opening, immediately hanging a piece.
867.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a knight (100% knight moves, 0% captures) to a square directly attacked by an opponent's pawn, hanging a full piece (100% 'hangs' outcome, median -2.0 material). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic damage—positions shift from drawn to losing with a median loss of 486 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' (73%) with tags like 'opening_blunder', 'pawn_captures_piece', and 'development', confirming this is an early-game piece placement oversight. The top boards make the concrete pattern unmistakable: knights placed on c3 when a d4 pawn attacks it, or knights developed to squares controlled by advanced central pawns. Maia's response is always a pawn capture (100%), cleanly winning the piece. This represents a fundamental failure to check pawn control of the target square before developing.

864.label: Trading or capturing pieces in endgames that fatally simplify into lost pawn endings or allow unstoppable passed pawns.
864.description: This feature fires on exchanges and trades (60% trade outcome) made predominantly in endgame/late-middlegame positions (52% endgame, 44% middlegame) that cost a median of 215 centipawns. The trajectory shows 76% losing->losing and 16% drawn->losing, indicating players in already difficult or balanced positions make trades that eliminate their defensive resources or simplify into hopelessly lost pawn endgames. The dominant motifs—pawn_endgame (31%), passed_pawn (15%), promotion_error (15%)—combined with tags like passed_pawn, king_activity, and connected_passers reveal the pattern: players trade off active pieces (rooks 36%, queens 20%) often capturing opponent's major pieces (queen 32%, rook 28%), but these exchanges remove the very pieces needed to blockade passed pawns or maintain defensive activity. The Opus summaries confirm this—trading away a queen to enter a hopeless pawn endgame, removing a defensive bishop for a worthless pawn, or capturing a piece that was actually blocking a lethal threat. Maia's preferred moves (80% non-captures) suggest the engine wanted to maintain piece tension rather than simplify, and 60% of the time a winning continuation was missed in favor of the losing trade.

870.label: Player makes a move (often a trade or capture) that ignores a stronger forcing line beginning with a check, costing significant evaluation.
870.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player executes a move—typically a bishop or king move involving a trade or hanging a piece—when a much stronger queen or rook check-first sequence was available. The Maia recommendation is overwhelmingly a queen move (83%) that delivers check (100%), indicating the missed line begins with a forcing check. The dominant motifs (king_safety 40%, discovered_attack 20%, fork 20%, back_rank 20%) and recurring tags like 'checks_before_captures' and 'checkmate_in_one' confirm the player violated the tactical principle of playing checks before captures or trades. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 218 centipawns, often converting a winning or drawn position into something worse. The concrete examples repeatedly describe scenarios where checking first would have won decisive material or delivered checkmate, but the player instead made an inferior capture, trade, or defensive move that forfeited the forcing advantage.

865.label: Player executes an apparently forcing move (check or fork) that is directly refuted by an overlooked defending piece.
865.description: This feature captures moves where the player launches what appears to be a forcing tactical shot—most often a knight fork or queen maneuver delivering check (43% checks, knight/queen moves dominate)—but critically overlooks that a defending piece guards the target square, resulting in material loss. The material signature shows 43% of moves 'hang' a piece (non-capture that drops material) while the rest appear superficially safe, with a median eval loss of 317 centipawns indicating severe blunders. The OPUS analysis explicitly identifies 'hanging_piece' (27%) and 'failed_fork' motifs, with multiple examples describing knight forks on c7 where the queen on d8 simply recaptures. The trajectory (29% drawn->losing, 14% winning->losing) shows these mistakes frequently convert holdable or winning positions into losses. The common 'tempo_loss' and 'pointless_check' tags reinforce that these are aggressive-looking but tactically flawed moves where the player saw the threat they created but failed to account for the opponent's defensive resources. The endgame-heavy phase distribution (57%) suggests players are especially prone to this when fewer pieces make forks seem more decisive, yet remaining defenders still cover key squares.

866.label: Moving a piece to an undefended square or away from a defensive duty, leaving material hanging for free capture.
866.description: This feature consistently fires on moves that hang a piece. The material signature shows 57% of moves result in 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) with a median net material loss of -1.0 (a full piece), while 90% of the triggering moves are non-captures themselves — the player simply moves a piece and leaves something en prise. The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif in 100% of cases, with recurring tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'missed_tactic.' The examples illustrate the pattern clearly: a knight moves away from defending a bishop (which then hangs), a bishop lands on an unguarded square where a queen scoops it up, a rook moves to a square where it can be captured for free. The eval trajectory shows a median cost of 209 centipawns, with most cases occurring in already-losing or winning positions (24% losing→losing, 10% losing→winning for opponent), indicating these are oversight blunders rather than desperate sacrifices. Maia's recommended moves (98% pawn moves, 61% pawn captures) suggest the correct play was typically a simple pawn advance or recapture — the blundering player instead chose an ambitious piece move that neglected basic piece safety.

869.label: In won endgames, advancing a pawn instead of capturing a critical enemy piece with the king, throwing away the win.
869.description: This feature fires on a highly specific endgame mistake: the player pushes a pawn (100% pawn moves, 0% captures) when the winning move was a king capture of an enemy bishop or knight (Maia's move is king 100%, capturing bishop 100%). The positions are universally endgames with passed pawns near promotion, where the player instinctively advances a passer but misses that capturing the enemy piece with the king was the only move that maintained the advantage. The eval trajectory is catastrophic—winning positions become drawn (67%) or even losing (33%), with a median loss of 647 centipawns. The tactical motifs confirm this: promotion_error (pushing toward promotion prematurely), hanging_piece (the enemy piece was free to take), and passed_pawn themes dominate. The top boards clearly show positions like Kf7 vs bishop on g7 with a g6 pawn, where Kxg7 wins trivially but advancing g4-g5 allows the bishop to blockade or sacrifice. The fundamental error is prioritizing pawn advancement over piece elimination in king-and-pawn endgames.

871.label: Trading queens with check that voluntarily enters a losing endgame, sacrificing dynamic compensation.
871.description: This feature fires on positions where a player trades queens (100% queen moved, 100% queen captured, 100% with check) in what is materially an equal exchange (net material 0.0), but the trade is strategically catastrophic. The eval trajectory shows these moves consistently convert drawn positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 237cp lost). The tactical analysis confirms this through tags like 'premature_simplification', 'queen_trade_error', 'bad_queen_trade', and 'dynamic_compensation_lost'. Maia's recommended moves consistently keep the queen on the board (100% queen move, 0% capture, 0% check), indicating the AI recognizes the queen's dynamic value in these middlegame positions. The concrete pattern across the top boards shows players impulsively trading queens with check—often recapturing on tempting squares—only to find themselves in hopeless rook or minor piece endgames where the opponent's structural advantages (passed pawns, better piece activity) become decisive. The check creates an illusion of forcing play, but the resulting simplification removes the player's only source of counterplay.

868.label: Playing a purposeless kingside pawn move (h3/g3/h4) while a decisive tactic or hanging piece goes unaddressed.
868.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player, often in a winning or advantageous middlegame/endgame, plays a slow, non-urgent kingside pawn move (h2h3, g2g3, or h2h4) instead of exploiting a critical tactical opportunity. The material signature shows 100% pawn moves with no captures, and 50% of these moves outright hang material. The eval trajectory is devastating: a median loss of 566 centipawns, with 60% of cases converting a winning position into a draw or loss. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly active pieces—rooks (60%) and queens (30%)—often delivering check (60%), confirming that the position demanded immediate tactical action. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring pattern: hanging pieces left undefended (40%), critical tempo squandered (40%), and back-rank threats ignored (20%). The concrete positions show a player on the kingside shuffling a pawn one square while their rook is en prise, a mating attack is available, or a passed pawn needs attention. This is the quintessential 'autopilot' mistake—a prophylactic-looking move played out of habit when the position screams for concrete calculation.

874.label: Moving the queen to a square where it can be captured with immediate checkmate.
874.description: This feature fires when a player moves their queen (86% queen moves) to a square that allows immediate checkmate, hanging the queen in a non-capture move (100% hangs, median material loss of -9.0 = queen value). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders with a median loss of 9168 centipawns, consistent with allowing checkmate-in-one. The dominant motif is king_safety (88%), and the recurring tags include checkmate_in_one (3), queen_blunder (4), and back_rank (2). Examining the concrete positions, the pattern is clear: players relocate their queen to a square where the opponent's queen can capture it with check or checkmate, often on back-rank or confined-king positions (e.g., Qg7 allowing Qxg7#, Qe2 allowing Qxe2#). The positions are predominantly middlegame (86%) with already-losing evaluations (57% losing->losing), suggesting players in desperate positions overlook that their queen move allows an immediate mating capture.

872.label: Player makes a quiet or pawn move, missing a forcing tactic (often back-rank or hanging piece) that wins major material.
872.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'safe' but passive move (often a pawn push or quiet rook/queen move — 78% safe, 72% no capture) while missing a powerful tactical shot that Maia identifies. The missed moves are predominantly rook moves (50%) and frequently deliver check (56%), with Maia capturing major pieces (rook 39%, bishop 17%, queen 11%). The dominant motifs are hanging_piece (40%), king_safety (20%), and back_rank (20%), indicating the opponent's pieces or king were vulnerable to a forcing sequence. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 346 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to merely drawn or from drawn to losing. The concrete positions confirm this: players push pawns that destroy their own king shelter (g2-g4 removing a critical shield), play quiet rook moves missing back-rank mates, or retreat queens when a knight fork or piece capture was available. The common thread is overlooking a forcing tactical blow — particularly one exploiting back-rank weakness or a hanging piece — in favor of a non-forcing move that squanders a decisive advantage.

873.label: Trading or simplifying in endgames when the player's active piece (often a queen) was the sole asset preventing defeat.
873.description: This feature captures endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where a player voluntarily trades or simplifies—most often giving up their queen (75% queen moves, 50% queen captures)—resulting in catastrophic eval losses (median 1331 centipawns). The material signature shows 50% trades and the rest losing/hanging outcomes, consistent with exchange decisions rather than simple blunders. The trajectory (50% winning->losing, 50% losing->losing) indicates these trades either throw away a winning position or seal the fate of an already difficult one. The Opus analysis confirms the recurring motif: queen_trade_blunder/error tags appear 5 times, with passed_pawn and pawn_endgame dominating. The concrete pattern across boards shows players trading queens into lost pawn endgames (e.g., Qxe6+ allowing king recapture supporting a passed pawn, Qxg5 entering a hopeless K+P ending, Qxe7 near promotion). The player eliminates the very piece providing dynamic counterplay (perpetual check threats, blockade ability) and enters a structurally lost simplified position where passed pawns decide.

876.label: Bishop retreats to a square where advancing pawns trap it in the opening.
876.description: This feature fires when a player moves their bishop (100% bishop moves, no captures) to a square where it becomes trapped by an opponent's pawn advance. The material signature shows the move itself appears 'safe' (nothing is immediately hanging), but Maia's response is always a knight-capturing bishop move (often with check), indicating the bishop is won. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic losses (median 357cp), predominantly converting drawn positions into losing ones (88%). The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'trapped_piece' (75%) as the dominant motif, with the concrete positions showing a recurring pattern: in opening theory (100% opening phase), bishops retreat to exposed squares (Ba5, Ba4, Bh4, Bh5) where they lack safe retreats and are corralled by pawn advances (b4, c5, g5-f4, etc.). This is a well-known theoretical pitfall especially in lines like the Nimzo-Indian and Ruy Lopez where the bishop ventures outside the pawn chain prematurely.

875.label: Developing pieces to passive squares or making aimless moves in the opening that hang material due to tempo loss.
875.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of early-game mistakes (100% opening phase) where players make moves that waste tempo and leave pieces hanging. The material signature shows 69% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median loss of 2.0 points, and 100% of positions miss winning material that was available. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (54%) and hanging_piece (23%), with common tags emphasizing development, piece_activity, and missed tactics. The eval trajectory is devastating: 75% of these moves turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 282 centipawns. The concrete positions reveal a clear pattern—players in sharp opening lines (mostly Italian Game and related e4-e5 systems) make developing-looking moves like Qe7, Nh5, Ng4, or b3 that appear natural but actually lose tempo against an active center, leaving pieces undefended or walking into tactical shots. Rather than maintaining tension or completing development efficiently, these moves allow the opponent to exploit the wasted time with immediate tactical threats.

877.label: Player makes a quiet or developing move while failing to capture an opponent's undefended piece that was freely available.
877.description: This feature fires when players overlook an opponent's hanging piece and instead play a passive, quiet, or developmental move. The material signature shows 72% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop material) and 85% involve no capture by the player, while Maia's recommended moves capture pieces 100% of the time (56% bishop, 28% knight, 9% rook, 6% queen). The tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif at 85%, with tags like 'missed_tactic', 'failed_recapture', and 'piece_activity' reinforcing that a free capture was available but ignored. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 460 centipawns with 44% of cases converting drawn positions to losing ones, indicating these are not minor oversights but game-deciding blunders. The top boards vividly illustrate this: a player developing a bishop with Be2 while an enemy bishop sits undefended on f3, or playing Rd8 while the opponent's queen hangs on d7. The pattern is concentrated in openings (56%) and middlegames (41%), where piece development can psychologically override the imperative to capture free material.

879.label: Player makes a non-defensive move while an immediate or near-immediate checkmate threat exists against their king.
879.description: This feature captures positions where a player moves a piece (rook, bishop, or knight) without addressing a critical king safety threat, resulting in hanging material or allowing a decisive attack. The material signature shows 67% of moves hang a piece (non-captures that drop material) with a median net loss of -1.0, while Maia's recommended moves consistently deliver check (100%). The dominant motifs are king_safety (67%) with recurring tags of checkmate_threat_ignored, exposed_king, and tempo_loss. The tactical analyses confirm this pattern: in one case White plays a completely non-defensive move when Qxh2# is unstoppable, in another White removes the only piece defending g2 allowing Qg2#, and in another a knight retreats from a crucial defensive square. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 147 centipawns with positions swinging from winning to losing (33%), confirming these are consequential oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The common thread is that players prioritize their own plan—whether attacking, repositioning, or promoting—while blind to an opponent's immediate mating threat that required urgent defensive attention.

878.label: King captures a knight instead of exploiting a stronger tactical opportunity, turning a drawn position into a losing one.
878.description: This feature fires when the player's king recaptures a knight (king moved 100%, captured knight 100%) in a middlegame position where a much stronger tactical continuation existed — specifically Maia consistently recommends a knight capturing a rook (Nxa1-type moves). The eval trajectory shows these moves uniformly convert drawn positions into losing ones (drawn->losing 100%, median 427cp lost), indicating the player chose a 'safe' or 'trade' recapture with the king while missing a winning tactical shot elsewhere on the board. The OPUS analysis confirms this: dominant motifs include hanging pieces left uncaptured, tempo loss, and missed tactics. The boards show positions where an enemy piece (often a rook) is en prise or a devastating tactic is available, but the player reflexively recaptures with the king on a knight rather than exploiting the more urgent opportunity. The self-blocking and piece activity tags further indicate these king recaptures often worsen coordination, severing defensive connections. This is fundamentally a 'missed tactic' pattern where a routine king recapture blinds the player to a decisive combination.

881.label: Playing a routine pawn move (typically h3 to challenge a pin) while missing a winning tactical combination in the opening.
881.description: This feature fires on opening positions (95% opening phase) where the player makes a 'natural' but passive pawn move (95% pawn moves, 100% non-captures) instead of finding a critical tactical blow. The dominant pattern is h3 played against a bishop pinning on g4, where the player reflexively kicks the bishop rather than exploiting the position with a sacrifice or fork (motifs: fork 31%, tempo_loss 31%, hanging_piece 23%). Maia's suggested moves are diverse (bishop 36%, queen 19%, knight 17%), often involving captures (36%) or checks (29%), confirming that strong tactical opportunities were available. The eval trajectory is devastating: 42% of cases go from winning to drawn, 20% from drawn to losing, with a median loss of 276 centipawns. The per-position analyses repeatedly describe missing Bxf7+ sacrifices followed by knight forks—brilliant tactical shots that the routine h3 completely overlooks. The material signature shows 'safe' in 88% of cases because the pawn move itself doesn't hang anything, but the opportunity cost of missing the tactic is enormous.

880.label: Giving a flashy queen check that allows a queen trade or escape, squandering a winning attack or forced mate.
880.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a queen check (queen moved 100%, check given 100%) that throws away a decisive advantage—typically a forced checkmate or crushing attack. The median eval loss is 370 centipawns, and 88% of the time the player missed winning material or a forced mate. The Opus analysis reveals the recurring pattern: instead of playing a quiet killer move (often a rook lift or a different piece delivering the decisive blow), the player opts for a superficially aggressive queen check that either allows the opponent to trade queens (queen_trade_error tag) or escape to safety. The material signature shows these checks are split between 'hangs' (47%, where the queen ends up en prise or trapped after the premature check) and 'safe' (47%, where the queen survives but the winning attack has evaporated). Maia's suggested moves frequently involve non-queen pieces (rook 29%) or quieter queen moves without check, confirming that the stronger continuation required restraint rather than the impulsive check. The trajectory (winning->losing 12%, winning->winning but with massive eval drop in many cases) shows these are predominantly cases of throwing away a won position by choosing spectacle over precision.

882.label: Moving a piece to a square where it (or another piece) is left undefended, losing significant material in the middlegame.
882.description: This feature consistently fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a bishop or rook and leaves a piece hanging or loses material without compensation. The material signature shows 50% hangs (non-capture moves that drop a piece) and 50% loses (capturing but losing more than gained), with a median net loss of 3.0 (roughly a minor piece). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic blunders: 50% convert winning positions into losing ones and 50% make already-losing positions much worse, with a median cost of 760 centipawns. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly identifies 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (73%), with common tags including undefended_piece, missed_tactic, and tempo_loss. Examining the boards confirms the pattern: pieces are moved to squares where they or other pieces become unprotected—rooks placed on files where they can be captured, bishops moved away from defense leaving material en prise. Maia consistently recommends bishop moves that maintain protection or win material, showing these players miss the defensive requirements of the position. This is a fundamental tactical oversight rather than a complex positional error.

884.label: Moving a rook (or other piece) to an undefended square where it can be captured for free by the opponent.
884.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a piece—most often a rook (60%)—to a square where it is immediately hanging and can be captured without compensation. The material signature is stark: 65% of moves are non-captures that simply hang a piece, with a median net material loss of -4.0 (consistent with losing a full rook). The eval trajectory shows these mistakes predominantly occur in already-losing positions (65% losing→losing), making a bad situation significantly worse (median 192cp lost), rather than throwing a winning game. The Opus tactical analysis confirms 'hanging_piece' as the universal motif across all examples—players overlook that their piece lands on or remains on an undefended square vulnerable to immediate capture. Common patterns include rook endgames where a rook moves actively but lands in a fork or capture path, move-order errors that leave a piece en prise, and 'free pawn grabs' that walk into recaptures. The positions span middlegame (55%) and endgame (45%), often featuring reduced material where one careless rook move proves immediately fatal.

885.label: Giving a check in an endgame that wastes a critical tempo without improving the position.
