The material signature shows the player moved king (44%), pawn (28%), or rook (22%) while almost never capturing anything (97% no capture), yet Maia's recommended move captures a knight 100% of the time. The boards consistently show an enemy knight on a dominant square (d6, f6, e4, c6, b5, etc.) that could have been captured but wasn't. The eval trajectory is devastating—median 477cp lost, with 54% of cases converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones. The tactical motifs confirm this: 64% hanging_piece (the knight was capturable), combined with missed_capture and missed_tactic tags. The per-position analyses explicitly describe scenarios like declining Rxf6 to capture a checking knight, or playing e5 attacking a knight instead of simply taking it with Bxd4. Players seem to reflexively move their king to safety or push a pawn when the correct response was to simply take the offending knight.

952.label: Playing a passive or tempo-losing bishop/rook move that hangs material while missing a forcing tactical opportunity.
952.description: This feature fires when players make non-forcing moves (primarily bishop 45% or rook 32% moves) that hang a piece (52% hangs) or are otherwise unsafe, while missing strong tactical replies that Maia identifies—often queen moves (39%), captures (58% of Maia's moves are captures), or checks (48% give check). The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (36%) and hanging_piece (21%), indicating the player chose a slow, non-urgent move when a sharp tactical blow was available. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 190 centipawns, with many positions converting from winning to drawn or losing (33% combined), confirming these are consequential missed tactics rather than minor inaccuracies. The concrete examples reinforce this: choosing a quiet Bb5 pin over capturing a free knight, playing a slow pawn advance instead of Qxa1+ winning a rook with check, or moving a queen off a critical tactical square. The pattern is consistently one of selecting a 'natural-looking' but passive piece move that loses tempo and material when an immediate forcing continuation (capture, check, or tactical combination) was decisive.

950.label: Moving the queen to a passive square in a queen endgame, converting a drawn position into a lost one.
950.description: This feature fires on queen moves in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player's queen retreats or repositions to an inferior square, turning a drawn position into a losing one (100% drawn->losing trajectory, median loss of 387 centipawns). The material signature shows queen moves (100%) that are not captures and not checks, with roughly half hanging the queen outright and half appearing safe but positionally catastrophic. The tactical analysis highlights king_safety, piece_activity, and back_rank themes—suggesting the queen is moved away from its optimal defensive/active post, often leaving the king vulnerable or ceding critical tempo. The boards consistently show simplified queen-vs-queen or queen-and-pawns endgames where only one precise queen placement maintains the draw, and the player chooses a passive or misplaced square (e.g., Qf3 instead of maintaining centralization, or Qe2 losing control of key squares). Maia's response is always a king move (100%), indicating the opponent calmly consolidates after the queen misstep. This is fundamentally a precision failure in queen endgames where the margin between a draw and a loss is a single accurate queen placement.

947.label: Bishop captures knight in the opening/early middlegame, surrendering the bishop pair and positional advantages for a materially equal but strategically inferior exchange.
947.description: This feature fires on positions where a bishop captures a knight (100% bishop moved, 82% captured knight) in what is materially an even trade (median net material: 0.0, 82% classified as 'trade'), but the exchange is strategically costly. The eval trajectory shows these trades are devastating positionally: 56% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 233 centipawns—far too large to be explained by material alone. The OPUS analysis confirms this with 70% positional_mistake motifs and recurring tags of piece_activity loss, tempo_loss, and development problems. Examining the top boards reveals a clear pattern: players capture knights on squares like f3, f6, c3, c6, or b7 with their bishops, often giving up the bishop pair and/or releasing tension in positions where maintaining the bishop was critical for attacking chances, king safety pressure, or long-diagonal control. Maia's recommended alternatives (82% non-captures, often knight or pawn moves) suggest quiet developing moves were far superior. The consistent opening/early-middlegame phase (65%/35%) indicates these are premature simplifying exchanges that relieve the opponent's positional problems while abandoning the player's own strategic assets.

948.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its optimal square in the opening, abandoning central control or defensive duties and allowing tactical exploitation.
948.description: This feature captures a recurring opening-phase mistake (76% opening) where players move already-developed pieces (knights 33%, bishops 21%) to inferior squares rather than continuing development or making the best pawn move (Maia recommends pawn moves 100% of the time). The material signature shows these moves are mostly 'safe' (58%) or 'hang' material (24%), meaning the piece itself isn't immediately captured but the repositioning creates tactical vulnerabilities that cost a median of 292 centipawns. The eval trajectory confirms these are position-ruining errors: 30% convert wins to draws and 27% convert drawn positions to losses. The tactical analysis reveals the underlying theme—pieces are moved away from strong central posts (e.g., knight leaving d5, king retreating to c8), causing tempo loss (8 occurrences), undermining development (7), reducing piece activity (6), and compromising king safety (6). The top boards consistently show positions where a piece had a strong role (defending f7, controlling the center, maintaining pressure) and was moved to a square where it either hangs or creates a structural/tactical weakness that the opponent can immediately exploit with forks or attacks on exposed pieces.

951.label: Developing a minor piece or retreating while overlooking an opponent's forcing queen exchange that wins hanging material.
951.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player moves a knight (59%), bishop (23%), or pawn (18%) — typically a developing move or retreat that appears natural — while completely missing that the opponent has a forcing queen capture/exchange (Maia's move is queen capturing queen with check 100% of the time). The eval trajectory shows these are costly errors (median 276cp lost), frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (55%) or winning positions to drawn ones (23%). The tactical motifs are split between hanging_piece (55%) and tempo_loss (45%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic, development, and queen_exchange. The concrete pattern visible in the top boards is striking: positions from well-known openings (Scandinavian, Petroff, Italian, Pirc) where queens face each other on an open d-file, and the player ignores the critical queen confrontation to make a 'developing' move (like Bg5, Nxe5, Ng4, Nd2), failing to realize that after the forced queen trade the resulting position leaves material hanging (typically the e4 pawn or a misplaced piece). The player prioritizes piece activity or apparent initiative over the concrete tactical reality that the queen exchange fundamentally changes the position's defensive requirements.

953.label: Player makes a rook/queen move that overlooks a hanging piece or back-rank threat, losing significant material.
953.description: This feature fires when players make moves (predominantly rook moves at 60%) that leave pieces undefended or ignore critical tactical threats, resulting in material loss (median -2.0 net material). The eval trajectory shows catastrophic losses (median 615 centipawns lost), with 80% of positions missing winning material that was available via Maia's recommended moves (which frequently deliver check at 80%). The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%), king_safety (25%), and back_rank (25%)—combined with tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'capture_with_check' reveal a consistent pattern: players execute routine-looking moves (exchanges, captures, retreats) while completely overlooking that their opponent has a forcing tactical shot available, typically involving check. The per-position analysis confirms this: examples include missing Qxd1+ winning an undefended rook, placing a rook on an undefended square where it's immediately captured, abandoning defensive duties allowing infiltration, and choosing the wrong capture order that ignores back-rank mate. These are not positional subtleties but concrete tactical oversights where the player's move appears reasonable in isolation but catastrophically ignores an immediate forcing reply.

954.label: Rook or king moves in the endgame that leave pieces or squares fatally undefended.
954.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame blunder pattern where players move their rook or king to an active-looking square but inadvertently hang material or fatally compromise their position. The material signature shows 60% of moves result in a hang (non-capture that drops a piece) with a median cost of -1.0 material, predominantly involving rook (40%) and king (28%) moves with almost no captures made. The eval trajectory confirms these are predominantly costly errors in already-difficult positions (45% losing->losing, but with a steep median 226cp loss), indicating moves that turn salvageable endgames into resignable ones. The tactical analysis ties it together: hanging_piece (50%), king_safety (20%), and tempo_loss (20%) motifs dominate, with concrete examples showing rooks abandoning critical defensive duties (back-rank weakness, undefended pieces) and kings walking into tactical sequences. The phase is 60% endgame, and the positions consistently show simplified material where a single misplaced rook or king step leaves something en prise or creates a fatal tactical vulnerability.

955.label: Player moves a piece away from a kingside attack, missing a decisive tactical continuation against the opponent's king.
955.description: This feature captures middlegame positions (98%) where the player has a significant attacking opportunity against the opponent's king but fails to find the critical continuation. The dominant motifs are king_safety (60%) and hanging_piece (40%), with recurring tags including missed_tactic, piece_activity, and tempo_loss. The player typically moves a queen (35%) or rook (26%) to a square that looks reasonable but abandons the attack—often retreating, capturing irrelevant material, or repositioning without urgency. The move itself frequently hangs material (42%) or is nominally safe (42%) but misses a devastating shot. Maia's recommendations show knight moves (33%) and checks (14%) that exploit king vulnerability, confirming the missed tactical blow. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 669cp lost), with 60% missing winning material, and positions spanning winning->losing (9%), drawn->losing (14%), and losing->losing (19%), indicating players at various disadvantages who had one critical chance to strike at the king but instead played a passive or misdirected move. The top boards consistently show open king positions with pieces aimed at the monarch where the player moves away from the attack rather than delivering the decisive combination.

956.label: Hanging a minor piece in the opening by ignoring tactical threats or moving to attacked squares.
956.description: This feature fires on opening-phase blunders (100% opening) where the player hangs a piece or loses significant material through a tactically naive move. The material signature shows 43% 'hangs' (non-capture moves that leave a piece en prise) and 43% 'slightly_down' outcomes, with a median net loss of -2.0 (consistent with losing a minor piece for a pawn or nothing). The eval trajectory confirms these are catastrophic mistakes: 43% turn drawn positions into losing ones and 43% turn winning positions into drawn ones, with a massive median eval loss of 452 centipawns. The tactical analysis layer reinforces this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (67%), supported by tags like 'piece_for_pawn', 'unprotected_piece', and 'opening_blunder'. The concrete positions show a recurring pattern: players move bishops or knights to squares where they can be captured for free, ignore opponents' hanging pieces they could win, or make developing moves that overlook simple one-move tactical threats. Unlike trade errors, these are not exchanges—they are uncompensated material losses from failing to account for basic piece safety in the opening.

957.label: Pawn advances (especially d5/e5/e4) that prematurely open the center, leaving pieces or pawns hanging.
957.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves—100% pawn played, 0% captures—that attempt a central break (d5, e5, e4, f4) at an inopportune moment. The material signature shows 55% of these moves hang material (median loss of 1 pawn), while the eval trajectory reveals devastating consequences: 40% convert drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 238 centipawns. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: premature breaks (tagged 'premature_break', 'center_control', 'pawn_structure') remove a pawn that was defending another piece or square, allowing the opponent to capture the advanced pawn and then collect additional material. The top boards overwhelmingly show d6-d5 or e3-e4 type advances where the pawn was serving a critical defensive role (guarding e5, protecting a piece, maintaining structure), and its advance leaves pieces undefended. This is not a tactical oversight of a specific tactic but a strategic misjudgment about when the position supports a central advance.

959.label: Playing a knight check that hangs the knight or loses significant material by moving a well-placed piece into a capturable square.
959.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers a check with a knight (67% knight moves, 78% checks played) that catastrophically loses material (61% hangs, median net material -2.0, median eval loss 338 centipawns). The dominant motif is hanging_piece (67%), and the tactical analysis reveals patterns of unnecessary checks, failed forks, and piece sacrifices without compensation. The player moves a knight to deliver check, but the checking square is covered by an enemy piece that simply captures the knight. Maia's recommended moves (king 33%, pawn 33%, knight 22%) suggest quiet, positional alternatives were available rather than the flashy but unsound check. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert winning or drawn positions into losing ones (winning->losing 17%, drawn->losing 22%, winning->drawn 11%), indicating players are throwing away good positions by being seduced by an aggressive-looking check that leaves the knight en prise.

958.label: Player moves a piece to an undefended square, hanging it or leaving another piece unprotected, while missing a winning tactical shot (usually a back-rank or capture combination).
958.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player moves a piece (most often a queen, knight, or rook) to an unsafe square, hanging material without compensation. The material signature shows 47% of moves result in a 'hang' (a non-capture that drops a piece) with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece), while 96% of the time the player misses winning material. The missed move (Maia's recommendation) is overwhelmingly a queen capture on a rook (59%) delivered with check (98%), indicating the player overlooked a forcing tactical blow—often involving back-rank threats or simple captures of undefended pieces. The dominant motifs confirm this: 55% hanging_piece, 27% back_rank, with tags like 'undefended_piece' and 'missed_tactic' recurring. The eval trajectory is catastrophic (median 791cp lost), with 31% of cases flipping from winning to losing and 16% from winning to drawn, confirming these are game-deciding oversights where a completely won position is thrown away by a single careless move that either leaves a piece en prise or abandons a critical defensive duty.

961.label: Pushing a non-critical pawn or making a slow move while the opponent's advanced passed pawns demand immediate attention.
961.description: This feature fires in endgame positions where the player is already losing and makes the situation dramatically worse (median 335cp lost) by playing a slow, safe pawn move instead of addressing the opponent's imminent promotion threats. The material signature shows the player's move is always a non-capturing pawn push that doesn't hang anything directly, yet Maia consistently identifies a rook capturing a pawn as the correct response—indicating the player needed to use active pieces to blockade or eliminate dangerous passed pawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: dominant motifs include passed_pawn (33%), hanging_piece (42%), and promotion_error (8%), with recurring tags of tempo_loss and missed_tactic. The concrete positions consistently show opponents with pawns on the 6th or 7th rank ready to promote, while the player wastes a critical tempo on an irrelevant pawn advance (h5h4, g4g3, f5f4), allowing the opponent's promotion to proceed uncontested. This is a classic endgame tempo error—prioritizing one's own slow plan over the opponent's immediately winning threat.

962.label: King moves that ignore a free queen capture available via pawn or piece, turning drawn positions into losses.
962.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (100% king moves) in a way that hangs material (median net -3.0, i.e., loses a piece) while completely missing that a simple capture of the opponent's queen was available — Maia's recommended move is always a pawn capturing a queen (pawn 100%, captures queen 100%). The eval trajectory shows these moves convert drawn positions into winning ones for the opponent (drawn->winning 100%, median eval lost ~100 pawns, indicating missed mate or decisive material). The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is a hanging piece (71%), with recurring tags of missed_tactic, missed_capture, and queen_hanging. The example narratives explicitly describe players ignoring pawn-takes-queen moves (e.g., c-pawn captures queen on b5, axb4 captures queen) in favor of aimless king moves or piece shuffles. This represents a specific blindness pattern where players overlook that a humble pawn can capture an exposed queen, instead making routine king moves that leave their own pieces en prise.

963.label: Player makes a safe-looking move in a winning position instead of executing an available forced checkmate sequence.
963.description: This feature fires when a player, already in a winning position, plays a quiet or preparatory move (typically a pawn push or king move) instead of capitalizing on an immediately available forced mate or decisive capture. The material signature shows 100% missed winning material with moves that are individually 'safe' or 'hangs' (non-captures that allow counterplay) rather than the crushing captures Maia recommends. The eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic median loss of ~9021 centipawns—characteristic of converting a forced mate into merely a winning or even losing position. The tactical analysis confirms this with tags like 'forced_mate_missed', 'missed_capture', and 'missed_tactic', along with example narratives describing players who had mate-in-8 or mate-in-16 but chose preparatory moves (h4 instead of fxg5, Qd2 instead of cxd3, Kf4 instead of addressing a critical pawn). The positions are predominantly endgames where the winning side has overwhelming material or positional advantage but fails to find the precise finishing blow, opting for slow 'improving' moves that squander the forced win.

966.label: Moves that ignore critical king safety threats, allowing immediate mating attacks or devastating back-rank tactics.
966.description: This feature captures moves where players neglect their king's safety in the middlegame, resulting in catastrophic losses. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (62%) that aren't captures—these aren't greedy grabs but quiet moves that fatally ignore tactical threats. The eval trajectory is devastating: median 408cp lost, with 29% going drawn->losing and 19% winning->losing, indicating players throwing away games. The tactical analysis strongly confirms this with king_safety (33%) and back_rank (33%) as dominant motifs, plus tags like mating_net and exposed_king. The best moves (Maia captures rook 24%, queen 10%) reveal that players missed winning tactical shots—often captures that would have addressed the threats or won material. The boards show positions with exposed kings (e.g., king on h5, back-rank vulnerabilities) where players made nonchalant developing or defensive moves while immediate mating threats existed. The piece types moved (knight 24%, king 19%, queen 19%) suggest reactive but inadequate responses to pressure rather than addressing the root tactical crisis.

969.label: Pawn capture in the opening that fatally opens a diagonal toward the king, allowing a devastating queen check.
969.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn moves (100% pawns, 100% opening) that appear materially safe but catastrophically weaken king safety. The boards consistently show positions where a pawn recapture on the e-file (typically fxe5 or dxe5) opens a critical diagonal (usually e8-h5 or a4-e8) that permits a crushing queen check (Qh5+). The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 294 centipawns—often converting a winning or drawn position into a losing one (winning->drawn 50%, drawn->losing 25%). The dominant motif is king_safety (73%), with queen_check and exposed_king as recurring tags. The missed tactic is nearly universal (100% missed winning material from the opponent's perspective). Players are lured by a seemingly safe pawn capture or development move that ignores the geometric vulnerability of their uncastled king along an open diagonal, while the engine's recommended move (typically Qh5+ or similar) exploits this immediately.

960.label: Knight jumps to e5 or g5 too early in Italian Game positions, hanging the piece to a simple recapture or leaving it undefended.
960.description: This feature fires almost exclusively in Italian Game and related open-game openings (100% opening phase) where White (or occasionally Black) prematurely lunges a knight from f3 to e5 or g5 (knight moves 100%) without adequate support. The boards are remarkably homogeneous: classical Italian setups with Bc4, Nf3 vs ...Bc5, ...Nc6, ...e5. The material signature shows the knight is either captured for a pawn (60% capture a pawn but end slightly down) or simply left hanging (40% non-capture that drops material), with a median loss of 2.0 material units—consistent with losing a minor piece. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic damage: every instance swings from a drawn/equal position to losing (median 310cp lost), equivalent to dropping a full piece. Opus analysis identifies the dominant motif as hanging_piece (86%), with recurring tags of development, missed_tactic, and opening_trap—the knight jump appears aggressive but ignores that the piece lacks support, often falling to a simple ...d6xNe5, ...Nxe5, or ...Bxf2+ sequence. This is a classic beginner opening trap where the lure of attacking f7 or creating threats leads to an unsupported knight incursion that simply drops material.

965.label: Failing to recapture an enemy bishop on c6 (or similar) that just captured a piece, leaving material hanging in the opening.
965.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where a player ignores an enemy bishop that has just captured one of their pieces (typically on c6 in Italian/Spanish-type structures). The material signature shows the player making non-capturing or pawn moves while Maia consistently recommends capturing the bishop — indicating the player missed an obvious recapture. The eval trajectory is severe (median 442cp lost, typically drawn->losing), confirming these are not subtle positional errors but concrete oversights costing a full piece. The tactical analysis overwhelmingly flags 'hanging_piece' (73%) with tags like 'failed_recapture' and 'missed_tactic', and the board positions repeatedly show an enemy bishop sitting on c6 (or similar invasion square) after having captured, while the player develops or grabs a pawn elsewhere instead of simply taking back. This is a classic beginner-level pattern recognition failure in the opening where the player loses track of the capture sequence.

968.label: Bishop captures a defended pawn in the opening, immediately losing a piece for one pawn.
968.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern: the player moves a bishop to capture a pawn (73% pawn captures) that is defended by a major piece (typically a queen), resulting in the immediate loss of the bishop for only one pawn — a net loss of approximately 2 pawns (median -2.0). The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic impact: 91% of cases transition from drawn to losing positions with a median loss of 447 centipawns. The tactical analysis consistently tags these as 'hanging_piece' (73%) with 'piece_for_pawn' and 'opening_blunder' being the most common descriptors. The top boards clearly show the pattern: Bf4xc7 where the queen on d8 recaptures, Bf5xc2 where the queen on d1 recaptures, Bg5xe7 where multiple pieces defend. In every case, the bishop moves to a square directly attacked by a defending piece, and the player fails to recognize that their bishop will be immediately captured with no compensation beyond the single pawn taken. This occurs exclusively in the opening phase where piece development tempts players into premature aggression with their bishops.

967.label: Bishop develops passively in the opening while ignoring a lethal knight fork threat on f7, hanging material.
967.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening blunder pattern where Black ignores an immediate tactical threat to the f7 square. The material signature shows bishops being moved 62% of the time with no captures, and the piece is effectively hung (100% hangs, median -1.0 material). The eval trajectory is uniformly drawn->losing with a median loss of 314 centipawns, indicating these positions were holdable before the mistake. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is a fork (62%), with tags overwhelmingly pointing to f7_weakness, knight_fork, opening_trap, and two_knights_defense. The top boards reveal the canonical position: Black faces White's Ng5+Bc4 battery targeting f7 (the Fried Liver/Two Knights Defense complex) and plays developing moves like Be7, Bd6, or Bg4 instead of the critical d5 counterstrike. The consistent pattern is a 'looks natural' developing bishop move that catastrophically ignores an immediate forcing threat, allowing a knight fork that wins material.

964.label: Player executes a greedy or impulsive capture/move before the correct intermediate move (often a queen check or trade), allowing a devastating counter-tactic.
964.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move-order error that squanders a winning or strong position (median eval lost: 893 cp, with 43% going from winning to losing). The material signature shows heavy rook and queen moves that frequently lose material (net median -3.0), while the best move (Maia line) almost always involves a queen delivering check (100% check rate) or forcing a queen trade first. The Opus analyses repeatedly describe the same pattern: the player captures greedily or makes an ambitious-looking move (grabbing a pawn, taking a rook) before executing the critical intermediate step—typically a check or forced queen exchange—that would secure the tactical sequence. Tags like 'missed_tactic', 'tempo_loss', 'move_order', and 'missed_queen_trade' confirm that the core error is sequencing: by not inserting the zwischenzug (intermezzo check or trade) first, the player leaves a piece hanging or allows a devastating counter-check that flips the evaluation. King safety and fork motifs arise because the missed intermediate check often exploits the opponent's exposed king, and skipping it lets the opponent exploit the player's own king instead.

970.label: Throwing away a winning endgame by allowing the opponent a critical tempo (counter-promotion, fork, or check) due to move-order errors.
970.description: This feature captures endgame positions where the player holds a winning advantage but squanders it through a tempo-related mistake, losing a median of 1210 centipawns and shifting from winning to drawn or losing. The material signature shows moves (pawn pushes or queen moves) that are either hanging or safe—not trades—indicating the player made a non-capturing move that overlooked a critical opponent resource. The tactical analysis reveals the unifying thread: promotion errors (premature promotion allowing counter-promotion with check), forks (placing pieces on vulnerable squares), and tempo losses (slow king moves or inaccurate move orders that hand the initiative to the opponent). The common tags—passed_pawn, tempo_loss, move_order, king_activity, counter_promotion—all point to endgame scenarios where precise timing is paramount and the player chose a natural-looking but fatally slow or missequenced move, allowing the opponent to equalize or win through a tactical resource that a correct move order would have prevented.

971.label: Passive rook or king moves in endgames that squander critical tempo against a stronger opponent.
971.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where the player makes a safe but passive move (typically with a rook or king) that loses crucial tempo. The material signature shows no captures and no checks, with the move being 'safe' materially—yet Maia consistently recommends moves that deliver check (100% check rate), revealing the missed tempo gain. The eval trajectory confirms these are mostly already-losing positions (83% losing->losing) where the median cost is modest (25cp), indicating subtle inaccuracies rather than blunders. The tactical analysis strongly reinforces this: 'tempo_loss' is the dominant motif (43%), with recurring themes of placing rooks on intermediate squares, failing to give interposing checks, or making king moves that allow the opponent better coordination. The positions are overwhelmingly Q-vs-R or rook endgames where the defending side must maximize activity through checks and precise placement, but instead drifts passively, allowing the stronger side to tighten the noose.

974.label: In the opening, player makes a routine developing move instead of capturing an undefended pawn on g7/g2 along the open long diagonal with a bishop.
974.description: This feature consistently fires on opening positions where the player has a bishop already developed on the long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1), and the opponent's g-pawn (g7 or g2) is undefended or inadequately protected. The player makes a 'safe' developing or routine move (material outcome: safe, no capture) while Maia's recommended move is always a bishop capturing a pawn (Bxg7 or Bxg2). The eval trajectory shows these moves uniformly convert a winning position into a drawn one (median loss: 324cp), indicating a serious missed opportunity. The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'hanging_piece' (85%) with recurring tags of 'undefended_pawn', 'exchange_win', and 'long_diagonal'. The boards show fianchetto or semi-fianchetto structures where the g-pawn is tactically vulnerable, often because the rook behind it is trapped or the pawn lacks adequate defense. Players appear to be on autopilot with standard development, completely overlooking that the long diagonal bishop has a concrete tactical shot available.

972.label: In the opening, player makes a routine pawn or minor piece move while missing a devastating queen tactic exploiting king safety weaknesses.
972.description: This feature fires on opening-phase mistakes where the player makes a seemingly natural move (pawn push 50%, minor piece or king move) that completely ignores a powerful queen-based tactic available to the opponent. The material signature shows Maia consistently recommends a queen move (100%) that would exploit the position, while the player's actual move is overwhelmingly safe in isolation (83% 'safe' material outcome) yet misses winning material 100% of the time. The eval trajectory is severe—median 265cp lost—with 39% of cases converting a winning position to drawn and 22% going from drawn to losing. The positional layer reveals king_safety (58%) as the dominant motif: the boards consistently show early Italian/Petroff-type positions where a knight sits aggressively on e5 or e4, and the player ignores the exposed king diagonal or f-file weakness (e.g., playing ...fxe4 or ...f6 into Qh5+ patterns, or ...Bg7/...O-O when a tactical queen blow is available). The tempo_loss tag (25%) reflects that these moves not only miss the threat but often waste developmental time, compounding the oversight. In essence, the player executes a 'normal-looking' opening move while blind to a concrete queen shot punishing their king's vulnerability.

973.label: Trading a bishop for a minor piece in the opening that relieves opponent's tension and surrenders a significant positional or tactical advantage.
973.description: This feature fires on opening-phase bishop trades (bishop moved 100%, capturing knight or bishop 50/50) that are objectively equal in material (net 0.0, pure trades) but cost a median of 289 centipawns—often converting a winning position into a drawn or losing one (winning->drawn 50%, drawn->losing 25%). The boards consistently show positions from well-known opening systems (London, Caro-Kann structures, Ruy Lopez-like setups) where the player resolves central tension prematurely by exchanging their actively-placed bishop. The Opus analysis confirms the pattern: the player captures in the wrong move order (e.g., Bxe7 before Nxe4, or Bxf6 when Bxh5 wins a hanging piece), releasing pressure and allowing the opponent's pieces to activate. Tags like missed_tactic (6), piece_activity (6), move_order (3), and tempo_loss (3) reinforce that these are not random trades but specifically premature exchanges that squander initiative, miss hanging pieces, or free the opponent's constrained position. The 100% 'missed winning material' rate confirms that in every case a much better option existed.

975.label: King moves that ignore an unstoppable passed pawn promotion, turning a drawn endgame into a loss.
975.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a 'safe' king move (no material lost immediately) while completely ignoring a critical passed pawn promotion threat. The material signature shows 100% king moves with no captures and no immediate material loss, yet the eval trajectory reveals a catastrophic drawn->winning shift (median -10062 centipawns), indicating the opponent goes from a holdable position to winning/mating. The Opus analysis confirms this: the dominant motif is 'promotion_error' (55%) with supporting tags of passed_pawn, promotion_threat, and tempo_loss. The concrete positions show patterns where the opponent has a pawn on the 2nd/7th rank about to queen, and Maia's recommended move is invariably a bishop capturing that pawn (Bxb2, Bxp) to eliminate the promotion. Instead, the player makes an aimless king move or prioritizes irrelevant tactics (like a meaningless check), permanently abandoning control of the promotion square. This is a classic endgame technique failure—missing that one precise defensive resource in favor of a natural-looking but fatal king move.

976.label: Giving a queen check that loses tempo or hangs material instead of executing a stronger continuation.
976.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a queen check (100% queen moves, 100% checks) that is either unnecessary or counterproductive. The material signature shows 64% of these checks hang material (median net -1.0), indicating the check allows the opponent to gain tempo or escape to a better square. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant motifs of tempo_loss (50%) and king_safety (38%), with tags like 'check_not_best', 'unnecessary_check', and 'queen_misplacement' appearing. The per-position summaries repeatedly describe scenarios where a check-first move order allows the opponent's king to improve its position (e.g., centralizing via Ke2) or wastes a critical tempo that should have been used for a direct winning continuation. The eval trajectory (median 189cp lost) shows these are costly mistakes spanning multiple game states—sometimes throwing wins into draws (21%) and sometimes worsening already losing positions (21%). The boards show queen checks like Qb1+, Qe1+, Qb8+, and Qd8+ where a non-checking move would have been decisively stronger. Maia's recommended moves are typically non-checking continuations (pawns 36%, rooks 21%) that execute concrete threats directly.

982.label: Player makes a quiet developing or repositioning move while an enemy piece hangs undefended, allowing opponent to seize a winning material advantage.
982.description: This feature identifies positions where the player moves a rook or bishop (quiet, non-capturing, safe moves with net material 0) while Maia's recommended move is a queen capturing a rook — indicating a completely free capture was available. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of cases swing from winning to losing with a median loss of 741 centipawns, confirming these are not subtle positional errors but catastrophic oversights. The Opus analysis reinforces this with dominant motifs of 'hanging_piece' (50%) and tags like 'missed_capture' and 'material_oversight' appearing repeatedly. The example summaries explicitly describe scenarios where a full rook sits undefended (e.g., on f3) and the player develops a piece or makes a quiet rook move instead of capturing it for free. This is a pure tactical blindness pattern — the player focuses on their own plan (development, repositioning) while failing to notice that an enemy piece is en prise and capturable immediately.

977.label: Rook moves to a passive or purposeless square, abandoning an active position and squandering a significant advantage.
977.description: This feature fires on rook moves (61% of activations) that are safe (76% don't hang material) yet cost a median of 215 centipawns, frequently converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones (26% drawn->losing, 13% winning->drawn). The positions are predominantly middlegame-to-endgame transitions (72% middlegame, 28% endgame) with strong rook-endgame and passed-pawn motifs. The tactical layer reveals the recurring story: players relocate their rook from an active, dominant post to a passive square—often chasing a defended pawn or retreating without purpose—while missing captures or tactical opportunities (missed winning material 56%). The Maia best moves frequently involve captures (39%) or checks (17%), indicating the opponent left concrete actions on the table. The top boards confirm this: rooks slide sideways to b2, d7, g6, a2, h5, a7, a1, c1, c4, h8—abandoning central control, active files, or attack on passed pawns. The tempo_loss tag (22%) and piece_activity tag reinforce that the core error is voluntarily making the rook passive when the position demanded decisive action.

980.label: Player captures material (often a queen) while missing a faster checkmate or decisive tactical blow.
980.description: This feature identifies positions where the player grabs material—typically capturing an opponent's queen or rook—while overlooking a forced checkmate or far superior tactical continuation. The material signature shows 67% queen captures with a median net gain of +2.0 (trades or safe captures), yet 100% of positions involve missed winning material according to Maia's evaluation. The eval trajectory confirms catastrophic cost (median 215 centipawns lost), with positions going from winning to drawn or even losing to winning being squandered. The tactical analysis is definitive: dominant tags include 'material_greed' (2), 'missed_mate' (3), and 'checkmate_in_one' (1), with explicit examples of players taking a hanging queen instead of delivering checkmate in one, or capturing with check instead of executing a back-rank mate sequence. The king_safety and back_rank motifs (50% and 12%) confirm that the missed continuations typically exploit the opponent's exposed king. This is a classic pattern of tunnel vision on the most obviously valuable capture while a lethal tactical shot goes unseen.

978.label: Losing critical tempo in drawn or losing endgame positions through aimless pawn or king moves that allow opponent's passed pawns or king activity to become decisive.
978.description: This feature detects a specific endgame error pattern where players squander tempo in simplified positions. The material signature shows mostly pawn (46%) and king (27%) moves with 91% non-captures—these are quiet repositioning moves, not tactical exchanges. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (86%), and the eval trajectory reveals that 50% of activations turn drawn positions into losing ones (median loss: 341 centipawns), which in pawn/bishop endgames is typically decisive. The tactical analysis confirms this with dominant tags of tempo_loss (5 occurrences), passed_pawn (4), and king_activity (4). The concrete positions show pawn endgames and bishop endgames where the player makes an innocuous-looking pawn push or king move (e.g., g2-g3, Kf4, b5-b4, Kb6) that fatally mismanages the tempo count, either creating opponent passed pawns, losing opposition, or abandoning control of critical squares. Maia's preferred moves (king 59%) suggest the engine recognized king activity was paramount, while the player chose passive pawn moves or misdirected their king.

979.label: Player makes a non-checking move when a forced checkmate via queen check was available.
979.description: All three signals converge on a single pattern: the player had a forced checkmate (or near-mate) available via a queen check but played a different piece move instead. Signal 1 shows that Maia's recommended move is a queen delivering check 100% of the time, while the player's actual move involves rooks (29%), queens (24%), or bishops (19%) with 0% checks—meaning they consistently failed to find the winning checking sequence. Signal 2 confirms catastrophic eval loss (median 227 centipawns, with examples losing 9000+ centipawns from forced mate to merely winning), and the trajectory shows many positions going from winning to drawn or staying winning but with massively reduced advantage. Signal 3's dominant motifs (king_safety 67%, hanging_piece 33%) and tags (forced_mate_missed, checking_sequence, exposed_king) confirm the opponent's king was exposed and vulnerable to a mating attack that was overlooked. The concrete positions show scenarios where queens and rooks are actively attacking near the enemy king, yet the player chose a quiet or irrelevant move (pawn push, rook lift, piece capture) instead of delivering the decisive check that would have led to checkmate.

981.label: Moving a knight to an undefended square where it is immediately captured, losing a full piece.
981.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where a player moves a knight (77% of cases) to a square where it hangs with no adequate compensation, resulting in a median loss of ~3 pawns worth of material (median eval lost: 324 centipawns). The material signature is striking: 63% of moves are 'hangs' (non-captures that drop a piece) and 30% are 'slightly_down', with no capture made 63% of the time—indicating the player is not trading but simply placing a piece en prise. The tactical motifs confirm this: 'hanging_piece' (33%) and 'king_safety' (67%) dominate, suggesting that players often misplace their knight under the illusion of creating a king-side attack or tactical threat that doesn't materialize. The concrete positions reinforce this: Na5 hanging to Nxa5, Nd4 walked into capture, Ne4 leaving the knight undefended. The eval trajectory shows these errors occur across all game states (losing->losing 27%, drawn->losing 13%) indicating that players at various evaluation standings make this same pattern of optimistic knight lunges that simply lose the piece.

986.label: Premature or misguided pawn advances in endgames that hang material or create fatal structural weaknesses.
986.description: This feature consistently fires on pawn moves (100% pawn moved) in endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player is already losing (83% losing->losing trajectory). The moves overwhelmingly hang material (83% hangs) with a median cost of -1.0 material and 85 centipawns lost. The boards reveal a clear pattern: players push pawns forward (g5g4, h4g3, e6e5, g7g5, b4b3, c3c4) in king-and-pawn or rook endgames, but these advances are premature — they break pawn structures, create passed pawns for the opponent, lose tempo, or leave pawns undefended. The tactical analysis confirms motifs of passed_pawn creation for the opponent, tempo_loss, and pawn_structure damage. Maia's responses (50% king moves, 50% pawn moves, no captures) suggest these pawn pushes simply allow the opponent to improve position or exploit the newly created weakness without needing to capture immediately. The player is typically already in a difficult position and the pawn push represents a further deterioration rather than a game-losing single blunder.

983.label: Player makes a developing or castling move while their own bishop hangs free on an open diagonal, throwing away a winning position.
983.description: This feature captures a highly specific opening blunder pattern where a player has a bishop hanging (usually on h6/g7 or a3/b2 diagonal) and instead of capturing the opponent's hanging piece (as Maia recommends with bishop captures in 83% of cases), they make a routine developing move—castling, fianchettoing, or repositioning a knight—that leaves their own piece en prise or fails to collect free material. The material signature shows 67% hangs with a median net loss of -3.0 (a full piece), and 100% of positions involve missed winning material. The eval trajectory is catastrophic: 67% swing from winning to losing with a median 1029 centipawn collapse, indicating these were already-won positions squandered by one inattentive move. The board positions consistently show Bxh6/Bxg7 or Bxa3/Bxb2 situations in the opening where one side's bishop is exposed on an open diagonal, and the player reflexively fianchettoes into the capture or castles while ignoring the tactic. The dominant Opus motif is hanging_piece (93%) with opening_blunder and missed_capture tags reinforcing that this is a pattern-recognition failure in familiar opening structures.

985.label: Moving a rook to a passive square that abandons critical defensive duties or blocks escape routes, allowing the opponent a forcing continuation.
985.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a rook (59% of cases) to a square that is not a capture and hangs material (68% hangs), typically in middlegame positions (91%) that are already losing or precarious. The key pattern across the boards is that the rook move abandons a critical defensive post (back-rank coverage, file control, or king protection) or actively blocks the player's own king escape route. Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly rook moves (96%) that deliver check (100%), revealing that the opponent had forcing continuations available that the player's passive rook placement fails to address. The tactical motifs—tempo_loss (50%), king_safety (25%), and back_rank (25%)—confirm that these rook moves gift the opponent tempo or expose fatal weaknesses. The eval trajectory shows many positions are already losing (27% losing->losing), meaning the rook move doesn't dramatically change evaluation but accelerates defeat by enabling mating nets or losing further material. The concrete examples show rooks moving to blocked squares (Re2 blocking king escape), retreating from active files (Rf8-d8 abandoning the f-file), or making aimless lateral moves while the opponent's pieces coordinate for a decisive attack.

988.label: In rook endgames, making a passive or aimless rook move that loses critical tempo against advancing passed pawns or active opponent pieces.
988.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (77% endgame phase) where the player moves a rook (69%) or king (23%) in a way that is materially 'safe' (77% nothing hangs) but positionally catastrophic, costing a median of 245 centipawns. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (27%), passed_pawn (18%), and positional_mistake (18%), with common tags emphasizing piece_activity, rook_endgame, and tempo_loss. The eval trajectory shows these are predominantly already-losing positions made significantly worse (50% losing->losing with large eval drops), where the player retreats or repositions the rook passively (e.g., Ra4-b4, Ra5-a3, Ra5-a4, Rh3-h1) instead of finding the one active defensive resource. Maia consistently recommends a rook move (100%), indicating the piece choice is correct but the square selection is wrong—the player picks a passive square that loses tempo against the opponent's advancing pawns or active king, transforming resistant defense into immediate hopelessness.

987.label: Developing or repositioning a minor piece passively when a concrete knight maneuver (often Nb5/Nd5) would exploit tactical pressure.
987.description: This feature fires on opening/early-middlegame positions where the player moves a bishop or knight to a natural-looking but passive square, missing a superior knight move (Maia's recommendation is 100% knight) that would seize the initiative through tempo, central control, or a tactical threat. The material signature shows the moves are overwhelmingly 'safe' (73%) or 'hangs' (20%) non-captures—these aren't blunders that drop a piece outright, but positional missteps that squander a significant advantage (median 261cp lost), frequently converting winning positions into drawn or losing ones (43% winning→drawn, 10% winning→losing). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motifs are tempo_loss and positional_mistake, with recurring tags around piece_activity, development, and knight_outpost. The concrete pattern across the top boards is consistent: in open positions with active piece play available, the player chooses a routine developing or repositioning move (Bd6, Bc5, Nf6, Bd2, d4, Bc4) instead of the one strong knight jump (Nb5, Nd5, or similar) that would have maintained tactical tension and initiative. The mistake is fundamentally about defaulting to general principles (develop, improve a piece) rather than calculating the specific forcing knight move that the position demands.

989.label: Unsupported central pawn advances in the opening that leave material hanging or create tactical vulnerabilities.
989.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern of premature pawn advances (50% pawn moves) during the opening phase (100% opening) that result in significant evaluation swings (median 253cp lost), typically converting drawn positions into losing ones (56% drawn->losing). The material signature shows moves that are 'slightly_down' (38%) or 'hangs' (31%), meaning the pawn push either directly loses material or leaves pieces undefended. The tactical analysis confirms this with 'hanging_piece' as the dominant motif (40%), supplemented by forks and discovered attacks that punish the overextension. Tags like 'premature_pawn_advance', 'central_overextension', and 'tempo_loss' reinforce that these are aggressive but unsupported central pushes (e4-e5, e2-e4, e3-e4) or piece lunges that create tactical holes. The concrete positions show repeated instances of e-pawn pushes that can be captured by knights or that open lines exposing the player's own pieces. Maia's responses are quiet non-captures (100%), suggesting the refutation involves simple development or piece repositioning that exploits the newly created weaknesses rather than immediate tactical fireworks.

991.label: King moves that surrender activity or tempo in critical middlegame/endgame positions, often allowing the opponent to advance passed pawns or seize the initiative.
991.description: This feature captures a recurring pattern where players make passive king moves (91% king moves) that are not captures (95% no capture) and frequently hang material (37% hangs). The positions are split between middlegame and endgame (54%/45%), and the dominant motifs—passed pawns (30%), positional mistakes (30%), and tempo loss—reveal that these king retreats or sideways shuffles fail to address critical threats like advancing passed pawns or maintaining king activity. The eval trajectory shows a median loss of 190 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn or drawn to losing, indicating these are not random blunders but systematic failures to keep the king active. Maia's recommendations (42% king but also 23% rook, 18% pawn) suggest the engine often preferred a more active king placement or an entirely different piece move. The top boards consistently show endgame or simplified positions where the king needed to advance toward passed pawns or maintain centralization, but instead retreated passively, ceding tempo and positional advantage to the opponent.

990.label: Player makes a safe-looking move in a won position that throws away a decisive advantage by losing tempo or missing a forced mate.
990.description: This feature captures positions where a player holds a winning or completely won position (often with forced mates available) but plays a 'safe' move—typically a queen or king move that doesn't hang material—yet catastrophically squanders the advantage. The material signature shows no captures or trades (67% no capture, 100% safe), ruling out greedy or exchange errors. The eval trajectory reveals massive centipawn losses (median 578cp), with positions going from winning to drawn or from mate-in-N to merely better. The dominant motifs are tempo_loss (50%) and missed_tactic/fork, with tags like forced_mate_missed, missed_tactic, and piece_activity confirming that these are cases where the player had a concrete winning continuation but chose a passive or aimless move instead. The phase is split between endgame (50%) and middlegame (50%), but the board positions overwhelmingly show simplified material (queen vs rook, rook endings, passed pawns) where precise calculation was required. Maia's suggestions (83% queen moves, 83% giving check) confirm that the engine wanted an active forcing continuation, while the player chose a quiet retreat or lateral move that surrendered the initiative entirely.

992.label: Advancing a passed pawn too early in the endgame, losing tempo or allowing the opponent to activate their king or pieces.
992.description: This feature captures a recurring endgame mistake where a player pushes a pawn (91% pawn moves) — typically a passed pawn — prematurely, losing critical tempo or positional control. The dominant motifs are passed_pawn (50%) and pawn_endgame (40%), with tempo_loss (8 tags) and king_activity (6 tags) being the most common strategic failures. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (64%) and the median eval loss of 281 centipawns is severe, with 32% of cases converting a winning position to drawn and 18% converting drawn to losing — classic 'threw a win' trajectories. The material signature shows these are mostly 'safe' moves (64%) or moves that hang material (27%), meaning the pawn push itself isn't a capture error but a positional/tempo blunder. Maia's preferred alternatives often involve king moves (46%) or rook moves (18%), suggesting the correct plan was to activate the king or maintain piece pressure rather than rushing the pawn forward. The top boards consistently show passed pawns being advanced one square too early, allowing the opponent's king to reach a critical square or creating a drawn position from a won one.

993.label: Player makes a quiet or routine move, missing a forced checkmate or crushing queen attack exploiting king safety weaknesses.
993.description: This feature fires when players overlook devastating king-safety tactics—most frequently missed checkmates or near-mates—in favor of routine, positionally-motivated moves. The material signature shows 73% non-captures (safe, quiet moves) while Maia's recommended moves are overwhelmingly queen moves (68%), often delivering check (18%). The tactical analysis confirms this: 62% of positions involve king_safety motifs, with 'missed_mate' and 'missed_mate_in_one' appearing frequently among the tags. The eval trajectory shows a massive median loss of 284 centipawns, with many positions going from winning to drawn (27%) or representing catastrophic blunders converting forced mates into mere advantages. The concrete positions repeatedly show open diagonals toward the opponent's king (e.g., Qxh2# patterns) where the player instead recaptures a pawn or makes a passive developing move. The player's piece choices (pawns 36%, bishops 18%) reflect these routine continuations, while the engine screams for the decisive queen strike. This is fundamentally a pattern-recognition failure: the player does not see the attacking geometry already present on the board.

996.label: Player moves a piece leaving their queen undefended, allowing it to be captured or exploited.
996.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move (most often a queen move, but sometimes another piece) that leaves their own queen hanging or undefended, costing significant material. The material signature shows 60% of moves 'hang' a piece with a median net loss of -1.0 (a full piece, likely the queen given context), while Maia's response is to capture the queen 100% of the time. The eval trajectory confirms these are costly errors (median 272cp lost), often converting drawn or winning positions into losing ones. The tactical analysis consistently identifies 'hanging_piece', 'undefended_queen', and 'tempo_loss' as dominant motifs, with multiple examples describing queens left unprotected due to move-order errors—players execute the right idea but in the wrong sequence, failing to first secure their queen via a trade or repositioning. The positions are all middlegame scenarios where tactical complexity masks the vulnerability of the queen, and players lose track of their queen's safety while pursuing other plans.

995.label: Trading an active bishop for a passive knight, releasing tension and squandering a dynamic advantage.
995.description: This feature detects positions where a player trades their active, well-placed bishop for a knight (bishop moved 92%, captured knight 85%) in what is objectively an equal material exchange (trade 100%, net material 0.0), but which constitutes a severe positional mistake. The eval trajectory shows these trades typically convert winning positions to drawn (54%) or drawn to losing (23%), with a median cost of 252 centipawns—indicating the exchange destroys significant positional or dynamic value. The tactical analysis confirms the dominant motif is positional_mistake (78%), with recurring tags of premature_exchange, premature_simplification, and releasing_tension. The concrete positions show a clear pattern: bishops on active diagonals (b4, g4, a6, g5) capturing knights on passive squares (d2, e2, f3, f6), often with check, which superficially looks forcing but actually relieves the opponent's coordination problems, invites simplification, and abandons attacking potential. The 38% check rate confirms players are seduced by the tempo of giving check while missing that the trade itself is the strategic error.

999.label: Player makes a trade or capture that squanders a winning tactical opportunity in the middlegame.
999.description: This feature fires when players make exchanges or piece-hanging moves (trade 42%, hangs 37%) that forfeit a much stronger tactical continuation. The median cost is 401 centipawns, with 63% of positions involving missed winning material. The dominant motifs—zwischenzug, move-order errors, and premature captures—reveal that players rush into an exchange without first inserting an intermediate move (check, threat, or rook activation) that would have won decisive material. The eval trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions to losing (26%) or squander winning advantages. The Opus analysis consistently identifies a stronger in-between move (e.g., an intermediate check, a rook lift, or a passed pawn advance) that the player skipped in favor of an immediate but inferior capture or trade. This is a middlegame pattern where the player sees the right idea but executes it in the wrong move order, collapsing a complex tactical position into one that favors the opponent.

997.label: Knight moves to seemingly active squares that walk into tactical refutations involving forks or hanging pieces.
997.description: This feature captures knight moves (100% knight played) that appear aggressive or active but are tactically flawed. The material signature shows 38% of these moves hang the knight and only 52% are safe, with a median eval loss of 251 centipawns—indicating serious tactical oversights rather than minor inaccuracies. The trajectory shows these moves frequently convert drawn positions to losing ones (14%) or throw away wins (8%). The Opus analysis reveals the dominant motifs are forks (33%), hanging pieces (33%), and king safety issues (33%), with recurring tags like missed_tactic and piece_activity. The concrete positions show knights jumping to central squares (e5, b5, f4, g5) that look active but allow the opponent to win material through counter-tactics—often the knight lands on a square where it can be captured or where it fails to compensate for what it leaves undefended. Maia's preferred alternatives are often quiet pawn or bishop moves, suggesting the knight leap is an overambitious deviation from solid play.

998.label: Trading an active, tactically potent piece for a passive one, squandering a winning or equal position.
998.description: This feature captures middlegame positions where the player initiates a piece exchange (bishop or knight for an opponent's piece of similar value) that is objectively catastrophic despite appearing materially neutral. The material signature shows 50% trades and 50% slightly-down outcomes with a median net of 0.0, confirming these are exchange decisions rather than outright blunders of hanging pieces. The eval trajectory is devastating: 100% of positions had winning material missed, with a median loss of 317 centipawns, converting winning positions to drawn or losing ones. The tactical analysis reveals the key pattern: the exchanged piece was the player's most active or tactically loaded piece—often a knight with fork potential, a dominating centralized piece, or a piece contributing to a kingside attack. Tags like 'piece_activity', 'missed_fork', 'knight_superiority', 'wrong_capture', and 'exchange_win_missed' all point to the same error: voluntarily trading away your best-placed piece for the opponent's worst-placed piece, releasing all tactical tension. The concrete positions confirm this—knights on e6 with fork threats traded for passive bishops, active bishops exchanged for inert pieces, and strong minor pieces swapped off when maintaining them would have preserved decisive advantages.

994.label: Moves that fatally weaken the player's own king position, often by castling into danger or removing critical defensive pawns/pieces.
994.description: This feature captures moves where the player critically undermines their own king's safety. The material signature shows mostly 'safe' moves (81%) with no captures (81%), indicating these aren't tactical blunders in the traditional sense—pieces aren't being hung through miscalculation—but rather positional decisions that catastrophically weaken the king. The pieces moved are predominantly pawns (38%) and kings (29%), consistent with castling into attacks or pushing pawns that expose the king. The Opus analysis confirms king_safety as the universal motif (100%), with examples including castling into danger (e1g1, e1c1), capturing pawns that were shielding the king (gxf5 removing the g6 guardian), and moving queens away from defensive squares. The eval trajectory shows a massive median cost of 517 centipawns, with positions transitioning from drawn->losing (29%) or already losing becoming much worse (33%), while 62% miss winning material—suggesting the player had better options available but chose moves that prioritized other concerns (development, material) over king safety. The combination of non-capture pawn/king moves, devastating eval drops, and consistent king vulnerability motifs points clearly to a pattern of neglecting one's own king safety.

1001.label: Moves that fatally compromise king safety by missing defensive or offensive king-related resources.
1001.description: This feature fires on moves where the player neglects critical king safety considerations, resulting in large evaluation losses (median ~595 centipawns). The material signature shows the player's moves often hang material or make disadvantageous trades (median net loss of 2.0), while the dominant motifs overwhelmingly involve king_safety (57%), back_rank threats, and tempo loss. The tactical analyses reveal a consistent pattern: the player makes a move that appears locally reasonable (capturing material, moving the king, advancing a pawn) but catastrophically overlooks how it weakens their own king's position or abandons a crucial defensive resource. Examples include removing a g-pawn shield to capture a rook (exposing the king to mate), moving the king away from a saving capture, or failing to interpose a check before capturing. The trajectory shows these mistakes convert drawn positions to losing (50%) or significantly damage already-won positions, indicating the player fails to prioritize king safety at critical moments where one tempo or one defensive move makes the difference between survival and collapse.

1000.label: Failing to recapture an enemy bishop sitting on f6/c3 in the opening, instead making an irrelevant move that hangs material.
1000.description: This feature fires on a highly specific opening pattern: the opponent has placed a bishop on a square where it can be immediately captured (most commonly Bxf6 in exchange-type positions), but the player ignores the recapture and plays a tempo-wasting or developing move instead (h6, Be7, d3, Qd2, O-O). The material signature shows 71% hangs (non-captures that drop a piece) with 100% missed winning material and a median loss of 524 centipawns. The tactical analysis confirms this: 'hanging_piece' is the dominant motif (58%), with 'tempo_loss' (25%) covering the cases where the player plays a move like h6 that does nothing to address the threat. The positions are uniformly in the opening phase (100%), often featuring a White bishop that has captured on f6 (or a Black bishop on f3/c3) that the opponent simply fails to recapture. Maia's recommended moves show 86% bishop captures, confirming the correct response was to take the intruding piece. The trajectory (86% drawn->losing) shows these were holdable positions completely thrown away by neglecting an obvious recapture.

1002.label: Moving a piece for material or activity while fatally neglecting king safety, allowing the opponent's attack to break through.
1002.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player moves a queen, bishop, or knight (often capturing a pawn or making a seemingly active move) while ignoring a critical king-safety obligation. The material signature shows 74% non-captures and 64% 'safe' outcomes on the surface—the moved piece itself isn't immediately lost—but the eval trajectory reveals catastrophic consequences: a median loss of 420 centipawns, with 41% of cases converting winning or drawn positions into losing ones. The dominant motif is king_safety (44%), supported by tags like exposed_king, queen_misplacement, and tempo_loss. Maia's recommended moves (45% rook, 36% bishop) suggest the correct response was typically a defensive or consolidating move rather than the aggressive/greedy piece maneuver chosen. The per-position analyses confirm the pattern: pieces are pulled away from defensive duties (e.g., Qxd5 abandoning f3's king cover, Nxb4 ignoring a queen on g7 threatening mate), leaving the king fatally exposed to coordinated enemy attacks. The player prioritizes a local gain or 'active' move while missing that their king position requires immediate attention.

1003.label: Giving a flashy but unsound check with a rook or queen that hangs material or squanders a winning position.
1003.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) with either a rook (57%) or queen (43%), but the check is premature or unsound—71% of the time the moved piece hangs, and the median material loss is catastrophic (median eval drop ~93 pawns equivalent, indicating missed forced mates or massive advantages thrown away). The Opus analysis confirms the dominant motif is 'tempo_loss' (50%) combined with 'premature_check' tags, where the checking move looks visually appealing but allows the king to escape or forces an unfavorable simplification. Maia's recommended moves are quieter (64% non-captures, often rook moves maintaining pressure), showing the correct approach was to build on the position rather than rush a check. The eval trajectory shows positions going from winning to drawn/losing or from mate-in-N to merely advantageous, confirming these are cases where an impulsive check sacrifices a decisive advantage for a flashy but hollow tactic.

1004.label: Advancing a central pawn too early in the opening, hanging it to a tactical refutation.
1004.description: This feature fires on opening-phase pawn advances (94% pawn moves) that constitute premature central breaks or aggressive pawn lunges before development is complete. The material signature shows 82% of these moves hang material (median -1.0 pawn), and the eval trajectory confirms devastating consequences: 94% transform drawn positions into losing ones, with a median loss of 215 centipawns. The tactical analysis reveals the recurring pattern clearly—players push d5 against Italian/Bishop setups or advance g-pawns against bishops (e.g., ...g5 against Bf4) without adequate support. The common tags (premature_central_break, king_in_center, development, tempo_loss) confirm these are structurally unsound pawn advances played before completing basic development, where the opponent punishes with simple captures or forks that exploit the newly created weaknesses. Maia's recommended moves (bishop 29%, knight 29%, pawn 35%) suggest quieter developing moves were available instead.

984.label: Ignoring a strong bishop check/attack in the opening by making a developing or pawn move that hangs material.
984.description: This feature captures a recurring opening mistake (88% opening phase) where the player makes a knight, pawn, or bishop move that hangs a piece or loses significant material (39% hangs, 23% slightly down, median -1.0 material), while Maia consistently recommends a bishop move that delivers check (100% bishop, 100% check). The missed move is always a material-winning opportunity (100% missed winning material), costing a median of 282 centipawns and frequently converting drawn positions to losing ones (31% drawn->losing). The top boards reveal standard Italian/Scotch/Sicilian opening positions where players make natural-looking developing or capturing moves (Nc6-a5, Nc6xd4, f7-f5, Nc6xe5) that leave pieces en prise, while overlooking a powerful bishop check that would win material or seize a decisive initiative. The dominant motifs—hanging_piece (50%) and king_safety (20%)—combined with tags like piece_activity, development, and tempo_loss confirm that these are tactical oversights in development where the player ignores the opponent's king vulnerability and plays a structurally or tactically flawed move instead of the crushing discovered or direct bishop check.

1005.label: Player ignores urgent king safety threats, allowing devastating attacks or forced mates.
1005.description: This feature captures moves where players neglect critical king safety concerns, resulting in catastrophic position collapses. The material signature shows 41% of moves hang material and 94% are non-captures, indicating passive moves made while the opponent has active threats. The dominant motif is king_safety (67%), with tags including exposed_king, king_hunt, and forced_mate. The eval trajectory is severe (median 658cp lost), with many positions swinging from drawn/winning to losing. The concrete positions consistently show exposed kings under attack (e.g., Qh6 with rook on e8, knight forks near kings, queens bearing down on weakened king positions). Players choose quiet moves like Kc5, Kf7, or piece shuffles instead of addressing the immediate tactical crisis—often missing simple defensive captures or interpositions that would neutralize the attack. The 33% promotion_error motif also fits: in endgame cases the king wanders into danger near promotion squares. Maia's recommended moves (35% queen, 29% bishop) suggest active defensive or counter-attacking resources were available but ignored.

1007.label: King or pawn moves that surrender critical tempo or opposition in pawn/rook endgames, turning drawn or close positions into losses.
1007.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (100% endgame phase) where the player makes a seemingly safe move (90% safe material outcome) — typically a king move (50%) or pawn move (20%) — that loses crucial tempo. The dominant motif is tempo_loss (42%), with passed_pawn (25%) and pawn_endgame (17%) as supporting themes. The eval trajectory shows these moves are catastrophic positionally: 40% turn drawn positions into losing ones, with a median cost of 265 centipawns. The Opus analysis consistently identifies the pattern: the player moves their king to the wrong square (losing the opposition), pushes a pawn without check when a tempo-gaining alternative existed, or fails to recognize that a passive-looking move hands the critical tempo to the opponent. Maia's recommended moves frequently give check (50%) — precisely the tempo-gaining resource the player missed. The positions are spare endgames (kings, pawns, occasionally a rook or minor piece) where a single tempo decides whether a passed pawn promotes or whether the opposition is held.

1006.label: Playing an attractive but purposeless check (usually with the queen) that squanders a winning attack or forced mate by giving the opponent's king an escape route.
1006.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where the player delivers a check (100% of activations) predominantly with the queen (80%), but the check fails to maintain or convert a winning advantage. The material signature shows these checks are mostly 'safe' (80%) — nothing is immediately lost — yet the player misses winning material 100% of the time, indicating a stronger non-checking continuation existed. The eval trajectory reveals that in 40% of cases a losing position flips to winning (suggesting the opponent just made the same type of error in reverse or the check accidentally helps), but in 20% a drawn position becomes losing and the Opus analysis repeatedly identifies 'pointless check' and 'missed mate' themes. The tactical summaries are remarkably consistent: players choose a forcing-looking check that actually improves the opponent's king position, allows interposition with development, or lets the king escape a mating net. Maia's recommended moves (rook 40%, queen 40%) never give check (0%), confirming the engine preferred quiet attacking moves that maintained pressure. The dominant tags — exposed_king, king_safety, king_hunt, tempo_loss — paint a picture of players in the middle of a king attack who reflexively play a check rather than tightening the net, burning a critical tempo and releasing the pressure.

1008.label: Player makes a non-forcing move in the opening, missing a strong bishop capture (typically Bxf3/Bxc3) that would have won material or maintained a significant advantage.
1008.description: This feature identifies positions where a player makes a quiet or non-critical move (pawn 27%, knight 23%, bishop 19%) that is overwhelmingly 'safe' (67%) or 'hangs' a piece (25%), while Maia consistently recommends a bishop capture (bishop 100%, capturing knight 94%). The positions are predominantly in the opening (71%) with developed pieces and active piece play. The eval trajectory shows severe consequences: drawn->losing (29%) and winning->drawn (27%) with a median loss of 283 centipawns, indicating the player is squandering a tactical opportunity. The motifs—tempo_loss (25%), hanging_piece (25%), fork (17%)—combined with tags like tempo_loss, piece_activity, and missed_tactic reveal that players waste time with moves like h6, Be7, or h4 instead of executing the critical bishop capture that would exploit a tactical vulnerability (often a pin on f3 or a capture that disrupts the opponent's coordination). The concrete positions show recurring patterns of bishops on g4/h5/b4 that should capture on f3/c3 immediately, but the player delays with an irrelevant move, allowing the opponent to consolidate or execute a counter-tactic.

1009.label: Developing or moving a piece to a square where it immediately loses tempo to an opponent's threat, squandering a winning or equal position.
1009.description: This feature captures moves that place pieces on squares where they are immediately challenged or forced to retreat, resulting in critical tempo loss. The material signature shows mostly safe moves (69%) with no captures (77%), indicating these aren't tactical blunders but positional misjudgments—pieces are developed to seemingly active squares that prove untenable. The dominant motifs (tempo_loss 40%, trapped_piece 30%) confirm the pattern: bishops placed where pawns attack them with tempo (Bc4 met by ...d5, Bb5 forced to retreat to e2), knights retreating to passive squares, and quiet moves that ignore the opponent's ability to gain time. The eval trajectory is devastating—median 262cp lost, with 38% of cases converting a winning position to drawn—showing these aren't minor inaccuracies but game-changing errors. Maia's recommendations (95% pawn moves) suggest the correct play was usually a simple pawn advance consolidating the position, while the player chose a 'clever' piece move that backfired. The top boards consistently show positions where a piece lands on a tactically vulnerable square in the opening/middlegame transition.

1010.label: In pure pawn endgames, the king moves to a suboptimal square, losing critical tempo in a pawn race or opposition battle.
